## A Blockchain-Based Framework for Secure Management of Government and Law Enforcement Records

## Himanshu S Shetty

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India himanshushettykt03@gmail.com

## Pratheek G Shetty

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India pratheekshetty934@gmail.com

Shifali Florine Lobo

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering and Management

Mangaluru, India

shifalilobo9@gmail.com

Abstract -The integrity, security, and accessibility of government and law enforcement records are fundamental to public trust. Yet, traditional centralized databases remain vulnerable to data manipulation, cyberattacks, and systemic inefficiencies that can compromise sensitive legal documents and undermine judicial processes. Blockchain technology offers a paradigm shift toward decentralized trust and cryptographic assurance. This paper presents a robust framework designed using Hyperledger Fabric to secure government legal records and enhance law enforcement procedures. We focus on the practical application of a permissioned blockchain, which is better suited for government use than public, cryptocurrency-based models. The architecture integrates smart contracts to automate legal documentation workflows and employs a hybrid on-chain/off-chain storage model to ensure scalability. Our results demonstrate a functionally complete, tamper-proof system that improves efficiency and provides a fully auditable trail for all record interactions. This work validates the feasibility of blockchain as a foundational technology for next-generation digital governance.

Index Terms -Index Terms-Blockchain, Hyperledger, Legal Records, Law Enforcement, Smart Contracts, Data Security, Government Applications, Tamper-Proof Systems, Judicial Data, Auditability.

## I. INTRODUCTION

In the digital governance era, one of the biggest challenges before public institutions is how to protect the sanctity of official records while making them accessible. Governments switching over from paper-based archives to digital infrastructure expose themselves to a new class of threats that includes sophisticated data breaches, unauthorized tampering, and systemic failures [5], [8]. In the sectors of law and order, this vulnerability assumes grave dimensions. A compromised

chain of evidence or a manipulated judicial record can trigger erosion of due process, obstruction of justice, and catastrophic damage to public confidence in the rule of law. Legacy systems are invariably incapable of combating such modernday threats; the shift to a more resilient and accountable digital infrastructure is not just a technological upgrade but a basic imperative for governmental legitimacy [10].

The solution described in this paper is based on blockchain technology-a decentralized ledger system, secure and transparent by design. Going beyond the cryptocurrency roots of blockchain [2], we utilize an enterprise-grade, permissioned framework, Hyperledger Fabric, which is designed to meet specific privacy and governance needs for institutions [3]. The immutable ledger and decentralized consensus at the heart of blockchain's core architectural principles provide a potent guard against data manipulation. Additionally, smart contracts integrate seamlessly and can automate and enforce legal and administrative protocols that reduce the possibilities of fraud and human error, while streamlining very complicated workflows [16], [18]. This proposed approach promises to build a new foundation of trust in judicial processes.

Beyond safety, advantages extend to the operational ability of a blockchain-based system by creating a fully auditable, transparent, chronological track of every transaction or data interaction-a feature very useful in both legal proceedings and internal audits [1]. This has already been exemplified by pioneering real-world implementations: Estonia integrated blockchain technology into its e-governance services to secure public records, while Georgia successfully deployed a similar solution in its land registry to reduce fraud [6, 7].

Despite this promise, there is still a gap between conceptual frameworks and holistic scalable solutions designed to meet the needs of the legal and law enforcement sectors. Much of the literature still remains conceptual or addresses very narrow applications that cannot be applied to the needs of a single record management system in the judiciary [11], [15].

This work directly addresses this gap. We propose a secure, tamperproof blockchain architecture for government legal records, designed and implemented on the Hyperledger Fabric framework. We elaborate on how to develop smart contracts that automate important procedures of the judiciary, critically analyze the system performance, and discuss tangible benefits and challenges while deploying such a framework. Our key contribution is primarily the validation of a hybrid onchain/off-chain architectural model that solves the scalability problem of storing large legal files combined with robust, rolebased smart contract logics to automate judicial access control.

## II. RELATED WORKS

Our research builds on works ranging from foundational blockchain theory, pioneering government pilot programs, to architectural solutions from parallel domains. The theoretical foundations of blockchain are well laid. Technical overviews such as Zheng et al. [4], detail the architectures and consensus protocols. While invaluable for the insight they provide, these foundational works primarily out- line the 'why' rather than the technical 'how' for public sector implementation

## A. Pioneering Implementations in the Public Sector

Some governments have moved from theory to practice. For example, Estonia's pioneering use of e-governance utilizes blockchain to secure the integrity of national data [6]. The Ministry of Justice of Georgia implemented a blockchain land registry system to provide transparency and reduce fraud [7]. Meanwhile, Dubai has committed to ambitious blockchain initiatives that involve operational benefits and legal challenges [24]. These large-scale projects are still limited to discrete areas, such as property or identity, and do not provide insight into the complex data flows that are present in the judicial and law enforcement data ecosystem.

## B. Applying Designs from Other Areas

Numerous technical challenges in our study such as data privacy, auditability, and interoperability have been confronted in other disciplines. A significant body of work on blockchain and healthcare data management, for example, resolves the challenges of ensuring sensitive patient records can be secured and readily translated to a form suitable for legal evidence [20], [22]. Similarly, user-based data sovereignty frameworks [17], verifiable digital credentials [18], and secure identity and authentication processes [26] introduce tested patterns with respect to managing access rights of varying legal entities. These architectural schemas offer promising building blocks but will need to be significantly modified to reflect the unique evidentiary processes and rules of the judicial environment.

## C. Identifying the Research Gap

The collective literature confirms a strong consensus on blockchain's capacity to bring unprecedented security and efficiency to government operations [1], [23], [29]. However, a critical gap persists between this potential and its comprehensive application within the legal and law enforcement domains. Much of the existing work remains either at a high conceptual level [9], is validated only within narrow, non-judicial pilots [6], [7], or lacks the empirical evidence that comes from a live, integrated deployment [25]. Our research directly addresses this deficiency by designing, implementing, and validating a holistic blockchain framework specifically engineered to meet the stringent requirements of a modern judicial system.

## D. Positioning Our Framework

While pioneering implementations in Estonia and Georgia validate blockchain for public records , they often focus on specific domains like identity or land registry. Similarly, frameworks from other sectors like healthcare provide robust patterns for privacy , but they are not tailored for the unique chain-of-custody rules and complex, multi-actor access policies required by the judicial system (e.g., judge, prosecutor, defense). Our framework addresses this gap by providing a holistic solution that specifically combines an immutable onchain ledger for metadata with a scalable, encrypted off-chain storage model for large evidence files , all governed by smart contracts explicitly designed to automate these complex legal workflows.

## III. SYSTEM DESIGN AND IMPLEMENTATION

The architecture and technical protocols adopted for our proposed system are discussed here. The development methodology has been directed by the basic core requirements of judicial data management, including the creation of a secure, tamper-proof, and efficient environment that is auditable and scalable. Permissioned blockchain, decentralized storage, and robust cryptographic techniques have been integrated to achieve this.

## A. System Architecture

We designed a hybrid architecture combining Hyperledger Fabric for the permissioned ledger and the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for decentralized storage. Hyperledger Fabric provides a controlled, auditable environment for immutable metadata and access rights which are critical for government systems while IPFS offers a resilient, efficient solution for storing large data objects, like evidence files, off-chain.

Hyperledger Fabric was preferred over other enterprise blockchains, such as Quorum or Corda, for its permissioned nature, modular architecture, and strong support for the 'channels' feature. This feature enables private transactions to take place between only some organizations, such as a prosecutor's office and one courthouse, perfectly meeting the needs brought about by judicial confidentiality. Besides this separation keeps the blockchain light and performant. The general architecture is represented in Fig.1.

## B. Secure Data Ingestion and Retrieval Workflow

The system's end-to-end process flow, illustrated in Fig. 2. The workflow begins at the User Interface. Requests are routed via an API Gateway to the central Backend Application Server, which acts as the orchestrator. The backend manages two distinct operations: it stores large, encrypted file chunks in Off-Chain Storage (IPFS) and submits the corresponding metadata as a transaction to the Blockchain Network. Within the network, the Smart Contract (Chaincode) validates and commits the transaction to the immutable Distributed Ledger, whose current state is maintained in the State Database. This architecture cleanly separates large file storage from immutable verification, ensuring both scalability and integrity.

A cornerstone of this framework is the secure, multi-step process for handling legal records, which guarantees confidentiality, integrity, and availability. The protocol, outlined in Table I, is executed by the backend server. It first generates a unique SHA-256 hash of the file for integrity verification and then encrypts the file using AES. The encrypted file is split into smaller chunks and uploaded to the decentralized storage (IPFS), which returns a verifiable Content Identifier (CID) for each chunk.

By storing only lightweight metadata on-chain, the blockchain remains efficient while providing a tamper-proof and auditable record of every file. Retrieving a file is the reverse process: the metadata is fetched from the ledger, the CIDs are used to retrieve the encrypted chunks from IPFS, and the file is reassembled and decrypted using the stored key.

Fig. 2. The end-to-end workflow for data ingestion, from the initial user request to the final blockchain transaction.

<!-- image -->

TABLE I SECURE DATA INGESTION AND STORAGE PROTOCOL

| Step                  | Description                                                                                                                                           |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| File Hashing          | A unique SHA-256 hash is generated to create a digital fingerprint of the file, enabling future integrity verification.                               |
| File Encryption       | The file is encrypted using AES with a unique key and Initialization Vector (IV) to ensure confidentiality.                                           |
| File Chunking         | The encrypted file is split into smaller chunks to facilitate efficient and reliable distributed storage on IPFS.                                     |
| Decentralized Storage | Encrypted chunks are uploaded to IPFS, where each receives a verifiable Content Identifier (CID).                                                     |
| Metadata Transaction  | The file's metadata (including its hash, AES key, IV, and the list of CIDs) is recorded as an immutable transaction on the Hyperledger Fabric ledger. |

## C. Multi-Layered Security Model

The framework implements a multi-layered security strategy. For authentication, we employ a stateless JWT system. Upon login, the backend issues an authToken that must be submitted as a bearer token for all subsequent requests. A

dedicated middleware validates this token's signature on every request, rejecting any tampered or invalid tokens.

Authorization is managed via a strict Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) policy, enforced at the middleware level of the backend server. This ensures users only perform actions permitted by their assigned role. The Hyperledger Fabric network itself is architecturally isolated and not directly exposed; only the trusted backend server is permitted to initiate communication with it. As a permissioned blockchain, all operations occur within a secure, private 'channel,' ensuring transaction data is visible only to authorized organizations. This model positions the blockchain not as the primary enforcer of access control, but as the ultimate, immutable auditor of all actions authorized by the centralized server.

## D. Automated Governance via Smart Contracts

Access to legal records is governed by smart contracts (chaincode) deployed on the Hyperledger Fabric network. These contracts function as self-executing digital agreements that autonomously enforce predefined access control policies.

Lst. 1 shows a simplified JavaScript implementation of our EvidenceContract , which inherits from the base Fabric Contract class. This chaincode is responsible for the final interaction with the ledger. Functions like storeEvidence and getEvidence are the core of this process. The storeEvidence function takes a stringified JSON object containing the evidence metadata and uses the putState command to write it to the ledger, keyed by its hash. Conversely, getEvidence retrieves the record using its ID.

```
'use strict'; const { Contract } = require('fabric-contract-api'); class EvidenceContract extends Contract { async initLedger(ctx) { console.info('Chaincode instantiated'); } async storeEvidence(ctx, evdString) { const {hash} = JSON.parse(evdString); await ctx.stub.putState(hash, Buffer.from( evdString)); return {success:true, hash:hash}; } async getEvidence(ctx, evID) { const evBytes = await ctx.stub.getState(evID ); if (!evBytes || evBytes.length === 0) { throw new Error('Evidence ${evID} does not exist'); } return JSON.parse(evBytes.toString()); } } module.exports = EvidenceContract;
```

Listing 1. Simplified JavaScript snippet of the Hyperledger Fabric chaincode

It is important to note that this chaincode is intentionally simple, as it represents the final, trusted step in the workflow. The primary security, including user authentication (JWT) and Role-Based Access Control (RBAC), is enforced by the backend server's submissionController before it invokes this chaincode. When a user requests a document, the backend first validates their permissions, and only then triggers the smart contract to execute the more granular validation logic detailed in Table II.

TABLE II SMART CONTRACT ACCESS CONTROL LOGIC

| Process Step          | Description                                                                                                                   |
|-----------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Identity Verification | The contract confirms the cryptographic iden- tity of the requesting user against the network's trusted member list.          |
| Permission Validation | The contract queries the ledger to verify the user's assigned role and permissions for the specific record being requested.   |
| Rule Execution        | The contract enforces any situational rules, such as time-based access restrictions or requirements for multi-party approval. |

Access is granted only upon successful validation by the smart contract. Crucially, every access attempt whether successful or denied is recorded as an immutable transaction on the blockchain, creating a comprehensive and undeniable audit trail. This automated enforcement minimizes the risk of human error or malicious circumvention of policies.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Our implemented prototype successfully demonstrates the feasibility of a decentralized, tamper-resistant platform that enhances data security and provides complete auditability.

## A. Achieving Data Immutability and Verifiable Integrity

A primary achievement is the framework's ability to guarantee the integrity of legal records. By hashing all files and anchoring their metadata on the Hyperledger Fabric ledger, we have created a system where any unauthorized modification to a file becomes immediately detectable. This cryptographic chain-of-custody is essential for legal proceedings, ensuring that digital evidence remains verifiable.

## B. Streamlining Processes with Smart Contract Automation

Our system leverages JavaScript-based chaincode (smart contracts) to automate the registration, validation, and access control of forensic and legal data. These smart contracts enforce business logic at the protocol level, which significantly reduces the reliance on manual oversight and minimizes opportunities for human error or malicious activity. This automation demonstrably accelerates traditionally timeconsuming workflows, such as evidence verification, while ensuring strict adherence to predefined policies.

## C. Performance Evaluation and Analysis

All performance benchmarks were conducted on a modest hardware setup, comprising an Intel Core i3-7100U CPU, 16GB of RAM, and an M.2 SSD, to establish a baseline performance profile. The results demonstrate the system's efficiency even on non-server-grade equipment, suggesting significant potential for enhanced performance in a production environment with enterprise-grade hardware.

The performance evaluation first confirmed the efficiency of our hybrid architecture for individual operations. As shown in Fig. 3, processing times for data ingestion and retrieval scale linearly with file size. This result is critical as it validates our design choice to store large files off-chain, preventing the blockchain ledger itself from becoming a performance bottleneck. The higher computational overhead of the ingestion process-which includes hashing, encryption, and consensus-naturally results in longer response times for the POST /upload endpoint compared to the simpler GET /getfile operation, as detailed in the API metrics in Fig. 4. This predictable performance trade-off is justified by the system's foundational advantage: a tamper-proof, immutable audit trail for every record.

Fig. 3. System processing time for handling files of various sizes, demonstrating a linear performance scaling that supports large files.

<!-- image -->

Fig. 4. A comparison of API response times, showing the higher latency of the ingestion process due to cryptographic and consensus overhead.

<!-- image -->

To assess the system's behavior under realistic conditions, we conducted scalability tests with concurrent users on the file retrieval route (Fig. 5). The results show a characteristic performance curve: as the number of virtual users increases from 20 to 50, the system's throughput (requests/sec) gradually decreases from a peak of approximately 1.2 to 0.6. Concur- rently, the average and percentile response times rise, peaking at 30-40 users before stabilizing. This indicates the system is reaching its saturation point, where additional load increases queuing time without improving throughput. The test confirms that the system remains stable under pressure but highlights a clear performance ceiling, providing a valuable benchmark for resource allocation and capacity planning in a production environment.

Fig. 5. System performance under concurrent load, illustrating the relationship between throughput and response time as user load increases.

<!-- image -->

## V. CONCLUSION

The challenge of managing legal and law enforcement records in a secure and trustworthy manner is a critical hurdle for modern governments. Traditional centralized databases, with their inherent vulnerabilities to tampering and their lack of transparent auditability, are no longer sufficient. This project demonstrates that a blockchain-based solution, built on a permissioned framework like Hyperledger Fabric, offers a robust alternative.

Our implemented system successfully creates a decentralized, transparent, and efficient environment for legal records. By integrating smart contracts, we have shown how key administrative processes can be automated, reducing both manual overhead and the potential for error or fraud. The immutable, time-stamped audit logs produced by the system guarantee that every interaction is recorded and verifiable, fostering unprecedented accountability. Furthermore, our hybrid architecture, which combines on-chain metadata with offchain storage, strikes a crucial balance between security and scalability, confirming that the system is not just technically sound but practically deployable.

In conclusion, this paper goes further than the theoretical discussion and proposes a pragmatic model for a transformative digital public service. By maintaining a robust database and preventing the modification of vital legal data, the proposed blockchain-based infrastructure can help improve institutional robustness and rebuild public trust. Such logical approaches can be developed and tested with necessary political support and will be a mainstay of digitalization of the public service.

Ayesha Saba Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning HKBK College of Engineering Bangalore, Karnataka, India 19p0051ayesha@gmail.com Tabassum Ara Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning HKBK College of Engineering Bangalore, Karnataka, India tabuara@gmail.com

Abstract - Electrocardiogram (ECG) analysis plays a vital role in diagnosing cardiovascular diseases, particularly valvular heart disease (VHD). Traditional ECG interpretation, however, is often hindered by noise interference, lead placement errors, and variability in waveform morphology, resulting in reduced diagnostic accuracy. This study presents a deep learning-based framework  that  leverages  ECG  images  to  detect  and  classify cardiac  abnormalities  with  a  focus  on  VHD.  The  proposed system employs a custom convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture  combined  with  image  preprocessing  and  signal processing techniques to enable automated diagnosis from 2D grayscale ECG images. The model includes Conv2D layers for feature  extraction,  MaxPooling  for  dimensionality  reduction, dropout for regularization, and a sigmoid classifier for binary classification.  ECG  images  are  converted  into  1D  signals  via column-wise  pixel  summation,  followed  by  R-peak  detection using find\_peaks() for  heart  rate  estimation  and  waveform analysis. The model was trained on 413 ECG images and tested on 104 samples, achieving an accuracy of 94.23%, precision of 0.96,  recall  of  0.91,  and  F1-score  of  0.93.  The  system  also generates comprehensive ECG reports including BPM, rhythm classification,  and  waveform  intervals,  offering  interpretable diagnostic insights. This approach demonstrates strong potential for scalable, automated ECG analysis in clinical and resource-limited settings.

Keywords- Electrocardiogram (ECG), Convolutional Neural Network  (CNN),  R-Peak  Detection, Heart Rate Estimation, Valvular Heart Disease (VHD), Image-Based Diagnostics.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Electrocardiography (ECG) is one of the most ubiquitous and  informative  non-invasive  diagnostic  tools  in  clinical cardiology. It records the electrical impulses generated during the cardiac cycle using surface electrodes strategically placed on the body, offering a window into cardiac rhythm, rate, and morphology. The output,  typically  visualized  as  a  series  of waveforms - P wave, QRS complex, and T wave serves as the foundation for diagnosing arrhythmias, myocardial infarctions,  ischemic  episodes,  and  structural  heart  diseases such as valvular heart disease (VHD)  [1]. Due  to its affordability and ease of acquisition, ECG is used globally as a  primary  screening  modality  for  cardiovascular  disorders, making  improvements  in  its analysis and interpretation critically important. 979-8-3315-7364-5/25/$31.00 ©2025 IEEE

Despite its clinical importance, manual ECG interpretation is  fraught  with  challenges. Noise  artifacts,  such  as  muscle tremors,  power  line  interference,  and  poor  lead  placement, often  distort  waveform  morphology  and  lead  to  diagnostic errors. Additionally, inter-observer variability among clinicians can contribute to inconsistent interpretations. These factors  compromise  both  the  sensitivity  and  specificity  of ECG  analysis  in  real-world scenarios  [2][3]. Moreover, traditional rule-based ECG algorithms, although reliable for basic rhythm detection, often lack the sophistication needed to recognize  subtle  morphological  anomalies  that  signal  early stages  of  complex  conditions  like  aortic  stenosis  or  mitral regurgitation. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL), have opened new avenues for automating ECG interpretation. Deep neural networks-especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs)-have demonstrated remarkable  capabilities  in  learning  spatial  hierarchies  from medical images and time-series signals. CNNs are especially adept  at  capturing  nuanced  features  in  ECG  waveforms, enabling  robust  classification  of  normal  and  pathological rhythms without manual feature engineering [4][5]. However, several  limitations  remain. Many  high-performing  models rely on large, annotated datasets, which may not be feasible in low-resource  settings. Additionally,  issues such  as  class imbalance,  overfitting,  lack  of  interpretability,  and  limited generalization across diverse patient populations continue to hinder widespread clinical deployment [6][7]. This research addresses these limitations by presenting a deep  learning-based  ECG  analysis  framework  that  works directly  on  image-based  ECG  inputs. Unlike  conventional approaches that require raw signal processing from biosensors or data acquisition systems, our method transforms existing ECG scan images into grayscale format and feeds them into a lightweight  CNN  for  classification. The  system  is  further enhanced  with  a  signal  projection  technique  that  extracts  a one-dimensional waveform from the image via column-wise pixel  summation. This  innovation  bridges  the  gap  between traditional  signal-based  and  image-based  methods,  enabling not  just  classification  but  also  clinical  feature  extractionsuch as R-R intervals, PR intervals, QRS duration, and heart rate estimation [8]. As shown in Fig. 1, the anatomical segments of the ECG waveform (P, QRS, and T waves) are used as key markers in our  signal  detection  process. Our  architecture  emphasizes robustness and interpretability. The CNN comprises multiple Conv2D and MaxPooling layers for spatial feature extraction, with dropout regularization applied to prevent overfitting. A

Fig 1. Labeled anatomy of a typical ECG waveform showing P wave, QRS complex, and T wave. <!-- image -->

sigmoid-activated dense layer outputs a binary classification, normal  or  abnormal. In  the  abnormal  case,  a  secondary pipeline  is  triggered  to  generate  a  full  diagnostic  report, including waveform analysis and rhythm interpretation. Importantly, this system is designed for accessibility and scalability. By eliminating the need for raw signal input and focusing instead on 2D image-based ECGs which are widely available  even  in  remote  or  resource-limited  settings,  the model becomes deployable in outpatient clinics, rural telemedicine units, and low-cost mobile applications. It also offers educational benefits, allowing trainees to visualize the correlation between morphological features and clinical diagnosis.

text: Moreover,  the  model's  integration  with  signal processing techniques enhances its transparency. Rather than being  a  "black  box,"  it  generates  clinically  interpretable metrics aligned with cardiological standards, thereby increasing clinician trust. Furthermore,  as  highlighted  in  Fig. 2,  proper  electrode placement  is  fundamental  to  acquiring  clean  ECG  signals. While  our  method  does  not  directly  interface with the acquisition process, it indirectly benefits from  correctly captured  inputs,  ensuring  that  the  downstream  analysis  is reliable. We emphasize that this system is intended to support, not replace, clinical judgment. Its role is to augment diagnostic capabilities,  reduce  burden  on  healthcare  professionals,  and provide an early-warning mechanism for critical cardiovascular conditions. To the best of our knowledge, this is among the first studies to combine ECG image classification with  signal  extraction  for  full  report  generation,  tailored specifically to valvular heart disease detection. We evaluate our model on a publicly available dataset of grayscale ECG images  and  check  its  accuracy. These results are then compared with state-of-the-art models. The manuscript is structured into key sections for clarity and scientific rigor. Section II reviews existing deep learning approaches  for  ECG  classification,  highlighting  algorithms, results,  and  research  gaps. Section  III  outlines  the  dataset, preprocessing steps, CNN architecture, and training procedure. Section IV presents  model performance metrics, visualizations, and clinical insights. Finally, Section  V summarizes key findings and proposes future directions for improving and deploying the system in real-world settings.

## II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Over the past two decades, the landscape of electrocardiogram  (ECG)  analysis  has  evolved  from  rulebased algorithms to highly sophisticated deep learning (DL) systems aimed at early and accurate detection of cardiovascular  conditions,  including  valvular  heart  disease (VHD). Early systems such as the Pan-Tompkins algorithm, implemented in Hamilton's open-source ECG toolkit, demonstrated high sensitivity (99.7%) and positive predictivity (up to 99.8%) for QRS detection and arrhythmia classification in low-resource settings [2]. Fig 2. Correct anatomical positioning of standard ECG electrodes on the chest and limbs to ensure signal accuracy and consistency. <!-- image -->

However,  the  lack  of  deep  learning  integration  and  limited coverage of structural heart conditions like VHD remained a shortcoming. Later, researchers such as Yan et al. proposed a morphology-focused method using mean-shift feature extraction and Gaussian Discriminant Analysis (GDA) combined with Support Vector Machines (SVM), achieving a promising 97.29% positive predictivity on the PTB dataset. Yet, their work was constrained by the use of only Lead I & II and lacked multi-disease scalability [9]. To bridge these gaps, hybrid models such as CNN+XGBoost  frameworks  were  introduced,  notably  by Ulloa-Cerna  et  al.,  who  trained  on  2.2  million  ECGs  and achieved an AUROC of 0.91 for predicting seven structural heart  conditions. However,  their  work  was  constrained  by single-system  deployment  and  underperformance  on  rare disease categories [6]. De  Riva et al. emphasized  the importance  of  12-lead  ECG  and  imaging  integration  for ventricular  tachycardia  localization,  noting  only  moderate accuracy (~70%) due to inconsistency in anatomical mappings and the lack of multimodal validation tools [10]. Meanwhile,  Maganti  et  al. focused  on  clinical  evidence reviews for VHD diagnosis, identifying echocardiography as a gold standard and stressing the lack of deep learning tools that integrate imaging with ECG for improved stratification of asymptomatic patients [11]. Recent studies have leveraged hybrid neural networks and multimodal  fusion  for  superior  classification  performance. For  instance,  Barman  et  al. introduced  a  multimodal  deep learning  pipeline  that  combined  ECG  data  with  patient metadata for comprehensive VHD detection. Their pipeline outperformed baseline models, emphasizing the significance of clinical context integration [12]. Neelima et al. proposed a deep hybrid neural network combining ECG and PCG signals to  enhance  multi-class  cardiac  classification,  outperforming traditional single-modality models in terms of accuracy and robustness  [13]. Similarly,  authors  in  [14]  implemented  an ensemble of decision trees and convolutional layers to process ECG  morphology,  enhancing  sensitivity across multiple datasets, yet the approach lacked interpretability. Authors in [15] developed a machine learning system for transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) detection in aortic stenosis patients using ECG features and multimodal inputs. Their system achieved high diagnostic precision, but logistic  regression  was  ultimately  favored  due  to  better interpretability in clinical workflows. Authors in [16] extended  this  model  using  a  fusion  of  logistic  and  random forest classifiers to classify VHD from ECG and echocardiographic features, demonstrating scalability across hospitals. Authors  in  [17]  explored  AI-driven  classification across echocardiographic and ECG data, revealing a significant improvement in early-stage disease detection using deep CNNs,  although limited by dataset heterogeneity. Authors  in  [18]  investigated  the  use  of  deep  multimodal networks  to  predict  outcomes  in  transcatheter  aortic  valve implantation  (TAVI),  focusing  on  success  prediction  using ECG and anatomical parameters, yet emphasized the need for improved  cross-cohort  validation. The  works  in  [19-29] demonstrate the effectiveness of CNN-based models for ECG classification across various domains, employing techniques like transfer learning, attention mechanisms, and spectrograms. These  research report high accuracy and clinical relevance, yet highlight challenges in generalization, data diversity, and deployment, paving the way for scalable, interpretable ECG diagnostic systems.

text: These works collectively also reveal the progressive shift from handcrafted features to fully automated, hybrid learning systems for cardiac classification. Despite notable advances, key gaps persist. Many systems still rely on annotated datasets with skewed distributions, underrepresenting minority conditions such as mitral prolapse or pericarditis. Additionally, there is a growing demand for explainable AI in clinical  environments,  especially  where  decisions  impact surgical or therapeutic  pathways. Furthermore, although multimodal  pipelines  have  demonstrated  higher  accuracy, deployment remains limited due to complexity, computational cost,  and  integration  challenges. Consequently,  there  is  a pressing need for lightweight, interpretable, and scalable deep learning frameworks, especially image-based systems that do not  rely  on  raw  ECG  signals  for  real-time,  low-cost  VHD detection.

## III. METHODOLOGY

This study proposes a deep learning-based, image-driven pipeline  for  automated  classification  and  interpretation  of electrocardiograms (ECGs) using grayscale images. The endto-end  framework  integrates  preprocessing,  convolutional neural  network  (CNN)  classification,  signal  transformation, clinical metric extraction, and report generation, as illustrated in  Fig.  3  (System  Architecture  Workflow).  The  following subsections outline each component in detail.

## A. Dataset and Image Specifications

The  model  was  developed  using  a  publicly  available dataset obtained from Kaggle's ECG Image Dataset. A total of  517  images  were  used,  comprising  413  training  samples and 104 testing samples. The original ECGs were stored in JPG format and subsequently converted to grayscale, standardizing input dimensionality to 224 × 224 pixels. Each image represents a single-lead ECG strip, enabling the system to  operate  independently  of  multi-lead  configurations.  This design improves  portability and scalability in resourceconstrained clinical settings.

Fig 3. Block diagram of the proposed custom CNN-based ECG diagnostic system architecture.

<!-- image -->

## B. Preprocessing pipeline

To  ensure  consistency  and  minimize  visual  noise,  a  robust preprocessing pipeline was implemented. This includes:

- Morphological filtering to remove background grid lines
- Grayscale normalization to improve contrast
- Resizing and padding to match the CNN's input dimensions
- Data augmentation techniques (e.g., random zoom, rotation,  horizontal  flip)  to  address  class  imbalance  and improve generalization

Furthermore, ECG signal transformation is performed by applying column-wise summation of pixel values to create a one-dimensional  waveform  from  the  grayscale  image.  This projected signal enables subsequent clinical metric calculations  such  as  heart  rate,  QRS  duration,  and  PR intervals.

## C. CNN Model architecture

The classification component utilizes a custom-designed CNN  built  using  TensorFlow  and  Keras  frameworks.  The architecture consists of:

- Convolutional layers (Conv2D) with ReLU activation for spatial feature extraction
- MaxPooling layers to reduce dimensionality and preserve dominant features
- Dropout layers for regularization, mitigating overfitting by randomly deactivating neurons during training

A  fully  connected  dense  layer  followed  by  a  Sigmoid activation function, yielding  binary  classification  output: Normal or Abnormal The network is trained using a Binary Crossentropy  loss  function,  which  is  well-suited  for  binary classification tasks. The optimization is performed using the Adam  optimizer  with  a  learning  rate  of  0.001,  ensuring efficient convergence. The CNN model was trained over 20 epochs  with a batch size of  32.  The  pseudo-code  for classification and feature extraction is mentioned in Table I. The detailed hyperparameter tuning parameters is shared in Table II.

## D. Classification and Signal Interpretation

Upon classification as Abnormal, the pipeline proceeds to the  signal  processing  stage.  The  previously  extracted  1D waveform undergoes:

- R-peak detection using SciPy's find\_peaks() function
- Interval calculation including:
- -Heart rate (BPM) via RR interval
- -PR interval
- -QRS duration
- -QT interval
- -ST segment metrics

These  temporal  features  are  compared  against  standard clinical thresholds, forming the basis of an automated diagnostic  report.  The  system  supports  real-time  waveform annotation  and  human-readable  outputs,  increasing  clinical interpretability.

## F. Evaluation Metrics

Model  performance  was  assessed  using  four  primary evaluation metrics:

- AccuracyIt measures the proportion of correctly predicted instances out of the total predictions, providing a general sense of model correctness.
- Accuracy = (TN+ TP) / (TP + TN + FP + FN) where TN/TP are true negatives/positives and FN/FP are false  negatives/positives.  It  is  a  basic  measure  of  how many instances are correctly classified. It gives a general sense of model performance but can be misleading if the classes are imbalanced in datasets.
- Precision- It is the ratio of true positive predictions to the total predicted positives, indicating the model's ability to avoid false positives.

Precision=TP/TP+FP

- Recall(or  sensitivity)  -  It  measures  the  ratio  of  true positives  to  the  total  actual  positives  ,  reflecting  the model's effectiveness in identifying all relevant cases.

Recall=TP/TP+FN

- F1-score - It is the harmonic mean of precision and recall ,offering a balanced metric that is particularly useful when dealing with imbalanced datasets.

F1 = (2 * Recall * Precision) / (Recall + Precision)

- Confusion  Matrix  -  It  is  used  to  visualize  the  model's classification  performance  across  normal  and  abnormal classes, showing  true  positives, true negatives, false positives, false negatives. It provides insight into specific types of misclassifications and supports a deeper interpretation  of  model  performance  across  the  binary classes (normal and abnormal ECGs).

These  metrics  provide  a  comprehensive  assessment  of classification performance, especially under class imbalance conditions common in medical datasets.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

This  section  details  the  outcomes  of  model  training, architectural  evaluation  of  the  neural  network,  and  feature extraction  from  ECG  signals.  The  analysis  encompasses training-validation performance trends, parameter efficiency assessments,  classification  evaluation  metrics,  and  clinical interpretation of extracted waveform features.

## A. Model Performance

The proposed CNN-based ECG classification model was evaluated  using  a  test  set  comprising  104  grayscale  ECG images.  The evaluation metrics used include accuracy, precision,  recall,  and  F1-score  as  indicated  in  Table  III, offering  a  comprehensive  understanding  of  the  model's predictive performance.

The  model  achieved  an  overall  accuracy  of  94.23%, indicating  strong  generalization  to  unseen  ECG  samples.  A precision  of  0.96  suggests  a  very  low  false  positive  rate, making the model reliable in correctly identifying abnormal ECGs. The recall of 0.91 reflects the model's sensitivity to detecting abnormalities, which is crucial for clinical applications  where  missed  diagnoses  could  be  critical.  The F1-score of 0.93 confirms a balanced performance between precision and recall.

## B. Diagnostic Signal Analysis

In  addition  to  classification,  the  system  performs  1D waveform  extraction  and  clinical  metric  analysis  for  cases predicted  as  abnormal.  Using  vertical  pixel  summation,  a pseudo-ECG signal is generated and processed to detect Rpeaks and extract waveform features such as the PR interval, QRS duration, QT interval, and heart rate. The derived values are  mapped  to  standard  cardiological  thresholds  to  assess conditions like tachycardia, bradycardia, and potential arrhythmic patterns.

| Interpretation | Normal sinus rhythm with borderline QRS width |

This  feature  not  only  validates  classification  results  but also enhances clinical interpretability, transforming the model from  a  black-box  classifier  into  a  hybrid  decision-support system.

The  progression  of  training  and  validation  accuracies across 20 epochs for the proposed CNN model is illustrated in Fig. 4. It is observed from the initial phase (Epochs 1-7) that both training and validation accuracies remain relatively flat, indicating  the  model  is  still  in  the  learning  phase,  possibly adjusting weights and biases with minimal improvement. In the  middle  phase  (Epochs  8-13),  a  sharp  rise  in  validation accuracy occurs around epoch 8, peaking near 0.9 by epoch 10.  This  reflects  a  successful  fit  to  the  dataset.  Training accuracy  also  steadily  improves,  suggesting  the  model  is learning  generalizable  features.  During  stabilization  phase (Epochs 14-20) both accuracies converge above 90%, with training accuracy nearing 98%  and  validation accuracy stabilizing around 92-93%. This indicates low variance and a well-regularized model with minimal overfitting.

The  model  demonstrates  excellent  generalization  from training to validation data, with strong predictive capacity and stable learning. The absence of significant divergence between  the  two  curves  confirms  the  effectiveness  of  the architecture,  regularization  strategies  (e.g.,  Dropout),  and preprocessing techniques.

## C. Comparative Insight

Compared to existing studies, the proposed model demonstrates superior or comparable performance. For instance, [9] achieved a positive predictive value of 97.29% using traditional GDA-SVM on the PTB dataset but lacked integrated signal interpretation. Meanwhile, composite deep learning  model  by  [6]  reached  an  AUROC  of  0.91  on  2.2 million  ECGs  but  required  massive  data  and  infrastructure. Our  lightweight  CNN  model  matches  or  exceeds  these benchmarks using a modest dataset (517 images) and standard computing hardware, demonstrating strong performance-cost tradeoff.

## E. ECG Signal Feature Detection from Images

The  proposed  system  includes  a  dedicated  pipeline  for detecting ECG waveform components directly from image- based signals.  A  projection of  pixel  intensities  is  computed from  the  grayscale  ECG  image,  transforming  the  visual waveform into a 1D signal suitable for peak detection.

Fig. 9 Detected ECG Waves on 1D Projection

As shown in Fig. 9, the resulting line plot highlights detected P, Q, R, S, and T wave points, each annotated using distinct color-coded  markers.  This  visualization  confirms  that  the system is capable of reliably identifying clinically significant wave components from raw image data.

From these detected peaks, the system computes important diagnostic  metrics  such  as  PR  interval,  QRS  duration,  QT interval,  and  ST  segment  duration,  as  well  as  waveform amplitudes. Each of these values is automatically interpreted based  on  established  cardiological  thresholds.  For  instance, prolonged QRS duration may indicate ventricular arrhythmia, while elevated T-wave amplitude can be associated with early myocardial infarction or hyperkalemia. These interpretations are  generated dynamically  for  each  ECG  input,  making  the method useful for automated, explainable diagnostic support.

Thus, the proposed CNN-based ECG classification model achieved a high accuracy of 94.23%, with precision of 0.96, recall of 0.91, and an F1-score of 0.93, demonstrating robust diagnostic performance. The confusion matrix confirms strong class separation with minimal misclassification (2 false positives,  4  false  negatives).  Additional  waveform  analysis accurately  identified  P,  Q,  R,  S,  and  T  peaks,  enabling  the extraction of clinical metrics like QRS duration and heart rate. The  model  is  computationally  efficient,  performs  well  on limited hardware, and offers interpretable outputs, making it highly suitable for real-time deployment in remote healthcare, telecardiology, and mobile diagnostic tools.

## V. CONCLUSION

This study presents an efficient CNN-based framework for ECG image classification and diagnostic waveform analysis. The model demonstrates strong performance with a classification accuracy of 94.23%, supported by high precision and recall. The integrated system not only classifies ECGs  as  normal  or  abnormal  but  also  extracts  clinically relevant features such as QRS duration and heart rate through 1D  waveform  projection.  This  dual  capability  enhances interpretability and aligns with real-world cardiological workflows.  The  system  is  lightweight  and  deployable  on standard hardware, making it ideal for point-of-care diagnostics in resource-constrained settings.

In future work, expanding the dataset to include diverse pathologies and multi-lead ECGs will improve generalization. Incorporating explainability tools  (e.g.,  Grad-CAM)  can enhance clinician trust. Additionally, real-time signal reconstruction  and  integration  with  wearable  or  IoT-based ECG monitors will further extend its applicability. A clinical validation phase and deployment in mobile health (mHealth) platforms are also key next steps.

Abstract -The  lungs  are  crucial  organs  for  sustaining  overall health, and their impairment can lead to severe consequences that impact  the  body's  overall  functionality.  Infectious  pulmonary diseases(IPD's),  including  Tuberculosis  (TB),  Pneumonia,  and COVID-19, are particularly challenging to diagnose due to their overlapping  symptoms  and  varying  presentations  in  medical imaging. To  overcome  these  challenges,  our  research  employs  a novel method where feature extraction from chest X-rays(CXR's) is  performed  using  advanced  techniques  such  as  Histogram  of Oriented  Gradients  (HOG)  and  Oriented  FAST  and  Rotated BRIEF (ORB). For classification, a fusion approach is used with Support Vector Machine (SVM) and Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) as base classifiers and Random Forest (RF) as the metaclassifier. The effectiveness of the proposed method was rigorously evaluated  across  three  distinct  classification  tasks.For  the  fourclass  classification  task,  the  method  achieved  a  test  accuracy  of 89.89%, precision of 90%, recall of 89.89%, and an F1 score of 89.86%. In the tertiary classification task, it demonstrated a test accuracy of 92.35%, precision of 92.44%, recall of 92.35%, and an F1 score of 92.35%. For the binary classification task, the method exhibited excellent performance with a test accuracy of 98.15%, precision of 98.16%, recall of 98.15%, and an F1 score of 98.15%.

Keywords  -  IPD,  feature  extraction,  HOG,  ORB,  Multiclass, XGBoost, SVM, RF

## I. INTRODUCTION

The  lung  is  the  most  essential  organs  for  maintaining  the healthy  functioning  of  the  human  body[1].  However,  several conditions  can  impair  lung  function,  leading  to  significant health issues. The goal of treating lung diseases is to manage their  severity  and  progression,  although  these  conditions  are often chronic and may not be fully reversible[2] . When the lung is damaged, it can lead to death, which highlights the need for early and accurate diagnosis. Respiratory diseases are becoming more common due to several factors, including higher pollution levels, smoking and use of biomass fuels, exposure to dust, and lifestyle changes . These factors lead to various lung conditions that  can  seriously  affect  a  person's  health  and  life  quality. Infectious pulmonary diseases are among the deadliest communicable diseases globally and rank among the top four leading causes of mortality [3]. Various methods and tools are

Studies show that X-rays of patients with respiratory diseases can show patterns like ground glass opacities, patchy consolidations, and other changes. This method is chosen because of its convenience and non-invasive nature.

Common  IPDs  include  pneumonia  (PN),  COVID-19,  and tuberculosis (TB). Each of these diseases has its own challenges in  diagnosis  and  treatment. The challenge lies in extending these successes to multiclass classification scenarios, where the need for accuracy must be balanced with computational efficiency.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Early diagnosis of infectious pulmonary diseases is crucial in medical diagnostics because of its significant impact on clinical outcomes and treatment outcomes. Pulmonary diseases, including Tuberculosis (TB), Pneumonia, and COVID-19, are widespread  and can lead to severe consequences  if not accurately  diagnosed. These  conditions  often  present  with overlapping symptoms which complicates the diagnostic process. Traditional  diagnostic  methods  can  be  limited  because  they often  depend  on  personal  judgment  and  interpretation  of symptoms and images. To improve accuracy, advanced computer vision techniques are used. These methods analyze clinical  images  more  objectively  and  effectively,  helping  to reduce mistakes in diagnosis. Many studies have been conducted on this topic, exploring how these advanced methods can enhance diagnostic efficacy. Fachrel et al.[6] conducted a study on classifying IPD's using CXR images, focusing on Corona virus, pneumonia, and also normal  cases. Their  highly  successful  model  featured  five convolutional units with a pair of LSTM layers and  achieved high F1 score with efficient training time. Mohan Bhandari et al.[7] explored the advance deep learning models for distinguishing CXR images into Corona virus disease, pneumonia disease and tuberculosis (TB) categories, leveraging explainable  artificial intelligence. Their lightweight  single CNN model achieved high  accuracy. Xuchun Wang  et  al.[8] aimed  to  improve  early  identification  of  chronic  respiratory disease  also  known  as  COPD  using  the  ML  methods. They applied supervised classifiers with techniques like class weighting and SMOTE resampling to handle imbalanced data, comparing models like Logistic Regression, RF,  LightGBM, XGBoost and Stacking. Patrik Szepesi et al.[9] addressed the challenge of automated pneumonia detection in medical imaging, emphasizing the subtle signs in CT and X-ray scans despite  its  significant  health  impact. Wataru  Uegami  and colleagues  in  [10]  addressed  the  diagnostic  complexities  of interstitial  pneumonia  (IP),  a  diverse  disease  with  significant clinical implications. Their study introduced MIXTURE (EAI with the integration of the recurrent training), a new method for creating deep learning models clinically relevant proficient in extracting  findings  with  minimal  input  from  experts. Ines Hilali-Jaghdam  et  al. in  [11]  developed  the  MOA-DLEDC (optimization algorithm with deep learning-enabled classification) method to diagnose Corona virus disease using CXR  images. This approach combines adaptive median filtering (AMF) for noise removal, the DenseNet model for the extraction of features, mother optimization algorithm (MOA) for hyperparameter tuning, and a sparse autoencoder (SAE) for classification. Bhosale et al. in [12] developed a model named PulDi-COVID,  designed  to  identify  various  lung  conditions, including  atelectasis,  bacterial  pneumonia,  COVID-19,  and pneumothorax, using CXR  images. This model uses a combination  of  transfer  learning  approaches,  incorporating architectures such as VGG19, VGG16, DenseNet169, MobileNetV2,  Resnet50,  NASNetMobile  and  DenseNet201. Kumar et al. in [13] highlighted the necessity of early-stage lung disease diagnosis using automated   methods based on deep learning, which generally depend on data from a single source like clinical imaging. Recognizing the limitations of  single  channel  analysis,  the  study  proposed  a  multimodal fusion  approach  integrating  clinical  imaging  data  combined with  medical  information  to  enhance  diagnostic  reliability. Rajasekar et al. in [14] investigated the prompt identification of cancerous cells in tissues of the lungs using deep learning, given its  significance  in  patient  assessment  and  management. The study  highlighted  deep  learning  model's  ability  to  identify lymphatic node engagement on histology slides, addressing the limitations of existing algorithms in precision, sensitivity and specificity. Sanida et al. in [15] focused on conditions such as fibrosis, tuberculosis, viral pneumonia. This framework makes use  of  a  CNN  architecture  to  improve  feature  learning  from CXR's. The approach was tested on a large data set and showed high performance in the infectious pulmonary disease diagnosis. Priyadarsini  et  al.

## III. METHODOLOGY

The  ultimate  aim  is  to  create  a  robust  and  efficient  stacking ensemble  method  for  the  prompt  identification  of  infectious pulmonary diseases by using CXR images. The methodology involves  using  a  fusion  of  SVM-XGBoost  as  the  primary classifiers  and  RF  as  the  stacking  classifier.  The  process includes data loading, preprocessing, feature extraction using ORB and HOG techniques, model training, and evaluation. The classification  tasks  are  categorized  into  binary  classification (Normal  and  TB),  tertiary  classification  (Normal  cases,  TB, Pneumonia), and four-class classification (TB, Pneumonia,Normal and the Covid19).

On  the  other  hand,  ORB  is employed  to  detect  keypoints  and  compute  their  descriptors, which encapsulate distinctive patterns and local features within the image. ## C. Model Training

From the training dataset, 15% was allocated for validation, and an entirely separate test set was used for final model evaluation. The classification framework for this study involves a stacking ensemble method with a fusion of SVM-XGBoost as the initial classifier and RF as the final classifier. In this study, the SVM classifier  was  utilized  with  linear  kernel.  This  kernel  was chosen due to its simplicity and efficiency, particularly when the data is linearly separable or when the dimensionality within the feature space is elevated.

In this study, XGBoost is used as an additional base classifier to complement the SVM. One of the standout features of XGBoost is its regularization term, which penalizes complex models to prevent overfitting [19].

In  this  research,  the  XGBoost  model  was  configured  with specific  hyperparameters  to  optimize  its  performance  for  the lung disease classification task. Abstract -Villagers living near forests face serious threats from wild animals, including crop damage, livestock loss, and risks to human safety. In order to overcome these problems generally the guards are appointed and cameras are installed. But these traditional methods require constant monitoring and the chances of failure increase. Sometimes there may be delays in the response, leading to false alarms. To avoid these challenges this research presents an Artificial Intelligence (AI) based system which helps in real-time detection and prevention of wild animal intrusions, especially in the villages and agricultural land near the forest areas. The proposed system uses motion sensors, thermal cameras and sound detectors to make accurate predictions when a harmful animal intrudes. For the real-time detection of wild animals, the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) model is used and this approach has achieved a precision of 98.4% at 30 frames per second. Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is used for detecting the animals and classifying them as harmful or harmless with an accuracy of 98.7%. Long Short Term Memory (LSTM) model is used to analyse the intrusion pattern and predict future intrusions with a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) value of 0.16. Once the system detects and identifies the animal, it sends alert messages to the villagers, forest officials and the concerned people via SMS and a mobile application is built using Flutter. The system also uses repellent tools like soundemitting devices and flashing lights to scare the animals away. The proposed approach provides a highly reliable and efficient solution to reduce human-wildlife conflict and enhance rural safety.

Index Terms -Artificial intelligence, machine learning, deeplearning, object detection, animal prediction, convolutional neural network, human-wildlife conflict.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Wild animal intrusions into agricultural lands and villages near forest regions have increasingly caused serious problems. Events like these lead to damaged crops, loss of livestock, and threats to both human life and safety [1]. Constant human attention is required for traditional methods such as appointing guards or installing cameras. However, these methods frequently lead to delayed actions, missed detections, and incorrect alerts. This approach uses artificial intelligence (AI) and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies to tackle these limitations [2]. Automated, real-time monitoring and aids in preventing wildlife intrusions are presented in the proposed approach. This system focuses on developing an AI-powered system that uses deep learning models to work with sensor data from thermal cameras and sound detectors to accurately detect wild animals in real-time and provide timely alerts to the concerned people such as farmers and local forest officers. The application of thermal cameras increases the predictions of dangerous animals even at night.

There are several studies that have explored the use of AI and IoT for reducing human-wildlife conflict [3]. Abed et al. [4] looked at different AI and sensor-based methods that help in protecting crops. Researchers discovered that combining sensors and AI models led to better predictions and more accurate animal detections. This also reduces the need for human guards and constant human supervision. Reddy et al. [5] created a system using a lightweight deep-learning frame- work. These models run on local devices to quickly detect animals that damage crops. Surya and Selvaperumal [6] have built a model for the detection of animals entering agricultural land. Their work explains how Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) can recognize different animals accurately. Waghmare et al. [7] combine AI models with motion sensors. Cameras usually fail to make accurate predictions when there is heavy rain fog or dust, so they have used seismic sensors that help in identifying dangerous animals in the regions near forests regardless of whether or time of day. Delwar et al. [8] combined the You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) model with advanced AI and IoT devices to detect wildlife near farms in real-time. Since regular cameras perform poorly at night, they have used thermal cameras to make accurate predictions even at night or when there is low light.

Fig. 1. Block diagram of the proposed hybrid intrusion detection system

<!-- image -->

Patil and Ansari [9] have built a system combining AI with IoT devices or sensors. They have used some tools like sound-emitting devices and light-emitting devices. The system first identifies animals and then scares them away using the repellent tools by emitting sounds and flashing lights. This eliminates the need for a human guard to protect villages and farms near forests. Siyanwal et al. [10] used fog-based architecture to combat wildlife poaching and for real-time detection. All these works demonstrates the use of different AI models like CNNs and long short-term memory (LSTM) for wildlife detection applications [11], [12]. The model helps in learning animal movement patterns and improves the prediction of future intrusions.

The proposed work integrates these insights by developing a hybrid deep learning system that uses YOLOv8 for realtime animal detection from thermal and visual inputs, a CNN to classify animals as dangerous or harmless, and an LSTM model trained on historical data to predict potential future intrusions [13]. The goal is to build a user-friendly web platform that provides live monitoring, quick alert messages via Short Message Service (SMS) and mobile apps, and uses tools like sound emitters and flashing lights to scare animals away. By using these safe and non-harmful methods the crops can be protected and conflicts between humans and wild animals can be reduced.

## II. METHODOLOGY

The proposed system is designed to provide a real-time solution to wild animal intrusions in agricultural and village areas located near forest boundaries. Fig. 1 represents the block diagram of the proposed system. The system architecture is designed to integrate multiple components working together efficiently. The first layer of the system is the data acquisition layer of various sensor inputs, followed by a pre-processing unit, a hybrid AI-based detection and prediction engine, and finally, a user interaction module delivered via web and mobile platforms. These components work together to enable not only detection but also prediction and automated deterrent control.

## A. Data Collection and Pre-processing

The data collection process is the core component of the system; it focuses on the strategic deployment of various sensors and surveillance devices near forest boundaries and agricultural zones. A multi-sensor setup consisting of thermal cameras, RGB cameras, microphones, and motion detectors is used to ensure reliable and continuous monitoring under varying environmental conditions. The technical specifications of the sensors used in the hybrid intrusion detection system are shown in Table I. Usage of FLIR Lepton 3.5 thermal camera helps us to detect heat signatures from animals up to 100 meters away, making them ideal for night-time surveillance and low-visibility scenarios [14]. High-resolution RGB cameras Logitech C920 is used for clear daytime imaging with effective coverage of up to 80 meters. Ambient sounds and specific animal vocalizations are captured using the omnidirectional capabilities of Microphones (Zoom H1n), by contributing to early detection based on auditory cues. Physical movement within a range of 3 to 7 meters is detected using the Motion sensors (HC-SR501 PIR module) which trigger the system only when necessary thereby reducing false alarms [15]. The use of these diverse sensors ensures extensive and contextaware data acquisition. All sensory inputs are transferred in real-time to a centralized local server, where they are queued for further preprocessing and analysis by the AI models.

TABLE I TECHNICAL SPECIFICATIONS OF SENSORS USED IN THE HYBRID INTRUSION DETECTION SYSTEM

| Sensor Type    | Model Used      | Detection Range   | Key Features                   | Usage Location          |
|----------------|-----------------|-------------------|--------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Thermal Camera | FLIR Lepton 3.5 | Up to 100 meters  | Night vision, heat mapping     | Forest edges, farmlands |
| RGB Camera     | Logitech C920   | 50-80 meters      | High-resolution, color video   | Entrance zones          |
| Microphone     | Zoom H1n        | Omnidirectional   | Sound pattern recognition      | Trees, posts            |
| Motion Sensor  | HC-SR501 PIR    | 3-7 meters        | Motion-triggered signal output | Near cameras/sensors    |

The raw sensor data is pre-processed before it is passed to the deep learning models. For image and video data, to maintain consistency across the dataset, preprocessing involves resizing frames to a standard resolution, usually 640x640 pixels. The process also includes the conversion of video footage into frames, noise reduction, and normalization of pixel values to reduce computational overhead. The audio signals are pre-processed by filtering out background noise and converting the raw waveform into spectrograms, which are more readable by machine learning algorithms. The purpose of preprocessing is to ensure that only clean, relevant, and high-quality data reaches the AI model to improve accuracy and reduce the possibility of misclassification.

## B. Hybrid Deep Learning Model

The system is built around a hybrid deep learning model that combines three components: YOLOv8, CNN and LSTM network [16]. YOLOv8 acts as the object detection engine and is responsible for identifying animals in real time from the video feeds. YOLOv8 consists internally three major components: a backbone that extracts fundamental features from the input images using multiple convolutional layers, a neck which combines the features across different scales using a Feature Pyramid Network (FPN) and a head which performs the final object classification and bounding box predictions. YOLOv8 is lightweight and its architecture allows to processing of frames at high speed, making it suitable for real-time applications.

After the detection stage, the identified animal images are passed through a CNN that is classified into two categories: dangerous (e.g., wild boars, elephants) or harmless (e.g., deer, monkeys). The CNN architecture consists of multiple layers of convolutions, max-pooling and fully connected layers that sequentially learn complex patterns and features. This classification step is crucial for decision-making, especially in determining whether deterrent mechanisms should be activated. The CNN is trained on a labelled dataset of animal images to improve accuracy in classification.

The system uses an LSTM model to improve its capabilities by analyzing patterns from previous intrusion data. LSTM networks are advanced Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN), which is capable of capturing long-term dependencies in timeseries data [17]. This model uses sensor activity, timing and environmental conditions as input to predict future outcomes. This prediction allows the system to act in advance and help farmers and forest officials by providing early warnings, allowing them to take action before an intrusion occurs.

text:
## C. Web and Mobile Interface

The final layer of the system includes both web and mobile applications that allow users to interact and monitor the system easily. These platforms help users including farmers, forest officials, and local authorities to interact with the system. The web application is developed using React.js and it is connected with the backend using RESTful APIs built using Node.js and Express, to make it compatible with the AI engine and databases. The backend services handle alerts, store user preferences, and logging intrusion data. Flutter is used as the cross-platform development toolkit for the mobile application. It enables cross-platform development, allowing the app to run smoothly on both Android and iOS devices with a single codebase. Firebase is utilized for real-time database and push notifications, enabling users to receive immediate alerts when intrusions are detected [18].

The web interface allows access to live camera feeds, visual heatmaps of intrusion zones, historical data analytics, and manual override controls for deterrent systems. The mobile application imitates these functionalities while being optimized for smaller screens and lower bandwidth use. It includes additional features such as SMS alert options and Global Positioning System (GPS) integration to locate intrusion spots quickly. These interfaces are designed with simplicity and usability in mind, featuring multilingual support and intuitive navigation, making them accessible to users with minimal technical expertise. Together, the web and mobile platforms ensure continuous awareness, quicker response times, and improved coordination between various stakeholders in mitigating human-wildlife conflict.

The models used for classification are well-known models such as Faster R-CNN, Single Shot MultiBox Detector (SSD), RetinaNet, YOLOv5, and MobileNet [19], [20]. These models are widely used for real-time detection of wildlife intrusions. The same pre-processing steps and environmental settings were maintained for consistency in evaluation. As shown in Table II, the performance metrics of each model clearly indicates that the proposed hybrid model that combines YOLOv8, CNN, and LSTM performs the best. As shown in Fig. 2, other models like MobileNet and SSD had higher RMSE values, meaning they were not as good at tracking patterns over time. The low RMSE proves that our system can learn from past animal movements, make accurate predictions, help send early warnings and automatically trigger deterrents, which is especially useful for reducing damage in rural areas and human-wildlife conflict. Beyond the core AI models, we also developed web and mobile interfaces that facilitate real-time interaction and monitoring. The screenshot of the designed web page is shown in Fig. 3. The web application enables forest officials and local authorities to view live camera feeds, analyse patterns of animal intrusion, and oversee sensor deployments effectively.

text:
## IV. CONCLUSION

This paper presents a hybrid deep learning-based wildlife intrusion detection system that integrates YOLOv8, CNN, and LSTM models with a multi-sensor network for real-time monitoring and prediction. An accuracy of 98.7%, precision of 98.4%, recall of 98.9%, and a low error rate of just 1.3% is achieved by the proposed model, outperforming several existing models in both detection and classification tasks. In addition, strong predictive capabilities with an RMSE of 0.16 is achieved by the LSTM model, enabling timely alerts and preventive actions. The system is designed to be practically deployable in rural and forest-adjacent regions, where humanwildlife conflicts are frequent. Automated detection and response mechanisms reduce the need for manual surveillance, mitigate crop damage, and livestock loss, and enhance safety. By providing mobile and web-based interfaces, it provides user-friendly access and real-time control for farmers and authorities. The system's modular design allows for scalable deployment and future enhancements, making it an efficient solution for wildlife conflict management and rural safety.

## A Novel Deep Learning-Based Framework for Early Diagnosis of Neurodegenerative Diseases

Dept of Master of Computer Applications Shree Devi Institute of Technology Mangaluru, India vidyas135@gmail.com Vidyarani UA

Abstract -Early detection of neurodegenerative diseases is critical for enabling timely intervention and improving patient outcomes. Currently, the diagnostic methods often detects pathology only at advanced stages, limiting therapeutic effectiveness. This paper extend a novel 3D CNN-Transformer-based framework designed for early diagnosis through automated neuroimaging analysis. The architecture combines local spatial feature extraction from 3D convolutional networks with long-range dependency modeling via Transformer encoders, supported by an optimized preprocessing pipeline that includes intensity normalization, spatial registration, and bias correction. While the framework is built for future multimodal integration of MRI, PET, genetic, and clinical data, this proof-of-concept evaluation focuses on structural MRI scans from Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Experimental results demonstrate strong baseline performance, achieving 91.2% accuracy and AUC = 0.94 in distinguishing early-stage Alzheimer's disease from healthy controls. These findings highlight the framework's potential as a foundation for interpretable, multimodal diagnostic systems for clinical decision support.

Index Terms -Deep learning, Magnetic resonance imaging, Dementia, Aphasia, Neurology, Convolutional neural networks, Diseases, Biomedical imaging, Medical diagnosis

## I. INTRODUCTION

Neurodegenerative diseases, such as Alzheimer's disease (AD), Parkinson's disease (PD), and Huntington's disease, are progressive disorders of the nervous system that lead to cognitive decline, motor impairments, and ultimately loss of independence. With the global aging population increasing, the prevalence of these conditions is rising sharply, posing significant clinical and socioeconomic burdens. Prior and accurate diagnosis is crucial for timely treatment, effective therapy, and better patient outcomes. However, conventional diagnostic methods-often based on clinical symptom evaluation, neuropsychological testing, and visual inspection of neuroimaging-tend to identify disease at advanced stages, by the time significant and permanent neuronal damage has taken place.

Over the past decade, machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) techniques have emerged as powerful tools for neuroimaging analysis, enabling automated detection of subtle structural and functional brain changes. Despite promising results, existing approaches face notable limitations. Many Nethravathi P S Dept of Master of Computer Applications Shree Devi Institute of Technology Mangaluru, India nethrakumar590@gmail.com rely on a single data modality, such as MRI or PET, which restricts the model's ability to capture complementary information. Others lack robust preprocessing pipelines, leading to inconsistent feature extraction, while limited interpretability hinders clinical trust and adoption.

To meet these challenges, we propose a novel deep learningbased framework for the early detection of neurodegenerative diseases. The framework incorporates an optimized preprocessing and feature extraction pipeline to ensure consistent and high-quality input data, improving model robustness. Using structural MRI scans from the Alzheimer 's disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), the system demonstrates high baseline performance in distinguishing early-stage AD from healthy controls. This work lays the foundation for a future multimodal, interpretable diagnostic platform capable of supporting clinicians in early disease identification.
