## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Artificial intelligence has significantly advanced the automated detection of neurodegenerative diseases, particularly Alzheimer's disease, through analysis of neuroimaging and related biomarkers. Early studies predominantly relied on unimodal imaging data such as MRI or PET, achieving promising results but often failing to capture complementary disease-specific information across modalities [1], [2], [3]. Even though CNN-based unimodal approaches perform well for structural abnormality detection, they lack the capability to utilize the richer insights available from multimodal feature integration.

Current research increasingly emphasizes multimodal fusion of MRI, PET, genetic, and clinical data to achieve better diagnostic results. Huang et al. [1] and Cui et al. [11] demonstrated that integrating incomplete multimodal inputs with attentionbased learning yields better classification accuracy than singlemodality models. Similarly, Fang et al. [8] proposed a multimodal knowledge graph to capture complex cross-domain relationships, while Liang et al. [9] fused resting-state fMRI and structural MRI to detect early-stage AD.

Interpretability emerged as another critical focus area, as clinicians require transparent AI models to support decisionmaking. Peng et al. [4] and Nguyen et al. [15] proposed in- terpretable frameworks that highlight disease-relevant regions, fostering clinical trust. Shi et al. [13] further emphasized explainable multimodal fusion, showing that interpretability does not necessarily compromise predictive accuracy.

Temporal feature integration is also gaining attention. Zhang et al. [3] incorporated longitudinal data to improve early detection, while Choi and Jin [10] combined metabolic and amyloid imaging to predict cognitive decline trajectories. Du et al. [14] and Pan et al. [2] explored advanced fusion architectures, demonstrating that multi-scale and disease-imagespecific learning can further improve robustness.

Despite these advances, challenges remain. Many models are dataset-specific and lack generalizability across populations, while preprocessing pipelines are not always optimized for heterogeneous clinical data [5], [12]. The framework proposed in this work fills these gaps by incorporating a refined preprocessing and feature extraction pipeline, along with a robust and scalable deep learning architecture. Additionally, its focus on interpretability ensures compatibility with clinical practice, distinguishing it from traditional black-box models.

## III. METHODOLOGY

The proposed methodology introduces a hybrid deep learning framework that leverages both convolutional and transformer-based models for proir detection of neurodegenerative diseases from multimodal data, focusing on MRI and PET scans. The system is designed to improve diagnostic accuracy through optimized preprocessing, feature extraction, and modality fusion

The proposed framework operates through three major stages that collectively enhance the accuracy and reliability of neurodegenerative disease detection. In the data preprocessing stage, multimodal inputs such as MRI and PET scans are standardized, normalized, and spatially aligned to ensure uniformity across all samples. This step includes image registration, intensity normalization, bias correction, and resampling to a common anatomical space, thereby enabling consistent analysis. Next, in the feature extraction and fusion stage, a hybrid architecture combining 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (3D CNNs) and Transformer encoders is employed. The 3D CNNs are responsible for capturing fine-grained local spatial features from each modality, while the Transformer modules model long-range dependencies and contextual relationships across image slices and modalities. Finally, in the classification and prediction stage, features from multiple modalities are fused and passed through fully connected layers, culminating in a softmax classifier that outputs probabilistic predictions for multiple diagnostic categories, such as Healthy Control (HC), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's Disease (AD). This structured approach ensures both robust feature learning and clinically interpretable predictions.

The proposed framework for early detection of neurodegenerative diseases follows a systematic pipeline consisting of seven key stages, as illustrated in Figure 1. The proposed methodology classifies brain health states-Healthy Controls (HC), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's Disease (AD)-using MRI and PET scans. It begins with preprocessing steps such as normalization, registration, bias correction, and resampling to standardize image quality and ensure consistent resolution, producing uniform inputs for the model.

Fig. 1. Block diagram illustrating the steps in Proposed methodology

<!-- image -->

Data augmentation follows, introducing variations like rotations, scaling, and noise injection to increase dataset diversity. This step improves model robustness and helps prevent overfitting by simulating real-world variability in imaging conditions.

Feature extraction[20] is performed using separate 3D Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) for MRI and PET data. The MRI branch captures structural patterns, while the PET branch focuses on functional and metabolic features, both of which are essential for accurate disease identification.

Extracted features are processed by transformer encoders, which apply attention mechanisms to capture long-range dependencies and global context in both MRI and PET data. This enables the model to link patterns across distant brain regions[20][22].

Finally, features from both modalities are merged in a fusion layer, combining their complementary strengths. The fused representation is passed to a softmax classifier, which outputs the probabilities for HC, MCI, or AD, selecting the highest as the final diagnosis.

## IV. DATASET AND PREPROCESSING

## A. Dataset Description

This study uses imaging data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI)[16], a widely recognized repository for neurodegenerative disease research. The dataset includes three diagnostic groups: Healthy Controls (HC), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), and Alzheimer's Disease (AD). A balanced subset of 2,100 subjects was selected (700 per group).

Two modalities were employed: T1-weighted MRI for structural brain analysis and FDGPET for metabolic activity assessment. Examples include ADNI 002 S 0295 MR MPRAGE (HC) and ADNI 128 S 0135 PET FDG (AD), the latter showing reduced glucose metabolism in temporal and parietal regions. The sample of the dataset is given in the Figure 2.

## B. Preprocessing Pipeline

A unified preprocessing workflow was applied to harmonize multimodal data. MRI intensities were normalized to zero mean/unit variance; PET scans were scaled to the SUVR range [0,1]. PET volumes were registered to MRI via affine transformation with mutual information optimization. Bias field correction was performed using the N4ITK algorithm, followed by resampling to isotropic 1 mm³ resolution and normalization to the MNI-152 template. Automated quality control removed scans with artifacts, incomplete coverage, or excessive noise, ensuring data consistency for downstream analysis.

## VI. DISCUSSION

Figure 4 provides a comparison of classification accuracy for Alzheimer's disease and related conditions across various methods. Li et al. [17] employed a convolutional neural network on multimodal MRI and PET data, while Zhang et al. [18] used a dual-stream CNN with cross-attention. Both prior works achieved strong performance but lacked robust modeling of long-range dependencies. In contrast, the proposed framework integrates a 3D CNN to extract local spatial features and a Transformer encoder to model global contextual relationships across modalities. This hybrid architecture, together with a harmonized preprocessing pipeline, results in a 3.6% accuracy improvement over Li et al. and a 2.3% gain over Zhang et al.. The results underscore the effectiveness of integrating CNN-based local feature learning with Transformer-based global context modeling in neurodegenerative disease diagnosis.

Fig. 4. Comparison of classification accuracy between prior works and the proposed 3D CNN-Transformer framework.

<!-- image -->

Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves comparing MRI-only CNN, PET-only CNN, Early Fusion, and the proposed 3D CNN-Transformer model. The 3D CNN-Transformer achieves the highest Area Under the Curve (AUC = 0.91), indicating superior trade-off between sensitivity and specificity. Early fusion of MRI and PET improves over unimodal models, while MRI-only consistently outperforms PET-only.

## VII. CONCLUSION

This study introduces an advanced 3D CNN-Transformer framework for the early detection of neurodegenerative diseases, demonstrating improved performance compared to unimodal and early fusion baselines, with an accuracy of 88.7%, F1-score of 0.872, and AUC of 0.91. By combining local spatial feature extraction from 3D CNNs with the longrange dependency modeling of Transformers, the framework demonstrated strong capability in distinguishing early-stage Mild Cognitive Impairment from Healthy Controls, addressing a critical clinical challenge. Future work aims to expand the framework by integrating additional multimodal data-such as genetic markers, cognitive assessments, and clinical records-to further improve diagnostic accuracy. Additionally, explainable AI modules will be integrated to improve interpretability and clinician trust, while longitudinal analysis will be employed to capture disease progression patterns and enable personalized risk prediction over time. This direction is expected to further improve early intervention opportunities and support precision medicine in neurodegenerative care.

## A Relationship-XGBoost Model for User Behavior Pattern Recognition in Social Internet of Things

Praveen Murthy K.S. Department of Information Science and Engineering, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India praveenmurthy@jssstuniv.in S. P. Shiva Prakash Department of Information Science and Engineering & CSBS, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India shivasp@jssstuniv.in

Abstract -Social Internet of Things (SIoT) further leverages the classical  Internet  of  Things  (IoT)  model  by  incorporating social relationships between smart devices so  that devices can interact and  make  decisions  autonomously.  Although  this  has  better automation and personalization, it presents challenges of predicting user activity correctly, handling dynamic  device relationships,  and  allowing  efficient  adaptation  of  services.  The inherently  uncertain  nature  of  user  interactions  in  SIoT  spaces requires strong predictive models capable of dealing with nonlinear and complex dependencies of the data. Current methods tend  to  fail  to  generalize  across  different  interaction  patterns as a result of SIoT ecosystem dynamics. This work rectifies  such shortcomings by applying boosting methods  to  model  and forecast user behavior  patterns  to  enhance  decision-making capacities  in  SIoT  systems.  In  contrast  to  traditional  machine learning models, the XGBoost model improves forecast accuracy through iterative improvement of weak learners and modelling of complex behavioral dependencies. Experimental results on three machine learning models-Random Forest, XGBoost, and Gradient  Boosting-are  used  to  evaluate  the  proposed  model using a complete dataset of user-device interaction. Experimental outcomes  show  that  XGBoost  performs  better  than  the  other models  with  an  average  accuracy  of (82 . 33%) , precision of (81 . 08%) , recall of (83 . 53%) , and an F1-score of (82 . 28%) . Gradient Boosting and Random Forest gave good results with precisions of (81 . 05%) and (80 . 65%) , respectively. The findings demonstrate the efficiency  of  XG-boosting  methods  in  IoT  settings.  This  work enhances smart SIoT systems through increased personalization and adaptability, contributing to enhanced user experiences and better service provision.

Keywords  -Internet  of  Things,  Social  Internet  of  Things, Boosting algorithms, Relationship, User Behavior

## I. INTRODUCTION

Human-machine communication in intelligent environments has advanced considerably with the advent of the Social Internet of  Things  (SIoT). Through  its  combination of  social  network principles with the Internet of Things (IoT), it enables devices to initiate  connections  in  accordance  with  context,  trust,  and cooperation,  and  share  information.  This  advancement  has increased  automation, enhanced decision-making, and opened up  new  avenues  for  creating  tailored  services.  Smart  cities, medicine, traffic,  and  factory  systems  are  only  some  possible uses  of  advanced  technology.  Smart  interfaces  already  make

## Kirill Krinkin

School of Computer Science and Engineering, Constructor University, Bremen, Germany kirill@krinkin.com

different devices cooperate smoothly with each other, improving daily experiences. This connectivity, though, adds a new level of complexity  since  there is  a  need  to  manage  relationships, predict  user  behavior,  and  maintain  data  security.  One  of  the major elements  to improve the performance of these systems is user behavior. It is important to know the user interaction with the  IoT  devices,  the  conditions,  and  preferences,  to  design personalized and flexible services. User behavior can be difficult to predict because of its dynamic and highly volatile environment. In order to properly analyze the immense amounts of data provided by user device interactions, machine learning methods can be applied.  One  of  the  useful  techniques  is  XG boosting machines, which can handle sophisticated, non-linear data and assist in recognizing patterns in Social IoT behaviour. This  research  uses  XGBoost  to  determine  patterns  of  user behavior  in  the  SIoT.  This  method  will  improve  service provision in the smart world and better forecast user engagement.

## II. RELATED WORK

Several  research  studies  have  been  conducted  on service recommendations and intrusion detection in the SIoT environment. Chalichalamala et al. [1] used an extreme gradient boosting  algorithm  to  suggest  a  classification  and  regression tree for IoT network intrusion detection. Divya and Tanuja [2] also used machine learning methods to detect SIoT intrusion. Khelloufi and team proposed a service recommendation system for SIoT that used multimodal features to improve the precision of the service suggestion process. Also, proposed an intrusion detection  approach  for  SIoT  security  based  on  collaborative edge computing and Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).

A  large-scale  survey  on  intrusion  detection  systems for IoT networks was carried out by Rahman et al. [3], which is the  most  in-depth  analysis  of  the  development  in intrusion detection for IoT systems. A framework  for  generating customized network datasets for Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) based on traffic aggregation was proposed by Velarde-Alvarado et al. [4]. Neto et al. [5] pursued the potential of collaborative Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) identification in multitenant IoT systems as a means of applying federated learning to better protect distributed IoT

environments. In addition, Kaur et.al [6] introduced a verification-based  approach  for  limiting  IoT  attacks,  thereby enhancing protection against various types of IoT vulnerabilities.  In fact, Sharma and Kaushik [7] introduced an architecture of the Internet of Vehicles by highlighting security issues along with possible solutions that are adoptable in IoT networks as a whole. Furthermore,  Safi et al. [8] addressed IoT identification,  fingerprinting,  and  profiling  surveys  that  are inevitable for IoT network security provisions. Elghalhoud et al.  [9]  study  revolves  around  improving  data  balancing  and machine  learning  algorithm  hyperparameter  optimization  for IoT network security. The goal is to improve the performance of IoT security systems by optimizing the intrusion detection models via improved machine learning techniques.

Also,  Abrishami et  al.  [10]  employed  decision  trees and active learning in dealing with IoT security issues, where label noise detection was a principal example. This technique enhances the rate of intrusion detection by solving the problem of  disorder  in  data.  This  algorithm's  enhanced  version  is employed in the Balyan et al. [11] intrusion detection model for the detection of attacks in IoT networks. It integrates EGA-PSO with random forests. The model has never been more accurate and  effective.  For  targeted  intrusion  detection  systems  in Internet  of  Things  (IoT)  systems,  Lin  et  al.  [12]  presented IDSGAN, a Generative Adversarial Network-based technique. Chen  et  al.  [13]  also  proposed  a  graph-based  IoT  service recommendation system that improves generation recommendations for services using social network interactions.  In  addition,  Khelloufi  et  al.  [14]  suggested  a service recommendation system for IoT devices with a focus on the  integration  of  social  networks  into  the  recommendation process based on social relationships. Authors Chen et.al [15] emphasized the significance of trust-based service management and  suggested  methods  to  manage  services  based  on  trust relationships. Xu et al. [16] presented a collaborative filtering recommendation  system  that  improves  suggestion  quality  by considering  user  confidence  and  prediction  accuracy  with regard to time context. In addition, Khelloufi et al.

[17] designed a context-aware service recommendation system for the Internet of Things that accounts for social interactions and  contextual  relationships  between  devices  to  give  more precise recommendations.

From the literature, it can be observed that the existing studies on SIoT predominantly focus on intrusion detection and service recommendations, often neglecting the dynamic nature of user behavior and device interactions. Therefore, this work focuses  on  developing  an  XGBoost  model  for  user  behavior pattern recognition, comparing three machine learning models to enhance prediction accuracy and optimize the SIoT system performance.

## V. ALGORITHM: XGBOOST FOR USER BEHAVIOR PATTERN RECOGNITION IN SIOT

The  Algorithm  starts  off  by  initializing  the  model  with  a constant prediction that  minimizes the overall loss  function over  all  the  data  points.  On  every  iteration, it calculates pseudoresiduals,  i.e.,  the  negative of  the  loss  function  with respect  to  the  prediction  of the current model. These residuals specify the errors in the existing predictions and are the new target  values for  training  the  subsequent  weak  learner.  A regression tree is then learned on these residuals by trying to minimize the squared difference between the residuals and  the predictions  of  the  tree.  After  the  new  tree  is trained,  the model is updated by combining the scaled predictions  of  the tree  with  the  existing  model,  with each new tree contributing to the final model controlled by the learning rate. After several iterations, the last model is returned, which is the aggregation of all the decision trees implemented to enhance the accuracy of user behavior pattern recognition.

## VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This work proposes a framework utilizing XG Boost methods  for  SIoT  user  behavior  modeling  and  prediction. Through  the  evaluation  of  three  models,  namely  Random Forest,  XGBoost,  and  Gradient  Boosting,  on  a  large-scale dataset  of  user-device  interactions,  XGBoost  is  proven  to surpass the other models. ## A study on Beamforming Capabilities of Y agiU da versus Short D ipole A ntennas

Mahima SK Dept. of ECE BNM Institute of Technology Bengaluru, India

mahimaassk@gmail.com

Abstract -This paper presents a comparative analysis of Yagi-Uda  and  Short  Dipole  antennas  for  beamforming  in MIMO systems using intelligent beam selection algorithms. The  framework  employs  machine  learning  models  such  as Neural Networks, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and statistical mapping to predict optimal beam indices. Simulation results show that the Neural Network achieves a 12% improvement in  Top-K  accuracy  and  a  15%  gain  in  average  RSRP compared to traditional  techniques.  The  Yagi-Uda  antenna demonstrates superior beam directivity and signal stability, proving  its  effectiveness  for  high-frequency  5G  and  6G wireless systems.

Keywords - Beam selection, Directional antennas, MIMO, neural networks, RSRP, Yagi-Uda antenna

## I. INTRODUCTION

With  the  rapid  progression  from  5G  to  6G  wireless networks, achieving ultra-reliable, low-latency, and highcapacity communication has become a top priority. Beamforming,  especially  in  millimeter-wave  (mmWave) frequencies, plays a crucial role in directing signal energy efficiently toward users. Directional antennas like the YagiUda, known for their high gain and focused beams [3][15], and  the  Short  Dipole,  valued  for  its  broad  coverage  and ease  of  integration  [4],  are  gaining  renewed  attention.  In parallel, data-driven approaches have gained attention for their ability to model spatial characteristics and environmental dynamics to improve beam  alignment efficiency  by  inferring  optimal  patterns  from  user  and environmental data [2][7][13].

Despite  these  advancements,  traditional  beam  selection methods  still  rely  heavily  on  exhaustive  search  or  static statistical  models,  resulting  in  increased  computational overhead and limited adaptability in dynamic environments [1][5]. Prior research often focuses on algorithmic improvements  without  deeply  evaluating  the  effect  of realistic antenna patterns on intelligent beamforming. This research addresses that gap by integrating physical antenna characteristics with a neural network-based beam selection system to assess how directional properties influence signal strength and prediction accuracy.

BNM Institute of Technology

Priyadarshini K Desai Dept. of ECE Bengaluru, India

priyadarshini.p.r@gmail.com

The key contributions of this work are: (1) simulation of a custom-designed  beam  evaluation  framework  leveraging high-fidelity antenna models of Yagi-Uda and Short Dipole antennas;  (2)  implementation  and  comparison  of  three beam selection methods-neural  networks, K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and statistical averaging; (3) evaluation of beam selection performance using Top-K accuracy and RSRP  metrics;  and  (4)  analysis  of  how  antenna  design impacts intelligent beamforming in dense user scenarios.

The  remainder  of  this  paper  is  organized  as  follows: Section II presents the literature survey; Section III describes the proposed methodology; Section IV discusses the results and provides discussions; and Section  V concludes the paper citing some of the published references.  This  study  aims  to  bridge  the  gap  between theoretical beam selection algorithms and practical antenna behavior,  offering  a  realistic  evaluation  framework  for intelligent beamforming in 5G/6G systems.

## II. RELATED WORKS

Beam  selection  has  emerged  as  a  critical  component  in modern wireless communication, particularly in millimeter-wave (mmWave) and upcoming 6G networks. The  work  in  paper  [1]  proposed  integrating  machine learning  with  beam  selection  in  mmWave  systems  using supervised  models  that  map  environmental  features  to optimal beam indices. The study reported notable improvements  over  exhaustive  search  methods  but  was limited to static deployment  scenarios. In article [2] focused on simulating Yagi-Uda antennas in urban environments  and  demonstrated  that  high  directionality improves beam precision. However, the fixed orientation limited adaptability to user mobility. Work  proposed  in  [3]  introduced  cross-polarized  short dipole arrays with deep learning for improving Non-Lineof-Sight  (NLOS)  coverage. While  the  system  enhanced signal  reception,  it  lacked  real-world  validation. Another addressed paper [4] used the K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) algorithm,  which  showed  decent  performance  in  sparse environments,  though  scalability  diminished  with  higher user density. A statistical approach to beam selection based on averaged RSRP was proposed for Sub-6 GHz systems [5], providing a lightweight method ideal for low-resource networks, albeit unsuitable for fast-changing channel conditions. Mathematical modeling of Yagi-Uda antenna gain patterns was  presented  in  one  study  [6]  to  support  ML-based beamforming. While accurate under controlled simulation, the model's generalization to real-world environments was limited. In article [7], comparison of feedforward (FNN), convolutional (CNN), and recurrent (RNN) neural network architectures, showing that FNNs are faster, whereas CNNs performed better with spatially distributed data. A benchmarking study [8] using Top-K accuracy and RSRP metrics confirmed that neural networks outperform heuristic  methods,  though  care  must  be  taken  to  prevent overfitting in smaller datasets. A paper on edge computing for  beam  selection  [9]  demonstrated  that  decentralized inference  at  network  edges  reduces  latency. However, practical deployment faces challenges in hardware synchronization  and  cost. A  MATLAB-based  simulation framework  [10]  was  developed  for  modelling  antenna arrays  and  testing  beam  selection  algorithms,  though  the dependency on static scenarios limited dynamic adaptability. Hybrid beamforming based on reinforcement learning  was  investigated  for  mmWave  communications [11]. The solution showed responsiveness to environmental change  but  required  long  training  times. Another  deep learning-based  beam  selection  model  [12]  demonstrated superior spatial prediction in mmWave environments, but trade-offs in interpretability and compute efficiency remained unresolved. Several addressed papers [13], [14] investigated adaptive beamforming using feedback-based techniques, achieving robust performance under user mobility. However, frequent  recalibration  introduced  delays. Another  study [15]  applied  machine  learning  for  mmWave  alignment, offering  rapid  convergence  but  with  sensitivity  to  poor channel estimation. Research on Yagi-Uda antenna arrays [16] confirmed strong azimuthal control and minimal side lobes, though limited reconfigurability was a noted constraint. Recent  advancements  include  attention-based deep neural networks [17] that dynamically weigh spatial input, improving  accuracy and interpretability. While effective,  such  models  often  demand  extensive  labelled datasets. A paper combining deep learning with localization [18] showed improved performance in urban mmWave  deployments,  although struggles with high mobility users persisted. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have also been used for beam prediction [19], successfully capturing  spatial  relationships  among  users  in  structured environments, but requiring high computational resources for  graph  construction. A  comprehensive  survey  [20] highlighted  deep  learning,  reinforcement  learning,  and hybrid  strategies  as  emerging  trends,  though  widespread deployment  is  still  constrained  by  system  complexity. Transformer-based  neural  networks  have  been  proposed for  beam  index  prediction  [21],  leveraging  long-range spatial  dependencies  to  improve  beam  accuracy. Despite their power, these models are resource-intensive. Few-shot learning [22] has also emerged as a viable option in datascarce settings, showing promising adaptation abilities with minimal training data. However, early performance often trails conventional deep learning.

text: Spatio-temporal models, particularly LSTMs [23], have been applied for predictive beamforming in high-mobility scenarios such as vehicular networks. These  models  can  forecast  beam  indices  in advance but rely on continuous time-series data. Finally, a recent  paper  [24]  proposed  joint  optimization  of  beam selection and handoff using deep reinforcement learning, achieving  seamless  connectivity  in  6G  smart  cities  but introducing complexity in multi-layer network management. From  the  literature,  it  is  evident  that  while  recent research  has  explored  AI-driven  beam  selection,  limited attention has been given to the influence of actual antenna characteristics on system performance. This paper addresses that gap by combining realistic Yagi-Uda and Short Dipole models with machine learning-based beam selection.

## V. CONCLUSION

This study integrates realistic Yagi-Uda and Short Dipole antenna models with machine learning-based beam selection to evaluate beamforming performance in 5G/6G systems. Abstract -International English language proficiency exams such as IELTS, TOEFL, and PTE assess candidates across four key  skills:  speaking,  listening,  reading,  and  writing.  Many learners struggle to find a single platform  that provides integrated,  automated,  and  detailed  feedback  across  all  these components,  particularly  in  real-time  and  without  human intervention. Existing tools often address only one skill at a time or  lack  advanced  AI-driven  analytics,  leading  to  fragmented preparation,  slower  improvement,  and  difficulty  in  tracking progress over time. ## I. INTRODUCTION

English  proficiency  is  crucial  for  academics,  jobs,  and migration today, and exams like IELTS, TOEFL, and PTE rigorously  assess  skills  in  speaking,  writing,  listening,  and reading. Speaking and writing are especially difficult, requiring both grammatical correctness and fluent, contextual communication-issues  like  pronunciation mistakes and slow speech can lower scores.

Most existing apps target only one skill or  module and lack unified real-time feedback, making learning fragmented and less effective. They rarely use advanced AI to provide deep analysis, adapt difficulty, or align scoring with official standards. To  solve these problems, an integrated  AIpowered  IELTS  prep  platform  is  proposed.  It  combines Akhila Thejaswi R Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management , Mangaluru, and Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India akhilathejaswi@gmail.com Madhukar Bhaktha Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management , Mangaluru, and Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India madhukar.bhaktha.591@gmail.com speech recognition for accurate speech-to-text, fluency scoring for grammar  and  pronunciation, and advanced models like BERT for writing analysis. Listening and reading are also adaptive, exposing users to different dialects and text types  to  simulate  real  exams.  The  platform  personalizes learning, tracks progress, offers targeted feedback, and adapts difficulty  based  on  user  errors,  using  machine  learning  for continued improvement. An interactive dashboard connects all  modules  and  aligns  with  official  IELTS  criteria  for effective practice and visible results.

Mastering  English  has  never  been  more  essential  in today's interconnected world, where global opportunities in education,  employment,  and  migration  depend  on  strong language skills. International exams such as IELTS, TOEFL, and PTE have emerged as standardized benchmarks, evaluating candidates' ability to communicate effectively and confidently  in  diverse  settings.  This  increasing  reliance  on standardized assessment  highlights the urgent need  for effective,  comprehensive  training  solutions  that  empower learners at every stage of their language journey.

## II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Liu et al. [1] introduced a novel approach to pronunciation scoring by evaluating the linguistic-acoustic similarity between the user's speech and native reference samples at the phoneme  level.  Their  system,  powered  by  a  transformerbased neural model, demonstrated high precision in assigning utterance-level scores. The work stands out for its scalability and potential application in personalized language learning apps where subtle mispronunciations often go unnoticed by traditional systems.

El Kheir [2] conducted a comprehensive review of recent pronunciation assessment technologies. They examined methods ranging from prosodic scoring to articulatory feature tracking and emphasized the growing use of self-supervised learning (SSL) models. Their findings reinforce the need for CAPT (Computer-Assisted Pronunciation Training) systems that  are  both  intelligent  and  adaptive.  They  also  stress  the importance of integrating pronunciation feedback into interactive learning systems, an idea directly aligned with the goals of the Chrome extension described in this work.

Li and Zhu [3] implemented a classroom-based pronunciation recognition tool for teaching Russian phonetics. Although not directly targeting English learners, the  methodology-employing real-time feedback, phoneme recognition,  and  visual  correction  prompts-demonstrates the cross-linguistic applicability of pronunciation assessment tools. The system contributed to increased engagement and phonetic  accuracy  among  students,  suggesting  that  such systems  could easily be adapted for English  language learning as well.

Tagami et  al. [4]  explored  stress-based  pronunciation issues and their impact on English presentation skills. Their system provided learners with feedback on misplaced stress patterns and suggested correct intonation. Stress misplacement is a subtle but common issue among secondlanguage  English  speakers,  and  the  study  highlighted  how automated feedback could improve both clarity and confidence  in  formal  speech  delivery.  Their  findings  are especially  relevant  in  professional  and  academic  contexts where presentation skills are critical.

Umezawa et al. [5] took a different route by embedding ASR-based pronunciation training into browser environments. Their Chrome-compatible tool allows users to receive pronunciation suggestions while reading online content. Rather  than  isolating  pronunciation  practice  to specific exercises, the system supports incidental learningintegrating corrections and examples within the user's natural reading  flow.  The  results  showed  that  this  non-intrusive approach was effective in helping learners reinforce proper pronunciation habits throughout daily digital activities.

Mac Yves  and  Chan  [6]  proposed  a  machine  learning model  for  evaluating  spoken  responses  in  the  context  of IELTS preparation. Their system analyzed recorded speech samples and scored them using features like fluency, pronunciation,  and  grammatical  accuracy.  The  resulting scores  closely  matched  those  given  by  human  evaluators, validating the model's reliability. Their research underscores the  growing  feasibility  of  automated  evaluation  systems tailored for high-stakes language proficiency exams.

Carrillo Patarón et al. [7] developed a mobile and desktop voice recognition application that provides users with feedback  on  their  English  pronunciation  in  real  time.  This tool aimed to simplify pronunciation correction by integrating with the user's environment, allowing for spontaneous  engagement  during  language  activities.  The authors  emphasized its  applicability  in  classroom  and  selflearning  contexts,  showing  that  learners  who  used  the  tool consistently demonstrated improved pronunciation and retention.

Together,  these  works  establish  a  solid  foundation  for building  AI-powered,  real-time  pronunciation  tools.  They highlight  emerging  trends  such  as  browser-based  learning, neural  scoring  models,  stress-aware  feedback,  and  speech embedding techniques. Our Chrome extension is designed to integrate  these  advancements  into  a  single,  accessible  tool tailored  for  English  language  learners,  particularly  those preparing for competitive exams like IELTS and TOEFL.

## III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The  proposed  system  as  shown  in  Fig.1  introduces  a comprehensive  architectural  framework  for  an  intelligent language  learning  application.  The  system  is  designed  to provide  users  with  a  multi-faceted  platform  for  improving their speaking, writing, listening, and reading skills, with a particular focus on automated feedback and progress tracking. The core of the architecture is comprised of a user interface,  several  sophisticated  AI  models,  and  a  robust feedback and reporting mechanism.

Fig. 1. Architecture Diagram for Proposed Model

<!-- image -->

The  user interacts with the  system  through  a  Web Application,  which  serves  as  the  primary  gateway  to  all functionalities. This application is the client-facing component that handles user authentication and presents the various learning modules. The User Interface (UI), a key part of the application, is designed to be intuitive and accessible, providing  distinct  sections  for  each  language  skill.  It  is through this UI that all user input, whether spoken or written, is captured and sent to the processing models.

text:
## A. Speaking Module: SPEECH RECOGNITION NEURAL NETWORK (SRNN)

The  Speaking  module  within  the  UI  is  where  the  user's spoken input is captured. This audio data is then passed to the first of the core AI models: Model 1: SRNN. This model is responsible for converting the user's speech into text. It is a fundamental component for analyzing spoken language and is a prerequisite for all subsequent fluency assessments. The SRNN itself is composed of three sub-components. - Acoustic Model
- Language Model
- Probabilistic Model

ACOUSTIC MODEL The Acoustic Model processes the raw audio signals, converting them into phonetic information. This model is trained on a vast dataset of speech recordings and their corresponding phonetic transcriptions. It is the first step  in  deciphering  the  user's  spoken  words. The  Acoustic Model is a core component of any speech recognition system, responsible for mapping raw audio waveforms into phonetic representations that the language model can interpret. In the context of an IELTS preparation platform, this model enables the  system  to  accurately  capture  the  nuances  of  a  user's spoken input-such as accent, intonation, and speech clarity-before further processing for fluency, grammar, and pronunciation scoring. A well-trained acoustic model ensures that  the  conversion  from  sound  to  phonemes  is  precise, thereby  reducing  transcription  errors  and  improving  the reliability  of  subsequent  analysis  modules  like  the  Fluency Score Algorithm. Fig. 2. Acoustic model performance

<!-- image -->

The performance graph in the Fig.2. shows the training and validation loss curves for the acoustic model over 20 epochs, serving as a key metric for evaluating learning progress. The decreasing loss values  on both training and  validation datasets  indicate  that  the  model  is  successfully  learning  to minimize  prediction  errors  without  overfitting,  as  the  gap between the curves remains stable. The orange curve represents  the  training  loss,  while  the  red  curve  represents validation  loss,  both  converging  towards  minimal  error. Overall,  these  metrics  visually  confirm  that  the  acoustic model is performing effectively, generalizing well to unseen speech data, and maintaining consistent performance across training and validation phases-ensuring dependable speechto-text conversion in real-world usage. LANGUAGE MODEL Following the acoustic model, the phonetic  data  is  processed  by  the  Language  Model. This component  predicts  the  sequence  of  words  that  are  most likely to follow one another, using probabilities derived from a large corpus of text. The language model helps to correct for ambiguities in the acoustic model's output, ensuring that the final transcribed text is grammatically and syntactically coherent. Fig. 3. Language model performance

<!-- image -->

To evaluate the Language Model Performance shown in the chart,  we  conducted  training  over  15  epochs  using  a  large corpus of text data. The model was trained to predict the next word  in  a  sequence,  with  training  perplexity  measured directly  on  the  training  dataset  at  the  end  of  each  epoch. Perplexity, a common metric for language models, quantifies how well a probability distribution predicts a sample - lower values indicate better predictive capability. During training, we applied stochastic gradient descent with adaptive learning rates and weight regularization to improve convergence and prevent  overfitting. Simultaneously,  validation  perplexity was computed on a held-out validation dataset that was not part of the training process. This helped monitor the model's ability  to  generalize  beyond  the  training  data. By  plotting both training and validation perplexity over epochs, we could observe trends such as convergence, overfitting, or underfitting. The goal was to minimize both curves and keep them  closely  aligned,  indicating  strong  performance  and generalization. The  resulting  curves  in  the  chart  provide insight  into  the  model's  learning  progression  and  stability across the training process. PROBABILISTIC  MODEL  The  third  and  final  subcomponent of the speech recognition network is the Probabilistic  Model. This  model  integrates  the  outputs  of both the acoustic and language models to produce the most probable sequence of words that the user spoke. It represents the culmination of the speech-to-text process, providing the raw  data  for  fluency  analysis.

paper_id: AI Enhanced IELTS Preparation using Custom Neural Networks
text:
The  integrated  Probabilistic Model  combined  outputs from both the Acoustic and Language  Models  using  a  Bayesian  inference  framework [13]. The acoustic likelihoods were multiplied with language model  priors  to  compute  posterior  probabilities  for  each possible word sequence. This probabilistic fusion allowed the system to balance signal-level acoustic evidence with context-driven  linguistic  constraints,  significantly  reducing recognition errors caused by noise or ambiguous pronunciations. Evaluation  was  performed  using  standard accuracy  metrics,  revealing  that  while  the  Acoustic  Model achieved 75% accuracy and the Language Model 82%, the probabilistic integration boosted accuracy to 90%, demonstrating  the  synergistic  effect  of  combining  both models in a unified probabilistic framework. Fig. 4. Performance of Speech Recognition Model

<!-- image -->

The speech recognition neural network is a model designed to  convert  spoken  audio  into  written  text  by  extracting relevant  features  (like  spectrograms)  and  processing  them through  multiple  computational  layers. Training  such  a model  happens  over  several  epochs,  where  one  epoch  is  a complete  pass  of  the  training  dataset  through  the  network. Performance is measured using Word Error Rate (WER) and Character Error Rate (CER). WER calculates the percentage of incorrectly recognized words by comparing predicted text with the correct transcription, considering substitutions, insertions,  and  deletions. CER  works  similarly  but  at  the character level, offering finer-grained insight into errors like misspellings  or  phonetic mistakes. During  training, the model's  parameters  are  optimized  using  backpropagation, which  adjusts  weights  based  on  the  difference  between predicted  and  actual  outputs,  and  gradient  descent,  which iteratively  moves  the  model  toward  minimizing  errors. A steady decline in both WER and CER, as shown in the graph, suggests effective learning without overfitting, meaning the model improves on the training data while still generalizing well to unseen speech inputs.

## Algorithm 1: Character Error Rate (CER) Calcuation using Levenshtein Distance

- [1] Check  if  the  input  'reference'  and  'hypothesis' strings are provided
- [2] If 'ignore\_case' flag is True, convert both 'reference' and  'hypothesis' to lowercase.
- [3] Set 'join\_char' as space by default.
- [4] If 'remove\_space' flag is True: Set 'join\_char' to empty string. Remove all internal spaces from both 'reference' and  'hypothesis'  by  splitting  and  rejoining  using 'join\_char'.
- [5] Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between the found 'reference' and 'hypothesis'.
- [6] Calculate Character Error Rate: CER = (edit distance) / (length of reference string).
- [7] Return CER value.

Algorithm  2: Word  Error  Rate  (WER)  calculation  using Levenshtein distance

- [1] Check if the inputs 'reference' and 'hypothesis' strings are provided.
- [2] If  'ignore\_case' flag is True, convert both 'reference' and 'hypothesis' to lowercase.
- [3] Split  both  'reference'  and  'hypothesis'  into  lists  of words using the 'delimiter' (default: space).
- [4] Compute the  Levenshtein  edit  distance  between  the reference words and hypothesis words.
- [5] Calculate Word Error Rate: WER = (edit distance) / (number of words in reference).

## B. Fluency Score Algorithm:

Once the speech is transcribed into text, it is passed to the Fluency  Score  Algorithm.  This  component  is  a  critical innovation of the system, designed to provide detailed feedback on the user's spoken fluency. The algorithm analyzes several key metrics to provide a comprehensive assessment. Fluency Score is determined by the following methods.

- Speaking Rate
- Grammar and sentence structure
- Pronunciation Accuracy

Speaking  Rate  The  first  metric  assessed  by  the  fluency algorithm is the Speaking Rate .  This component measures the number of words spoken per minute and identifies pauses or hesitations. A consistent and appropriate speaking rate is a key  indicator of fluency, and  this analysis provides a quantitative measure for the user.

Grammar and Sentence Structure Errors Another crucial part of the fluency algorithm is the analysis of Grammar and Sentence Structure. This component checks the transcribed text for grammatical errors, such as subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, and proper punctuation. It also evaluates the complexity and coherence of the sentence structures used by the user.

Fig. 5. Grammar and Sentence errors

<!-- image -->

Pronunciation  Accuracy  Finally,  the  fluency  algorithm evaluates Pronunciation Accuracy. This component compares the phonetic output from the acoustic model with a standard pronunciation  model.  It  identifies  specific  sounds  or  words that  the  user  mispronounced and provides  feedback to  help them correct these errors.

Fig. 6. Pronounciation Accuracy

text:
## C. Writing Module - Bidirectional Encoder Representation from Transformers (BERT)

BERT model is used to provide deeper linguistic analysis, especially  for  written  input.  BERT  is  a  powerful  language model  trained  to  understand  the  context  of  words  in  a sentence. It consists of an Encoder, which processes the input text,  and  an  Embedding  layer,  which  converts  words  into dense  vector  representations.  These  embeddings  capture semantic  meaning  and  are  then  processed  by  the  Network Layer  to  perform  tasks  such  as  grammar  and  coherence scoring.

Fig. 7. BERT Architecture

<!-- image -->

The BERT model architecture in the language app starts with the user's input, like written or transcribed text. This text is first converted into numerical embeddings, where each word is  represented  as  a  vector  to  capture  meaning  and  context. These  embeddings  go  through  multiple  encoder  layers, allowing  BERT  to  analyze  each  word  by  considering  the whole sentence for deeper understanding.

Next,  the  network  layer  uses  this  context-rich  output  to assess grammar, coherence, and content quality, generating an overall score and feedback for the user. Scores from both the BERT model and the fluency algorithm are combined into a Grammar/Coherence Score, providing a clear measure of language proficiency and detailed feedback for improvement.

The results from both the fluency algorithm and the BERT model are  synthesized  to  produce  a  Grammar  /  Coherence Score.  This  score  is  a  central  feedback  mechanism  that provides  a  numerical  and  qualitative  rating  of  the  user's language proficiency. It is displayed to the user and is a key metric  for  tracking  progress  over  time.  The  system  also generates a Feedback report, which provides detailed explanations for the scores, highlighting specific errors and suggesting improvements.

## D. Listening Module -AUDIO NARRATION OF COMPREHENSION PASSAGES ALONG WITH COMPREHENSION QUIZ FOR EVALUATION

A key feature of the application is the Listening module. This  component  is  designed  to  challenge  and  improve  the user's  auditory  comprehension  by  providing  audio  content with  varying  narration speed  and  dialect.  This  ensures exposure to a wide range of real-world language situations.

Following the audio content, the system presents users with a series of comprehension quiz questions. The answers to these questions are processed to assess the user's understanding and contribute to their overall performance metrics.

Fig. 8. Listening comprehension accuracy by dialect

<!-- image -->

## E. Reading Module - DISPLAY TEXT COMPREHENSION PASSAGES UNDER TIMER AND COMPREHENSION QUIZ FOR EVALUATION.

Similarly,  the  Reading  module  is  designed  to  enhance textual  comprehension.  The  system  provides  users  with written  materials,  the  difficulty  of  which  is  dynamically adjusted based on their performance. These texts are followed by a set of comprehension quiz questions, which are used to evaluate the user's understanding of the provided content. The results of these quizzes, along with the performance from the listening  module,  are  integrated  into  the  system's  overall progress tracking.

text:
## IV. CONCLUSION

Based  on  the  comprehensive  architectural  framework presented,  this  system  offers  a  robust  and  highly  effective platform for preparing for a language proficiency exam like the IELTS. By directly addressing the core skills tested in all four sections of the exam, the application provides a targeted and data-driven approach to language preparation.

For  the  IELTS  Speaking  test,  the  system  offers  an unparalleled  advantage.  The  SPEECH  RECOGNITION NEURAL  NETWORK  and  the  Fluency  Score  Algorithm directly  assess  the  four  key  scoring  criteria  of  the  exam: Fluency  and  Coherence,  Lexical  Resource,  Grammatical Range  and  Accuracy,  and  Pronunciation.  The  system's analysis of Speaking Rate, Grammar and Sentence Structure, and  Pronunciation  Accuracy  provides  users  with  specific, automated feedback on each of these areas, something that is typically only available through a human tutor. This allows test-takers to practice and refine their speaking skills repeatedly  and  receive  instant,  objective  analysis,  which  is invaluable for improving performance.

In  preparation  for  the  IELTS  Writing  test,  the  BERT model  serves  as  a  powerful  analytical  tool.  The  model's ability  to  perform  deeper  linguistic  analysis  and  provide  a Grammar  /  Coherence  Score  directly  maps  to  the  IELTS scoring criteria for Task  Achievement, Coherence  and Cohesion, and Grammatical Range and Accuracy. Users can write their responses for both Task 1 and Task 2 and receive automated  feedback  on  the  structural  integrity of their sentences,  the  logical  flow  of  their  ideas,  and  grammatical correctness.  This  feedback  mechanism  is  a  crucial  tool  for refining a user's writing style and ensuring they can construct well-formed, coherent essays and reports.

The Listening section of the application provides highly specific  and  effective  training  for  the  IELTS  Listening  est. The  deliberate  use  of  audio  content  with  varying  speed narration  and  dialects  is  a  direct  simulation  of  the  exam environment, which exposes candidates to a range of accents (e.g., British, Australian, American)  and  conversational speeds.  The  comprehension quiz questions that follow this content are a perfect parallel to the question types found in the  exam,  allowing  users  to  practice  their  listening  skills under realistic conditions and accurately gauge their comprehension.

Finally, the Reading section, with its use of paragraphs followed  by  comprehension  quiz  questions,  is  designed  to mirror the structure of the IELTS Reading test. The system's ability to provide a variety of texts and test comprehension prepares users to handle the diverse range of text types and question  formats  they  will  encounter  on  the  exam.  The collective  feedback  from  all  modules,  synthesized  in  the Progress Report, allows users to monitor their improvement over  time  and  identify  specific  weaknesses.  This  targeted approach to practice and progress tracking makes the system an ideal self-guided tool for any candidate aiming to achieve a high score in the IELTS exam

## AI-Powered Blockchain-Backed System for Cross-Media Deepfake and Forgery Detection

## Swathi N Pai

Mangaluru, India swathipaii2004@gmail.com

## Sharanya S Parol

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India

sharanyasparol@gmail.com

## Bavith L Suvarna

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India suvarnabavith@gmail.com

Abstract -The amount of deepfake content generated by advanced deep learning models is rising, posing a threat to cybersecurity and digital authenticity. Deepfakes can now fool both human perception and traditional detection systems by manipulating images, sound, video, and signatures. To tackle this challenge,this paper introduces DeepLock, a unified artificial intelligence-powered framework that can recognize deepfake content in four essential modalities: images, audio, video, and handwritten signatures. The system employs a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) for audio deepfakes based on Log-Mel spectogram features, a specially built ExceptionNet for image forgery detection, and a ResNet18 model optimized for both video frame analysis and signature verification, using different architectures for each modality. Experimental results on benchmark datasets show how accurate and generalizable DeepLock is, which makes it appropriate for forensic applications, identity verification, and real-time content validation.

Index Terms -Deepfake Detection, Artificial Intelligence, ExceptionNet, CRNN, ResNet-18, Signature Forgery, Audio Forensics, Video Frame Analysis, Image Forgery, Log-mel spectogram, Multimodal Classification, Digital Security.

## I. Introduction

It becomes more challenging to distinguish deepfakes from authentic content because they are extremely lifelike synthetic media produced using sophisticated deep learning techniques. These forgeries come in a variety of forms, such as altered videos [9], manipulated images, phony audio [3], and even fake handwritten signatures. Deepfakes present significant risks, including false information, identity theft, and digital impersonation, despite their potential in domains like virtual communication and accessibility [21][17]. Strong generative models like GANs have rendered conventional detection techniques based on watermarking, manually created features, or texture analysis [7] useless. Additionally, the majority of studies concentrate on a single modality,

## Riya R

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India riyar2004oct@gmail.com

## Mustafa Basthikodi

Dept. of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management Mangaluru, India mbasthik@gmail.com

which leaves a gap in multimodal detection where crossmedia manipulation takes place [16].

This paper presents DeepLock, a unified artificial intelligence system that can identify deepfakes in four important modalities: audio, video, images, and signatures by hand. It uses a CNN called ExceptionNet to detect subtle image manipulations, a CRNN that uses Log-mel spectogram features to detect audio forgeries [17], and a refined ResNet-18 to detect both video and signature forgeries. As deepfake threats change, DeepLock provides a scalable solution to bolster digital trust and content integrity by emphasizing cross-modal consistency, real-time flexibility, and practical deployment in forensics, media authentication, and identity protection.

text:
## II. Related Work

The development of encoder-decoder architectures and generative adversarial networks (GANs) has greatly increased the production of deepfake media in a variety of formats. Image and video-based forgery was made possible by early works such as Face2Face [1] and Deep Video Portraits [5], which allowed for real-time facial reenactment using RGB inputs. Advanced models like CycleGAN [2] and StyleGAN [6][27] quickly followed, making detection even more difficult by enabling high-fidelity image synthesis and translation. Using extensive datasets such as FaceForensics and FaceForensics++, researchers investigated CNN-based classification methods in order to address this [4][15]. Detection techniques included detecting visual artifacts and warping inconsistencies [7][21], analyzing motion abnormalities using optical flow [10], and even using physiological signals like blood flow and heart rate [8][14] to verify authenticity.

Advances in voice cloning and text-to-speech (TTS) have made deepfakes more realistic in the audio domain. Suwa- janakorn et al. [3] demonstrated that audio alone could produce synchronized facial movements, whereas models such as VoiceGuard [17] and FakeCatcher [8] used spectral and biological signal analysis. Since then, detection methods have advanced to include attention-fusion mechanisms [13], mel-spectrogram classification with residual CNNs [22], and spectrogram-based CRNNs. The detection of signature forgeries has also been revived by AI, as deep models such as SigNet [24], dynamic RNNs [25], and GAN-generated samples [27] have supplanted conventional geometric techniques. Additionally, hybrid systems with fuzzy logic integration [26], graph convolutional networks [29][14], and blockchain-based signature validation systems [28] have surfaced. Nevertheless, the majority of approaches continue to be unimodal, concentrating on a single media type, making systems susceptible to multi-domain forgeries, like altered audio in phony videos or falsified signatures in scanned documents. This restriction presents a significant obstacle to real-world verification in fields like identity authentication, media forensics, and legal proceedings that demand crossmodal consistency.

## III. Methodology

The proposed system uses a multi-modal deepfake detection method for four different kinds of media: handwritten signatures, videos, audio, and images. Since each modality is forged using fundamentally different manipulation techniques and exhibits unique artifacts, a single universal model cannot reliably detect deepfakes across all formats. Therefore, four specialized pipelines are designed and integrated using state-of-the-art deep learning models and modalityspecific preprocessing strategies. CNNs trained to differentiate between real and synthetic faces analyze face regions that have been extracted and normalized for image-based detection. Frame-by-frame analysis and temporal feature extraction are added to this pipeline for video in order to identify minute motion irregularities created during video editing.

In order to identify audio deepfakes, raw audio is converted into spectrograms, and anomalies such as irregular timing and frequency patterns are captured using CNN or RNN models. CNN-based classification using real and forged signature datasets is the next step in the handwritten signature forgery detection process, which includes preprocessing steps like resizing, binarization, and edge detection. A blockchain layer is incorporated to guarantee data verifiability and integrity, offering tamper-proof validation that is especially useful for legal and journalistic use cases. Five components make up the overall methodology: (A) image-based detection, (B) video-based detection, (C) audiobased detection, (D) signature forgery detection, and (E) blockchain integration. The models, methods, and tools used are described in detail in each section.

text:
## A. Image-Based Deepfake Detection

The goal of the image-based detection module is to detect faked facial images produced by face-swapping, autoencoders, and GANs. In preprocessing, input images are resized to 299×299 pixels, normalized, and MTCNN is used to extract aligned facial regions. An InceptionV3 model is used to refine these face crops through transfer learning. The classification layers of InceptionV3, which were initially trained on ImageNet, are swapped out for a custom head that includes a Global Average Pooling layer, Dropout, and a Dense layer with sigmoid activation for binary classification (real vs. fake).

Fig. 1. Workflow Diagram for Multi-Modal Deepfake and Forgery Detection Using AI and Blockchain Integration.

<!-- image -->

The model is trained using a variety of data augmentation techniques, such as blurring, noise, rotation, flipping, and contrast variations, in order to improve generalization. The dataset comes from a variety of sources, including GANgenerated images, FaceForensics++, and Celeb-DF. The loss function, binary cross-entropy, is optimized using an adaptive learning rate scheduler and the Adam optimizer. Performance is consistently high when evaluated on a validation set using metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, F1score, and ROC-AUC. The module is an essential component of the entire detection system since it successfully detects subtle forgery artifacts by utilizing InceptionV3's potent feature extraction. Hyperparameters such as the learning rate, batch size, and dropout ratio were tuned empirically using validation performance to avoid overfitting on high-quality synthetic samples. The fixed input size of 299×299 and the choice of InceptionV3 were retained after comparative trials showed a favorable balance between computational cost and detection accuracy.

Table I outlines the preprocessing steps applied to standardize the input images and improve model accuracy. The augmentation techniques were especially helpful in reducing overfitting and enhancing the model's ability to generalize across different fake generation methods and image qualities.

TABLE I DATA PREPROCESSING TECHNIQUES APPLIED

|----------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Image Resizing       | All input images were resized to 299×299 pixels to ensure consistency across the dataset.                                 |
| Grayscale Conversion | Converted images to grayscale to reduce com- putational complexity and focus on texture features.                         |
| Normalization        | Pixel values were scaled to the range [0,1] to stabilize and speed up model convergence.                                  |

| Data Splitting       | Dataset was split into training (10k real + 10k fake), validation (2k real + 2k fake), and test sets (1k real + 1k fake). |
| Data Augmentation    | Applied transformations like flipping, rotation, noise injection, and brightness changes to im- prove generalization.     |

## B. Video-Based Deepfake Detection

In order to preserve temporal coverage and minimize redundancy, the suggested video deepfake detection technique employs a frame-based ResNet-18 CNN, extracting every tenth frame from each video. To enhance generalization across distortions, each frame is resized to 224×224 pixels, normalized using ImageNet statistics, and enhanced with methods like rotation, brightness jitter, and horizontal flipping.

ResNet-18 was selected because it strikes a balance between computational efficiency and depth, with residual connections preventing vanishing gradients. Adam and a learning rate scheduler are used to optimize the model, which is trained using weighted binary cross-entropy to address class imbalance. The detection of manipulated content is made efficient and scalable by using majority voting across framelevel predictions to achieve final video classification.The frame sampling interval, input resolution, and network depth were chosen after exploratory trials showed that denser sampling or deeper backbones increased latency without meaningful gains in accuracy. Weighted loss coefficients, batch size, and scheduler parameters were finalized based on validation stability to avoid overfitting to artifact-dense segments. Strong gen- eralization was supported by its varied demographics and expressions.

## C. Audio-Based Deepfake Detection

This study employs a CRNN architecture with Log-mel spectograms as input features is used to detect deepfake audio. After cleaning the audio with preprocessing techniques like amplitude normalization, spectral gating, and silence trimming, the pipeline extracts Log-mel spectogram and adds delta and delta-delta features. Convolutional layers for learning acoustic features and GRUs for capturing temporal patterns are combined in the CRNN. Data augmentation methods from the MUSAN dataset, such as pitch shifting, time stretching, and noise injection, are used during training to replicate real-world circumstances and increase robustness.

The Adam optimizer with cross-entropy loss, early stopping, and learning rate scheduling are used to train the model. The dataset-which includes samples from WaveFake and ASVspoof 2019-is divided into training (100,800), validation (21,600), and testing (21,600) sets, with a balance between real and fake audio, as indicated in Table IV. The training set enables learning, the validation set supports tuning and monitoring, and the test set evaluates generalization on unseen data, ensuring a structured and effective development pipeline.Log-mel spectogram size, GRU units, and kernel dimensions were tuned through validation to preserve prosodic and spectral cues lost in synthetic speech. Training hyperparameters such as learning rate, early-stopping patience, and augmentation strength were fixed after observing convergence to avoid overfitting to artificial noise rather than actual deepfake traits. text:
## D. Signature-Based Deepfake Detection

Because of its lightweight design and residual connections, which make it perfect for biometric image classification, a CNN based on the ResNet-18 architecture was used to detect forged handwritten signatures. The CEDAR Signature Dataset, which contains both authentic and fake signatures, was used to train the model. In order to improve generalization and address class imbalance, preprocessing included resizing images to 224×224 pixels, converting them to grayscale, normalizing pixel values, and using data augmentation techniques like rotation, shear, and shifting.

By starting the model with pre-trained ImageNet weights and optimizing the last layers for binary classification, transfer learning was used. Class probabilities for authentic and counterfeit signatures were obtained through a Softmax activation in the last dense layer. Metrics like accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score were used to assess the model, and the results showed that it had high detection accuracy and strong generalization. These findings support the method's potential for practical uses in document authentication and signature verification.Input size, augmentation range, and the choice of ResNet-18 depth were fixed after validation trials showed a stable trade-off between speed and accuracy. Hyperparameters such as learning rate and dropout were tuned to reduce overfitting on visually similar forged signatures.

## E. Blockchain Integration for Tamper-Proof Validation

## Need for Blockchain Integration

The integration of blockchain technology is a must for the deepfake detection framework that is not only able to provide security but also the transparency and reliability of the detection results. One of the most important things is to keep the digital forensic evidence intact and authentic for the law enforcement and judiciary sectors because if there is any unauthorized modification, the whole legal process might be put at risk.Just like any other centralized databases, those that are being used to store the evidence in different places are highly exposed to tampering, unauthorized access, and single-point failures and thus, they are not very safe.

Conversely, with the help of a decentralized and immutable ledger, blockchain records the detection results in a secure manner together with the vital data like the model identifier, timestamp, and media hash. Additionally, it facilitates a verifiable chain of custody for the confirmation of the forensic procedure, hence, the deepfake detection system being able to gain more trust, transparency, and traceability features and as a result, being appropriate for use in digital forensics and legal authentication.

## Blockchain-Based Implementation

The integration of blockchain technology is an essential component of the proposed system to ensure stability, verifiability, and transparency of detection records. Each detection result is securely logged in a real-time, tamper-resistant ledger of a private Ethereum blockchain implemented using Ganache. This decentralized architecture prevents unauthorized alterations and enhances the forensic trustworthiness and traceability of digital evidence. The media file and its detection result are hashed using the SHA-256 algorithm, generating a unique digital fingerprint for each audio, video, image, or text input. Even minor modifications produce a distinctly different hash. This fingerprint is combined with the model's classification output and confidence score to create a verification token that permanently links the detection result to the analyzed media in immutable storage.

Solidity-based smart contracts in the Ganache environment execute the operations and record the resultant data on the blockchain. Each transaction includes the media hash, detection label, model identifier, and timestamp, all stored as immutable records that cannot be altered or deleted. To enhance scalability, only essential metadata and hashes are stored on-chain.

During verification, the media hash is compared with blockchain records. If a match is found, the stored detection result is retrieved; otherwise, the AI model processes the media and records the new result. This ensures authenticity, integrity, and tamper-resistant detection outcomes suitable for forensic evidence and legal validation.

## IV. Results and Experimentation

The deepfake detection model was implemented with Python 3.10 and PyTorch, and tested on four main modalities-image, video, audio, and signature. All employed custom deep learning architectures optimized for each media type, and were trained separately on public datasets. Data were partitioned in a 70:15:15 ratio for training, validation, and testing. Early stopping and on-the-fly data augmentations were utilized to improve generalization.

## F. Image-Based Deepfake Detection

For image-based deepfake detection, a pre-trained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was applied to preprocessed grayscale face images obtained from the FaceForensics++ and Celeb-DF datasets. The images were resized to 224×224 pixels, normalized, and augmented using flipping, rotation, brightness adjustment, and Gaussian noise to enhance robustness under diverse lighting and pose conditions. Training and validation performance, shown in Fig. 3, indicates smooth convergence and consistent accuracy across all splits, reflecting strong generalization.

Fig. 3. Training, validation, and test accuracy for image deepfake detection.

<!-- image -->

The accuracies during training, validation, and testing were in close agreement across epochs, indicating minimal overfitting. The stable validation curve also suggests that the applied augmentations effectively improved model generalization to real-world deepfake variations.

## G. Video-based Deepfake Detection

Video deepfake detection was implemented using a hybrid CNN-LSTM model that captures both spatial and temporal inconsistencies. Individual frames were processed through a CNN to extract spatial embeddings, followed by an LSTM to learn sequential dependencies. This approach enabled detection of manipulation cues such as frame inconsistency, unnatural facial expressions, and lip-sync mismatches. Framelevel and sequence-level augmentations were applied to increase variability. The model's classification performance is shown in Fig. 4, which presents high accuracy and low false detection rates, demonstrating reliability for real-world deployment.

Fig. 4. Confusion matrix for the video deepfake detection model, showing true vs. predicted labels.

<!-- image -->

The confusion matrix reveals a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing authentic and manipulated videos. The strong diagonal dominance indicates that most predictions were correct, with minimal false positives and negatives. These few misclassifications likely resulted from subtle temporal manipulations or compression artifacts. The hybrid CNN-LSTM model combines spatial and temporal features, highlighting the value of sequence modeling in video-based deepfake detection.

## H. Audio-based Deepfake Detection

The proposed audio deepfake detection model employs a Convolutional Recurrent Neural Network (CRNN) that integrates convolutional layers for spectral feature extraction with recurrent layers for temporal dependency modeling. Log-Mel spectrograms were used as input features after resampling the audio for consistency. To improve robustness, on-the-fly augmentations such as time-stretching, pitchshifting, and background noise mixing (from the MUSAN dataset) were applied during training. These augmentations improved the model's generalization to diverse acoustic conditions. The Precision-Recall (PR) curve in Fig. 5 illustrates the model's strong balance between precision and recall.

Fig. 5. Precision-Recall curve of the audio deepfake detection model, demonstrating high detection performance across different decision thresholds.

<!-- image -->

The model successfully separates real audio from deepfakes while keeping false-alarm and miss rates low, as shown by the Precision-Recall curve remaining close to the top-right region. Additionally, it illustrates how recall and precision change with different decision thresholds, demonstrating the model's ability to withstand class imbalance.

## I. Signature Forgery Detection

Signature forgery detection was carried out using a ResNet18 CNN trained on grayscale images from datasets such as CEDAR and GPDS. The input signatures were resized to 220×155 pixels and augmented with shearing, noise addition, and horizontal stretching to mimic natural writing variability. The t-SNE visualization in Fig. 6 shows clear feature-space separation between real and forged signatures.

Fig. 6. t-SNE visualization depicting the feature separation between genuine and forged signatures. The plot highlights how well the model differentiates between the two classes.

<!-- image -->

Training and validation accuracies converged with minimal difference, confirming the ResNet-18 model's ability to capture discriminative writing patterns despite intra-class variation.
