The video model exhibited slightly lower recall, possibly due to minor inconsistencies in frame-level data.

## K. Blockchain

The blockchain module was experimentally tested through a private Ethereum network built with Ganache and the module was evaluated for its effectiveness, reliability, and forensic credibility. After every AI-generated detection result was converted into a SHA-256 cryptographic hash, a Solidity smart contract stored the data on the blockchain. The blockchain recorded all transactions successfully without any data loss or inconsistencies, thus it was the integrity of on-chain storage that was verified. Different media samples were forcibly changed to test tamper resistance. In fact, each manipulation was found to be correct because the recalculated hashes did not match the existing blockchain entries, thus 100

As per the performance analysis, the system delay is almost negligible as the average transaction execution and block confirmation times were between 1 and 2 seconds. The hybrid storage method that keeps large media files off-chain and only stores hashes and metadata on-chain has proven to be both scalable and efficient. Such outcomes show that the use of blockchain has a significant positive impact on nonrepudiation, auditability, and forensic traceability without affecting real-time detection performance at all. Hence, the blockchain component elevates the deepfake detection system not only in terms of reliability but also as a source of evidence.

## V. Discussion

The legitimacy and dependability of digital communications are seriously threatened by the growing prevalence of deepfake media, especially in the fields of identity verification, forensics, and journalism. The proposed modular multimodal deepfake detection framework integrates specialized deep learning models, including CNN-LSTM for spatiotemporal video analysis, CNN for image forgery detection, ResNet-18 for signature forgery via pressure and stroke dynamics, and CRNN with log-mel spectrograms for audio anomaly detection. By extracting fine-grained spatial and temporal features for every modality, this architecture improves performance. However, generalization to real-world scenarios involving noise, compression, and linguistic variation is limited by the small diversity of datasets (FaceForensics++, WaveFake, ASVspoof2019, and CEDAR). Additionally, the cross-modal reasoning needed to identify synchronized multimodal forgeries is absent from the modular design. To ensure global applicability, future developments should concentrate on decision-level fusion, collaborative multimodal learning, model compression, and shared inference pipelines for real-time efficiency. Additionally, attention-based visualization should be used to improve explainability, and more diverse, multilingual, real-world datasets should be included.

## VI. Conclusion

Reliable and scalable deepfake detection systems are now essential as synthetic media makes it harder to distinguish between authentic and fraudulent content. This issue is addressed by DeepLock, a unified multimodal framework that uses architecture-specific models like ExceptionNet for images, CRNN for audio, and ResNet-18 for both video and signature verification to detect forgeries across audio, video, images, and handwritten signatures. Across a variety of modalities, its modular yet integrated design guarantees precise, effective, and flexible detection while facilitating explainability and practical implementation. DeepLock shows great promise for use in digital forensics, identity verification, and media authentication by focusing on crossmodal detection to identify intricate, multimodal forgeries that are frequently overlooked by unimodal systems. To further increase its dependability in security-critical settings, future research will concentrate on improving adversarial robustness, interpretability, and real-time performance.

## AI-Powered Detection of Potato Leaf Diseases Using Deep Neural Networks

Alapan Ghosh ∗ , N. D. Adesh ∗ , Raghavendra S ∗ , and Devidas Bhat †

∗ Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal-576104, India

† Department of Information Science, NMAMIT, NITTE

Email: alapanghosh3@gmail.com, adesh.nd@manipal.edu, raghavendra.s@manipal.edu, devidasbhat@nitte.edu.in

Abstract -The potato (Solanum tuberosum), a crop essential to global food security, faces significant yield threats from diseases like Early and Late Blight. Traditional diagnosis via visual inspection is often inefficient and subjective, delaying necessary action. To overcome these limitations, this study evaluates six deep learning architectures for the automated identification of potato leaf diseases from images. A custom-built Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) is a benchmark against five prominent pre-trained models using transfer learning and subsequently investigates the impact of fine-tuning the top-performing architecture, EfficientNetB0. Experiments on the public PlantVillage dataset show that the fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 delivers a superior accuracy of 99.22%. A real-world test case provides strong support for this quantitative result, demonstrating the fine-tuned model's ability to correct a misclassification made by its nonfine-tuned counterpart. The proposed work provides a clear benchmark for model selection and confirms that a strategic fine-tuning process is a critical step for achieving robust, stateof-the-art performance in agricultural computer vision and this research also contributes to SDG 9 by developing an innovative and robust deep learning framework to enhance the technological capabilities of the agricultural industry.

Index Terms -Deep Learning, Computer Vision, Plant Disease Detection, Transfer Learning, Fine-Tuning, EfficientNet, Innovation.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Potato ( Solanum tuberosum) is a central component of the global food system, but crop sustainability faces a constant threat from diseases such as Early Blight (Alternaria solani) and Late Blight (Phytophthora infestans), which can rapidly destroy leaves, leading to significant yield reduction and economic losses [1]. Traditionally, the first line of defense is visual inspection by agricultural specialists, a procedure often prone to bias, time-consuming, and not easily scalable, resulting in delayed diagnoses and treatment [2].

The emergence of deep learning has fundamentally transformed the landscape of computer vision with computeraided image inspection, where Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have emerged as the dominant method for nearly all computer vision tasks [3].

In this work, a rigorous comparative study is conducted to determine an optimal deep learning framework for automatically categorizing potato leaf diseases. A performance baseline is established with a custom-designed CNN and systematically

979-8-3315-7364-5/25/$31.00 ©2025 IEEE

evaluate it against five prominent pre-trained architectures: VGG16 [4], ResNet50, MobileNetV2, DenseNet121, and EfficientNetB0 [5]. The core of this investigation assesses the performance differential between using these architectures as fixed feature extractors (transfer learning) and adapting their weights to the specific domain of plant pathology (fine-tuning). This is demonstrated by isolating the top-performing model, EfficientNetB0, and conducting a second training phase to fine-tune its parameters.

The principal contributions of this paper are threefold: 1) A direct, controlled performance benchmark of six deep learning models on the public PlantVillage dataset [6] is provided; 2) The performance gains achieved by fine-tuning a state-of-theart architecture for this specific task are empirically quantified; and 3) A qualitative case study from a practical application is presented that validates the higher reliability of the fine-tuned model's diagnoses when applied to practical examples.

The remainder of this document is structured as follows: a review of prior research on potato disease identification using artificial intelligence is presented in Section II, and Section III presents the dataset and model design. Section IV specifies the experimental setup and its conditions. The findings and analysis are addressed in Section V and Section VI briefs the concluding thoughts.

## II. RELATED WORK

Deep learning, particularly regarding Convolutional Neural Networks, is one of the active research for plant pathology. It automates feature extraction of visual information to detect plant diseases, with superior performance compared to traditional methods using hand-crafted features [7].

The work by Mohanty et al. highlighted the potential of this method by applying a GoogLeNet model on the PlantVillage dataset [8] for the detection of 26 different diseases affecting 14 crop varieties, in turn recording accuracy as high as 99.35% and setting a concrete base for further studies [9]. For potato diseases, some subsequent works are Tiwari et al. [10], with 97.8%, who used VGG19 as its base network, and Mahum et al. [11], which looked into deeper models such as DenseNet201, with an accuracy of 97.2%. These works confirm their suitability.

While many studies have focused on one architecture, the comparative works such as Chakraborty et al. [12] have benchmarked models including VGG16, VGG19, MobileNet, and ResNet50, concluding that in that specific experimental setup, the best performance was by VGG16. Further research has involved even more advanced techniques; for example, a recent study utilized a feature fusion ensemble of VGG16 and ResNet-50 to improve classification accuracy beyond that of the individual models [13]. Another key focus has been lightweight models, with Picon et al. [14] demonstrating a customized MobileNet for on-device deployment, emphasizing the performance-cost balance.

Fig. 1. Sample of data augmentation applied to a potato leaf image.

<!-- image -->

However, one important challenge, as noted by Ferentinos, is the gap in performance from 'lab-to-field' for models that have been trained on clean datasets such as PlantVillage [8] [15]. Furthermore, the particular added value of fine-tuning compared with standard transfer learning is often not well investigated. Recent work by Ali et al. [16] on apple leaves has shown, however, that a fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 significantly outperformed its standard version, reaching 99.78% accuracy. This result points to fine-tuning as a crucial variable in obtaining robust state-of-the-art results [17].

With these insights in mind, the present work provides a comparative study that includes fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 and takes a close look at the improvements from fine-tuning for better benchmarking in potato disease management.

## III. METHODOLOGY

This section of the paper describes the dataset characteristics, the design of the models evaluated, and the training approaches used in this work.

## A. Dataset and Preprocessing

These experiments utilized images from the publicly available PlantVillage dataset [8] supplemented with extra images of healthy leaves to make the overall collection more balanced. This produces a final dataset of 2,864 images of potato leaves. There are three classes: Potato Early Blight (1000 images), Potato Late Blight (1000 images), and Potato Healthy (964 images). This is a slightly imbalanced dataset with the 'Healthy' class being the minority class compared to the two disease classes. For these experiments, the complete image set was divided into training (80%), validation (10%), and test sets (10%). All the images within the dataset were resized to the standard dimension 256 x 256 pixels -a standard input size for many pre-trained architectures such as those in this work, where computational efficiency must be balanced against retaining relevant visual detail - and normalised into the [0, 1] range of pixel values. In an effort to boost the models' generalization performance and to address the class imbalance, the training data was subjected to dynamic data augmentation in real-time(on-the-fly). This technique does not permanently add to the overall count of images in the dataset; instead, it generates modified versions of the training images dynamically in memory for each training epoch. This process, which included random horizontal and vertical flips (each with 50% probability) and random rotations (within a range of 15 ± degrees), effectively exposes the model to a much larger and more varied set of training examples without altering the original dataset size [18]. Fig. 1 shows a sample image from the dataset, as well as an example of this augmentation process.

## B. Model Architectures

An evaluation of six separate CNN-based architectures was conducted.

1) Custom CNN: A baseline sequential CNN was designed from scratch. Its design includes six convolutional layers using 3 x 3 kernels and ReLU activation, with a max-pooling operation following each layer. The network concludes with a flatten layer and two dense layers, with the final output layer using a softmax activation function.

2) Pre-trained Architectures: Five pre-trained models were employed: VGG16 [4], ResNet50 [19], MobileNetV2 [20], DenseNet121 [21], and EfficientNetB0 [5]. For these models, a transfer learning approach was used, as illustrated in Fig. 2. The convolutional base of each model was pre-trained on ImageNet. It was instantiated without its top classification layer, and its weights were frozen. To prevent the pre-trained layers from being updated during training, their weights were frozen, thereby preserving the rich and generalized visual features learned from the massive ImageNet dataset. A new trainable classification head was added, consisting of a Global Average Pooling 2D (GAP) layer, a Dropout layer for regularization, and a final Dense layer with softmax activation. During this initial training phase, only the weights of this new head were updated.

Fig. 2. Architecture of the transfer learning pipeline used in this study.

<!-- image -->

## C. Transfer Learning and Fine-Tuning Strategy

The primary training methodology for the pre-trained models was a two-stage process, which is visualized in Fig. 3.

Fig. 3. Visualization of model performance during training and fine-tuning.

<!-- image -->

- 1) Transfer Learning Phase: In the initial phase (Epochs 1-20), the convolutional base of each pre-trained model was frozen. During this stage, the training process was limited exclusively to updating the weights of the newly added classification head. This phase enables the model to learn to map the generalized characteristics from the base to the specific potato disease classes.
- 2) Fine-Tuning Phase: For the top-performing model, EfficientNetB0, a second phase was implemented (Epochs 2130). The entire base model was unfrozen, and the model was re-compiled with a very low learning rate ( 1 × 10 -5 ). Training was then continued for an additional 10 epochs. This step enables the model to make small, precise adjustments to the learned feature representations, specializing them in the nuanced visual characteristics of potato leaves [22].

## V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

This section provides a thorough comparison of the seven experimental setups. Specifically, the discussion will be done in three stages: first, a multifaceted quantitative comparison; second, an in-depth analysis of the best performing model; and third, a qualitative case study to emphasize practical relevance.

## A. Quantitative Performance Comparison

All the models were carefully assessed in terms of their performance using the unseen test dataset. The comparison in Table II takes into account not just key classification metrics but also the approach for feature extraction, model complexity, and computational cost.

This observation has yielded a number of lessons. Firstly, all the models performed excellently, with various test accuracies above 97% according to Hossain et al. [27]. The Precision, Recall, and F1-Scores close to perfection of most models show high balances between true disease cases and not raising unnecessary alarms. Among these, ResNet50 achieved the highest raw accuracy, a result well aligned with observations from other studies on agriculture where residual architectures have been particularly effective [28].

A more nuanced picture, however, comes from multiple metrics. MobileNetV2 and the standard EfficientNetB0 - both designed for efficiency - showed sharply faster training times. The performance of MobileNetV2 is most relevant to the potential deployment on mobile devices where computational resources would be thin [20]. The most important observation is the impact of training strategy, starkly visible in the 'Feature Extraction' column. Using fixed 'ImageNet Pre-trained' features performed well, but allowing the model to adapt these into 'Fine-Tuned Features' elevated the performance of EfficientNetB0 to the most robust and reliable overall [24].

## C. Qualitative Analysis: A Practical Case Study

A prototype diagnostic application was developed to translate these quantitative metrics into a real-world context and validate the practical utility of the models. This tool features a simple Graphical User Interface (GUI) that permits a user to upload a potato leaf image. Upon upload, the application loads the saved, pre-trained model weights, preprocesses the input image to match the required 256 x 256 format, and feeds it to the model to generate a real-time prediction of the disease class and a corresponding confidence score. Using this application, a qualitative analysis was conducted. While the standard EfficientNetB0 model performed exceptionally well on the curated test set as shown in Fig. 6, its generalization capabilities were limited when faced with novel data. This limitation is demonstrated in a compelling case study shown in Fig. 7, where both the standard and the fine-tuned models were tested on a challenging image of Late Blight not seen during training or testing.

Fig. 6. A representative example of a correct classification by the standard EfficientNetB0 model on a test image.

<!-- image -->

Fig. 7. Qualitative case study comparing the standard transfer-learned model (left) with the fine-tuned model (right) on a challenging image.

<!-- image -->

Although it performed exceptionally well on the test set, the standard EfficientNetB0 model incorrectly classifies the image as Early Blight with a low confidence of 58.56%, indicating its uncertainty. In stark contrast, the fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 model correctly classifies the same image as Late Blight with a very high confidence of 98.75%. This case study provides powerful empirical evidence that fine-tuning does more than just incrementally improve aggregate metrics; it enhances the model's discriminative capabilities and robustness, allowing it to overcome ambiguity and make reliable diagnoses in practical scenarios [31]. The following will further detail the differences in robustness suggested by this case study. Table III presents a qualitative analysis summarizing how each model architecture is expected to perform under common real-world challenges.

## VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This paper presented a comparative evaluation of six deep learning architectures for potato leaf disease detection, focusing on the specific performance benefits of fine-tuning. The findings clearly demonstrate that the training strategy is the critical factor for creating a genuinely dependable diagnostic tool. A strategically fine-tuned EfficientNetB0 achieved stateof-the-art accuracy (99.22%) and proved its superior realworld reliability in a case study by correcting a misclassification made by its non-fine-tuned counterpart. This confirms that for specialized tasks like plant pathology, the finetuning methodology is more impactful for achieving robust performance than the initial choice of architecture alone. Although the model performed exceptionally, future work must concentrate on validating its robustness on more challenging 'in-the-field' datasets and exploring model optimization for deployment on low-power mobile devices, transforming this research into an accessible tool for farmers.

## Adaptive Urban Traffic Control Using Camera Vision and Emergency Vehicle Mobile Interface

Shilpa B L Dept of CSE, ATME College of Engineering Mysore, Karnataka, India-570028

email:blshilpa@gmail.com Mayank M Dept of CSE, ATME College of Engineering Mysore, Karnataka, India-570028

email:mayankmjain16@gmail.com

Abstract -Urban traffic congestion is a significant concern in the daily operations of commuters and emergency responders. Existing systems based on timers do not have the ability to adjust density and prioritize emergency calls. This paper  offers  an  integrated  intelligent  traffic  management system based on density-related signal reordering, including emergency  vehicle  preemption.  This  system  uses  existing surveillance cameras and a custom-trained Roboflow object detection  model  (mAP@50  =  99.5%)  to  provide  vehicle counts,  allowing  for  lane  priority  reordering,  rather  than routine signal timing changes. A dedicated mobile app allows only the emergency vehicle's to pre-declare its route, and the backend system looks for green-signal  precedents when the emergency vehicle is within a 500 meters distance approach window. Real-time control of signal precedence is accomplished by using a network of LED modules connected to  the  ESP32  development  board.  The  system  also  reduces average  wait  time  by  up  to  35%  and  keeps  the  emergency vehicle  moving  without  obstructions.  The  results  show  the experiment, an effective system compared to existing work, including  an  analysis  of  the  existing  YOLO-based  systems, and  discussion  of  limitations  and  applicability  to  scalable smart-city development.

Keywords -Intelligent Traffic Management, Emergency Vehicle Preemption, Image Processing, Object Detection, Smart City, Traffic Signal Prioritization, Real-Time Monitoring, Vehicle Counting.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Urbanization has significantly increased vehicle traffic, making  congestion  one  of  the  main  problems  facing modern cities. This leads to delays and frustrates commuters. This also negatively impacts emergency response services. Traditional traffic control systems usually operate on fixed timer cycles. Their rigidity makes it  hard  for  them  to  adapt  to  changing  traffic  patterns  or emergencies.

Recent advancements in Intelligent Transportation Systems (ITS) demonstrate how technologies like computer vision, embedded hardware, and mobile communication can be used to manage traffic dynamically. One  notable  aspect  of  density-based  signal  control  is  its ability to use video feeds to monitor vehicle counts in real time  and  adjust  signal  behaviour  accordingly.  However, many of  these  systems  mainly  focus  on  changing  signal durations, which can create synchronization problems.

In  addition  to  traffic  optimization  efforts,  emergency vehicle  preemption  has  become  an  important  part  of modern smart city designs. Traditional methods that rely on RFID,  GPS,  or  manual  overrides  are  often  heavy  on Md Fakruddin S Dept of CSE, ATME College of Engineering Mysore, Karnataka, India-570028

email:zayed.fakruddin@gmail.com

infrastructure, expensive, or slow to respond. In contrast, mobile-application-based signal preemption using estimated time of arrival (ETA) offers a scalable and realtime solution for providing green corridors [13], [14].

This paper proposes a unified intelligent traffic management  system  that  addresses  both  routine  traffic congestion  and  emergency  vehicle  routing.  The  solution combines image-based vehicle density detection for prioritizing traffic signals with a mobile app for declaring emergency routes and preempting signals based on estimated  arrival  times.  The  system  includes  real-time location-aware routing, LED  signal control using a microcontroller,  surveillance  cameras,  and  cloud-hosted object detection through Roboflow [9], [10]. Nonemergency  vehicles  cannot  access  the  mobile  interface; only  registered  emergency  fleets,  like  ambulances,  fire engines, and police patrols, have access credentials. This ensures controlled use of the preemption feature.

The proposed system brings these components together to give emergency responders quick, uninterrupted passage. This reduces average wait times through dynamic lane  prioritization.  This  approach  supports  smart  city integration and promotes safer, more  efficient urban mobility.

## II. RELATED WORK

Extensive research into intelligent transportation solutions has been fueled by the increasing need for traffic control systems that can adjust. Inefficient vehicle flow and prolonged  congestion  often  happen  because  traditional systems cannot handle real-time changes in traffic. They depend  on  fixed  signal  cycles.  In  response,  researchers have  suggested  density-based  control  strategies  that  use sensors, computer vision, and machine learning, as shown in  Table  I.  These  methods  help  manage  traffic  based  on flow patterns and vehicle counts.

## A.   Density-Based Adaptive Signal Control

Several studies have looked at traffic signal control that uses real-time vehicle density estimation, often employing computer  vision  and  object  detection  techniques.  For instance,  Ghosh  et  al.  [11]  developed  a  YOLOv5-based vision system to dynamically adapt traffic signals, demonstrating high precision in traffic density measurement. Similarly, Mehar and Singh [12] proposed an OpenCV-based solution for real-time lane-wise vehicle counting and adaptive timing.

The majority of these strategies concentrate on modifying signal durations in response to traffic accumulation. Congestion is lessened, but less congested lanes  may  experience  unfair  delays  and  synchronization problems as a result. In order to overcome these issues, our system employs a different approach that maintains fixed signal durations while dynamically adjusting lane priorities in  response  to  current  vehicle  counts.  This  approach ensures that the most congested lanes are served first, while still  maintaining  fairness  through  a  rotating  sequence  for the other directions [1]-[3], [5].

## B.   Emergency Vehicle Preemption Systems

Prioritizing  the  movement of emergency vehicles has been  an  important  focus  in  intelligent  traffic  research. When an emergency vehicle is detected, traditional systems change traffic signals using GPS, RF-based transmitters, or Vehicle-to-Infrastructure  (V2I)  communication  [6],  [7]. However,  these methods often depend on expensive infrastructure, such as RFID readers or manual coordination by traffic officers. Density-based optimization or emergency preemption typically operates independently. Few systems provide a combined approach that integrates both objectives.

TABLE I. SUMMARY OF KEY CONTRIBUTIONS IN RELATED WORK

| Reference       | Approach Used                             | Technology Used                         | Limitations                                         |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| [1], [2]        | Density- based control                    | Image processing (OpenCV), timers       | No emergency vehicle handling                       |
| [3]             | Signal preemption                         | Basic priority logic                    | Lacks real-time ETA routing                         |
| [5], [11]       | Adaptive signal timing                    | YOLO, Camera vision                     | Duration-based control, fairness issues             |
| [6]             | RFID & GPS-based preemption               | RFID, GPS modules                       | Costly infrastructure                               |
| [7]             | Timed Petri Nets for preemption           | Formal modelling                        | Complex implementation                              |
| [13]            | GPS + mobile app                          | Android app, GPS                        | No general traffic density handling                 |
| [14]            | IoT-based green corridor                  | IoT, real-time communication            | Lacks adaptive signal reordering                    |
| Proposed System | Integrated density control and preemption | Roboflow (YOLO-like), Mobile app, ESP32 | Dependent on cloud; limited night vision evaluation |

## III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE AND COMPONENTS

The proposed system merges emergency vehicle prioritization  and  traffic  signal  control  based  on  density. This uses a mobile app along with a cloud backend, camera feeds, cloud-hosted machine learning models, and a microcontroller-based signal actuation unit. The design is modular  and  supports  real-time  data  processing,  routeaware signal preemption, and remote monitoring.

The system collects real-time traffic data from surveillance  cameras.  This  applies  the  Roboflow  Instant model for vehicle detection and adjusts lane priorities based on density. Emergency vehicles send their routes through a mobile app. This allows the system to change signals ahead of their arrival.

## A.   Existing Camera Infrastructure and Video Processing

Existing  traffic  surveillance  cameras  at  intersections support  the  system.  A  Python  application  accesses  and processes the continuous video streams from these cameras, frame by frame. Selected frames are sent through HTTP requests to an Instant  model  hosted  on  Roboflow Universe, which is specifically trained for vehicle detection.

## B.   Roboflow Cloud Model for Vehicle Detection

The Roboflow model processes incoming frames and returns structured JSON responses. These responses contain  vehicle  bounding  boxes  and  class  labels.  The output  is  processed  in  Python  to  count  the  number  of vehicles at each intersection.

Fig. 1. The proposed Intelligent Traffic Management System integrating vehicle detection, density-based signal reordering, and emergency vehicle signal preemption.

<!-- image -->

## C.   Traffic Signal Control via ESP32 Module

Traffic signals in the demonstration use colored LEDs connected  to  an  ESP32  Wi-Fi-enabled  microcontroller. Based  on  the  traffic  density,  control  commands  are  sent over a local Wi-Fi network from the Python program to the ESP32.  The  microcontroller  reads  these  commands  and turns on the appropriate LED (green, yellow, or red). This setup mimics real-world traffic signals.

- D.   Emergency Vehicle Route Preemption Mobile App

A  React  Native  mobile  application  was  created  to improve routing for emergency vehicles. To plot routes, the app uses the Directions API and the Google Maps SDK for iOS  and  Android.  The  backend  gets  the  route  when  a destination is specified and calculates the estimated time of arrival  (ETA)  for  each  intersection.When  the  emergency vehicle  is  about  500  meters  from  a  junction,  the  system changes the signal to green, overriding the density-based logic.  This  helps  the  emergency  vehicle  move  smoothly along the selected path.

## E.   Backend and Cloud Services

The system's backend is built with Node.js and Express.js.  These  technologies  manage  the  app's  server operations.  The  backend  stores  and  organizes  user  and route information in a cloud database. Responders log in securely using Firebase Authentication with their email and password. The app gets updates about signals and routes via  web  APIs.  User  sessions  are  managed  securely,  and passwords are encrypted to protect user data. Cross-origin access is set up to ensure the app works safely on different devices. This setup is in line with the system pipeline in Fig. 1.

## F . Real-Time Communication and Hosting

During the demonstration phase, the backend APIs and ESP32 communication work over a local Wi-Fi network or LAN  server.  The  setup  can  also  be  deployed  on  cloud platforms  like  Render  or  Heroku  for  scalable  use.  The system design allows integration into smart city infrastructure with minimal hardware changes.

## IV. WORKING METHODOLOGY

The  proposed  system works  in  two  synchronized modes:

- density-based  traffic  signal  control  using  live camera feeds and cloud-based object detection.
- emergency  vehicle  signal  preemption  through mobile app-based routing.

The following steps explain how the system operates in real time.

## A. Real-Time Frame Acquisition from Existing Cameras

Traffic  surveillance  cameras  installed  at  intersections provide a continuous video feed. A Python script extracts frames  at  regular  intervals  to  capture  real-time  traffic conditions without overloading the system. These frames are  transmitted  to  a  remote  object  detection  model  for analysis.

## B . Cloud-Based Vehicle Detection via Roboflow

Captured frames are sent to a Roboflow Instant model hosted on Roboflow Universe. The model performs object detection and returns vehicle classes and bounding boxes. The Python program parses this response to count vehicles in  each  lane  of  the  intersection.  The  accuracy  of  this detection  is  illustrated  in  Fig.  2,  which  shows  highconfidence  predictions  with  a  mAP@50  of  99.5.  This vehicle  count  serves  as  the  input  for  the  density-based decision logic.

Fig. 2. Vehicle detection along with Confidence (mAP@50 = 99.5)

## C.   Dynamic Lane Prioritization Based on Density

Unlike  traditional  fixed-sequence  signal  systems,  the proposed method calculates traffic density for all four lanes and  determines  which  lane  has  the  highest  number  of vehicles. The system does not modify the duration of green signals, which remains fixed (e.g., 20 seconds per lane), but changes the signal order to prioritize the densest lane first.

After the most congested lane is served, the remaining three  lanes  are  cycled  through  in  a  rotating  manner  to ensure fairness and avoid starvation. This approach optimizes  traffic  flow  while  maintaining  equal  access across all directions.

## D.   Signal Execution using ESP32 Microcontroller

The traffic  signals  are  simulated  using  colored  LEDs connected  to  an  ESP32  microcontroller.  Signal  control instructions,  including  the  updated  lane  order,  are  sent through Wi-Fi from the Python program. The ESP32 turns on the LEDs based on the received sequence. Each signal stays green for a set time before changing to the next one.

## E.   Emergency Vehicle Routing via Mobile Application

Emergency vehicle operators use a React Native mobile app to enter their destination. The app employs the Google Maps SDK and Directions API to create a route. The App also sends the vehicle's live GPS location to the backend using expo-location.

## F.   Signal Preemption Based on ETA

The  backend  calculates  the  estimated  time  of  arrival (ETA) of the emergency vehicle at each junction along its route.  When  the  vehicle  is  about  500  meters  from  an intersection, the backend sends a signal override command to  the  ESP32.  This  interrupts  the  current  signal  cycle, turning  the  corresponding  lane  green  so  the  emergency vehicle can pass through.

## G.   Mode Switching and Recovery

While emergency routing is active, the system suspends density-based priority and gives full control to the emergency vehicle's route. Once the vehicle has cleared the intersection, the system automatically reverts to the regular density-based prioritization cycle.

## V. ALGORITHMS AND TECHNICAL IMPLEMENTATIONS

The  proposed  intelligent  traffic  system  relies  on  a combination of geolocation tracking, real-time communication, signal control logic, and hardware interfacing  to  enable  both  density-based  and  emergencypriority signal management.

At  the  centre  of  the  system  is  a  proximity  detection algorithm that calculates the distance between emergency vehicles and nearby traffic signals. This uses the Haversine formula to find the geodesic distance between two sets of latitude and longitude coordinates. If a vehicle is within a defined radius, such as 500 meters, the system considers that signal for possible preemption.

To keep things responsive in real time, the mobile app tracks the emergency vehicle's location using highaccuracy  GPS  updates  at  regular  intervals,  like  every  3 seconds or 10 meters. The backend processes this data to estimate  the  ETA  and  the  distance  to  reach  the  next intersection. If the distance is less than 500 meters, the app sends a green light override command for that signal.

Signal control employs a predictive timing mechanism to ensure a smooth flow for emergency vehicles. Once the vehicle has passed, the system switches back to the normal density-based rotation. The density-based mode organizes traffic  lanes  based  on  vehicle  count  but  maintains  fixed signal durations for fairness. The system follows a stagebased  logic  that  shifts  from  planning  and  detection  to override and recovery once the emergency vehicle clears the intersection.

Security  and  reliability  are  managed  through  JWTbased user authentication, Aadhaar number validation, and encrypted storage for user credentials. To support offline performance  and  improve  responsiveness,  local  caching techniques like FIFO queues and async storage are used for destination history and route persistence.

Hardware communication occurs through HTTP commands  sent  to an ESP32  microcontroller, which controls  the  signal  lights.  A  dual-backend  architecture guarantees that even if the cloud fails, fallback mechanisms ensure safe and reliable operation.

Performance  tracking  is  enabled  through  continuous logging  of  ETA  accuracy,  journey  times,  and  signal responsiveness .  This  helps  assess  system  efficiency  and supports data-driven refinement for future iterations.

## B.   Haversine Distance Algorithm

```
function getDistanceInKm(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2) { const R = 6371; // Radius of the earth in km const dLat = deg2rad(lat2 - lat1); const dLon = deg2rad(lon2 - lon1); const a = Math.sin(dLat / 2) * Math.sin(dLat / 2) + Math.cos(deg2rad(lat1))*Math.cos(deg2rad(lat2))* Math.sin(dLon / 2) * Math.sin(dLon / 2);
```

```
const c = 2 * Math.atan2(Math.sqrt(a), Math.sqrt(1 - a)); return R * c; // Distance in km }
```

This is a  geodesic distance calculation algorithm that computes the great-circle distance between two points on Earth's surface using their latitude and longitude coordinates.

## C.   Signal Proximity Detection Algorithm

The system implements a proximity-based signal triggering algorithm that:

Monitors the emergency vehicle's distance from predefined traffic signals.

Filters signals based on their position relative to the route Sorts signals by distance from origin to destination.

The proposed system  was  evaluated  under  controlled demonstration  conditions  using  real-time  video  feeds, mobile routing simulations, and signal actuation via microcontroller hardware. text:
## VII. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORKS

This paper introduced a smart traffic signal system that combines density-based signal reordering with emergency vehicle  prioritization  using  a  mobile  app.  By  utilizing existing cameras, cloud-hosted object detection, and microcontroller-based signal control, the system achieved high detection accuracy and reliable real-time management. The method ensured that the lane  with the highest vehicle density received priority while still keeping fairness  through  fixed-duration  signals  and  a  rotating sequence. The mobile app allowed emergency responders to follow optimized routes and automatically trigger green signals  within  a  500-meter  range.  Experimental  results showed over 99% detection accuracy, stable ESP32-based signal switching over local Wi-Fi, and consistent preemption performance, demonstrating real-time responsiveness without impacting system stability.

Despite  the  positive  results,  the  system  has  some limitations.  Cloud-based  processing  relies  on  network connectivity, and performance in low light conditions has not yet been assessed. Additionally, deploying the system on  a  large  scale  would  require  improvements  for  edge processing and integration with centralized traffic databases.

In the future, the system could be expanded by adding local  processing on edge devices to cut down on delays, integrating predictive analytics for forecasting traffic patterns, and allowing for multi-vehicle emergency coordination. Cloud-based dashboards, real-time analytics, and  integration  with  government  portals  might  further enhance smart city initiatives.

While  the  system  is  accurate  and  responds  quickly, cloud processing introduces delays and connectivity issues in handling images. The system's performance in low light and bad weather has yet to be tested. Future work will focus on  implementing  edge  processing  to  eliminate  delays, adding  night-vision  capabilities,  enabling  multi-vehicle emergency coordination, and conducting large-scale trials with real traffic control hardware.

## Adversarial Prompting and Jailbreak Attacks in Large Language Models: Detection and Mitigation Strategies

Abdul Muqeet Armar Department of CSE Beary's Institute of Technology Mangalore, India abdularmar6@gmail.com Nubila Jaleel Department of CSE Beary's Institute of Technology Mangalore, India nubilajaleel@gmail.com

Abstract -The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs)  such  as  GPT-4  and  similar  architectures  into  realworld applications has revolutionized natural language understanding, but it has also unveiled pressing security challenges. Among the most critical are adversarial prompting and jailbreak attacks, wherein attackers craft subtle or  cleverly engineered inputs to exploit model loopholes,  bypassing built-in safeguards  to  elicit  unintended,  inappropriate,  or  harmful outputs.  Addressing  these  evolving  threats  demands  solutions that are not only accurate but adaptive and comprehensive. In  this  study,  we introduce JBSHIELD -a unified detection and  mitigation  framework  that  leverages  both  supervised classification  and  unsupervised  anomaly  detection  techniques. The  proposed  system  employs  multi-stage  feature  extraction and ensemble decision-making to identify a broad spectrum of hostile  prompts in real time.  Our  mitigation stack  consists  of prompt  filtering,  robust  response  sanitization,  and  dynamic policy  enforcement,  working  together  to  dramatically  reduce successful attack rates. Through rigorous experimentation on a synthetic benchmark containing 5,000 diverse prompts, including 2,000 maliciously crafted  examples,  JBSHIELD achieves a detection accuracy of 96.4% and reduces the attack success rate from a baseline of 45% to just 5%. These results highlight the framework's potential as a proactive defense for next-generation  AI  applications,  promoting  safer  and  more trustworthy deployment of LLMs in sensitive domains.

Keywords -Adversarial  prompting,  jailbreak  attacks,  large language models, Anomaly detection, machine learning security, multi-tiered mitigation.

## I. INTRODUCTION

In  recent  years,  large  language  models  (LLMs)  such  as GPT-4  and  PaLM  2  have  fundamentally  transformed  how machines  understand  and  generate  human  language.  These models now power a wide spectrum of real-world applications -ranging from intelligent chatbots and automated assistants to educational tools and support systems -bringing unprecedented convenience and capability to users across industries.

However, this rapid progress has not come without risks. As LLMs become more ubiquitous, they also present new and unexpected opportunities for misuse. Among the most serious issues  are  adversarial  prompting  and  jailbreak  attacks -techniques  where  adversaries  deliberately  craft  inputs  that trick the model into circumventing safety mechanisms, often coaxing the system into producing inappropriate, unsafe, or confidential content.

This  challenge  is  compounded  by  the  very  strengths  of LLMs:  their remarkable ability to generalize, adapt to Mohammed Sinan Marikattay Department of CSE Beary's Institute of Technology Mangalore, India meetsinan@gmail.com

ambiguous inputs, and provide reasoned, nuanced responses. Ironically,  these  capabilities  can  sometimes  allow  cleverly designed prompts to slip past basic safeguards, undermining the intended integrity of the system. As attackers continue to invent  new  prompt  strategies and exploit  subtle  model behaviours, defensive measures that once seemed sufficient quickly become outdated.

Consequently,  ensuring  the  responsible  use  of  LLMs demands security solutions that are not only precise, but also agile -capable of detecting and adapting to evolving threats in real time, without unduly limiting the usefulness of these powerful models. In this context, our work seeks to address the urgent need for robust, layered defences against adversarial and jailbreak attacks, paving the way for safer and more trustworthy AI deployments.

## II. MOTIVATION

While  the  capabilities  of  large  language  models  are impressive,  their  openness  and  flexibility  have  also  made them appealing targets for sophisticated adversarial attacks. Traditional defences -such as static keyword filters, blacklist/whitelist  approaches,  or  hard-coded  safety  rules -are  rapidly  being  outpaced  by  attackers  who  continually develop  new  ways  to  bypass  these  safeguards.  With  the growing integration of LLMs into high-stakes environments such as healthcare, finance, legal advice, and content moderation, the risks are no longer theoretical: even a single successful  jailbreak  incident  can  lead  to  the  leakage  of proprietary information, harmful recommendations, or violations of ethical and legal standards.

Compounding the problem is the speed at which adversarial  creativity  evolves.  Attackers  can  easily  exploit weaknesses  through  subtle  prompt  modifications,  iterative probing, or by chaining instructions together across a multiturn conversation. These  adaptive strategies expose the insufficiency of any single-layer or static defence.

Moreover,  the  very  nature  of  LLMs -designed  to  be context-sensitive, helpful, and  flexible -means that the line between benign and adversarial inputs can be blurry. Overly aggressive filters may prevent genuine users from receiving accurate  or  helpful  information,  frustrating  end  users  and reducing real-world usefulness. Conversely, lenient controls create  opportunities  for  abuses  that  quickly  spiral  out  of control.

As  a  result,  the  development  of  robust,  adaptive,  and context-aware security frameworks is essential. Such systems must not only accurately detect and intercept adversarial or jailbreak attempts in real time, but also minimize disruptions to  legitimate  use.  Furthermore,  effective  solutions  should adapt as new attack patterns emerge -all without relying on constant manual updates or sacrificing user experience. This urgent  need  for  resilient,  multi-layered  defences -and  for systems that evolve alongside the threat landscape -drives the development  of  JBSHIELD,  our  proposed  comprehensive approach to adversarial and jailbreak mitigation in LLMs.

## III. RELATED WORKS

The  growing  adoption  of  large  language  models  has spurred  intensive  research  on  understanding  and  mitigating their vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks and policy circumvention.  Early  defensive  techniques  were  primarily centred around simple blacklist and whitelist filtering, intended to block obviously harmful terms or phrases. While straightforward, these static rule-based approaches have proven insufficient as  adversaries rapidly  invent new  attack strategies that evade detection, such as through paraphrasing, code words, or semantic manipulation.

Sun  et  al.  [4]  and  Li  et  al.  [5]  have  each  investigated various approaches for identifying adversarial inputs, ranging from deep grammar and syntactic feature analysis to perplexity-based anomaly detection. More advanced adversarial methods have been explored in recent years. For instance, Wallace et al. demonstrated how carefully engineered 'adversarial triggers' could  consistently  prompt LLMs to produce restricted responses, exploiting the sensitivity  of  these  models  to  specific  input  patterns  [1]. Similarly,  Wei  et al.  showcased  that manipulating  chain-ofthought reasoning -wherein prompts guide the model through stepwise logic -could be exploited to bypass intended  output  controls,  even  for  questions  that  would normally be blocked [2].

In  parallel,  the  phenomenon  of  jailbreak  attacks  has received  significant  attention.  Researchers  like  Perez  et  al. have detailed  how  automated prompt optimization and iterative  refinement  can  systematically  reveal  prompts  that circumvent both internal model filters and external API-layer safety systems [3]. These attacks, often crafted through trialand-error or algorithmic generation, highlight the shortcomings of static defence mechanisms and the ease with which determined attackers can discover new vulnerabilities.

Detection strategies have also evolved. Sun et al. and Li et al. have each investigated various approaches for identifying adversarial inputs, ranging from deep grammar and syntactic feature  analysis  to  perplexity-based  anomaly  detection  with language  models [4][5]. Supervised learning techniques leverage curated datasets of benign and dangerous prompts to train classifiers, while unsupervised models such as autoencoders  attempt  to  flag  statistical  or  semantic  outliers without relying on labelled attack samples.

Despite  these  advances,  significant  gaps  remain.  Many published  mitigation  techniques -including  reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), output postprocessing, and multi-agent oversight -offer partial solutions but often lack adaptability to shifting attack methods and realworld  complexity  [6][7][8]. Furthermore, few  integrated systems comprehensively combine high- accuracy detection with a multi-layered, context-aware mitigation stack that can be updated dynamically as the threat landscape evolves.

This environment of rapidly advancing threats and piecemeal defences underscores the need for novel frameworks -like the approach proposed in this paper -that blend supervised and unsupervised detection, deep semantic analysis, and adaptive, multi-phase response systems to ensure the security and reliability of LLM applications.

text:
## IV. RESEARCH GAP

Despite significant progress in understanding and hardening  large  language  models  against  various  forms  of adversarial abuse, pronounced limitations remain in securing these systems against persistent, creative,  and evolving attack strategies.

To  begin  with,  many  existing  defences -for  example, static blacklist filtering, keyword matching, or isolated prompt rewriting -are  vulnerable  to  evasion  through  paraphrase, code  substitution,  and  conversational  context  manipulation. These  approaches  can  stifle  legitimate  interaction  without providing lasting robustness, as attackers quickly adapt their methods to circumvent known filters. Meanwhile, detection methods rooted in simple statistical modelling or single-layer anomaly  detection  often  fail  to  generalize  when  confronted with unseen or highly obfuscated attack vectors.

Recent efforts to strengthen LLM security have explored supervised classifiers, autoencoder-based anomaly  detection, and output post-processing. However, these solutions typically  operate  in  isolation,  are  tuned  for  specific  threat instances, or struggle with timely adaptation as attack patterns evolve.  Critically,  very  few  published  strategies  integrate these disparate elements into a cohesive, layered framework that unites real-time detection, robust multi-stage mitigation, and ongoing system learning.

Furthermore, the fast-changing nature of adversarial prompting -where new 'jailbreak' methods or instructional prompts can emerge rapidly -necessitates solutions that are not  only  accurate  but  adaptive,  leveraging  feedback  and continuous monitoring to close vulnerabilities as they  appear. Many  studies  also overlook the practical challenge of maintaining a low false positive rate: aggressive defences may disrupt legitimate users, while lax policies open the  door to subtle, damaging exploits.

Lastly, very few approaches take a holistic perspective that combines  both  supervised  and  unsupervised  learning,  deep contextual semantic analysis, and  flexible,  policy-driven response  layers,  all  orchestrated  within  a  feedback  loop  to ensure up-to-date protection. There remains an urgent need for security  frameworks  that  are  comprehensive,  modular,  and able to evolve in tandem with adversarial ingenuity.

Addressing these gaps, our work introduces JBSHIELD: a hybrid detection and mitigation pipeline designed to provide not  only  accurate  identification  of  adversarial  and  jailbreak prompts, but also multi-tiered, adaptive response mechanisms that continually update in line with the threat landscape.

## V. METHODOLOGY

This section describes the architecture, components, and workflow of JBSHIELD, our proposed framework for realtime detection and mitigation of adversarial prompting and jailbreak attacks in large language models.

## A. System Architecture Overview

JBSHIELD is designed as a modular, multi-stage pipeline that systematically analyses and secures user prompts before they reach the core language model. The flow of the system is  illustrated  in  Figure  1  (see  suggested  diagram  layout below).

Fig. 1. System  architecture  of  the  JBSHIELD  detection  and  mitigation framework

## Main components:

1.  Input  Handling  &  Preprocessing: All  user  prompts  are standardized  via  normalization  (lowercasing,  punctuation removal) and tokenization. This ensures consistent feature extraction and model behavior for varied linguistic styles.

## 2. Feature Extraction:

Each prompt is converted into multiple feature sets:

- a) Syntactic features: Parse trees, sentence length, and n-gram frequencies.
- b) Semantic  features:  Embeddings  from  pre-  trained language models, capturing nuanced context.
- c) Statistical  features:  Prompt  rarity,  character-level statistics, and lexical diversity.

These  features  enable  robust  detection,  even  for  cleverly paraphrased attacks.

3. Hybrid Detection Module:

JBSHIELD employs a dual-branch detection approach:

- a) Supervised Learning: A Random Forest classifier  is  trained  on  a  labeled  dataset  of  benign, harmful,  and  known  jailbreak  prompts.  This  model leverages  human-  curated  features  to  capture  diverse attack styles.
- b) An  autoencoder  is  trained  exclusively  on  benign prompts.  Inputs  resulting  in  high  reconstruction  error  are flagged  as  outliers,  surfacing  novel  or  unseen  adversarial cases.
- c) This hybrid detection strategy ensures broad coverage: the supervised branch captures known malicious patterns  (based  on  our  labeled  training  data),  while  the autoencoder flags novel anomalies. We  calibrate each detector's threshold on validation data to balance recall and precision. In practice, the system flags an input as adversarial if any branch exceeds its threshold. This ensemble approach maximizes  detection  coverage  across  diverse  attack  types without manual rule tuning.

## 4.

- Concept Subspace Comparison:

To  capture  deeper  semantic  shifts  characteristic  of jailbreak attacks, our system learns low- dimensional 'concept vectors' that distinguish:

- i. Harmful vs. benign prompts (toxic subspace) ii. Jailbreak vs. harmful prompts (jailbreak subspace)

This is achieved through Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of LLM hidden state differences, as detailed in Section V.B.

5. Ensemble Decision Logic: Input  prompts  are flagged  as adversarial  if  any  of  the  detection components (Random  Forest, autoencoder, subspace analysis) exceed calibrated, empirically optimized thresholds. This ensemble approach maximizes both recall and precision against a wide range of attack strategies.

## 6. Multi-Tiered Mitigation Stack:

- i. Prompt Filtering: Regular expression and semantic  similarity  filters  block  known  exploit phrases and their variants.
- ii. Response  Sanitization: The  model's output  is post-processed using toxicity classifiers and policy rule-checkers. Policy-violating outputs are masked, rewritten, or suppressed.
- iii. In our implementation, flagged outputs undergo automatic sanitization using a suite of tools. We apply pre-trained toxicity  classifiers and  custom policy  filters  to  identify  banned  content,  then mask or  paraphrase  any  offending  segments.  In extreme  cases  (e.g.  high-severity  or  sensitive violations),  the  system  can  completely  block  or rewrite  the  response  to  remove  the  violation,  in line with recommended best practices this clarifies  that  harmful  model  outputs  are  either automatically removed or rewritten.
- iv. Dynamic Policy Enforcement: High-risk scenarios  trigger  immediate  escalation -either stricter model parameters or human- in-the-loop intervention -helping limit false negatives without degrading user experience for legitimate queries.
7. Continuous  Learning  and  Feedback  Loop: The system logs model and user interactions, including adversarial and  borderline cases. This  data is fed back into retraining pipelines, ensuring  that  the  detection  models  remain current as attack techniques evolve.

## C. Training and Evaluation

a) Dataset Construction: A dataset of 5,000 prompts (3,000  benign,  1,500  harmful,  500  jailbreak)  was  created using a combination of handcuration  and automated adversarial  prompt  generation  (paraphrase,  synonym  swap, logical manipulation).

b) Model  Training: Random  Forest  and  autoencoder models were trained using scikit-learn and PyTorch, respectively.  Hyperparameters  (e.g.,  number  of  trees,  layer size)  were  tuned  via  cross-  validation.  Concept  subspaces were fit  using calibration pairs from the same dataset.

- c) Threshold Calibration: Detection thresholds were set to optimize F1-score on a validation set, balancing false positives and attack miss rate.

## VI. FRAMEWORK AND WORKFLOW

The JBSHIELD framework was developed using Python 3.9,  leveraging  a  robust  ecosystem  of  libraries  tailored  for machine  learning  and  natural  language  processing.  Core components  were  implemented  using  PyTorch  for  deep learning tasks such as training the autoencoder and extracting hidden states from large language models. The Random Forest classifier  and  feature  engineering  components  employed scikitlearn, while Hugging Face's Transformers library facilitated  seamless  integration  with  pretrained  LLMs  like GPT-2, GPT-4, and PaLM 2, enabling extraction of contextual embeddings from intermediate layers. Matrix operations and singular value decomposition for concept subspace extraction were performed with NumPy and SciPy.

To  train  and  evaluate  the  system,  a  dataset  comprising 5,000 prompts  was assembled,  including 3,000  benign user inputs,  1,500  harmful  prompts,  and  500  jailbreak  prompts. The latter two categories were generated through a combination of manual curation of known attack patterns and automated  augmentation  techniques  such  as  paraphrasing, synonym substitution, and instruction perturbation. All prompts  underwent  standardized  preprocessing  involving lowercasing, punctuation trimming, and tokenization consistent with the target LLM's vocabulary.

The Random Forest classifier was trained on a balanced subset of this dataset, utilizing engineered features including n-gram frequencies, syntactic parse patterns, prompt length, and embedding-based statistics. Hyperparameters, such as the number of trees and maximum depth, were optimized using five-fold crossvalidation to maximize predictive performance.  The  autoencoder  employed  a  fully  connected architecture with multiple hidden layers designed to reconstruct benign prompt embeddings; deviations in reconstruction error were used to identify anomalous adversarial  inputs.  Critical  transformer  layers  were  selected for embedding extraction based on ablation studies to maximize  discrimination  between  benign  and  adversarial prompts. Singular  Value  Decomposition  was  applied  to differences  between  harmful  and  benign  hidden  states  to derive the toxic concept vector, and similarly to harmful and jailbreak states to obtain the jailbreak vector. Thresholds for detection scores were calibrated on a validation set to manage trade-offs between true and false positive rates.

In operation, the system functions as a real-time inference pipeline.  Prompts  enter  through  a  preprocessing  module before undergoing feature extraction, after which three detection mechanisms operate in parallel: the Random Forest classifier, autoencoder anomaly detector, and concept subspace scoring. If any detector flags a prompt as adversarial or suspicious, the system immediately routes the input to the mitigation stack, which applies regex-based prompt filtering, sanitizes model outputs using toxicity and policy checks, and, when  appropriate,  engages  human  oversight  via  dynamic policy  escalation.  The  full  pipeline  is  containerized  with Docker, enabling streamlined deployment across environments. Performance benchmarks  indicate average processing  latency  below  120  milliseconds  per  prompt  on commodity 8-core CPUs supplemented by NVIDIA GPUs for efficient embedding extraction.

Comprehensive logging records every flagged input alongside  mitigation  outcomes.  This  repository  of  security events  and  model  responses  feeds  a  scheduled  retraining pipeline, where fresh adversarial samples and user feedback are  incorporated  to  refine  detection  thresholds  and  update classifier  models.  This  continuous  learning  loop  endows JBSHIELD  with  resilience  and adaptability against the dynamic  landscape  of  adversarial  prompting  and  jailbreak attacks.

## VII. RESULTS

To  rigorously  assess  the  capabilities  of  the  proposed JBSHIELD framework, we conducted comprehensive experiments  using a  diverse  dataset  of  5,000  prompts.  This dataset included 3,000 benign user inputs, 1,500 intentionally harmful prompts, and 500 advanced jailbreak attack examples generated  through  both  manual  and  automated  methods -such as paraphrasing, synonym swaps, and manipulation of instruction intent -to simulate the tactics of real-world adversaries.

The system's hybrid  detection  approach,  which  blends supervised classification with unsupervised anomaly detection,  delivered  impressive  results.  Across  the  entire evaluation set, JBSHIELD achieved a detection accuracy of 96.4%, successfully identifying most adversarial and jailbreak attempts.  The  system  maintained  a  strong  recall  rate  of 94.1% -effectively  balancing  sensitivity  to attacks  with the need to avoid excessive false alarms. Importantly, the false positive rate remained low at 2.8%, meaning legitimate user prompts were seldom misclassified as threats.

The system's hybrid detection approach (combining supervised classification and unsupervised anomaly detection)  delivered  strong  results.  JBSHIELD  achieved  a detection accuracy of 96.4%  across the evaluation set, successfully identifying the vast majority of adversarial and jailbreak attempts. The system maintained a high recall rate of 94.1%, effectively balancing sensitivity to attacks with a low miss rate. Importantly, the false-positive rate remained only 2.8%, meaning benign user prompts were rarely misclassified as threats.

Beyond  simple  detection, the multi-tiered mitigation strategy proved its value. Without any defences, nearly half (45%) of all adversarial and jailbreak attacks were successful, underscoring the vulnerability of even cutting-edge language models to determined adversaries.

Once  JBSHIELD's  full  stack  was  appliedincluding prompt  filtering,  response  sanitization,  and  dynamic  policy adjustments -the success rate of these attacks plummeted to just 5%. This highlights how layered, adaptive defences can make a tangible difference in the security posture of AI-driven systems.

The system was also designed with practicality in mind. Real-time benchmarks found that JBSHIELD operates at an average  processing  latency  of  under  120  milliseconds  per prompt,  ensuring  timely  detection  and  intervention  suitable for deployment in live applications.

## VIII. DISCUSSION

The  experimental  results  demonstrate  that  JBSHIELD provides  a  robust,  adaptive  framework  for  detecting  and mitigating  adversarial  prompting  and  jailbreak  attacks  on large  language  models.  The  hybrid  detection  mechanism effectively  balances  high  sensitivity  to  a  broad  range  of malicious inputs while maintaining low false positive rates, which is  critical  for  preserving  user  experience  in  practical deployments.  The  multi-tiered  mitigation  strategy  further strengthens security by combining pre-emptive prompt filtering, output sanitization, and dynamic policy escalation, significantly reducing the attack success rate.

One key advantage of JBSHIELD is its modular design, allowing continuous learning and rapid incorporation of new adversarial  examples  into  the  system.  This  adaptability  is crucial  in  the  arms  race  against  adversaries  who  frequently alter their tactics. Additionally, the system achieves real-time inference  speeds  compatible  with  production  use,  avoiding bottlenecks that could impede user interaction.

In  our  experiments,  JBSHIELD  processed  each prompt  in  roughly  120  ms  on  standard  server  hardware (8-core  CPU  with  GPU  acceleration).  This  sub-200  ms overhead  is  modest,  indicating  that  the  framework  can operate in real time without perceptible delay to users.

Despite  these strengths, several  challenges  remain. Highly  sophisticated  zero-day  attacks,  especially  those mimicking benign prompts closely or exploiting semantic nuances, may still evade detection. The reliance on humanin-the-loop for uncertain cases introduces potential latency and  operational  overhead.  Future  improvements  could involve  integrating  explainable  AI  techniques  to  provide better interpretability of detection results and further automating the escalation pipeline to reduce human workload.

Finally, extending JBSHIELD's methodologies to multimodal  models,  which  process  images,  audio,  and video alongside text, represents  an important  direction to address the evolving landscape of AI threats.

## IX. CONCLUSION

This paper presents JBSHIELD, a comprehensive framework integrating supervised and unsupervised learning for  real-  time  detection  and  multi-layered  mitigation of adversarial prompting and jailbreak attacks in large language models.  Through  a  synthetic  benchmark  study  involving 5,000  prompts, including  challenging  adversarial  examples, JBSHIELD  achieved  a  detection  accuracy  of  96.4%  while decreasing  attack  success  from  45%  to  5% .  The  system's adaptive, modular architecture offers a practical path forward for  safeguarding  LLM  deployments  in  sensitive  and  highstakes environments.

Moving forward, we aim to refine detection on zero-day prompt  variants,  reduce  human  intervention  latency,  and expand the framework to encompass multimodal AI models. JBSHIELD's strong performance and design principles make it  a  promising  foundation  for  enhancing  the  security  and trustworthiness of future AI systems.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The core mission of this platform is to unify various job search, career coaching, and training capabilities into one integrated system. Platforms include job-recommendations, AI-resumed writers, mock interviews with feedback on performance, industry trend dashboards, and cover-letter builders. While static and rule-based legacy systems tend to be cumbersome and obsolete, modern platforms employ the power of NLP and deep learning models-goal-oriented and performance: for instance, BERT for skill extraction with full context [1], RAG for retrieving knowledge from chunks of realtime or offline data [11], and LSTM for scoring sequential user responses in mock interviews [12]. We also use Google Gemini or GPT for natural language generation where it suits, such as resume and cover letter writing. Utilizing a vector database such as FAISS or Pinecone, with pre-embedded PDF documents and job data, lets us robustly construct a RetrievalAugmented Generation (RAG) pipeline that powers several modules [3].

According to this need, we are working on the AI Career Coaching Platform, which encompasses multiple essential features in a single locational hub: job recommendations, AI resume generation, mock interviews with feedback, an industry trends dashboard, and cover letter generation [4], [6], [7]. While an old-class system works on static data or rule-based logic, our system-with modern NLP and deep learning models such as BERT for context-aware skill extraction [10], RAG for knowledge retrieval from real-time or chunked data [11], and LSTM to evaluate the people sequential responses in mock interviews [12]-executes intelligent operations. In other words, we may use Google Gemini or GPT for natural language generation wherever required, i.e., resume and cover letter generation. FAISS or Pinecone vector databases pre-embeds PDF documents and job data utilized by us for creating a powerful RAG pipeline, which injects life into different modules.

With such architecture, the system was made modular and scalable, having efficiency as a primary consideration regarding web technologies such as Next.js for the frontend and Node.js or FastAPI for backend APIs. Clerk is used for user onboarding and authentication, while model orchestration is facilitated using microservices that connect the Pythonbased NLP backends to the main application. In this say, the decoupled architecture allows for deployment and optimization of each feature independently. For example, resume sourcing might occur through a Gemini API call or could switch to a custom pipeline of BERT + RAG + LSTM based on availability or cost factors. By adjusting and applying each module with the best-suited AI technique, we guarantee that end users get intelligent, real-time feedback on an individual profile and for the roles being targeted [8], [9].

## II. RELATED WORK

In years gone by, many platforms have surfaced to assist an individual in navigating his or her career path through automation and artificial intelligence. For example, LinkedIn does job recommendations via collaborative filtering and profile matching [12]; however, the suggestions offered by the company are very surface-level and not really tailor-cut to the skill sets evolving at the user's end or to intent [2], [18]. Similarly, some other platforms such as CareerExplorer and Glassdoor will provide skill-based assessments and career guidance based on personality, but sadly, those services will stand on the sidelines concerning real-time adaptability and deep integration with recent NLP advancements [7], [13].

AI-based systems for resume creation and optimization, such as JobScan and Rezi, are concerned with an applicant's alignment of keywords with job description keywords. This is handy in bumping up the score on ATS, but it does not measure semantic relevance from the perspective of candidate intent. Meanwhile, more informally, job seekers themselves are using ChatGPT or Google Gemini to write their resumes, cover letters, and mock interviews [15], [16]. However, these systems operate independently of each other and without any memory or data retention capabilities; moreover, they do not provide one single user experience combining resume generation, job search, and interview simulation within one cohesive pipeline.

The modern NLP technologies presented through BERT for semantic understanding [6], [10], RAG for retrieval-augmented generation [3], and LSTM for evaluating sequential responses [5] have presented new avenues for developing intelligent, personalized career counseling platforms. While some of these models are studied on their own, very few systems actually use them integrated into fully modular end-to-end coaching platforms.

Additionally, frameworks using FAISS or Pinecone for document vector search and Clerk for secure user onboarding are rarely incorporated in academic or commercial career platforms [3]. Our proposed system addresses this gap by offering a seamless, real-time AI assistant for job seekers using state-of-the-art models and tools in a cohesive architecture.

## III. PROPOSED SYSTEM / METHODOLOGY

## A. System Overview

The system is currently under the title of AI Career Coach, an intelligent web platform that provides diversity, equity and inclusion support for individuals to navigate their career path through a personalized AI-based experience. The system is composed of four major components: Job Recommendations [4], [6], [7], Resume Generation [3], Mock Interview Simulation, and Industry Insights (for employee market insight) [9]. Each of these components are built using NLP and machine learning models, i.e., BERT [10], LSTM [12], RAG [11], Gemini AI and provide contextual understanding, relevance and interactivity.

User experience is done with an easy-to-use user interface through React, and back-end noting is done through Node.js, Firebase and vector databases such as Pinecone [18], which assist systems to process data and store (using embeddings). Gemini AI helps to generate personalized resumes and the content used for training on the industry content, while BERT [10] and RAG [11], [19] are used to contextualise inputs from user and provide both relevant job suggestions or video-based interview simulations. The goal is to create an interactive endto-end AI ecosystem to support all job application phases of the user.

## B. System architecture

Fig. 1. System Architecture

## C. Model Selection & Justification

RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation): RAG uses retrieval functions alongside generative language models [11],

[19]. It's used to produce industry-specific insights that are well-detailed, using relevant and timely information found either in document databases or online [18], and generating a smooth response.

BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers): BERT [10] is being utilised for semantic analysis of user profiles and job descriptions to rank job recommendations according to how well the candidate skills match the job.

LSTM (Long Short-Term Memory Networks): LSTM networks [12] are used to simulate interview-style question generation and response analysis, where the model can track and understand sequential context in user answers.

## Gemini AI (from Google):

Gemini AI serves multiple roles: it generates personalized resumes, crafts real-time industry insights, and aids in mock interview simulations with human-like conversations. Its large multimodal capabilities make it suitable for dynamic and creative content generation.

## D. Data Flow

The data flow architecture enables seamless and customized user experiences through multiple AI-enabled components. Each of the front-end [20] and back-end [21] components interacts with each other and with advanced NLP models as well as APIs to support resume upload, parsing, career insights, job-role matching, interview simulation, and custom document creation. The data movement is explained as follows:

## Step 1: User Onboarding / Authentication

The users will use the application via a web interface built with Next.js [20]. Users can either register as new users or log in as existing users. Authentication is managed through Clerk [22], where a user will be authenticated securely. When a user logs in, the user metadata is stored in NeonDB [23]. The backend system also synchronizes user activity and preferences in real-time with Firebase to provide analytics.

## Step 2: Resume Uploading and Parsing

After logging in, users can upload their resumes as PDF files. The uploaded resumes are stored in Firebase Cloud Storage. The backend system, built in Node.js [21], sends the file contents from the uploaded resume to the Gemini API, which parses the resume into structured information such as skills, experience, and education. The AI generates a draft version of an ATS-compliant resume template and intersperses relevant AI-generated suggestions throughout the text [3].

## Step 3: Dynamic Career Insights via RAG Pipeline

The system uses a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline [11], [19] to retrieve weekly-updated industry trends and skills in demand. The pipeline retrieves relevant documents from either a web scraping API or curated dataset, processes them with a large language model (e.g., Gemini), and embeds the processed content and index in a Pinecone vector database [18] for semantic search. When a user selects a career insight, the backend requests relevant results from Pinecone and sends them to the dashboard.

Fig. 2. User Onboarding and Authentication Flow

<!-- image -->

## Step 4: Job Role Matching using BERT

When the user requests job recommendations, the backend executes a fine-tuned BERT model [10] to match the user's resume data and preferences to curated job datasets. BERT computes semantic similarities between the user's skills and job requirements, then ranks matched job positions.
