text:
## Step 5: LSTM-Driven AI Mock Interviews

For mock interview attempts, the user selects a target job title. The system generates role-specific questions in real time using either predefined templates or fine-tuned LSTM models [12] trained on domain-specific interview corpora. After the user responds (by typing or recording), the model scores the answers semantically with contextual scoring, generating performance scores and improvement tips. This feedback loop allows users to progressively improve their interviewing skills.

## Step 6: Personalized Cover Letter Generation

The user can upload a job description (JD) to generate a personalized cover letter. The parsing engine extracts information from the JD, parses the user's resume, and calls the Gemini API [3] to generate an ATS-compliant cover letter. This letter is formatted and organized with a tone appropriate for the target company and role. Both the mock interview and cover letter tools allow full editing control before submission.

## IV. IMPLEMENTATION

The implementation of the AI Career Coach converts the proposed architecture into a working prototype that integrates model inference, retrieval, and generation services with a responsive frontend [20]. The system follows a strict top-tobottom flow: user input is captured by the Next.js frontend, routed to backend API endpoints, processed by a sequence of AI modules (BERT → RAG → optional LSTM → Generative LLM), and the outputs are returned to the frontend for display and user interaction.

An overview of the complete system architecture is shown in Fig. V.

Fig. 3. Overall architecture of the AI Career Coach system.

<!-- image -->

## A. Data Acquisition and Preprocessing

Data sources feeding the platform include:

- User-provided inputs (resume text, job descriptions, interview responses),
- Periodically harvested industry documents (PDF reports, salary surveys, job postings),
- Curated skill taxonomies.

Incoming textual inputs are normalized (Unicode normalization, lowercasing), cleaned (removal of headers, footers, and PII where required), and tokenized using the same WordPiece/BERT tokenizer applied in model inference [10]. Long documents are chunked into overlapping windows (e.g., 5001,000 tokens) to produce manageable retrieval units for the RAG index.

Structured numerical data (e.g., salary ranges, skill frequency time series) are normalized and aggregated for dashboard visualizations and LSTM forecasting [12].

## B. Model Implementation and Interaction

Model responsibilities reflect the modular pipeline in Fig. V:

- 1) BERT Model: Performs request classification and entity extraction [10], [24]. First, user intent is identified (dashboard query, resume generation, interview session, cover letter). Then, relevant entities such as skills, job titles, companies, and time spans are extracted.
- 2) RAG Component: Uses extracted entities as retrieval keys. Embeddings for document chunks are stored in a FAISS/Pinecone [18], [25] vector index. The retriever returns the top-k context passages relevant to the query [11], [19]. This retrieved context, along with BERT outputs, forms the context window for the generative LLM.
- 3) Optional LSTM Layer: Acts as a refinement and scoring stage. Invoked when:
- Multi-turn interview context must be evaluated [12],
- BERT/retriever confidence falls below a set threshold,
- System is in detailed mode .

The LSTM processes sequential inputs (e.g., interview answers, resume bullet points) and outputs quality scores and rephrasing suggestions.

- 4) Generative LLM: (Gemini, GPT family, fine-tuned T5) Produces final human-readable artifacts such as ATSfriendly resume sections, tailored cover letters, interview feedback, and dashboard summaries [3], [26]. The LLM is always RAG-conditioned: prompts concatenate BERT entities, top-k retrieved evidence, and a system instruction template enforcing format, tone, and keyword coverage. Post-processing checks validate keyword coverage and length; low-confidence outputs trigger optional LSTM re-scoring before delivery.

## C. Backend Orchestration and API Design

The backend orchestration layer [21] routes frontend requests to the appropriate model microservices:

- APIs accept structured JSON payloads,
- Perform limited validation and sanitization,
- Send requests to the BERT service for initial parsing.

Based on BERT results, the orchestrator decides whether to:

- 1) Call the retriever,
- 2) Invoke LSTM scoring,
- 3) Call the generator directly.

All model services expose RESTful endpoints and are containerized for scalability. Responses are returned as a single JSON object containing:

- Generated text,
- Metadata (matched skills, relevance scores),
- Suggested actions (e.g., "improve bullet point X" ).

## D. Frontend Integration and UX Flow

The Next.js frontend [20]:

- Captures and locally validates user inputs,
- Provides editing interfaces for resumes/cover letters,
- Displays interactive dashboards (skill trends, salary charts).

When an action is requested:

- 1) The frontend calls the corresponding backend API.
- 2) While models are processing, progress indicators are displayed.
- 3) Results are returned in editable form, allowing the user to refine or request alternative outputs.

For the mock interview module, the frontend supports:

- Real-time streaming of prompts and results,
- Progress charts,
- Session data persistence for longitudinal LSTM scoring.

## E. Deployment, Monitoring, and Protections

Model services deploy on cloud instances with GPU acceleration when required, while lightweight tokenization/routing runs in CPU containers.

A caching layer anticipates frequent retrieval contexts, reducing latency for repeated queries.

Logging and telemetry track:

- Per-request latency,
- Model confidence,
- Error rates.

Logs are anonymized, enabling:

- Scheduling of index refreshes,
- Triggering model retraining.

From a privacy perspective:

- PII is removed before any external API call ,
- Role-based access controls restrict stored artifact access.

## V. RESULTS AND EXPECTED OUTCOMES

Evaluators of the proposed intelligent career coaching system studied many performance measures: Job Classification, Entity Extraction, and Recommendations. Overall, there were substantial improvements in performance using a combination of BERT for semantic understanding, RAG for contextual retrieval, and LSTM for sequence prediction over baseline models [4], [6], [7]. The ATS resume generator module benefits by successfully generating an end-user ATS optimized F1-score of 0.92 versus conventional keyword comparison methods [3], [28]. The AI-powered interview module achieved an 88% rolespecific accuracy in generating interview questions. The skillgap analysis component generated a precision score of 90%, indicative of promising performance of our NLP pipeline. Table I summarizes the performance metrics.

The system's real-time dashboard allows the main user interface to automatically update industry trends weekly while ensuring context relative to each user remains consistent with the demands of the labor market. Initial usability testing has shown an improvement in user satisfaction rates, producing career-contextualized recommendations in comparison with static recommendation or suggestion boards.

## VI. CHALLENGES AND LIMITATIONS

While some useful results have been obtained, the proposed architecture has certain limitations. First, large pre-trained models like BERT [10] and RAG [11], [19] inherently increase the computational cost when using these components for inference, and real-time inferencing is difficult without hardware acceleration [29]. Performance also depends on how frequently workforce data are updated, particularly when forecasting skills with the LSTM model [12]. Another limitation is the precision of entity extraction from unstructured job postings, as differences in formatting and terminology may reduce accuracy [24]. Furthermore, while the system performed well with English, extending its capabilities to multilingual job markets would require retraining for multiple domains, which could be resource-intensive [30]. Data privacy is also a concern [27], requiring strong anonymization and encryption protocols for handling sensitive career and resume information.

text:
## VII. FUTURE SCOPE

Future iterations of the system will aim to improve both performance and adaptability. We plan to investigate the use of transformer-based time-series models, such as Temporal Fusion Transformers (TFT), to replace LSTM modules for skill trend forecasting [31]. Expanding the data footprint to include multilingual and multi-domain job postings will improve global applicability [30]. We also aim to implement reinforcement learning to optimize recommendation strategies based on user feedback, increasing personalization over time [32]. Low-latency inference can be achieved through model quantization and edge deployment [29]. Additionally, we plan to add explainable AI (XAI) layers for increased transparency and trust in recommendations [33].

## VIII. CONCLUSION

In summary, we presented an intelligent career coaching system that integrates BERT for semantic understanding, a RAG agent for retrieval-augmented generation, and an LSTM for sequential forecasting to deliver a comprehensive, adaptive, and user-centered career guidance solution. Our system supports ATS-optimized resume building, AI-powered mock interviews, skill-gap identification, and trend-based career recommendations. Experimental findings suggest that our multicomponent architecture outperforms conventional career advisory systems in terms of accuracy, personalization, and alignment with industry trends. However, challenges remain in improving computational efficiency, multilingual adaptation, and privacy-preserving processing.

## An Energy-Aware Routing Framework for SIoT Using Relationship-Based K-Means Clustering

Anusha R.S Dept. of Information Science and Engineering, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India anushars@jssstuniv.in Shiva Prakas S P Dept. of Information Science and Engineering, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India shivasp@jssstuniv.in

Abstract -Social  Internet  of  Things  (SIoT)  improves  the conventional  IoT  networks  by  infusing  social  features  into device interactions to realize intelligent and autonomous networking.  Yet,  routing  protocols  in  use  fail  to  consider  the social relationships between devices and concentrate mainly on energy or topology-related metrics, resulting in inefficiencies in dynamic and resource-limited settings. Bridging this need, this research introduces an energy-aware routing framework that incorporates  relationship-based  clustering  based  on  the  KMeans  algorithm.  The  proposed  model  exploits  both  social parameters -device interaction frequency and  relationship strength -and  traditional  network  metrics  like  energy  levels and communication range to form socially consistent, energyefficient clusters. Routing  decisions  become  context-aware within such clusters, thus making it more adaptive and reducing overhead. Simulation results indicate that the proposed framework performs significantly better than standard protocols like LEACH and HEED with 98.1\% packet delivery ratio, 91.4\% energy efficiency, reduced routing cost of 0.0148, and enhanced residual energy. The outcomes confirm that social context in conjunction with energy-aware clustering facilitates enhancing routing performance, scalability, and network lifetime in SIoT systems.

Keywords -Social  Internet  of  Things  (SIoT),  Energy-Aware Routing,  K-Means  Clustering,  Relationship-Based  Networking, Context-Aware Networking

## I. INTRODUCTION

The global spread of the Internet of Things (IoT) has given rise  to  a  hyper-connected  world  where  billions  of  physical devices  interact,  exchange  information,  and  make  various applications intelligent. Traditional IoT systems rely primarily on the physical connectivity of devices and fail to recognize the  social  attributes  that  come  with  real-world  interactions. Efforts to address this limitation have led to the development of the Social Internet of Things (SIoT). SIoT introduces social relationship  models  into  IoT  networks,  enabling  devices  to communicate based not only on proximity or service characteristics but  also  on  social  and  contextual  ownership, co-location, collaboration, and shared interest. This shift from a technically centered network to a socially aware infrastructure  opens  new  possibilities  for  more  intelligent, adaptive, and human-centered device communications.

Herein, in this context, this work introduces an EnergyAware Routing Framework for SIoT Based on RelationshipBased K-Means Clustering. The originality of the introduced model is that it is capable of exploiting social relationships between  IoT  devices  to  establish  dynamic  context-aware communication clusters. Unlike traditional clustering that is based  on  spatial  proximity  or  network  metrics  only,  this Kirill Krinkin School of Computer Science and Engineering, Constructor University, Bremen, Germany kirill@krinkin.com method  includes  relationship  types  like  ownership  object relationships  (OOR),  social  object  relationships  (SOR),  cowork relationships (CWOR), and guardian object relationships  (GOR),  among  others.  These  provide  a  rich context  for  device  behavior  understanding  and  identifying efficient routing paths. The contributions of this work can be outlined as follows:

- Development  of  a  new  routing  framework  based  on  KMeans clustering and relationship-aware SIoT context.
- Development of a multi-feature clustering strategy considering spatial, interactional, and relational features to form efficient communication groups.
- Development  of  an  energy-efficient  routing  mechanism that avoids unnecessary data transmission and maximizes network lifetime.
- Performance evaluation of the framework through simulated  experiments  based  on  the  SIoT  relationship datasets.

The remainder of the paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the related work and highlights the shortcomings of  current  energy-aware  and  social  routing  approaches. Section 3 summarizes the system design and the clusteringbased routing scheme. Section 4 provides details about the dataset setup, simulation framework, and performance measures. Section 5 presents the experimental findings and comparative study. Lastly, Section 6 wraps up the paper and provides directions for future research, such as the integration of reinforcement learning and distributed trust assessment.

Devices communicate autonomously in SIoT environments based on social relationships to enable intelligent services. Conventional routing protocols, however, ignore the social awareness and energy restrictions of devices, resulting in wasteful communication and decreased network lifetime. The absence of adaptive, relationship-based routing protocols  raises  overhead  and  power  waste,  particularly  in dynamic and resourcerestricted  SIoT  networks. ## V. PROPOSED ALGORITHM

The suggested algorithm is outlined in 1. The algorithm seeks to enable energy-efficient, socially-aware routing within SIoT  environments.  It  carries  out  its  functionality  in  three general phases: grouping the devices into clusters, choosing a cluster head for each cluster, and lastly, routing the data with an  energy-aware  method.  The  first  step  is  clustering  the devices into groups using the K-means clustering algorithm. Once clusters are formed, a representative device for  every cluster is chosen and made the head of the cluster. The node is  selected  based  on  various  parameters:  it  should  have sufficient energy, good communication, and good connections with other members in the cluster. Once the cluster heads have been  selected,  the  algorithm  proceeds  to  the  routing  phase. Devices in a cluster directly communicate with their cluster head to reduce the energy used for longdistance communication. When data must be transmitted to a device in another cluster, it is relayed by the cluster head to other cluster heads,  and  they  choose  routes  that  are  socially  stable  and energy-efficient. This multi-hop routing over trusted cluster heads  minimizes  the  total  energy  consumption  within  the network and ensures very high reliability.  By  incorporating social  context  into  routing,  the  algorithm  assures  that  data passes through devices that are more likely to have stable and cooperative relationships.

## VI. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

Dataset  Preparation: A  synthetic  SIoT  dataset  containing 1,00,000 samples was generated, where each sample corresponds to a unique device. The dataset includes attributes such as device ID, type, brand, and model, along with inter-device distance in kilometers, mobility status, and ownership  percentage.  Communication  parameters  such  as communication type (e.g., WiFi, BLE, ZigBee) and relationship  type  (e.g.,  STOR,  GSTOR,  SOR)  were  also included. Additionally, each entry specifies peer brand and type,  a  binary  relationship  indicator  (is-related  status),  and associated application and service IDs. This data set simulates a dynamic and diverse SSIoT scenario.

The  clustering  was  done  using  a  Relationship-Based  KMeans  Clustering  algorithm,  which  groups  devices  into clusters based on relationship type (represented numerically, ownership  percentage,  mobility  features,  communication mode, and proximity among devices. The aim was to create socially  compact  clusters  with  low  geographical  spread  so that  routing  becomes more efficient and the energy cost is minimized.  After  the  formation  of  clusters,  an  energyefficient routing protocol was applied to each of them. The routes were decided based on factors like the available energy at the devices, communication success rate in terms of packet delivery  ratio,  physical  distance  between  nodes  that  are communicating, and the  strength  of  the  social  connections between them. A weighted shortest path algorithm based on customized weights was used through the networkx package to find the optimum routes.

Evaluation  Metrics: The  performance  of  the  model  was evaluated based on a few important metrics. Energy Efficiency  was  quantified  as  the  ratio  of  devices  with adequate residual energy after communication rounds.

Intra-cluster Distance was evaluated as the average physical distance between devices in every cluster. Routing Cost aggregated energy usage, physical distance, and social relation  strength  into  an  integrated  cost  metric. Packet Delivery Ratio (PDR) showed the communication reliability by  expressing  the  ratio  of  delivered  packets. Residual Energy expressed the average residual energy (in joules) of devices  after  the  routing  process.  To  analyze  the  effect  of social  cohesion  on  the  performance  of  the  system,  the relationship match ratio -calculated as the percentage of socially comparable devices in a cluster -was changed from 70% to 100%. It assisted in determining the effect of social affinity  on  clustering  and  routing  performance  through quantification.

## VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This study introduced a Relationship-Based K-Means Routing Framework specifically designed for SIoT environments. The  model  strategically combines  social parameters -such as device interaction frequency and relationship strength -with traditional network features like energy efficiency and communication range. Through the use of K-Means clustering, socially-aware clusters were formed, enabling efficient and context-driven routing decisions.The performance results showed remarkable improvements over existing  routing  protocols  like  LEACH  and  HEED.  The model resulted in better delivery ratios, less energy consumption,  and  less  routing  overhead.  These  are  due  to combining social context with energyaware clustering, which enhances scalability, reliability, and performance in heterogeneous and dynamic IoT systems.

One  of  the  promising  extensions  is  to  design  dynamic clustering techniques to accommodate mobile IoT nodes and changing  social  relations,  typical  of  SIoT  applications  in reality.  Another  trend  lies  in  integrating  security  and  trust mechanisms into routing design. This encompasses instantaneous assessment of node trustworthiness and the use of secure communication protocols to protect against potential threats or malicious actions.

## Analysis of Kannada Tweets for Depression using Machine Learning Models

## Praveen V D

Electronics and Communication Engg Srinivas Institute of Technology Mangaluru, India vdpraveen2@gmail.com

## Soorya Krishna K

Electronics and Communication Engg Srinivas Institute of Technology Mangaluru, India ksooryakrishna1@sitmng.ac.in

## Aishwarya

Electronics and Communication Engg Srinivas Institute of Technology Mangaluru, India kotianaish@gmail.com

Abstract -The expanding role of social media has positioned platforms like X, Facebook, and WhatsApp as critical spaces for individuals to convey their thoughts and emotions instantaneously. This study focuses on the classifying users as depressive or non-depressive based on their social media posts in Kannada using machine learning techniques. Kannada's distinct linguistic characteristics and scarcity of language resources create specific challenges for Natural Language Processing. In the present work, Machine Learning algorithms are used to find the indications of depressive thoughts of the user based on the tweets. This can then be used further for providing necessary aid and counselling to the depressed persons. A labelled dataset of Kannada tweets, adapted from the Sentiment140 corpus, was utilized in this study. Preprocessing techniques including tokenization, stop-word removal, vectorization and lemmatization using Word2Vec were applied. Logistic Regression, Extreme Gradient Boost, Ridge Classifier, Linear Discriminant Analysis and Stochastic Gradient Descent Classifier were trained using the vectorized dataset with their performance being evaluated using metrics accuracy and the Area Under the Curve score. The Linear Discriminant Analysis outperformed the chosen models with 79.95% accuracy.

Index Terms -sentiment140, Word2Vec, Kannada, Machine Learning, Depressed

## I. INTRODUCTION

Depression is a mood disorder that causes a persistent feeling of sadness and loss of interest [1]. Depression affects a person's behaviour and can lead to physical and emotional problems. With growing connectivity and collaboration, people use social media frequently to express their opinion, feelings which can be a great source of information. We selected a popular social media platform, X (formerly Twitter), for studying the people's behaviour through their tweets.

The present generation is tech-savvy and use social media platforms like X, Facebook, Instagram and so on, to express their emotions, thoughts, and mental states through short text posts. In Kannada-speaking regions, mental health awareness is still evolving, and early detection of depressive tendencies

by the way of analysis of social media posts could aid in providing timely support. However, there is an absence of automated tools to analyze Kannada-language tweets for depression detection due to limited datasets, linguistic complexity, and informal language variations. It is nearly impossible and impractical to manually analyze vast amount of data obtained from social media. Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques and ML algorithms can be used to analyze the social media posts . NLP helps us to process and extract features from human language. ML algorithms can use these features to classify the data based on predefined classes. Several studies have focused on sentiment classification from tweets due to X's concise and real-time nature. A classification of political tweets was carried out in [2] using Random Forest, Decision Tree, and Logistic Regression classifiers. It was observed that meticulous preprocessing and Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency vectorization significantly influence model performance. The researchers in [3] developed a Bidirectional-Long Short-term Memory (Bi-LSTM)-Random Forest model in which 3,000 Facebook posts in Bengali language were classified as mild, moderate and severe levels of depression. They employed manual annotation for labelling the posts and compared the performance of Bi-LSTM, Bi-LSTM-Random Forest and Bi-LSTMXGBoost models. Among the selected models, Bi-LSTMRandom Forest produced best accuracy of 93.67%. The authors of [4] developed a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-LSTM model with pretrained embeddings for tweet classification into depressive and non-depressive classes. As a comparison, they evaluated ML models such as Naive Bayes, K-Nearest Neighbor and Random Forest. The hybrid model produced an accuracy of 98.47% and RF produced 97.69% among the ML models. The authors of [5] applied Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) to tackle imbalanced Flipkart review data and compared multiple classifiers

(LR, DT, NB). Their TF-IDF and n-gram-based approach was particularly effective after hyperparameter tuning. Hybrid ML approaches were employed in [6], [7]. They achieved better accuracy in comparison with traditional classifiers. The authors of [8] addressed the sentiment analysis in code-mixed Indian texts (Kannada-English, BengaliEnglish, Hindi-English). Using distributed representations like Doc2Vec, FastText, CNN, and Bi-LSTM, they demonstrated that Deep Learning models better handle noisy and unstructured multilingual data. In [9], the researchers developed a sentiment analysis model in Kannada. Unlike typical binary classification, they included emotions like anger, sadness, and happiness. Among various classifiers tested, Linear Support Vector Machine yielded the best accuracy. The authors in [10] analyzed customer reviews with the help of SVM, DT, and NB. The study underscores the value of ML in automatically classifying reviews into positive or negative sentiments, enabling efficient customer feedback processing. In [11], the researchers performed a comparative analysis of ML classifiers for sentiment detection, particularly in movie review datasets. They outlined several forms of sentiment analysis, such as fine-grained, aspect-based, and emotion detection, providing a detailed taxonomy of sentiment classification strategies. The authors of [12] explored NB and SVM and compared their performance in analyzing social media sentiment. They focused on identifying model-specific strengths and limitations and emphasized the significance of preprocessing techniques like text normalization and feature extraction on classification accuracy. The researchers in [13] employed supervised ML techniques using the Internet Movie Database dataset to conduct binary classification (positive/negative) of movie reviews. A sentiment analysis on Hindi and Kannada tweets using ML classifiers such as NB, KNN, DT, and RF was carried out in [14] that addressed the challenges in multilingual sentiment classification, especially for languages with limited annotated datasets. In [15], Na¨ ıve Bayes model is applied to classify sentence polarity into four categories: positive, negative, neutral, and mixed. The paper [16] demonstrates the use of Logistic Regression, SVM, Na¨ ıve Bayes classifiers for classifying tweets for negative and positive frequencies with Logistic Regression achieving highest accuracy. The authors of [17] used classifiers such as RF, SVM, DT, XGBoost, LR, and Gaussian Naive Bayes (GNB) for sentiment analysis of tweets about National Education Policy. The tweets were classified into negative, positive and neutral categories based on sentiment scores generated by TextBlob. DT classifier produced highest accuracy among the ML models used. From the previous literatures, it is observed that NLP and ML has been applied mostly on English language text with a few studies attempting to classify text in regional language such as Kannada. Also, the accuracy and other metrics depend on the methods of preprocessing of the dataset.

## II. MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

In this section, a brief introduction of the various ML models of interest to the present work is presented. The classifier algorithms such as Logistic Regression, Ridge Classifier, Extreme Gradient Boosting, Linear Discriminant Analysis and Stochastic Gradient Descent are presented. These models were chosen for classifying Kannada social media posts into depressive and non-depressive categories for their ability to effectively learn patterns and relationships from textual data, even in low-resource language settings.

## A. Logistic Regression

Logistic Regression is a statistical and ML method widely used for binary classification tasks, in which the dependent variable assumes one of two possible classes - such as spam vs. non-spam or depressed vs. non-depressed [18].

## B. Ridge Classifier

Ridge regression alters the loss function by incorporating a regularization component that discourages large coefficient magnitudes, resulting in coefficient estimates that minimize the modified residual sum of squares [19].

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

The complexity parameter α ≥ 0 controls the amount of shrinkage. The classifier recasts the binary classification task as a regression problem by representing targets as { -1, 1 } , enabling optimization of the same loss function. The sign of the output indicates the category. For multiclass problems, the model performs multi-output regression and selects the class with the highest predicted value.

## C. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) Classifier

XGBoost is based on Gradient Boosting. It is an ensemble technique that combines multiple weak learners to create a strong predictive model. The weak learners are usually Decision Trees. Trees are built sequentially, with each successive tree focusing on correcting the mistakes of the previous ones, and the final prediction is obtained by combining the outputs of all trees in the ensemble [20].

## D. Linear Discriminant Analysis

Linear Discriminant Analysis is a supervised classification problem that helps separate two or more classes by converting higher-dimensional data space into a lower-dimensional space. It determines a linear combination of features that most effectively distinguishes between classes in a dataset [21].

## E. Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) Classifier

SGD is an effective method for training linear classifiers and regressors using convex loss functions, including linear SVM and Logistic Regression [22]. SGD is highly effective for managing large-scale and sparse datasets, which are encountered in text classification and NLP tasks.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## A. Description of the dataset

The sentiment140 dataset [23], comprising 1.6 million tweets collected via the Twitter API, was utilized for this study. The tweets have been annotated (0 = negative, 4 = positive).

## B. Data Cleaning and Transformation

The dataset from the previous step is filtered to remove the weblinks, hashtags, usernames from the tweets. The tweets with negative polarity were recategorized as depressive and non-depressive by computing the average polarity of words highly correlated with depression [24] and then comparing the polarity of each tweet with it [25]. The tweets were translated into Kannada using Google translate and were manually checked and cleaned for unsupported language and symbols. The labels were encoded as 0 for depressive and 1 for non-depressive tweets.

The sentences were tokenized, followed by removal of stop words and lemmatized using indic-nlp library. The dataset was balanced so as to include 100000 tweets each for both depressive and non-depressive categories.

## C. Feature Extraction and Training

The Word2Vec model is employed to transform the lemmatized tweets into vector representations of suitable dimensions. The vectorized dataset is divided in the ratio of 80:20 for training and testing purposes. The selected models are trained and evaluated. This task was carried out in the Google Colab Pro environment, with the specifications outlined in Table I.

## Attention-guided multi-scale feature fusion for HER2 scoring in HE-images based on histopathology images trained model

Pateel G P Dept. of CS & E (Nitte Deemed to be University) NMAM Institute of Technology (NMAMIT) Nitte, India pateel.gp@nitte.edu.in

Roopashree Nayak Dept. of ECE SCEM Mangalore, India roopashree.ec@sahyadri.edu.in

Abstract -The Human Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor 2 (HER2) gene is responsible for promoting the growth of aggressive tumors, and its accurate assessment is crucial in selecting targeted therapies. The traditional immunohistochemistry (IHC) method is prone to variation due to subjective interpretation and staining artifacts. Automated HER2 evaluation from hematoxylin-eosin (HE)-stained slides offers an improved option for reproducibility, cost-effectiveness, and efficiency, ultimately leading to better patient care. In this work, we present an attention-steered deep learning model that directly predicts the HER2 score from hematoxylin-eosin (HE)- stained images. We leverage the pre-trained model, similar to the DenseNet-121 model, KimiaNet, to learn multi-scale features from its four Dense Blocks. It employs global average pooling followed by cross-attention for feature fusion, which leverages inter-scale dependencies. The fused representation is fed to a classifier for end-to-end prediction of the HER2 score. This system offers a cost-effective and dependable alternative to the IHC test, facilitating the standardization of HER2 scoring and potentially improving diagnostic routines in clinical settings.

Index Terms -HER2 scoring, HE histopathology, KimiaNet, cross-attention, Breast cancer, deep learning, Feature fusion.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Breast cancer is the leading malignancy in women globally, with an estimated 46% increase in incidence by the year 2040 [1]. Improvements in screening, early diagnosis, and management have enhanced cure rates [2]. Of subtypes, HER2positive breast cancer is aggressive, characterized by early recurrence, metastasis, and poor survival. It presents in 15-25% of cases and is a key determinant of the direction of targeted therapy [3]. HER2 overexpression is an early occurrence of tumorigenesis and increases the metastatic risk by 50-80%

[4]. Currently, guidelines recommend routine HER2 testing in patients with invasive, recurrent, and metastatic breast cancers [5]. Hematoxylin-eosin (HE) staining is used for morphological tissue evaluation, while immunohistochemistry (IHC) identifies biomarkers such as HER2, estrogen (ER), and progesterone (PR) receptors [6]. IHC scoring for HER2 varies between 0 and 3+, with 0/1+ representing negative, 3+ positive, and 2+ equivocal, and subject to verification by fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) [7]. Proper HER2 assessment is essential for the selection of eligible patients for HER2-targeted therapies [8]. Timely and regular evaluations are, however, discouraged by global pathologists and diagnostic resource shortages [9], [10]. HER2 scoring is conducted according to guidelines provided by the College of American Pathologists (CAP) and the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO) to provide uniform interpretation in laboratories [7]. The criteria for scoring are in Table I. Manual HER2 determination by IHC is time-consuming and requires extensive infrastructure for handling, storage, and processing of specimens [11]. Expertise is necessary for interpretation, but it remains subject to subjectivity. Staining variability in intensity and uniformity is a source of both interobserver and intra-observer discrepancies, with inaccuracies reported to be as high as 20% [12], [13]. TABLE I IHC scores and corresponding HER2 interpretation as per American Cancer Society guidelines.. | IHC Score   | Status                     | Treatment Recommendation                                                                                                                           |
|-------------|----------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|

|             | Equivocal                  |                                                                                                                                                    |

The stained glass slides are scanned using high-resolution digital scanners to produce whole-slide images (WSIs), allowing for a close examination of cellular morphology and protein expression, which are crucial in assessing HER2. A number of computer-assisted HER2 scoring systems have been created, such as Visiopharm's Arrayimager and Automated Cell Imaging System's HER2-CONNECT TM [14]. These online platforms enhance diagnostic effectiveness and precision in scoring. Yet, they are very expensive and therefore restrict access to low-resource environments. Additionally, the majority of solutions remain reliant on human actions, introducing subjectivity and potential diagnostic errors that can impact clinical outcomes. Over the last few years, deep learning has emerged as a robust solution to overcome the shortcomings of conventional HER2 classification, enabling uniform and precise judgments by capturing subtle patterns that are beyond human vision [15] [16]. Although imaging methods such as mammography [17], CT [18], ultrasound, and MRI [19] provide diagnostic information, histopathology is still the gold standard for final breast cancer diagnosis and molecular subtyping. Existing HER2 testing through immunohistochemistry (IHC) is subject to subjectivity, with human interpretation causing interand intra-observer variability, according to research, which may lead to inconsistent scoring results of up to 20%. Furthermore, IHC is inherently time-intensive and expensive, requiring specialized reagents, skilled personnel, and specialized infrastructure, which makes it challenging to scale up in resource-limited environments. To overcome these limitations, we introduce an attentionguided multi-scale feature fusion for HER2 scoring using HEstained images, based on histopathology images trained by KimiaNet, which utilizes the DenseNet-121 architecture. ## II. RELATED STUDY

Several HER2 classification studies on histopathological images have used handcrafted features and classical classifiers. Mukundan et al. [20] extracted texture and intensity features for logistic regression and SVMs, reporting 93% and 89% accuracy, respectively. Cordova et al. [21] used statistical region descriptors and logistic regression on IHC slides, reaching 83% accuracy but only 53% HER2-positive recall.

Traditional ML methods suffer from reliance on manual feature design and limited scalability to complex image data.

Fig. 1. Sample H&E-stained image patches from the BCI dataset: (a) 0, (b) 1+, (c) 2+, (d) 3+.

<!-- image -->

Deep learning, on the other hand, can learn hierarchical features directly from HE images.

Oliveira et al. [22] used weakly-supervised CNNs with multiple-instance learning, achieving 83.3% accuracy on finetuned IHC but only 53.8% on external data. Wang et al. [23] proposed HER2-ResNet, a 38-layer model achieving 93% on four-class classification. Zheng et al. [24] introduced WPNet, a pyramid-based IHC classifier, reporting 96.98% for binary classification.

Generative methods have also emerged. Shah et al. [25] used DCGANs for data augmentation, and later explored ensemble CNNs [26], [27]. Suleman et al. [28] proposed SmartMobiNet, a MobileNet variant for skin cancer detection with 89% accuracy.

Shamai et al. [29] predicted ER/PR/HER2 from HE using ResNet with AUCs of 80%, 75%, and 74%. Tewary et al. [30], [31] used ensemble transfer learning and AutoIHCNet, achieving 98% WSI and 96% patch-level accuracy. Shovon et al. [32], [33] used Xception and DenseNet ensembles, reaching 97.12%. Mridha et al. [34] proposed convoHER2 with 85.10%. Our prior HER2-ETNET [35] utilized a weighted ensemble of CNNs, achieving 97.84% accuracy on BCI.

Despite progress, most studies focus on IHC-stained images, which require costly laboratory procedures. Few address multi-class HER2 scoring from HE-stained images under realworld class imbalance, limiting robustness and generalization.

## III. MATERIALS AND METHODS

In this section, we describe the dataset used in this study and the proposed method.

## A. Dataset

This work employs the BCI dataset [36], a HER2 classification benchmark consisting of 4870 paired IHC and H&E image patches of dimension 1024 × 1024 , cropped from 600 WSIs digitized at 0.46 µm/pixel with a Hamamatsu NanoZoomer S60. The WSI was partitioned into 16 blocks. HER2 score labels (0+, 1+, 2+, 3+) by expert labeling were labeled for H&E images based on matching IHC labels, rendering BCI the sole publicly available dataset providing four-class HER2 labels per CAP/ASCO guidelines [7].

- 1) Patch extraction and processing : To preserve critical histopathological details, each high-resolution HE-stained image ( 1024 × 1024 ) is divided into 16 non-overlapping patches of size 256 × 256 ; also, the patches with no tissue information are discarded. In contrast to general ImageNetpretrained models, KimiaNet was trained from scratch on more than 240,000 high-resolution patches (each 1000 × 1000 pixels at 20 × magnification) taken from 7,126 whole-slide images (WSIs) over about 30 types of cancer obtained from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA). The patches were judiciously chosen using a high-cellularity mosaic strategy to create morphological richness. By learning from histopathological patterns directly, KimiaNet acquires domain-specific features, such as cell structure, tissue organization, and staining patterns, which lead to improved performance in downstream tasks, including image retrieval, classification, and slide-level diagnosis. It's publicly available, and pre-trained weights offer a robust and efficient starting point for transfer learning in medical image analysis, specifically for tasks involving HEstained histopathology slides. - 3) Multi-Level Feature Representation from Dense Blocks : To obtain useful representations at different semantic levels, we utilize the results of all four Dense Blocks in KimiaNet. ## IV. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

This section presents a detailed analysis of the results obtained from the proposed attention-guided multi-scale feature fusion for HER2 scoring in HE-images.

To measure the performance of a classifier quantitatively, we used the confusion matrix to obtain several different performance measures. The most widely used evaluation metrics, Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-score, are used in this study.

The deep domain-specific transfer learning model KimiaNet utilized in this study was trained for 50 epochs on the HER2 multi-class BCI dataset. The hyperparameters were chosen based on empirical trials. In the presented framework, a learning rate scheduler was employed with an initial learning rate of 0.01, which is relatively high. The learning rate was reduced by a factor of 10 every 20 epochs. This rapid initial learning rate enables the model to take larger weight updates at the beginning of training, allowing it to converge more quickly and achieve better accuracy in fewer steps. The trajectories of accuracy during epochs are shown in Figure 3, which indicates the dynamics of learning.

As can be seen, the training and validation accuracy of the proposed model demonstrate better performance, with a training accuracy of 97.81% and a validation accuracy of 95.71%. The performance on the test set is tabulated and is as shown Table III.

## V. CONCLUSION

This new framework presents a multi-scale feature fusion model driven by attention for end-to-end automated HER2 scoring from HE-stained histopathology images. By employing a domain-specific, pre-trained model and multi-semanticlevel feature extraction, the proposed approach effectively extracts both local and global fine-grained tissue features and learns inter-scale relationships as well. Incorporating a crossattention mechanism enables more robust fusion of these multi-scale features, concentrating the model on diagnostically meaningful regions. Experimental results demonstrate improved classification accuracy and robustness over HER2 scoring classes, indicating the model's capacity to assist pathologists and enhance diagnostic consistency in breast cancer assessment. The model is based on high-quality, wellannotated histopathology datasets and may be sensitive to variations in staining protocols or scanner settings, which could potentially compromise its generalizability. Robustness will be improved through stain normalization and domain adaptation methods in future work, and the framework will be extended with explainable AI for further clinical interpretability.

Abstract -With the ever-growing exponential rise in digital platforms, user registration credibility is a critical challenge to maintain. Fake users created  with duplicated or  manipulated textual  information,  such  as  names,  emails,  and  identification numbers,  have  the  potential  to  undermine  the  security  and integrity of the platform. The current paper presents a strong fake user identification framework  that incorporates the MERN (MongoDB, Express.js,  React,  and  Node.js)  stack  for full-stack web development and the Billiards Optimized Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural  Network  (DSCNN-BilOA). It begins with a data capture module, where the user  inputs  structured  textual  information-such  as  name, email, telephone, and discretionary government ID-through a React-based  front-end.  The  input  from  the  user  is  validated and  stored  securely  in  MongoDB  prior  to  the  conversion  to numerical vectors  appropriate  for  deep  learning.  The  vectors are  passed  through  the  Depthwise  Separable  Convolutional Neural  Network  (DS-CNN)  model, which  classifies  users  into learned registration patterns. With its minimized computational  complexity  in  delivering  model  accuracy,  it  is the best choice in real-time usage. For further improvement in the detection performance, the Billiards Optimization Algorithm  (BilOA)  is employed  for  hyperparameter  finetuning. Experimental results are presented, which validate that the proposed DS-CNN-BilOA model has superior performance with 99.21% classification accuracy, 98.97% precision, 99.06% recall,  and 99.01% F1-score. Concurrently, this framework is an efficient, scalable solution to fake user identification based on  the  user  input  of  textual  data  alone-biometric  inputs unnecessary-appropriate for secure, responsive MERN-based platforms.

KeywordsBilliards Optimization Algorithm,  Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network, Fake User Identification, MERN Stack.

## I. INTRODUCTION

In  today's  digital  age,  it  is  more  evident  that  there  is  a need  to  distinguish  real  from  the  fake  users.  As  online platforms  expand,  they  make  excellent  targets  for  such fraudulent acts as impersonation, spamming, and abuse [1].

## S.Balaji

To  address  this,  there  is  a  need  to  have  a  robust  and adaptable  web  application  framework.  Among  the  most practical  frameworks  to  achieve  this  is  the  MERN  stack, which employs MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js to create dynamic and secure applications [2].

MongoDB, being a NoSQL database, provides flexibility in  the  storage  of  user-related  information,  such  as  profiles, behaviour history, and access metadata. Express.js is a lightweight web application framework for Node.js that facilitates  efficient  server-side  logic  and  API  (Application Programming  Interface)  development.  React.js  is  an  opensource front-end JavaScript library that facilitates development  of  interactive  and  real-time  user  interfaces,  a necessity in verifying user activity and feedback. Node.js, in its  role  as  a  runtime  environment,  effectively  processes asynchronous requests and background activities [3].

Positioning  data-driven  sophisticated  mechanisms  atop this  stack  enables  the  analysis  of  usage  patterns,  device fingerprints,  and  history  to  mark  suspicious  behavior  [4]. Such insight enables developers to detect anomalies that can indicate the presence of bot  users  - like  frequent account creations from a single IP address, aberrant usage patterns, or form input consistency anomalies [5].

With  the  increasing  demand  for  secure  and  trusted platforms,  integrating  user  verification  procedures  into  a MERN solution is preventive and remedial [6]. As identity verification  overlays  or  behavioural  monitoring  modules, the  MERN stack provides an elastic and extensible canvas upon which to effectively detect and prevent malicious users and uphold platform integrity and trust.

## Contributions:

- The system integrates the MERN stack to create a scalable, real-time platform that collects and manages structured user registration data.
- A Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network (DS-CNN) processes the encoded textual

- data to detect anomalies and identify fake or duplicated user patterns with high efficiency.
- The  DS-CNN  architecture  reduces  computational complexity  and  enables  fast  inference,  making  it suitable for real-time web-based classification tasks.
- To maximize detection accuracy and model performance, the Billiards Optimization Algorithm (BilOA) fine-tunes hyperparameters, ensuring optimal  learning  configurations  through  collision inspired metaheuristic search.
- The  combined  DS-CNN  and  BilOA  framework enables the system to accurately distinguish between  genuine  and  fake  users,  enhancing  the security  and  trustworthiness  of  digital  platforms without requiring facial or biometric verification.

The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents a review  on  related  works;  Section  3  details  the  proposed methodology;  Section  4  presents  results  and  discussions; and Section 5 concludes the paper.

## II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Among various applications of MERN stack, few related works were listed below:

In  2021,  Alisha,  M.,  et  al.  [7],  have  introduced  a  deep learning (DL)-based model for recognizing traffic signs and providing real-time auditory alerts to drivers through Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The system identified various road signs and converted them into voice notifications,  enhancing  driver  awareness  and  road  safety. Built using the MERN stack integrated with DL models, the method  improved  accident  prevention  by  reducing  driver distraction.  However,  limitations  included  dependency  on high-quality  input  images,  possible  misclassifications  in poor  lighting,  and  computational  overhead  for  real-time processing.

In  2023,  Cam, N.T. et al. [8], have developed In 2023, Cam,  N.T.  et  al.  [8]  developed  a  machine  learning-based framework called UIT-DGADetector for detecting domains generated by algorithms (DGA), commonly used by botnets to circumvent traditional security mechanisms. This framework  incorporated  bigram  analysis,  long  short-term memory networks (LSTM), and a hybrid LSTM with onehot encoding, enhanced through an ensemble classification mechanism. To manage and balance traffic, Kafka was used for efficient request queuing, while the  MERN  stack supported the system's deployment. The model demonstrated  high  detection  accuracy;  however,  it  showed reduced effectiveness against word-based DGA botnets and exhibited queue latency that warranted further optimization.

In 2025, Hapsari, K.N.C., et al. [9], have examined the utilization of the MERN stack in developing an online quiz platform to identify and counteract the influence of misleading content disseminated via social networking platforms.  The  research  utilized  qualitative  data  gathering methods and utilized Scrum method to build the system in incremental chunks. The strengths were increased flexibility,  cross-platform  compatibility,  and  a  consistent JavaScript environment, whereas weaknesses were inflexible  sprint  frameworks  and  possible  user  interaction issues.

In  2025,  Ahsan,  R.,  et  al.  [10],  have  suggested  the development of a comprehensive end-to-end recommendation  system  tailored  for  crowdsourced  road monitoring applications using machine learning (ML). The article  tackled  significant  crowdsourcing-related  problems, such  as  low  or  biased  feedback,  by  using  a  multi-stage validation  process  for  the  data.  Modular  features  were facilitated using a client-server multi-tiered architecture and the  MERN  stack.  Flexibility,  prediction  using  regression through  cloud  computing,  and  numerical  user  feedback support were the benefits, but reliance on the quality of user input and network latency were major drawbacks.

## Problem Statement

This  growing  dependence  on  user-generated  content  in web apps has given rise to fake users, largely affecting the authenticity  and  trustworthiness  of  online  platforms.  The problem is to identify and filter the fake users accurately, as the  latter  are  highly  adept  at  easily  manipulating  systems through  spam,  misinformation,  or  malicious  attacks.  The problem  is addressed through the creation of a  more advanced  identification  system  for  fake  users  using  the MERN stack for complete full-stack development, coupled with deep learning techniques to carry out both behavioral and  content-based  analysis.  The  platform  is  designed  to detect anomalies in user behavior, providing secure, scalable,  and  efficient  real-time  user  authentication  and upholding the integrity of the platform.

## III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The proposed methodology integrates  the  MERN  stack with  cutting-edge  deep  learning  for  accurate  identification and prevention of fake or duplicate user registrations. First, ordered  text  data  is  obtained  from  users  in  a  secure  web interface and saved in MongoDB. This is then analyzed with a Depthwise Separable Convolutional Neural Network (DSCNN), which effectively detects suspicious patterns in user input.  To  refine  detection  precision,  the  DS-CNN  is  finetuned with the Billiards Optimization Algorithm (BilOA), a metaheuristic  billiard  ball-inspired  algorithm.  This  method guarantees  a  lightweight,  efficient,  and  dependable  system that  is  able  to  verify  users  in  real  time  without  biometric inputs. Figure 1 presents the blocked diagram of the proposed methodology.

Fig.1. Block Diagram of DS-CNN-BilOA Framework

## A. Data Collection

The  system  begins  with  the  Data  Collection  phase, where it collects and authenticates structured text input from users.  When  a  user  uses  the  web  application  developed using React.js (the front-end part of the MERN stack), they need  to  register  or  login  by  filling  a  form  with  necessary information  like  full  name,  username,  email  ID,  phone number, and optionally, government-approved identification numbers  (such  as  an  Aadhaar  number,  national  ID,  etc.). This data is fed into well-structured fields that are validated on  the  client  side  through  schema  validation  to  confirm format accuracy. Once valid verification, the validated data is securely stored in a MongoDB database in JSON format.

This  collected  data  is  then  processed  for  Fake  User Identification  using  the  MERN  Stack  and  a  Depthwise Separable  Convolutional  Neural  Network  (DS-CNN).  DSCNN is selected  over  traditional  CNNs  due  to  its  reduced computational complexity and lower memory usage, making it  highly  efficient  for  real-time  user  classification  on  webbased platforms

## ClearFlow: Deep Learning-Based Fluency Enhancer for Stuttered Speech

Suketha Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management, Mangaluru, and Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India suketha.bcroad@gmail.com Vrinda U N Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management, Mangaluru, and Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India vrindaun@gmail.com

## Brundha Hegde

Sahyadri College of Engineering & Management, Mangaluru, and Affiliated to Visvesvaraya Technological University, Belagavi, Karnataka, India hegdebrundha@gmail.com

Abstract -Stuttering, a common speech disorder, disrupts the smooth flow of communication, often undermining an individual's self-confidence and social engagement. While conventional speech therapy methods provide effective intervention, they frequently fall short in terms of accessibility, affordability, and the ability to offer immediate corrective feedback. In this work, we present ClearFlow, a deep learning-driven fluency enhancement system capable of detecting and addressing stuttering patterns such as repetitions, prolongations, and speech blocks in real-time scenarios. The system employs a hybrid architecture combining Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) for acoustic feature extraction and Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks for modeling temporal speech sequences. Furthermore, ClearFlow incorporates Delayed Auditory Feedback (DAF) and Altered Auditory Feedback (AAF) mechanisms to deliver realtime, context-sensitive corrections through auditory and visual prompts. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets like UCLASS and FluencyBank demonstrates an overall detection accuracy of 89.2, maintaining reliable performance even in noisy environments. ClearFlow offers a portable and scalable solution, making fluency enhancement tools more inclusive and widely accessible.

Keywords -Stuttering, Speech Fluency, Deep Learning, RealTime Feedback, CNN-BiLSTM, Assistive Technology.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Speech is a primary way humans communicate thoughts, feelings, and ideas. For most people, speaking fluently is a natural process. However, for individuals who stutter, producing smooth and uninterrupted speech can be a daily struggle.Stuttering is a speech disorder that causes disruptions such as repeating sounds or words, stretching sounds for too long,or suddenly blocking speech altogether. These

interruptions can make communication difficult and lead to frustration,embarrassment, and social withdrawal [1].

Beyond just affecting speech, stuttering often has a significant emotional and psychological impact on individuals. Many people who stutter experience low self-confidence, anxiety, and avoid situations where they need to speak. This can affect their personal lives, academic performance, career opportunities,and overall quality of life. Addressing stuttering is not only about improving how a person speaks but also about helping them regain confidence and participate fully in society [2].

Speech therapy has been the most common method used to manage stuttering. Therapists work with individuals to practice speaking techniques, improve breathing control, and reduce disfluencies over time. While effective for some, these therapies have certain limitations. Regular sessions are costly and require consistent attendance, which is not always possible for individuals in remote or underprivileged areas. Moreover, therapy often lacks real-time feedback, meaning individuals do not receive corrective cues while speaking in everyday situations [3].

With advancements in technology, there is now a growing possibility to assist people who stutter using intelligent systems. [8] [34], [36], [38] Artificial Intelligence (AI) and deep learning have shown great promise in analyzing speech patterns, detecting irregularities, and offering instant feedback. These technologies can support individuals in real-time, even outside clinical settings, making therapy more accessible and practical [4],

In this paper, we introduce ClearFlow, a deep learningbased fluency enhancer designed to detect and correct stuttering patterns as they happen. ClearFlow uses a combination of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) to extract important features from speech and Bi-directional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks to understand how speech patterns change over time. [28], [33] This combination allows the system to accurately identify disfluencies like repetitions, prolongations,and blocks during real conversations [5].

One of ClearFlow's key features is its real-time feedback system. Unlike traditional therapy that provides feedback after a session, ClearFlow gives immediate auditory and visual cues when a stuttering event is detected. [35] It uses Delayed Auditory Feedback (DAF) and Altered Auditory Feedback (AAF) techniques, which are proven methods to help reduce stuttering. [9]These cues guide the user to adjust their speech fluency on the spot, making the learning process more effective and interactive.

ClearFlow is designed to be lightweight and portable. It can run on smartphones and making it accessible to individuals who may not have access to traditional therapy. Whether at home, school, or work, users can carry ClearFlow with them and benefit from real-time fluency support wherever they are. This portability ensures that fluency enhancement is not limited to clinical settings but is available during daily conversations.

In addition to helping correct speech in real time, ClearFlow also keeps track of a user's progress. It records information about how often stuttering events occur and provides detailed reports that can be shared with speech therapists. As technology keeps evolving, ClearFlow has the potential to become even better. Future versions of the system could include userspecific customization, learning to adapt to person's unique speaking style. Support for multiple languages and more advanced feedback features could also be added.ClearFlow represents a big step towards making speech therapy tools more accessible,practical, and empowering for people who stutter, helping them gain confidence and communicate more freely [6].

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Recently, researchers have shown increasing interest in applying artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning to support speech therapy. One of the key focus areas has been stuttering, a disorder that causes unintentional disruptions in speech like repeating words, stretching out sounds, or sudden pauses. This section reviews important studies that have worked on using deep learning models to analyze speech and provide corrective feedback, with the aim of improving fluency in real time.

## 1.Early Clinical and Behavioral Research

Early research focused on how stuttering affects not just speech but also emotional well-being. Vanryckeghem et al. [22] observed that children who stutter tend to develop negative self-perceptions. Menzies et al. [21] highlighted that many adults who stutter also experience social anxiety, recommending Cognitive behav ior therapy (CBT) as a supportive therapy. Kelman and Nicholas [20]introduced the Palin Parent-Child Interaction(PCI) approach, involving parents in early treatment to create a more supportive environment. These studies laid the groundwork for treating stuttering as both a speech and psychological condition.

## 2. Deep Learning Models for Disfluency Detection

Deep learning has brought a new level of efficiency and accuracy to the detection of stuttering patterns. [10], [11], [13], [18], [24] Abubakar et al. [1] introduced StutterNet, which uses a combination of convolutional and recurrent networks to identify speech disfluencies from audio features. While the approach is effective, its performance depends heavily on the quality and balance of the dataset used. [30], [37] Kourkounakis et al. [2] proposed FluentNet, which combines deep learning layers with attention mechanisms to better focus on the important parts of speech. This helped improve the system's ability to detect different types of stuttering in natural conversations.More recently, Liu et al. [17] used wav2vec2.0 and transformers to capture deeper context from speech. Their model can handle variations in language and speech length, making it more adaptable to real-world situations.

## 3. Multimodal and Context-Aware Modeling

Contextual and multimodal modeling has become essential in differentiating between fluent and disfluent speech. Mohapatra et al. [26] introduced DisfluencyNet, which utilized contextual embeddings and improved data labeling techniques for better detection. Wagner et al. [29] combined acoustic features with large language models (LLMs) trained on ASR hypotheses for multi-label classification of disfluencies in English and German.Romana et al. [27] focused on acousticonly models and demonstrated that such systems could outperform text-dependent ones in noisy environments, making them viable for real-world applications where accurate transcripts are not always available. [23], [31]

## 4. Feedback Systems for Stuttering Correction

Arjun K. N. et al. [14] proposed a signal processing-based system that not only detects but also corrects disfluencies The system uses MFCC and LPC features along with energybased thresholding to achieve high accuracy with minimal delay, making it suitable for time-sensitive applications. Suttarwala et al. [4] developed an IoT-enabled wearable device that integrates sensors and machine learning models (SVM and CNN) to detect stuttering patterns and deliver real-time auditory feedback.

## 5. Limitations in Existing Studies

Several systems have been developed to detect stuttering, but many still face real-world limitations. Models that perform well in controlled environments often struggle with background noise, varied accents, or spontaneous speech. A common challenge is the lack of standardized, balanced datasets, which makes it harder to detect less frequent stuttering patterns like blocks or silent pauses. Most tools focus only on detection and don't provide real-time feedback. [12], [16], [19], [25],

[32] Even when feedback is offered, these systems typically rely on high-end devices or strong internet connections, limiting their use on mobile or low-resource platforms. [7]

## 6. Summary and Research Gap

Although deep learning-based stuttering detection has shown promising results, most existing systems fall short in terms of real-time performance, contextual accuracy, and mobile readiness. This study addresses these gaps by:

- 1) Utilizing balanced and labeled datasets for robust model training.
- 2) Implementing and evaluating both CNN and BiLSTM architectures for disfluency classification.
- 3) Integrating real-time feedback mechanisms such as DAF and AAF.
- 4) Optimizing the system for deployment on smartphones to enhance accessibility.

These datasets provided a wide variety of speech recordings, including different types of stuttering events like repetitions, prolongations, and blocks. The diversity of speakers in terms of age, gender, and accents ensured that the system would be able to generalize well to real-world scenarios. ## C. Audio Preprocessing and Feature Extraction

- Noise Reduction : Remove unwanted background sounds to ensure clarity of speech signals.
- Feature Computation (MFCCs) : Extract MelFrequency Cepstral Coefficients to capture essential frequency characteristics.
- Additional Features (Pitch & Energy) : Extract pitch variation and energy levels to provide dynamic speech patterns.

Noise is eliminated to ensure only relevant speech information is retained. The cleaned audio is then transformed into numerical features, primarily through Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCCs), which effectively capture the key frequency components of speech.

## D. Model Architecture Design (CNN-BiLSTM)

- CNN Layers for Feature Extraction : Capture localized patterns in spectrograms, such as frequency peaks indicating disfluencies.
- BiLSTM Layers for Sequence Learning : Analyze temporal dependencies and context in speech sequences.
- End-to-End Hybrid Architecture : Enable the system to learn spatial and sequential speech features for accurate detection.

The CNN-BiLSTM model consists of three convolutional layers with filter sizes of 64, 128, and 256, each followed by a ReLU activation and max-pooling operation. These layers extract spatial and frequency-related features from the MFCC input. The output feature maps are then flattened and passed into a Bi-LSTM layer with 128 hidden units in each direction to capture temporal dependencies in both forward and backward contexts.The final dense layer with a softmax activation outputs class probabilities corresponding to the stuttering types like repetition, prolongation, and block. Dropout layers with a rate of 0.3 are used to prevent overfitting, and batch normalization is applied after each convolutional block to stabilize training.

## E. Training Strategy

Once the model architecture was finalized, the training phase involved feeding the CNN-BiLSTM model with annotated examples of fluent and stuttered speech. Data augmentation techniques such as modifying pitch and stretching time sequences were applied to improve model generalization. After training, the model's accuracy and reliability were assessed using a separate test set. Performance metrics like Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1-Score were used for evaluation. ClearFlow achieved an overall detection accuracy of 89.2%.The model was trained for 50 epochs using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.001 and categorical crossentropy as the loss function. The dataset was divided into 70% training, 20% validation, and 10% testing splits. Early stopping was implemented to prevent overfitting by monitoring validation loss. Data augmentation techniques, including pitch shifting, time-stretching, and noise injection, were applied to improve model generalization,robustness against real-world variations.

## F. Evaluation and Deployment

- Feedback Mechanisms (DAF & AAF) : Provide auditory corrections via Delayed and Altered Auditory Feedback.
- Visual Feedback Interface : Display real-time visual prompts to assist users during speech.
- Portable Deployment : Optimize system to run on mobile devices and embedded platforms like Raspberry Pi.

When a stuttering event is detected, ClearFlow activates the real-time correction module that is DAF and AAF techniques. In the DAF mechanism, the user's speech is played back to them with a short delay of 200 ms, which encourages slower , controlled speech production. The AAF module simultaneously alters the pitch of the feedback by ± 10%, helping users monitor their speech rhythm and articulation more consciously. The corrections are delivered through headphones or speakers with minimal latency (under 100 ms), ensuring that feedback aligns closely with live speech.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

models. The CNN-BiLSTM model converged steadily, with both training and validation accuracy improving over time. The validation accuracy closely followed the training curve, which indicates good generalization and little overfitting. The loss curves supported this, showing a consistent decline in both training and validation losses throughout the epochs. In contrast, the CNN-only model started to overfit around the 30th epoch. This is evident from the increasing gap between training and validation loss. paper_id: ClearFlow Deep Learning-Based Fluency Enhancer for Stuttered Speech
text:
## C. Result Discussion and Feedback Validation

The results clearly demonstrate that the proposed CNN-BiLSTM model performs significantly better than the baseline CNN, BiLSTM, and SVM models, achieving an overall accuracy of 89.2%. The CNN layers effectively capture short-term acoustic variations such as pitch peaks, pauses, and sudden energy changes, while BiLSTM layers model the temporal flow of speech, allowing the system to distinguish between similar-sounding but temporally different disfluencies such as repetitions and prolongations.The confusion matrices further confirm that ClearFlow maintains balanced accuracy, with fewer misclassifications compared to single-model approaches. The steady convergence of both training and validation curves indicates that the model doesn't overfit, which validates the effectiveness of the applied data augmentation and training strategies.Therefore it provides a reliable and efficient foundation for real-time stuttering detection in assistive speech technologies.

To evaluate the practical performance of ClearFlow's realtime feedback system, preliminary DAF and AAF modules was conducted using pre-recorded disfluent speech samples from the UCLASS dataset. In this setup, a delay of 200 ms was applied for DAF, and a pitch alteration of ± 10% was used for AAF both parameters are widely recognized in clinical speech therapy for improving fluency. The feedback response latency averaged 85 ms, ensuring that corrective cues were delivered almost instantaneously after stuttering events were detected. Informal testing with a small group of participants suggested noticeable improvement in speech rhythm and reduced frequency of repetitions when the feedback mechanisms were active. Although this small study was limited in scope, the results indicate that the integrated feedback module operates effectively and is suitable for real-time use.

## D. Future Integration Plan

To improve the robustness and predictive accuracy, future work will explore a hybrid ensemble strategy. This will combine the fast convergence and localized feature extraction of CNNs with the sequence modeling abilities of BiLSTMs and other advanced architectures, the system could better adapt to different speaking styles, disfluency patterns, and acoustic conditions. Techniques like weighted majority voting or stacked generalization may help the model make more reliable predictions, especially in edge cases or noisy situations. Optimization-based speech enhancement methods, such as those by Mishra et al. [15], have demonstrated that parameter tuning can further improve the fluency correction performance of speech recognition systems.This ensemble approach also enables more reliable real-time deployment on mobile and embedded devices, making the technology easier to access in resource-limited or remote areas. These improvements would support ClearFlow's long-term goal of providing effective, portable, and user-friendly speech fluency support for people who stutter.

## V. APPLICATION OF THE PROPOSED IDEA

The proposed ClearFlow system enables users to communicate their thoughts clearly to others, reducing speech interruptions, and improving overall fluency. The model can be applied to real-world scenarios, such as classrooms, workplaces, and therapy sessions, to improve communication confidence. It can also be deployed on mobile and IoT-based platforms, supporting both home and clinical applications. Its portability, low latency, and real-time feedback promote a continuous and accessible fluency enhancement.

## VI. CONCLUSION

This study presents a practical and innovative approach to detecting stuttering patterns in speech using deep learning techniques. By evaluating both a baseline CNN and a hybrid CNN-BiLSTM architecture, we showed that adding temporal context significantly improves model performance. The CNNBiLSTM model achieved an accuracy of 89.2 percent, outperforming the CNN's 84.3 percent. This result highlights its ability to capture the dynamic and sequential nature of disfluent speech. Our method is non-invasive, cost-effective, and designed for realtime deployment. This makes it suitable for mobile platforms,home-based therapy tools, and low-resource clinical settings.Despite these promising results, challenges such as differences between speakers and background noise still exist. Future work will focus on increasing the diversity of the dataset, exploring ensemble learning to boost generalization, and optimizing the system for low-power, edge devices. Despite these promising results, limitations such as the small dataset size, need for comprehensive statistical validation, and refinement of the real-time feedback mechanisms remain areas of ongoing work, which will further enhance ClearFlow's contribution to assistive AI systems for speech fluency improvement.

Abstract -Cross-border remittances are important sources of financial support for families, especially in developing countries, facilitating access to basic human necessities like education and healthcare. In spite of their stability through international crises like COVID-19, and India being the largest recipient in 2024, conventional remittance systems based on SWIFT and Correspondent Banking persist with high costs, lagged processing times, and low transparency. This paper suggests a blockchainbased remittance platform that overcomes these limitations by removing intermediaries, facilitating real-time peer-to-peer transfer through automation of smart contracts. The platform makes use of stablecoins to provide volatility resistance. Secure custodial wallets, as well as strict KYC/AML compliance, provide user authentication and regulatory compliance. The designed architecture improves speed, lowers the cost of transactions, and provides regulatory trust-showing a scalable, secure, and inclusive alternative to traditional remittance systems.

Keywords -KYC/AML, Decentralized Finance, Digital Wallets, Financial Inclusion, Regulatory Compliance

## I. INTRODUCTION

There has been a surge in the growth of Cross-Border Remittance and the global remittance market in recent times, owing to several factors, namely the rise in global migration, the Growth of Digital Payment Systems & Fintech, and the Rise in high-income destinations and strong labour markets, and growth in the gig economy and remote work. For a significant chunk of the population in developing countries, remittances from abroad contribute to a considerable part of their financial standing. 'Remittance' refers to money sent across different countries to individuals, families or businesses. For some low-income countries, these funds account for over 10-15% of their annual GDP. India comes up as one of the top recipients of international remittances. And according to the World Bank, India was the world's largest recipient of international remittances in 2024. India received an estimated $129.1 billion in 2024, which was 14.3% of the world's total remittances [1]. This was the highest amount ever received by any country in a single year.
