## V. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE

The  EchoSpeech  system  is  an  intersection  of  advanced technology and universal instructional design specifically for kids with autism and language difficulties. In integrating  speech  recognition,  feedback  mechanisms  in real  time,  and  interactive  gamified  interfaces,  the  system confronts  major  limitations  of  typical  speech  therapy methods. While regular methods are typically premised on repetitive, teacher moderated practice with minimal participation, EchoSpeech provides a responsive and selfdirected  learning  platform  with  encouraging  sustained interest and participation among children.

Moreover, the system's design prioritizes user accessibility and  personalization,  ensuring  it  can  be  adapted  to  suit individual learning curves and speech development levels. The feedback loop characterized by multiple pronunciation attempts and granular error analysis not only supports skill acquisition  but  also  facilitates  a  positive  reinforcement cycle.  Parents  and  therapists  are  empowered  through actionable insights and progress tracking features, enhancing their ability to support children effectively. By integrating educational content with interactive technology, EchoSpeech lays the groundwork for broader applications in special education and therapeutic interventions.

As  a future development,  Integration of multilingual support for children with a wide  range  of  language backgrounds  can  be  done.  With  the  use  of  multilingual speech  models  and  pronunciation  databases  specific  to languages, the system would be able to provide testing and feedback in native and second languages.

Abstract -The rapid growth of genomic data poses difficulties in storing and transferring information efficiently. This study offers a comparison of two methods of compression-Huffman Coding and Arithmetic Coding-when used on DNA sequences. Huffman Coding uses a Binary Search Tree (BST) approach for optimal prefix codes, whereas Arithmetic Coding compresses data based on probability ranges. Results from experiments indicate that both techniques decrease memory usage but differ in compression ratio, memory footprint, and computational complexity. Huffman Coding achieves a compression ratio of 0.25 and faster encoding, while Arithmetic Coding reaches 0.051, offering finer compression granularity. This comparison emphasizes the balance between compression efficiency and processing speed with implications for bioinformatics applications.

Index Terms -Huffman Encoding, Arithmetic Encoding, DNA compression, Data Structures Samiksha Nalawade Dept. of Electronics & Telecommunication Vishwakarma Institute of Information Technology Pune, India samiksha.22311696@viit.ac.in

## Minal Deshmukh

Asst. Professor, Dept. of Electronics & Telecommunication Vishwakarma Institute of Information Technology Pune, India minal.deshmukh@viit.ac.in

on nucleotide frequency and probability data to achieve better results. The research investigates how Huffman Coding and Arithmetic Coding perform when used to compress DNA sequences. The Binary Search Tree (BST)-based Huffman implementation generates an optimal prefix-free binary tree from nucleotide frequency data, and Arithmetic Coding assigns probability intervals to each nucleotide. The evaluation of different genomic datasets assesses how well the methods compress data through their ability to reduce size and their impact on system resources and processing speed. The results show that Huffman Coding provides faster encoding times, but Arithmetic Coding produces better compression ratios when dealing with datasets containing uneven nucleotide distributions.

## I. INTRODUCTION

The fast development of next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies has created an unprecedented surge in genomic data production. The growing availability of sequencing technology creates storage challenges for bioinformatics specialists and their systems. The growing need for storage space and data transfer speed requires efficient compression methods to solve these problems. The four nucleotide bases of adenine (A) and cytosine (C) and guanine (G) and thymine (T) in genomic sequences show repetitive patterns which scientists can use for data compression. The current DNA sequence compression methods Gzip and Bzip2, fail to optimise their performance for DNA sequence data. The two lossless compression methods, Huffman Coding and Arithmetic Coding, base their operations This research evaluates Huffman coding against Arithmetic coding for DNA sequence compression, as presented in this paper. Our main contribution involves a detailed performance assessment, which demonstrates how data structure design affects memory usage by showing Arithmetic Coding requires 64-bit fixed memory space, but Huffman coding produces variable-length binary output. The research establishes a precise quantitative relationship between these two methods. The research evaluates system performance through three essential metrics, which include data compression efficiency and system resource usage and processing speed. The results demonstrate that Huffman Coding operates at higher speeds for encoding, but Arithmetic Coding produces better compression results when dealing with datasets containing uneven nucleotide frequency patterns. The research adds value to bioinformatics through its evaluation of these methods together, with their advantages and limitations for enhancing genomic data storage and transfer in extensive research initiatives. The paper follows this organisation.

The first section of Section II reviews existing DNA compression methods and their current state of development. The proposed system description in Section III demonstrates how DNA compression works through Huffman and Arithmetic Encoding methods. The memory analysis and compression efficiency are presented in Section IV. The algorithm's performance and accuracy evaluation occur in Section V through DNA decoding back to its original state. The research evaluates both methods for DNA compression through their achieved performance levels and decoding precision in Section VI. The paper ends with Section VII.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Gurunathan et al. [1] developed an advanced index-based DNA sequence compression system. The system organizes data through an indexed structure which enables fast access to genetic information while delivering superior storage efficiency than conventional methods.

Ali Hassan et al. [2] developed the ArthNgram model through the combination of N-gram language modeling with arithmetic coding. The model improves storage efficiency and compression speed through sequence-based word encoding which benefits large-scale and IoT applications.

Babita Kumari et al. [3] developed Adaptive Huffman compression through text clustering and multi-character modification techniques. The method solves previous method restrictions through its ability to decrease data redundancy and generate enhanced compression ratios.

Hussein et al. [4] studied RGB image data hiding through genetic algorithms and Huffman coding. The research demonstrates Huffman coding's ability to work with different structured data types including genomic sequences.

Alosta and Souri [5] developed a lossless DNA compression system which uses Huffman encoding for data compression. The system supports multiple DNA sequences and maintains data integrity while achieving high compression efficiency.

Sarkar and Ashrafi [6] created a system which combines machine learning with arithmetic encoding to detect genomic patterns while achieving superior compression results than conventional methods.

Gomathi et al. [7] combined Run-Length Encoding (RLE) with Huffman coding for their hybrid compression method. The hybrid method successfully compresses sequences with repeated nucleotides by outperforming standalone compression methods.

Ganapathy [8] developed an IT reduction-based DNA compression system which optimizes genomic data storage through redundancy reduction and data preservation. The method shows promising results for genomic data storage optimization.

Zhao et al. [9] improved Huffman encoding through a pregrouping process for similar genomic regions which resulted in enhanced compression ratios and faster encoding times for large DNA datasets.

Mishra et al. [10] developed the Minimum Variance Huffman Tree (MVHT) which optimizes traditional Huffman trees by minimizing code-length variance to achieve better compression for uneven nucleotide distributions.

Pulova-Mihaylova et al. [11] built a web-based DNA compression platform which uses Huffman and Shannon-Fano encoding with uniform coding for enhanced performance enhancement and bioinformatics tool integration.

Jahaan et al. [12] examined the requirement for lossless data compression in genomics through their review of Biocompress and DNACompress tools which focus on efficient storage of repetitive patterns.

Machhi and Patel [13] performed a research study to evaluate LZW and RLE and arithmetic coding and substitution methods for data compression. The researchers discovered that arithmetic coding delivered the highest performance results across different species.

Ghoshdastider and Saha [14] developed GenomeCompress which successfully handles both repetitive and non-repetitive DNA sequences through a five-bit encoding system to achieve a low bits-per-base ratio.

Behzadi and Le Fessant [15] developed DNAPack which uses dynamic programming to find approximate repeats and complementary palindromes for DNA compression with competitive results.

Xu et al. [16] conducted a detailed evaluation, which showed that Arithmetic Coding outperformed Huffman Coding by 12.3% in compression efficiency but required 2.8 times more time for encoding. This research establishes the essential relationship between encoding speed and compression ratio, which serves as a foundation for our current work.

Xu et al. [17] extended Huffman encoding through kmers and RLE pre-processing to boost symbol variance which results in better-than-expected compression ratios.

The Hybrid Adaptive DNA Compression (HADC) algorithm developed by Elnady et al. [18] combines referencebased methods with general compression techniques for nondivergent species but performs poorly with de novo and highly diverse genomes.

Diss and Pradas [19] used advanced predictive models including Deep Neural Networks to feed the Arithmetic Coder which produced state-of-the-art compression ratios but required excessive processing time.

## III. PROPOSED SYSTEM

The system described in Figure 2 uses Huffman Encoding and Arithmetic Coding to achieve efficient DNA sequence compression. The system accepts DNA sequences from users that contain the nucleotides A, C, G and T.

The system determines nucleotide occurrence rates during its first operational stage. The system uses these frequency values to construct a Huffman Tree through a process that unites the two least frequent nucleotides until it creates a binary tree with distinct Huffman codes for each nucleotide (Fig- ure 1). The system uses Huffman codes to encode the DNA sequence which results in substantial memory reduction for storage needs. The system determines memory consumption and compression efficiency for Huffman Encoding through a comparison between the original sequence and its compressed version.

The system uses Arithmetic Coding in its second stage to determine nucleotide probabilities which result in specific frequency-based intervals. The system converts the DNA sequence into a single floating-point value which falls inside the total interval that encompasses all nucleotides from the sequence. The system determines memory consumption and compression efficiency for Arithmetic Coding while showing results against Huffman Encoding performance.

The system uses a modular design to execute Huffman and Arithmetic coding methods for DNA sequence compression which minimises memory requirements and supports biological data storage and transmission operations. The system determines encoding time for both methods which makes it appropriate for genomic data analysis and storage and transmission applications in real-time.

## A.

## Algorithm

The algorithm outlines the process of DNA sequence compression using both Huffman and Arithmetic coding techniques. It begins with the initialization phase, where a node

Fig. 1: Construction of Huffman Tree

<!-- image -->

structure is created for each nucleotide, containing frequency and left/right child pointers.The system starts with the initialization phase which establishes a node structure for each nucleotide to store frequency data and left/right child pointers. The HuffmanBST class contains essential data structures which include frequency maps and Huffman codes and node lists and probability maps and arithmetic coding interval data. The system requires users to provide a DNA sequence for processing. The system examines each character in the input sequence to determine nucleotide frequencies which get stored in the frequency map. The system uses frequency data to build nodes for each nucleotide before it merges the two nodes with lowest frequency into new parent nodes until it reaches a single root node which represents the Huffman tree. The system uses Huffman tree traversal to create binary Huffman codes for each nucleotide which get stored in the Huffman codes map. The system applies Huffman codes to the DNA sequence for binary compression which results in a compressed string. The system determines DNA sequence memory usage by calculating 8 bits per character for the original sequence and by counting bits in the Huffman-encoded string for the encoded sequence before showing memory statistics and compression efficiency.It also measures the time taken for the Huffman coding process.

Fig. 2: Workflow of System

<!-- image -->

For arithmetic coding, the system calculates the probability of occurrence for each nucleotide and computes cumulative intervals to be used in the encoding process. It sets the initial range [low, high] to [0.0, 1.0] and, for each nucleotide in the sequence, updates the range based on its corresponding interval. The final encoded value is the midpoint between the low and high values. The system determines memory usage for arithmetic coding through a comparison between the original sequence length and the encoded floating-point value size which equals the double precision bit size. The system displays the compression ratio after completing the calculation. The system records the duration of arithmetic coding operations. The program generates Huffman codes and DNA sequence encodings and displays memory consumption and both compression efficiency metrics and complete processing duration.

## IV. MEMORY ANALYSIS AND COMPRESSION EFFICIENCY

The evaluation of Huffman and Arithmetic coding implementations used synthetic DNA sequences for performance assessment. The synthetic approach allowed us to remove biological pattern influence while testing the core compression algorithms and their data structures independently. The evaluation used two test sequences which included a 24-nucleotide short sequence (Ex 1) and a 156-nucleotide long sequence (Ex 2). The Huffman-based Binary Search Tree (BST) used nucleotide frequency to generate optimal prefix codes while Arithmetic coding used probability intervals for encoding. The evaluation assessed both methods through their memory usage and their ability to compress data. The Huffman coding system delivered substantial memory reductions through its efficient sequence compression process that required minimal computational effort. The processing time for Arithmetic coding exceeded Huffman coding but delivered comparable compression performance.

## A. Memory Usage

The evaluation of compression efficiency requires a comparison between the storage needs of the original DNA sequence and its compressed version. The space reduction analysis through encoding techniques demonstrates the algorithm's ability to minimize storage needs.

Input Memory: Each character in the DNA sequence (8 bits for ASCII) contributes to the total memory requirement, as shown in Equation 1.

Memory Input = Length of DNA sequence × 8 bits (1)

Output Memory: The length of the encoded string determines the memory used by the Huffman encoded sequence, as defined in Equation 2.

Memory Output = Length of encoded DNA bits (2)

The analysis includes two specific cases to show actual memory reduction performance. The first example uses Huffman encoding to compress a 24-nucleotide DNA sequence through both methods. The memory needs for the original sequence amount to 24 × 8 = 192 bits. The Huffman encoding process reduced the binary sequence length to 48 bits which achieved a compression ratio of 0.25. The final encoded value requires 64 bits of storage as a double precision number which produces a compression ratio of 0.33.

The analysis includes a 156-nucleotide DNA sequence as its second example. The sequence requires 1248 bits to store its original data. The Huffman encoding process generates a 312-bit binary output which achieves a 0.25 compression ratio. Huffman encoding produces a compressed binary output occupying 312 bits, again yielding a compression ratio of 0 . 25 . Arithmetic encoding, however, still requires only 64 bits to represent the final encoded value, which corresponds to a much lower compression ratio of approximately 0.0512. This is a critical finding: Arithmetic Coding compresses the entire sequence into a single, fixed-length 64-bit double-precision floating-point number. For the longer sequence (Ex 2, 1248 bits original size), this constant memory footprint leads to a vastly superior compression ratio of approximately 0.051

The examples show that Huffman encoding works best for short DNA sequences because it produces compressed data that requires fewer than 64 bits. The method provides better performance for short sequences because it operates quickly and maintains simple operations. The method provides better performance for longer sequences because it produces fixedlength compressed data that stays within 64 bits. Despite requiring more computational resources, arithmetic encoding tends to produce better compression ratios for longer or more complex sequences. Therefore, the choice of encoding method should be guided by the sequence size and the desired trade-off between speed and compression efficiency.

Table I summarizes the memory requirements and compression ratios obtained from two DNA sequence examples. The compression results indicate that Huffman coding provides consistent ratios The compression results indicate that Huffman coding provides consistent ratios (0.25), while Arithmetic coding shows variable results depending on the sequence7. The consistency of the 0.25 Huffman ratio is inherent to the balanced nature of the synthetic DNA sequences used, where the four nucleotides (A, C, G, T) appear with nearequal frequency. Under these conditions, Huffman's optimal prefix codes assign a fixed 2 bits per nucleotide (BPB) code to each symbol (since log 2 (4) = 2 ). Given the original ASCII representation is 8 bits per character, this results in a fixed theoretical compression ratio of 2 / 8 = 0 . 25 , while Arithmetic coding shows variable results depending on the sequence.

## V. PERFORMANCE AND ACCURACY EVALUATION

To ensure the reliability of the compression methods, we assessed the accuracy of DNA sequences after decompression.The Huffman and Arithmetic coding algorithms maintained lossless compression according to Figures 4 and 5 because they allowed perfect reconstruction of the original sequences without any information loss. The comparison between original and decompressed sequences through multiple tests proved that all nucleotide sequences matched perfectly. The maintenance of exact data fidelity stands as a vital requirement for bioinformatics because it enables reliable genomic analysis and interpretation.

## VI. APPLICATION AND USE CASES

The two lossless data compression algorithms Huffman coding and Arithmetic coding function differently based on their operational efficiency and system complexity requirements.

The ZIP and GZIP compression tools use Huffman coding to shorten frequent symbols which results in smaller data sizes. The compression algorithm Huffman coding works with transformed data to compress multimedia formats through its application in JPEG image and MP3 audio compression. Huffman coding serves two purposes in communication systems by reducing data redundancy and improving error detection and correction capabilities.

The technique of Arithmetic coding outperforms Huffman coding because it encodes symbols as fractional bit lengths, achieving theoretical entropy limits. The modern multimedia codecs H.264, HEVC (H.265), and AV1 use Arithmetic coding for video and audio compression to achieve high-quality streaming at reduced bit rates. Arithmetic coding stands out in error-resilient systems through its tight data compression because it helps applications that need to correct small errors. JBIG2 uses Arithmetic coding for file compression to achieve better performance than Huffman coding under specific conditions. Both techniques function together in various practical applications to achieve optimal performance through balanced compression efficiency and system complexity.

text:
## A. Limitations and Real-World Challenges

While both Huffman and Arithmetic coding realize very good lossless compression, there are certain limitations in practical applications. The first is scalability: currently, the provided implementations were tested on synthetic sequences of up to a moderate length of 156 nucleotides. Real-world genomic data can span billions of base pairs and would be difficult or impossible to handle by these techniques, instead requiring more complex, adaptive, and block-based schemes. Error resilience is a second significant differentiator. Because Arithmetic Coding reduces the entire sequence to a single fractional value, a single bit error in the encoded value during transmission would likely corrupt most or the entirety of the decoded sequence. Huffman coding gives much stronger localized error resilience, where one error would affect just one or two code words.The analysis of real-world genomic datasets from NCBI reveals complex non-random patterns which general-purpose symbol coding tools fail to detect at the level of domain-specific tools Biocompress and DNACompress.

## VII. CONCLUSION

The paper conducts a comparative evaluation of Huffman and Arithmetic Coding methods for DNA sequence compression because bioinformatics requires better data management solutions. The implemented systems proved that both methods decrease genomic data storage requirements through lossless data preservation. The Binary Search Tree (BST)-based Huffman coding method delivered quicker encoding operations but Arithmetic coding produced better compression performance for datasets containing uneven nucleotide patterns.

These compression methods demonstrate their ability to boost genomic data storage and transmission performance which makes them essential tools for researchers who handle extensive genomic information. Researchers should develop new compression systems which unite the advantages of Huffman and Arithmetic coding to achieve better results in bioinformatics operations. The development of Huffman and Arithmetic Coding systems for real-time applications including streaming and IoT requires optimization. The integration of AI with these compression methods and their development for error-resistant networks and high-resolution media formats and quantum computing applications represents potential future research areas.

## VIII. FUTURE WORK

The development of hybrid methods which use Huffman encoding for fast local pattern processing and Arithmetic Coding for better output compression will enhance results in various bioinformatics applications.

The development of optimized methods for real-time applications including streaming and IoT systems alongside integration with genomic compression software for specific domains represents potential future research directions.

text:
## Efficient Parallel Processing of Structured Big Data Using Scala and Apache Spark

Sampath Kini K Department of Computer Science and Engineering Nitte (Deemed to be University),NMAM Institute of Technology Karkala, India sampath@nitte.edu.in

Abstract -As the volume and complexity of structured data continue to grow, there is an increasing need for scalable and efficient  processing  methods.  This  paper  explores  the  use  of Scala in  conjunction with Apache Spark for parallel big data processing, focusing specifically on structured datasets such as CSV and relational formats. By leveraging Spark's in-memory computing  capabilities  and  Scala's  functional  programming strengths, we develop a parallel processing model that enhances execution  speed  and  resource  utilization.  The  study  evaluates performance  using  real-world  datasets  and  compares  results across  various  workloads.  Our  experimental  results  show significant  improvements  in  processing  time  and  scalability, particularly  when handling large volumes of  structured  data. The findings demonstrate that combining Scala and Spark is a practical and effective approach for real-time big data analytics, especially  in  educational  and  research-oriented  environments. This work also outlines areas for further optimization, including dynamic  workload  balancing  and  integration  with  machine learning pipelines.

Keywords-Big Data, Apache Spark, Scala, Parallel Processing, Structured Data

## I. INTRODUCTION

In  today's  digital  era,  organizations  are  generating  vast amounts  of  structured  data from  sources  like relational databases, enterprise software, and transaction systems. While this data offers tremendous potential for analysis and decisionmaking,  the  challenge  lies  in  processing  it  efficientlyespecially as traditional methods begin to fall short when it comes to scale and speed [1], [2].

Over the past few years, parallel and distributed computing models have emerged as practical solutions to this problem. Among them, Apache Spark has become a leading choice for big data processing due to its in-memory computing capabilities and flexible APIs [3]. Spark's ability to handle a variety of workloads-from SQL queries to machine learning-makes  it  particularly  useful  in  handling  complex data  pipelines.  Moreover,  its  native  support  for  Scala,  a concise and expressive programming language, offers additional advantages for building scalable data applications [4], [5].

This paper explores how the combined use of Scala and Apache  Spark  can  improve  the  processing  of  structured datasets. By leveraging Spark's distributed computing framework and Scala's functional programming features, the Sreekantha Desai Karanam Department of Computer Science and Engineering Nitte (Deemed to be University),NMAM Institute of Technology Karkala, India sreekantha@nitte.edu.in goal is to evaluate improvements in performance, scalability, and overall code maintainability. We also examine real-world scenarios  to  demonstrate  how  these  technologies  can  be effectively applied in academic and enterprise environments.

text:
## II. BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORK

In the field of big data analytics, earlier systems such as Hadoop  MapReduce  were  pivotal  in  enabling  distributed computation  across  large  datasets.  However,  due  to  their reliance  on  disk-based  operations,  these  systems  frequently encountered  latency  issues,  particularly  for  iterative  and interactive workloads [6]. This has led to growing interest in more responsive and memory-efficient platforms.

Apache  Spark  emerged  as  a  powerful  alternative  that addresses many  of the limitations of traditional batch processing frameworks. Spark enables in-memory data caching, reducing the overhead associated with disk I/O and allowing for significantly faster execution of repeated computations. Its flexible architecture supports a wide range of  workloads-from  batch  jobs  and  interactive  queries  to machine learning and real-time stream processing-making it highly adaptable for various big data scenarios.

A  key factor in Spark's efficiency is its seamless integration  with  Scala,  the  language  in  which  it  is  natively developed.  Scala  combines  object-oriented  and  functional programming  paradigms,  which  makes  it  well-suited  for expressing  complex  data  transformations  in  a  concise  and readable  format.  Developers  benefit  from  Scala's  advanced type system, pattern matching, and immutable collections, all of  which  contribute  to  writing  robust  and  scalable  data pipelines [7], [8].

Several academic and industrial studies have highlighted the advantages of using Scala with Spark for structured data processing. Scala's tight coupling with Spark allows for more direct API interactions, reducing boilerplate code and improving runtime performance [9]. Furthermore, in comparative  assessments  with  other  distributed  processing tools like Apache Flink and Storm, Spark continues to perform favourably  in terms of throughput, fault tolerance,  and ecosystem support [10].

Given these developments, the combination of Spark and Scala offers an efficient and developer-friendly environment for  processing  structured  datasets.  This  paper  extends  the ongoing research by evaluating how these technologies can be applied to enhance data processing performance and scalability in both academic research and enterprise applications.

## III. RESEARCH GAP

Before  Despite  considerable  advancements  in  big  data processing frameworks, several critical gaps remain unaddressed,  particularly  in  the  context  of  structured  data handling  using  parallel  and  distributed  approaches.  While Hadoop  MapReduce  initially  laid  the  foundation  for  largescale data analysis, its lack of in-memory processing and realtime  capabilities  limits  its  applicability  in  dynamic  data environments [11].

Apache Spark has been widely recognized for its improved performance over MapReduce, especially due to its support for  in-memory  computation  and  DAG  (Directed  Acyclic Graph)-based  execution  models.  However,  existing  studies have  primarily  focused  on  unstructured  or  semi-structured data,  leaving  a  noticeable  research  gap  in  the  systematic evaluation  of  Spark  and  Scala's  efficiency  with  structured datasets,  such  as  relational  databases  or  tabular  enterprise records [12].

Moreover, although Scala is Spark's native language and offers a blend of functional and object-oriented programming paradigms, comparative analyses of Scala-based Spark applications versus Python (PySpark) or Java implementations are limited. This raises the need for empirical studies that quantify the performance, readability, and maintainability trade-offs of using Scala in real-world structured data pipelines [13].

Additionally, while Spark supports SQL-based querying through Spark SQL, limited research exists on how parallelism at the code level (e.g., using RDD transformations vs. DataFrames or Datasets in Scala) impacts overall processing  efficiency.  Most  academic  work  overlooks  the influence  of  code-level  parallel  constructs  and  optimization techniques that can further enhance performance [14].

Furthermore, benchmarks involving educational or enterprise datasets are rare, which inhibits broader adoption and reproducibility. There is also a scarcity of investigations into  how  mini-projects or academic prototypes  can  scale  to enterprise-level applications, especially when using Scala in combination with Spark's parallel architecture [15].

This  study  aims  to  bridge  these  gaps  by  evaluating  the effectiveness of Spark-Scala integration for processing structured data using real-world educational datasets. The goal is to provide empirical insights and practical benchmarks that can guide both academic researchers and industry practitioners in optimizing big data workflows.

text:
## IV. METHODOLOGY

This research adopts an experimental approach to evaluate the performance of Apache Spark in combination with Scala for processing structured datasets.  The methodology is divided  into  four  major  phases:  Dataset  Selection,  System Setup, Implementation, and Evaluation Metrics. Fig.1 shows the flow of all the tasks involved in this research project.

Working  with  structured data in Spark  using Scala involves  several  important  steps  that  contribute  to  efficient data handling and processing. Everything starts with initializing  the  SparkSession,  which  serves  as  the  main gateway for using Spark's DataFrame and SQL features. Next comes data ingestion, where datasets-commonly in CSV or Parquet formats-are read into Spark DataFrames for further processing.

Once the data is loaded, it goes through a preprocessing stage. This step is essential to ensure data quality and usually includes cleaning operations like removing null or inconsistent values, converting data types, or applying simple filters  to  prepare  the  data  for  analysis.  The  transformation phase follows, where operations like map, filter, and groupBy are applied.

To improve performance, caching is often used. By storing frequently accessed data in memory using df.cache(), Spark avoids recalculating results in repeated operations, which can save a  lot  of  time  in  large  workflows.  Finally,  the  system's performance  is  evaluated  using  key  metrics  like  execution time and memory usage. This helps determine how well the setup scales as the dataset size grows, ensuring the approach remains efficient even with larger volumes of data.

Fig. 1. Parallel Big Data Processing Using Scala and Spark.

<!-- image -->

## A. Dataset Selection

For the purpose of this study, we use publicly available structured datasets relevant to education and business analytics.  Notably,  the  Student  Performance  Dataset  from UCI Machine Learning Repository and Retail Sales Transactions from Kaggle were selected due to their variety, schema complexity, and real-world applicability [16], [17].

## B. System Setup

The  experiments  were  conducted  using  Apache  Spark 3.4.1  running  on  a  4-node  cluster  built  with  commodity hardware. Each node is configured with 16 GB RAM, quadcore processors, and Ubuntu 22.04 OS. Scala 2.12 was used as  the  programming  language,  and  Hadoop  HDFS  was integrated for distributed file storage. Spark was deployed in standalone  mode  to  simulate  mid-scale  enterprise  scenarios [18].

## C. Implementation

Multiple  data  processing  pipelines  were  created  using Spark's  RDD,  DataFrame,  and  Dataset  APIs  in  Scala.  The goal was to compare performance across different abstraction levels while applying parallel operations such as map, filter, groupBy, and join.

In addition, we implemented SQL-based transformations using Spark SQL to simulate business intelligence operations like  data  warehouse  style  aggregations.  The  pipelines  were tested with and without in-memory caching to understand the effect of memory optimization techniques. Scala's support for immutable  data  structures  and  parallel  collections  was  also utilized  to  design  parallel  workflows  that  minimize  side effects [19].

## D. Evaluation Metrics

We measured performance using a variety of quantitative metrics:

- Execution Time (ET): Time taken to complete a job from ingestion to final output.
- Scalability  Index  (SI):  Variation  in  performance  as data volume increases.
- Code Complexity (CC): Measured using Cyclomatic Complexity and Lines of Code (LoC).
- Programmer Efficiency (DE): Time required to implement pipelines in Scala versus other languages (Python, Java) for similar tasks.

We also performed comparative benchmarking between Spark-Scala and Spark-Python implementations for selected queries  to validate Scala's  efficiency in structured  data processing.

## V. ALGORITHMS USED

text:
## A. Structured Data Ingestion Using Spark and Scala

This algorithm outlines the process of ingesting structured datasets,  such  as  CSV  or  Parquet  files,  into  Apache  Spark using  Scala.  The  goal  is to  create  a  clean  and  usable DataFrame that conforms to a specified or inferred schema. The  steps  are  designed  to  ensure  robust  and  efficient  data loading while handling common issues such as missing values or inconsistent data types.

- 1) Step 1: Begin by initializing a SparkSession with the necessary configurations. This session acts as the main entry point for interacting with Spark functionalities in a structured application.
- 2) Step  2: Define  the  schema  S  for  the  dataset.  The schema can either be manually specified to enforce strict data typing or automatically inferred by Spark based on the input file.
- 3) Step  3: Load  the  input  dataset  D  into  a  DataFrame called DF using Spark.read operations. Depending on the file format, appropriate options (e.g., header, delimiter, inferSchema) should be set to ensure correct parsing.
- 4) Step 4: Perform data cleaning by addressing missing or  null  values  and  resolving  any  data  type  inconsistencies. This step ensures that the data is reliable for further processing and analysis.
- 5) Step 5: Return the cleaned and structured DataFrame DF, which can now be used for transformation, analysis, or storage.

These steps enable a streamlined approach to data ingestion  that  is  scalable  and  well-suited  for  handling  large volumes of structured data in big data applications.

## B. Parallel Processing of Structured Data Using Spark and Scala

This algorithm outlines an efficient approach to processing structured data in parallel using Apache Spark with Scala. The objective is to apply a set of transformation rules to a given DataFrame and obtain a processed version, DF\_trans, optimized  for  further  analysis  or  storage.  The  algorithm leverages Spark's distributed computing capabilities to achieve scalability and speed.

- 1) Step 1: Begin by partitioning the input DataFrame DF using an optimal strategy. Techniques such as hash partitioning  or  range  partitioning  help  distribute  the  data evenly  across  the  cluster  nodes,  enabling  better  parallel execution.
- 2) Step 2: Apply the defined transformation rules R using high-level Spark operations such as map, filter, groupBy, and withColumn.  These  transformations  are  executed  lazily, allowing Spark to optimize the execution plan.
- 3) Step  3: If  the  transformed  data  will  be  reused  in multiple operations, persist it in memory using the .cache() or .persist() method. This helps avoid recomputation and improves performance for iterative workloads.
- 4) Step 4: Trigger the computation by executing one or more Spark actions such as count(), show(), or write(). These actions  force  Spark  to  evaluate  the  transformation  pipeline and return the result.
- 5) Step 5: Finally, return the resulting DataFrame DF\_trans, which now contains the cleaned and transformed data ready for downstream processing.

## C. Performance Evaluation and Metric Computation

This algorithm outlines a systematic approach to evaluating the performance of a Spark-based data processing workflow. By analysing key runtime metrics such as execution time and scalability, developers and researchers can better  understand  how  the  system  behaves  under  various workloads and optimize it accordingly.

- 1) Step  1: Start  by  capturing  the  current  system  time (t\_start) just before initiating the main  actions on  the transformed DataFrame (DF\_trans). This provides a baseline for measuring processing duration.
- 2) Step  2: Perform  the  desired  action(s)  on  DF\_trans, such  as  writing  the  data  to  disk  or  performing  a  complex computation.  These  actions  serve  as  the  workload  under evaluation.
- 3) Step 3: Immediately after the action completes, record the current time again (t\_end). This timestamp marks the end of the operation.
- 4) Step 4: Calculate the total execution time by subtracting  t\_start  from  t\_end.  This  value  represents  how long the system took to complete the task.

- 5) Step  5: Use  Spark's  Web  UI  or  application  logs  to monitor memory consumption during execution. This helps assess resource efficiency and identify potential bottlenecks.
- 6) Step 6: To evaluate scalability, repeat the above steps with  different  dataset  sizes.  Observe  and  document  how execution time changes relative to the data volume. A welloptimized system should exhibit near-linear scalability under increased loads.

7) Step 7: To Consolidate the collected information into a  set  of  performance  metrics  M,  including  execution  time, memory  usage,  and  scalability  indicators.  These  metrics provide valuable insights into the effectiveness and efficiency of the Spark-Scala processing pipeline

This performance evaluation framework enables practitioners  to  make  data-driven  decisions  about  system tuning, infrastructure scaling, and algorithmic improvements in large-scale data processing environments.

- The solution scaled effectively, maintaining performance as dataset sizes increased.

Abstract -Autonomous drones are powering the revolution in delivery,monitoring,rescue, and surveillance operations, where the real-time navigation of complex 3D environment is crucial. Nevertheless, conventional methods are usually required to choose between power efficiency and adaptability to changing conditions. A hybrid reinforcement learning and A*-based energy-efficient motion planning system with local dynamic obstacle integration is presented in this paper. The energy-aware heuristic is obtained from a physics-based engineering model that considers both horizontal and vertical components of the motion energy, thus making sure that optimization is carried out in a fair manner.Voxelized 3D Grid along with a LiDAR-like sensing mechanism facilitates Dynamic Obstacle Perception and Local Path Re-planning. The innovative adaptive architecture changes the ratio of energy and distance costs based on the battery condition, hence increasing durability and safety. Simulations indicate that this hybrid will be A*+RL approach achieves 92.4% success, 65% fewer collisions and 24% improved energy efficiency compared to conventional A*. The system has realtime adaptability and scalability for Larger environments and considerable enhancement in energy- Aware UAV navigation.

Index Terms -autonomous drones, path planning, obstacle avoidance, 3D navigation, A* algorithm, dynamic rerouting, energy efficient, reinforcement learning

## I. INTRODUCTION

The proliferation of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in logistics, surveillance, agriculture, and disaster management krishnaraj.chadaga@manipal.edu

has accelerated the need for efficient and autonomous navigation [1], [8]. Traditional path planning approaches such as Dijkstra's or Breadth-First Search guarantee optimality but are computationally heavy and unsuitable for real-time aerial systems [2]. A* search, with its heuristic-guided optimization, provides a balance between computational efficiency and optimality.

However, most existing 3D A* applications minimize distance, not energy, despite UAVs being highly energyconstrained systems [10]. Power usage depends heavily on altitude changes, accelerations, and hover durations. A path which is based solely on distance can still be very energyconsuming if there are again and again altitude changes or if the air is turbulent.

## A. Background on A* Algorithm

A* is an extensively used informed search technique that tries to achieve a balance between efficiency and accuracy by employing heuristic functions [4]. Conventional A* works out the minimum-cost route from a given starting point to a goal with the help of the below evaluation function:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where f(n) is the estimated total cost from start through node n to goal, g(n) is the actual cost from start to node n, and h(n) is the heuristic estimated cost from n to goal. Common heuristic functions for 3D space include Euclidean distance and Manhattan distance.

However, standard A* has critical limitations to be used for UAV navigation [11]: it does not consider energy consumption differences between horizontal and vertical movements, it treats all free cells equally despite the proximity of obstacles, cannot handle dynamic environmental conditions, and static heuristics without taking into consideration vehicle dynamics and wind.

To overcome this, we propose an energy-aware cost function, taking the propulsion, lift, and drag forces into account. Such a cost dynamically updates based on the battery level of the drone, thus guaranteeing energy efficiency during its mission. Real-time obstacle detection has also been enabled through the LiDAR-based virtual sensor, with dynamic replanning whenever new obstacles show up [5]. In our approach, an RL component fine-tunes the local movement decisions within the A* framework [14]. The RL agent will learn corrective actions to avoid a collision and to optimize smooth trajectories without recomputing the entire path.

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

For UAV navigation, a number of algorithms have been investigated, each of which addresses particular constraints [9]. Due to their high computing costs, early methods like Bellman-Ford and Dijkstra's promised shortest paths but failed in huge 3D grids. A* used heuristics to increase search efficiency, but traditional distance-based cost models disregarded energy restrictions.

For large-scale planning, Holte et al.'s Hierarchical A* [2] abstracts complex settings into manageable layers, although it is highly dependent on the quality of the abstraction. Koenig and Likhachev's D* Lite [3] allows incremental path updates for dynamic situations, although frequent adjustments result in overhead. Although Field D* made any-angle pathways smoother, it was still computationally demanding for onboard devices.

A* for UAVs was improved by a number of experiments using multi-objective optimization, which included risk, safety, or smoothness but ignored physical energy costs. Li et al. [6] used reinforcement learning for energy-efficient UAV swarm planning, exhibiting adaptive learning skills but encountering difficulties with reality gaps and high training demands.

Although learning-based techniques, such as policy gradient approaches and Deep Q-Networks (DQN), increased adaptability, they were difficult to interpret and required a lot of training. A thorough review of RL in robotics was given by Kober et al. [7], who noted difficulties in integrating it with heuristic methods for real-time path planning but emphasized its promise for navigation. Introduced by Phillips and Likhachev [5], Safe Interval Path Planning (SIPP) incorporates temporal safety to avoid both static and dynamic barriers, making it appropriate for time-sensitive situations like as urban airspace navigation.

While deep learning techniques continue to show promise for collision-free navigation in congested spaces [19], recent developments in control theory have improved UAV stability and responsiveness [18]. Cooperative missions with distributed job allocation are made possible by multi-agent coordination frameworks [20], [24].

Recent developments include hybrid models that combine learning and search [14]. By incorporating a physics-based energy model into A* for accurate cost computation, adding adaptive λ -weighting between distance and energy cost based on battery level, using LiDAR-based perception for dynamic environment updates, and incorporating local reinforcement learning refinement, our suggested framework expands on these developments.

## III. MATERIALS AND METHODS

Our approach combines heuristic path planning and reinforcement learning to accomplish effective 3D navigation while optimizing energy consumption and enabling real-time system adaptation.

## A. Environment Modeling and Dataset Configuration

A 3D voxel grid is used to depict the space, with each cell labeled as free, occupied, or restricted [11]. Static and dynamic barriers are dispersed at random, and the start and goal points are established in the workspace.

Mission Parameters: The objective sites were selected from the entire area, the minimum path was 30 voxels, the energy budget was 1000 units, and the start places were randomly selected within a low altitude range (Z: 0-10m).

A perception model inspired by LiDAR simulates sensing: Sensor Noise ± 0 . 2 m, Range 20m, Field of View 120 ◦ Gaussian [28]. ## IV. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS

The experimental scenarios covered sparse, clustered, and dense environments in which the performances of three agents: Random, A*-only, and Hybrid(A*+RL) were compared.

## A. Performance Metrics - Definitions

Success Rate (%) [17]: Episodes achieving target without collision/energy depletion. Target: > 90% .

Collision Rate (%): Episodes resulting in collision. Acceptable: < 10% .

Avg Path Length (m): Average distance covered, signifying efficiency.

Energy (J): Overall consumption (hover + motion + altitude).

Time to Goal (s): Mission completion time.

## B. Comparative Performance Analysis

Success rose 24% (74.5% to 92.4%), collision lowered 65% (20.8% to 7.6%), energy fell 24% (414J to 314J), time improved 35% (27.1s to 21.8s), and path length decreased 15% with the hybrid planner. These findings show how energyaware A* planning and adaptive RL refinement work well together.

By effectively reducing vertical variations by 31%, the altitude penalty ( α = 0 . 05 ) of the energy-aware heuristic directly contributed to battery conservation. The dynamic balancing strategy was validated by the adaptive λ -weighting mechanism, which avoided energy depletion in 94% of lowbattery circumstances compared to 73% for fixed-weight alternatives. Stability during fast maneuvers is further improved by advanced control strategies [18].

## V. DISCUSSION

## A. Energy Efficiency and Hybrid Architecture

Complementary benefits result from combining A* and RL. [14]: While RL allows for dynamic obstacle reaction and adaptive tactical corrections, A* guarantees global optimality and deterministic behavior. This division maintains real-time responsiveness while reducing computing overhead (A* 120180ms initial planning, RL 3-5ms each action, replanning 45ms).

Hovering (8-12W/motor for normal 250mm frames [16]), horizontal motion (linear drag), and vertical motion with asymmetric climb penalty ( α = 0 . 05 ) are all captured by the physics-based energy model. Using favored horizontal routing, moderate altitude transitions, and aggregated elevation changes, empirical validation demonstrates 18-21% energy savings compared to distance-only optimization. In real deployments, energy optimization techniques [21] are crucial for increasing operating range.

## B. Collision Avoidance and Barrier Detection

Robust spatial reasoning is provided by the voxelized occupancy grid ( 11 × 11 × 11 perception, 5.5m radius) with a 2-voxel safety margin. Four steps are used to handle dynamic obstacles: linear trajectory prediction, incremental replanning, temporal collision checking (3s horizon), and velocity estimation ( v obs = ( p t -p t -1 ) / Δ t ). As a result, collisions decreased from 20.8% to 7.6% (a 65% improvement). For better obstacle recognition, complementary sensory modalities are provided by vision-based detection techniques [23].

## C. Performance Decomposition

Individual contributions are isolated through decomposition (Table III). While energy awareness avoids premature depletion, RL's taught avoidance offers crucial tactical response that pure A* does not. The 15% path reduction shows that efficiency is increased rather than decreased via energy optimization. For swarm applications, learning-based guidance systems [24] are still promising.

## D. Computational Feasibility and Real-World Deployment

Suitability for embedded platforms (Jetson Nano, Pi 4) is confirmed by memory footprint (4MB total: 500KB grid, 2.1MB DQN, 1.5MB A* structures) and timing constraints. LiDAR (SLAMTEC A2, Velodyne VLP-16) [28], RTK-GPS (u-blox ZED-F9P), 9-DOF IMU (MPU-9250), sensor fusion (EKF/UKF, ROS2), and safety mechanisms (geofencing, battery monitoring, redundancy) [29] are necessary for real-world transition. While sensor interface and uncertainty handling are the key areas of change, core algorithms are essentially unaltered.

An increased operational range is made possible by the 24% energy reduction, which increases flight time by 20-25% (e.g., 20 to 24 minutes). By resolving insurance and regulatory needs, the 65% collision improvement improves safety for populous areas. Single-policy deployment across several contexts without retraining is made possible by cross-environment generalization.

## VI. CONCLUSION

An energy-efficient hybrid navigation framework for 3D drone motion planning that combines A* and RL is presented in this work [6], [14]. Better path quality, energy efficiency, and dependability are achieved by combining a physics-based energy model, adaptive λ -weighting, and LiDAR-driven obstacle awareness.

## Key Contributions:

- 1) Physics-based energy heuristic capturing altitude penalties, propulsion costs, hover energy
- 2) Adaptive λ -weighting sensitive to battery percentage
- 3) Real-time LiDAR-based replanning for dynamic obstacles
- 4) Hybrid architecture combining A* optimality with RL adaptivity

Improvements are confirmed by simulations: 92.4% success rate, 7.6% collision rate, and 24% energy savings compared to baseline A*. Robust generalization ( > 85% success across all circumstances) is demonstrated via cross-environment validation. The framework demonstrates how intelligent adaptive planning combined with physiologically meaningful energy modeling greatly increases UAV endurance and mission effectiveness.

## VII. ACKNOWLEDGMENT

The authors thank the Manipal Institute of Technology's Department of Computer Science and Engineering for resources, the project supervisor for advice, and their peers for comments that helped to improve this work.

## VIII. FUTURE WORK

Critical extensions addressing reviewer concerns and advancing practical deployment include:

Multi-Agent Coordination: Swarm intelligence for cooperative missions (surveillance, area coverage, distributed delivery) with collision avoidance and task allocation protocols [20], [24].

Real-Time Sensor Integration: Hardware validation with actual LiDAR (SLAMTEC A2) [28], RTK-GPS (u-blox ZED-F9P), IMU (MPU-9250), RGB-D cameras (RealSense D435) [23] for ground-truth environment mapping and obstacle detection under sensor noise and uncertainty.

Transfer Learning and Domain Adaptation: Bridging simulation-reality gap through domain randomization, progressive neural networks, and adaptive parameter tuning to handle real-world variations (lighting, weather, GPS drift).

Advanced Energy Modeling: Incorporating wind disturbances (anemometer-based measurement or IMU estimation), aerodynamic drag coefficients from CFD analysis, payload variations, and battery discharge nonlinearities [29] for accurate flight dynamics.

Edge Computing Optimization: Onboard neural network quantization (INT8), model pruning, and TensorRT optimization for real-time inference on resource-constrained embedded platforms (Jetson Nano, Pi 4) with < 100ms latency requirements.

Hardware Flight Testing: Physical UAV deployment with Pixhawk/Navio2 flight controllers, validating energy model accuracy, collision avoidance robustness, and generalization performance across outdoor environments (urban, forest, agricultural fields) [27].

Failure Mode Analysis: Systematic evaluation of GPSdenied scenarios (indoor, urban canyons) using visual-inertial odometry or UWB localization, communication link failures, and degraded sensor conditions to ensure operational reliability [25].

Ultimately, building fully autonomous, energy-aware UAV systems for safety-critical applications: urban search-rescue, medical delivery, precision agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and planetary exploration [9], [12], [13].

S.V.N. Sreenivasu 1 , Meesala Sivaiah 2 , Manikanta Mallela 3 , Ikkurthi Dhanush 4 , Karanam Madhavi 5 , Dodda Venkata Reddy 6

Abstract -With a data-driven approach to workforce management, forecasting employee attrition is crucial for reducing organizational disruption and maximizing human capital strategy. Fair-ExplainHR is an improved, explainable, and fairnessaware machine learning model for ethically transparent attrition prediction proposed in this work. Inspired by the shortcomings of current models-largely their lack of attention to interpretability, fairness, and human-focused cues-this effort incorporates new behavioral (burnout), engagement, and economic signals into the prediction pipeline. Based on the IBM HR Analytics dataset, the approach combines strong preprocessing with SMOTE for imbalance management, feature engineering, and sophisticated model tuning using Optuna. The prediction engine consists of a deep stack ensemble of GRU-based neural networks, XGBoost, and TabNet, with a meta-classifier coordinating decision-level fusion. In contrast to earlier hybrid models that were limited to 95 % accuracy, Fair-ExplainHR recorded a higher accuracy of 96 % , with heavy gains through deep learning integration and explainability. SHAP analysis also provides transparent model decision insights, tackling ethical AI issues.it also promotes responsible AI practices, serving as a benchmark for future attrition prediction systems within corporate HR analytics.

Index Terms -Employee Attrition Prediction, Explainable AI, Fairness-Aware Machine Learning, GRU, TabNet, XGBoost, Deep Stacking Ensemble.

text:
## I. INTRODUCTION

Attrition of employees is a pervasive and expensive issue for companies, usually interfering with workflows, dampening morale, and increasing operational expense related to rehiring and retraining [4]. Although conventional machine learning techniques have been used in predicting employee turnover, most are not transparent, ethically sound, or sufficiently informed about human resource realities [6]. Responding to this, this research proposes Fair-ExplainHR-a fairness-aware, explainable, and ethically responsible predictive model which uses state-of-the-art deep learning methods to precisely pinpoint attrition risks.

As opposed to traditional approaches, this model improves predictive capability by adding engineered features that express burnout inclinations, employee engagement levels, and financial stressors like inflation and employment rates-features usually neglected but pivotal in human decision-making scenarios. These attributes were selected via correlation analysis to remove redundancy and ensure relevance, thus improving both interpretability and model performance [9]. The IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition dataset employed in this research provides a rich and structured description of organizational employee records, including demographic, behavioral, and performance-related attributes. The dataset includes over 1,400 employee records and 35+ features such as job title, overtime, environment satisfaction, and monthly income-forming a robust foundation for developing attrition prediction systems. To preprocess the data, label encoding, standardization, and SMOTE were used to resolve class imbalance between active and attrited employees.

The Fair-ExplainHR architecture is built on a deep stacking ensemble that leverages the capabilities of GRU (Gated Recurrent Unit) for temporal pattern recognition [3], XGBoost for high-performance gradient boosting [2], and TabNet for interpretable learning on tabular data. Hyperparameters were optimized using Optuna, and SMOTE was used for class imbalance. The model achieved 96 % accuracy and 0.978 F1-score, outperforming hybrid models that averaged 95 % accuracy [14]. To ensure transparency, SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) was used, helping stakeholders understand feature-level contributions and addressing the black-box issue of deep models [10]. Recent literature surveys, as summarized in our background analysis, show that most studies used traditional classifiers like Decision Trees, SVM, and Random Forests with limited feature diversity and performance below 90 % [14]. By closing this gap, Fair-ExplainHR contributes to the development of more ethical, interpretable, and highperforming attrition prediction systems.

text:
## II. RELATED WORK

Ahmad et al. (2025) highlighted how conventional decisionmaking mechanisms in HR were handicapped by manual processing and predictive limitations [1]. To fill this gap, they developed a machine learning-based model to predict employee attrition based on important HR indicators such as job position, work experience, and satisfaction level. ## A. Dataset Description

The model is trained on the dataset from IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition containing the data of 1,470 employees. The dataset is usually utilized to determine why the employees are departing from the company. It contains 35 features as: Personal details: Age, Gender, Marital Status. Job details: Department, Job Title, Salary, Company Years. Work behavior: Overtime, Job Satisfaction, Work-Life Balance. The target variable is Attrition, meaning whether the employee was retained or attrited from the firm. This information is useful because it helps in the understanding of patterns with regard to employees' engagement, performance, and burnout. It also helps in the creation of machine learning models that can predict who the most likely employees are to leave and therefore allow HR teams to intervene early.

## C. Model Training

In the Fair-ExplainHR system, three models-XGBoost, TabNet, and GRU-were trained on engineered features obtained from behavioral, engagement, and synthetic economic features. ## V. CONCLUSION

This study presents an interpretable and fairness-focused deep ensemble model, Fair-ExplainHR: Ethical and Transparent Attrition Prediction with Engagement, Economic, and Behavioral Signals. It aims to accurately identify employee attrition while maintaining ethical transparency. The framework includes preprocessing steps like standardization and SMOTE oversampling to address class imbalance. It also features engineered metrics related to burnout risk, engagement level, and economic stress. The model combines GRU, TabNet, and XGBoost in a stacked ensemble. With the help of Optuna for hyperparameter tuning, 10-fold stratified cross-validation, and held-out testing, the ensemble outperformed individual models with an accuracy of 96

The model's interpretability is equally important. SHAP analysis was used to create both global and local explanations. This provided insights into how the engineered features and HR-specific metrics contribute to attrition predictions. These explanations enhance the framework's ethical transparency and uphold responsible AI standards. Diagnostic visualizations like confusion matrices, ROC curves, and training-testing performance graphs further confirm the reliability of model predictions and training consistency.

By integrating human-centric features with deep learning and explainability, Fair-ExplainHR balances predictive ability, clarity, and fairness. This model acts as a reliable decisionsupport tool for HR departments that want to reduce employee turnover with clear, data-driven insights.

In the future, the Fair-ExplainHR framework will be incorporated into real-time Human Resource Information Systems (HRIS) to support ongoing monitoring and proactive attrition alerts. Additionally, it will undergo cross-industry external validation using diverse workforce datasets to ensure generalizability and fairness across different organizational settings. Future improvements will aim at enhancing computational efficiency for large-scale deployment and expanding the model to track employee behavior over time, promoting responsible and inclusive AI use in human capital management.

## Explainable Multi-task Deep Learning and Vis-NIR Spectroscopy for Non-Destructive Mango Quality Assessment

Shana Santhosh Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Institute of Engineering & Technology,  Srinivas University, Mangaluru, India shanadigil@gmail.com

Abstract -  Non-destructive  evaluation  of  mango  quality  is crucial  for  ensuring  consumer  satisfaction,  optimizing  postharvest management, and reducing losses in the supply chain. This  study  presents  an  explainable  multi-task  deep  learning framework integrating Visible -Near Infrared (Vis -NIR) spectroscopy with a one-dimensional convolutional neural network (1D-CNN) for simultaneous prediction of key physicochemical  attributes  and  detection  of  internal  disorders  in mangoes. Spectral data (400 -1100 nm) from 3,950 calibration and 725 test samples covering multiple cultivars and maturity stages were analyzed to estimate dry matter (DM), soluble solids content (SSC), titratable  acidity  (TA),  and  firmness.  The proposed multi-task 1D-CNN model outperformed conventional regression methods such as PLSR, PCR, MLPR, and SVMR, achieving  coefficient  of  determination  (R²)  values  above  0.85, lower RMSEP, and higher residual prediction deviation (RPD > 3.0).  For  classification  of  internal  disorders,  it  attained  91  % accuracy with an F1-score of 0.90. SHAP-based interpretability analysis  identified  influential  wavelength  bands  between  750 and 900 nm corresponding to key biochemical absorptions. The proposed  model  demonstrates  strong  generalization  across cultivars and seasons, offering a scalable, explainable, and realtime solution for practical mango quality assessment.

Keywords -Visible-Near  Infrared  Spectroscopy  (Vis -NIR), Multi-task  Deep  Learning,  Spectral  Feature  Analysis,  SHAP Explainability, Mango Internal Disorder Detection.

text:
## I. INTRODUCTION

Quality control of mangoes is a paramount issue in a quest to serve the global markets with their ever-growing demands and expectations. Internal quality parameters measured include dry matter content (DMC), total soluble solids (TSS), an indicator of sweetness, titratable acidity (TA), and firmness and  have  effects  on  the  postharvest  shelf-life,  flavour,  and grading  decisions. Conventional  methods  are  based  on  the destructive method of sampling, when fruit is opened up in the laboratory to make assays which compromises throughput and is associated with loss of samples. Thus, there exists a lot of interest  in  designing  quick  and  non-invasive  methods  of assessing  internal  quality  parameters  that  can  effectively estimate information about a given fruit by maintaining fruit integrity. The  use  of  visible  as  well  as  near  infrared  (Vis-NIR) spectroscopy has gained enormous consideration as a potential non-destructive method used in estimating internal fruit traits. The spectral reflectance in the 400-1100nm or long range NIR (up to 1650-2500nm) has been shown in several studies to give robust calibration models of mango DMC, TSS

Dheeraj Hebri Department of Master of Computer Application, Srinivas Institute of Technology,  Srinivas University, Mangaluru, India

dheeraj.h7@gmail.com

and vitamin C using chemometric techniques such partial least squares regression (PLSR) or multi-predictor local polynomial  regression  (MLPR)  [1]. As  an  example,  the spectrum of absorbance 1000-2500nm provided PLSR models to predict TSS and vitamin C with correlation coefficients of ~0.86 and good RPD values of ~2.3-2.0. Similarly, the study [2],  showed  that  MLPR  had  a  higher  pH  and  TSS  Gadung Klonal 21 mango prediction accuracy than the support vector regression and kernel PLSR,  with  an  average  absolute percentage error of less than 10 on each ripening stage. Quantitative traits estimation has already reached maturity, and physiological disorders inside the body still pose a quality control bottleneck. Such conditions as frothy flesh, spongy tissue, black flesh, jelly seed and soft nose trimming tend to show up only after the fruits have been allowed to ripen and cause rejection of a complete batch of fruits despite the fruit looking okay on the surface [3]. Current research trends with portable Vis-NIR spectral instruments showed some high promise of accurate detection of these internal faults. As an example, Alves et al. (2025) designed models that distinguished  several  disorders  based  on  growth  stages  of cultivars and harvest and storage stages with high classification  accuracy  of  both  current  disorder  status  and predictions of the future events of disorder occurrence using spectra  at  harvest. In  the  same  manner,  Patil  et  al. (2024) achieved  a  classification  with  up  to  96.7 %  accuracy  on SIMCA classification of spongy tissue in Alphonso mango by using spectral features in 670-970nm [4]. Most of the previous research has treated each measure of quality independently or individual types of defects individually,  even  though  it  is  acknowledged  that  quality measures are intertwined with each other, and there are several types  of  defects. There  are  not  many  studies  that  combine multiple traits and interior turned over detection into a single predictive model. In  addition,  the majority of  strategies  are based on  existing  chemometric  regression  and  discriminant methods,  the  existing  data  rarely  support  the  use  of  deep learning or multi-task models with their ability to use a single spectrum to predict multiple quality indicators. The explainability  of  model  insights  is  also  unexplored  in  most cases, yet with research in other systems, recent research on fruit  quality  alternatively  uses  attention  maps  and  feature attribution methods to correlate spectral bands with biochemical components [5,6]. In the same way, field or orchard ports of portable VisNIR systems have also been restricted in their application by the  calibration  drift,  instrument  instability,  and  season-to- season model generalization between cultivars.

paper_id: Explainable Multi-task Deep Learning and Vis-NIR Spectroscopy for Non-Destructive Mango Quality Assessment
text: Although the earlier studies have shown that handheld Vis-NIR can be used to screen mango DMC and discrete disorder, problems are still encountered  when  it  comes  to  developing  and  constructing models that can be used on new equipment or during a later harvest. In this context, this paper presents a whole holistic method of mango quality determination by compact Vis-NIR spectroscopy and predicting the main quality factors (DMC, TSS,  TA,  firmness)  and  internal  defects  categories  (e.g., spongy tissue, black flesh) with a single spectrum using the multi-task deep learning model. We take advantage of a big data set comprising a combination of multiple cultivars and physiological stages of ripening (~3950 calibration and tuning samples,  and  ~725  independent  test  samples). We  add:  (1) creation of a unified 1D-CNN multi-task model to perform regression and classification simultaneously; (2) strict validation via cross-season/cultivar/instrument transfer as well  as  comparison  to  PLSR,  MLPR,  and  SVMR  baseline models; (3)  application  of  explainable  artificial  intelligence concepts to determine the most influential wavelength bands; and (4) demonstration of high robustness and generalization of trained models, for easy portability as bookshelf or staff in field. Our  integrative  approach  to  non-destructive  quality monitoring of mango seeks to develop a higher quality of nondestructive models in mango as opposed to being single-trait models,  but  to  achieve  an  overall  method  that  includes interpretability and generalizability, which can be of practical value to exporters, growers, and those directly concerned with quality determinations.

text:
## II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Spectroscopy techniques have contributed enormous traction  in  the  last  several  years  in  evaluating  the  mango quality  without  destroying  them. In  [7]  Lamptey  et  al. employed the use of a handheld near-infrared (NIR) spectrometer  (7401070  nm)  to  predict  total  soluble  solid (TSS) and pH of a total of 198 mangoes belonging to three varieties based on chemometric-based models. Of the available preprocessing and classification methods, the LDASVM method  achieved  a  substantial  respectable  prediction accuracy of 97.44%, whereas the Si-PLS regression approach offered nothing but satisfying R 2 values (0.63 and 0.81 of TSS and pH, respectively), which demonstrates the efficiency of handhelds in-field. Generalizing it to a sample of fruit purees analysis  treatment,  [8]  Pimpen  et  al. subjected  the  Fourier Transform  NIR  (800-2500  nm)  to  Partial  Least  Squares Regression (PLSR) to estimate the composition of the TSS and Titratable Acidity (TA) in purees of mango  and mangosteen  and  reported  a  good  r2  measurement  of  0.955 within the TSS checks of mango juice, demonstrating that the estimation can be quickly implemented in processing lines. In the  meantime,  [9]  Kusumiyati  et  al. employed  SSC  and vitamin C intact mangoes using NIRS (10002500 nm), where the  correlation  in  both  cases  reached  0.88  and  0.87  after smoothing  the  spectra  and  normalizing  them  using  PLSR, which  enhanced  the  capacity  of  the  technique  to  deal  with several dimensions of quality at once. The study by Polinar et al. examined  1,200  mango  fruits  by  NIR  spectroscopy  to determine  maturity  achieved  with  PLSR  and  PCA-LDA algorithms  that  provided  R2  values  of  0.946  and  0.839  in terms  of  maturity  and  TSS  levels,  respectively,  and  the classification  accuracy  to  predict  a  maturity  level  was  86

percent demonstrating the usefulness of the model in taking harvest decisions. To  predict  sweetness,  [11]  Al-Sanabani  et  al. achieved high prediction performance (R2 = 0.96 training, 0.95 testing) on a handheld NIR spectrometer (900-1700nm) using SVM, outperforming the PLS. Indicatively, [12] Xu et al. incorporated hyperspectral imaging (HSI) and twodimensional CARS with PLSR to assess damage impact in mangoes using high predictive accuracy in the determination of pulp firmness (0.84), TSS (0.90), and chroma (0.94), which enables damage detection after transport. O Brien et al. in their comparative  study  [13]  used  Vis-NIRS  and  Laser  Doppler Vibrometry (LDV), finding that Vis-NIRs was more effective than  LDV,  particularly  when  IQI  models  were  used  to incorporate sugar into the models (R 2 = 0.729), in predicting internal quality properties of sweetness and firmness. Regarding  the  defect  detection,  [14]  Guru  and  Nandini employed PLS-DA with dimensionality reduction and machine learning classifiers (SVM, RF, LR) and made 93.78 percent accuracy in classifying Alphonso mangoes according to  the  spectral  characteristics  of  the  obtained  NIR  spectra, thereby establishing a new standard in defect detection. The evaluation  of  texture  has  been  investigated  by  [15] Sharma and Sirisoomboon, who correlated textural properties (rupture force, penetration energy) with FT-NIR spectra via PLSR,  and  achieved  moderate  validation  accuracies  (r  = 0.703-0.754), unusable  by  small-scale  texture screening. text: further scaled it up combining sound models to  estimate  DMC  through  4  seasons  and  10  varieties  when using  short-wave  NIRS  (684-990nm)  [16]. The  analysis identified that cultivar-specific and ANN-based global models are successful and the best predictor is the physiological stage. On an industry  site,  [17]  Sharma  et  al. have  used  Vis-NIR spectroscopy (400-1000nm) combined with a conveyor belt line to make online TSS predictions with RMSEC of 0.690% and RMSEP of 0.765%, which shows that it is already ready to  assimilate  into  automated  grading. On  the  issue  of  peel interference, [18] Phuangsombut et al., compared spectral data of peeled and non-peeled mangoes, with higher accuracy of flesh-based models and effective minimization of the error of prediction  via  empirical  spectral  compensation. In  another wider classification study by Kusumiyati et al, UV-Vis-NIR spectroscopy was applied using PCA to differentiate six types of fruit with ideal classification (100 per cent accuracy) in one project  using  MSC  as  a  pre-processing  tool  and  NIPALS based PCA further demonstrating the flexibility of the model to other fruits than mangoes [19]. Moving on to non-mango fruits, [20] Amoriello et al. also compared HSI and portable Vis-NIR models to measure apricot quality and found that the HSI-based ANN-MLP models would yield better R2 values (0.918  and  0.904  in  DM  and  TSS  respectively),  advancing cross-commodity applications. In [21] Bellotto et al. modified VIS-NIR  spectroscopy  to  culture  and  orchard  location  to accurately predict the SSC and DMC in apples, which gave additional validation that the method is versatile across fruit and storage condition. Though the number of researches proving the usefulness of NIR and Vis-NIR spectroscopy in non-destructive experiments and optimization of mango quality continue to increase, the list of gaps still remains open. The majority of the existing works consider few quality parameters (translucent solid solids or firmness), or are limited to a few varieties of mango, and thus cannot be applied to represent numerous varieties and growing regions. Also, the effects of other external influences like peel thickness, maturity level, and  surrounding  noise  on  spectral  accuracy  are  not  well researched. Additionally, the different machine  learning models have been applied but no comparison has been made to include the latest methods of machine learning such as the use of DL and the combining modelling process. This is why a multi-parameter, cultivar-free scheme that exploits sophisticated  computational  models  on  real-time  and  fielddeployment applications to measure mango quality is needed.
