text:
## III. METHODOLOGY

## A.

## Dataset Description

We  used  a  full  dataset  of  about  3,950  calibration  and model  training  spectra  and  an  independent  test  set  of  725 spectra. To identify variation in internal quality indicators, the data  were  collected  over  a  range  of  mango  cultivars  and ripening conditions: hard green, and ripen states. A portable Vis-NIR spectrometer was used to measure spectral response in the range  of  400 ∼ 1100nm  in  wavelength,  with  the spectrometer capturing reflectance. This band offers absorption  waves  related  to  pigments  and  the  water  bands (~970nm) well known to be linked to compositional qualities in mango.  The  probe  used was  a near-contact diffuse reflectance  probe  with  controlled  lighting  conditions  with consistent integration time and distance parameters to guarantee spectral repeatability which are similar concepts to that of standard handheld Vis-NIR applications of assessing fruit quality.

Preparation  of  spectral  data  as  input  to  be  modelled compared raw reflectance observations with multiple spectral preprocessing  methods  in  order  to  maximize  signal  quality and model fit. Based on other available literature on mango spectroscopy, we added Savitzky-Golay smoothing, standard normal variate, multiplicative scatter correction and Gaussian smoothing. As an example, when using PLSR, PCR, or SVM regression models of a prediction study of Arumanis mango pH  it was  found  that second-derivative  Savitzky-Golay filtering  yielded  better  results  than  raw  spectra  [22].  In addition to preprocessing, we considered spectral reflectance indices (SRIs) as small feature representations. Driven by the research on proximal sensing, including a large-scale analysis of  mango  and  strawberry  stages  where  SRIs  were  used  in conjunction  with  ML  models  to  improve  the  prediction  of biochemical parameters, we calculated and  contrasted  SRIs and full-spectrum modelling. Such systematic ways of preprocessing and feature extraction guarantee robust, interpretable  learning  of  mango  quality  characteristics  and internal disorders.

## B. Modelling Approach

The  suggested  approach  uses  Vis-NIR  spectroscopy  in combination  with  a  multi-task  DL  model  to  conduct  nondestructive evaluation of the mango internal quality attributes and classification of the mango internal disorder, functional block  diagram  is  shown  in  Fig. 1. The  pipeline  starts  with spectral analysis in which the reflectance spectra of mangoes, in  the  wavelengths  of  400-1100nm  are  measured  on  the surfaces  of  the  mango  fruits  using  a  Portable  Vis-NIR instrument. Pre-processed SRIs are passed to a 1D-CNN with shared low-level spectral feature extraction layers and differentiating task-specific  output  heads  with  different  sets  of  spectral be the input spectra wavelengths. The  shared  convolutional features on different tasks. Let 𝑋 ∈ ℝ 𝑛∗𝑑 of 𝑛 samples  and 𝑑 feature extractor applies as in Eq. 1. <!-- formula-not-decoded -->

where ∗ denotes 1D convolution, 𝑊 (1) are the convolutional  weights,  and 𝑏 (1) the bias term. Multiple convolutional layers capture hierarchical spectral patterns. In this setup, we are using regression heads (represented in Eq. 2) to predict three important fruit quality traits: DM, TSS, and TA. Each of these traits is modelled using a linear transformation of the shared hidden representation (denoted by 𝐻 ). <!-- formula-not-decoded -->

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

This means that the predicted value (denoted by 𝑦 ̂ 𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑡 ) is computed by taking the dot product of a weight matrix 𝑊𝑟𝑒𝑔 with the hidden representation 𝐻 , and then adding a bias term 𝑏𝑟𝑒𝑔 . This  is  a  standard  linear  regression  operation  used  in neural networks. We use a loss function, Mean Squared Error (MSE)  to  train  the  model  so  that  it  can  make  accurate predictions. It  is  the  average  of  the  squared  differences between the predicted values ( 𝑦𝑖 ) and the actual values ( 𝑦 ̂ 𝑖 ) of the entire samples in this dataset. Fig. 1. Proposed Model Framework

<!-- image -->

The  traits  are  managed  with  the  help  of  classification heads. The shared hidden representation ( 𝐻 ) is then mapped to  a  set  of  output  scores  ( 𝑧 ),  controlled  by  each  of  the classification heads, which corresponds to each of the possible classes. These  scores  are  linearly  transformed. In  order  to transform these raw scores 𝑧𝑗 to probability over the various classes, we transform the scores using the SoftMax function where the outputs are confined within the range of 0 to 1 and adding to 1. Then applied the categorical cross-entropy loss to gauge the performance of the classification heads. This loss is a penalization of incorrect predictions given the discrepancy between predicted probabilities and the actual class labels. It is calculated as in Eq. 3. <!-- formula-not-decoded -->

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

The categorical cross-entropy loss is calculated based on a few key components. Here, 𝑛 represents the total number of samples in the dataset, while 𝐶 denotes the number of possible classes  for  the  classification  task. The  term 𝑦𝑖𝑗 is  a  binary indicator  variable  that  takes  the  value  1  if  the 𝑖 𝑡ℎ sample belongs  to  the 𝑗 𝑡ℎ class,  and  0  otherwise. This  acts  as  the ground  truth  label. On  the  other  hand, 𝑝̂ 𝑖𝑗 represents  the predicted probability that the model assigns to the 𝑖 𝑡ℎ sample belonging  to  the 𝑗 𝑡ℎ class. The  loss  function  is  designed  in such a way that it penalizes the model more heavily when the predicted  probability  for  the  true  class  is  low. Therefore, minimizing this loss encourages the model to assign higher probabilities  to  the  correct  classes,  ultimately  improving classification accuracy.

text:
## C. Model Training & Generalization

In  order to  achieve  robustness,  we  deploy  a  crossvalidation protocol that is nested. This is in terms of inner loop when hyperparameters are tuned and outer loop when it comes to  the  unbiased evaluation of the model. Generalizability is tested by leave-cultivar-out and leave-season-out schemes. In transferability, calibration transfer methods are used. Also, a semi-supervised learning approach introduces the unlabelled spectra, with robust loss functions which facilitate the downweighting of possible outliers and domain mismatches being inspired by the recent developments in mango spectroscopy calibration.

## D. Explainability

Transparency of a model in making its predictions is the key to gaining trust and making it fit to be applied to the real world, particularly  in  scientific  and  agricultural  context.  To fulfil this requirement of interpretability of a model we apply a methodology called SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations). SHAP offers a principled method to explain a machine learning models output by measuring the contribution  of  each  input  feature-which,  in  the  case  of  a spectrum, would be each wavelength-to the final prediction of the model in regards to a certain trait (such as dry matter, sugar content, or acidity). Mathematically (Eq. 4) SHAP decomposes  the  prediction  of  a  model 𝑓(𝑥) into  sums  of contributions of each feature, which is contained in the SHAP values.

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

In this equation, 𝑓(𝑥) represents the model's prediction for a  given  input 𝑥 .  The  term ∅0 is  the  base  value,  which corresponds to the average prediction across the entire dataset. Each ∅𝑖 denotes the SHAP value for the 𝑖 𝑡ℎ feature, reflecting its individual contribution to the prediction. The corresponding 𝑥𝑖 is the actual value of that input feature. This approach  allows  an end-to-end pipeline utilizing signal processing, machine learning, and explainability capabilities to provide a simple and accurate non-destructive solution to evaluating the quality of mango fruits

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

To assess the performance of the suggested framework, an extensive  selection  of  indicators  was  used  for  both  the regression  and  classification  problems.  The  metrics used to evaluate the regression tasks (predicting DM, SSC, TA and firmness)  were  the  coefficient  of  determination  (R 2 ),  root mean  square  error  of  prediction  (RMSEP)  and  residual prediction  deviation  (RPD).  In  the  classification  task,  the classification  problem  of  discovering  internal  disorders  in mangoes,  accuracy,  precision,  recall,  and  F1-score  were calculated.

## A. Regression Performance

The  results  of  a  comparative  analysis  of  R 2 values  of baseline models with the proposed 1D-CNN on the four traits of mango quality are presented in Fig. 2. The 1D-CNN model achieves better scores than baseline models across all environment  measurements  under  consideration  DM,  SSC, TA,  and  Firmness.  SSC  and  DM  predictions  evidence  the greatest enhancement as R 2 values rise to 0.85 and 0.89 out of the former 0.72 and 0.78 respectively. This clearly shows the higher predictive power of the multi-task 1D-CNN, perhaps because  of  the  possibility  to  capture  hierarchical  spectral feature and exploit inter-task-dependencies.

Using the RMSEP comparison plot in Fig. 3, an evident decrease in the error of prediction is identified when using the 1D-CNN model compared to the baseline methods in all the four traits. The 1D-CNN results in lower values of RMSEP, with greatest differences occurring with DM and SSC, which value decreases ~1.6 to ~1.0 and ~1.8 to ~1.2 respectively. It means that 1D-CNN model more accurately and consistently predicts the data, and the method of non-destructive identification  of  the  quality  of  mangoes  becomes  more reliable.

Such  advances  imply  that  the  1D-CNN  model enables  not  only  reduced  prediction  error  but  also  greater robustness and reliability of the model, which would enable the implementation of the model in practical applications in the non-destructive quality assessment of mangoes.

The regression outcomes firmly assert the competence of the  given  multi-task  1D-CNN  model  in  the  non-destructive assessment  of  mango  quality.  The  model  achieved  high success in predicting all traits, DM, SSC, TA, and Firmness by learning the shared spectral representations combined with a  trait-specific  mapping,  at  the  same  time.  The  significant increases  in  the  parameters  of  R 2 ,  RMSEP,  and  RPD  also testify  to  the  strength  of  the  DL  model  not  only  to  prove versatile  in  terms  of  generalization  across  cultivars  and seasons. Elevated RPD levels especially above 3.0 on the traits of  interest  such as DM and SSC consider this method very appropriate when it comes to high-throughput and field-level screening operations. ## B. Classification Performance

The proposed 1D-CNN model to detect internal disorders in mangoes was examined against the standard measures of classification performance in terms of a confusion matrix and standard classification metrics. A baseline SVM in the role of internal disorder detection recorded 82 percent, whereas 1DCNN classifier was an absolute 91 percent, with an F1-score of 0.90. This indicates that the convolutional model was able to  pick  on  spatial  variations  in  spectra  that  signify  internal tissue damage or chaos, despite not destructive sampling.

Of the 40 actually belonging to the  disorder,  32  were  correctly  classified  and  there  were  8 incorrectly classified into the healthy category. ## C. Model Explainability

To  identify  which  spectral  bands  most  influence  the model's predictions, a SHAP analysis was performed. This method  clarifies  how  each  wavelength  contributes  to  the model's output. The heatmap in Fig. 7 shows SHAP values across the 400 -1100nm range, revealing a strong high-impact region between 750nm and 900 nm. This range provides the largest positive contribution to detecting internal disorder and aligns with known water absorption and chlorophyll-related bands, indicating that tissue degradation is effectively captured within this spectral interval.

Fig. 7. SHAP-Based Wavelength Importance

<!-- image -->

Conversely,  wavelengths  outside  the  central  spectral bands exhibit much smaller SHAP values, indicating limited influence  on  the  model's  decisions.  Notably,  the  negative SHAP values point to spectral regions that reduce confidence in detecting internal disorder, likely corresponding to absorption patterns typical of healthy mango tissue. Thus, the SHAP visualization not only clarifies how the model makes decisions but also aligns well with known physiological traits of  mangoes.  This  alignment strengthens  trust  in  the  model and supports its  practical  use  in  real-world  mango  grading and quality assessment systems.

text:
## V. CONCLUSION

This experiment developed and tested an effective methodology  of  non-invasive  quality  and  internal  disorder discrimination in mangoes based on portable Vis-NIR spectroscopy device and new DL architecture multi-task 1DCNN. The developed model showed an excellent outcome in predicting several (important) fruit quality characteristics, as DM, soluble SSC, TA, and firmness all at once, and the model is efficient in grouping the existence of internal physiological disorders. In comparison with traditional ML benchmarks of PLSR,  PCR,  SVMR,  MLPR,  the  offered  1D-CNN  model drastically enhanced the regression quality (R 2 >0.85), reduced RMSEP, and increased RPD to the level beyond the threshold that components can be used in practice.

In addition to performance improvements, the explainability results generated using SHAP showed valuable clues  in  partitions  of  the  spectrum,  where  information  can most  leverage  the  decision-making  and  boost  the  scientific validity  of  the  system  along  with  the  possibility  of  deploy ability. It  is  worth noting  that  the  wavelengths of  the  range 750-900 nm were singled out as having critical impacts, as were  physiological  markers  related  to  the  occurrence  of internal decay. The overall pipeline had a good generalization across season and cultivars, and thus it could be deployed at the field level. With promising commercial applications that could  transform  the  way  the  mango  industry  assesses  the quality at post-harvest and grade the mangoes to be exported, this solution offers the mango industry a scalable, interpretable, and real-time functional alternative to the current destructive quality assessment mechanism, a technique  that  is  not  only  expensive  to  implement  but  also exceedingly time consuming.

## Harnessing Technology for Precise Detection and Classification of Cervical Cancer

Ashwini B NITTE (Deemed to be University), Dept. of Information Science and Engineering, NMAM Institute of Technology, Nitte, Udupi 574110, India

ashwinib@nitte.edu.in

Shriraksha Adiga Technical Lead Oracle India Pvt. Ltd., Bengaluru, India shrirakshaadigan@gmail.com

Abstract -Cervical  cancer  is  one  of  the  most  prevalent  diseases among women and the leading health concern for the increase in the  female  mortality  rate  globally.  With  approximately  500000 new cases reported annually around the world, the early detection and analysis of cancer have become critical. Traditional Screening techniques such as Pap smears, colposcopy, Human Papillomavirus  (HPV),  and  biopsies  are  well-known  screening approaches for the  detection of cervical cancer often  associated with challenges like time-consuming, costly, invasive, and requiring highly skilled pathologists, which increases susceptibility  to  human  error.  Overcoming  the  challenges  of traditional  screening  approaches,  the  advancement  of  medical image  processing, and  artificial intelligence with innovative solutions have enabled more accurate and efficient cervical cancer detection.  This  study  proposes  a  hybrid  CNN  approach  for detecting and analyzing cervical cancer cell attributes from papsmear  images.  An  automated  tool  is  designed  with  a  simple graphical  user  interface  to  identify  cervical  cancer  and  its  five types of cancer tissues. The  region extraction and  feature extraction are implemented using SIPaKMeD  and Herlev datasets.  Overall,  the  proposed  model  demonstrates  89.13% classification accuracy for five cervical cell variants.

Keywords-Cervix, Cervical Cancer (CC), GLCM features, Morphology, Pap-smear, Segmentation, UNET.

## I. INTRODUCTION

Cancer is a  complex, intricate condition and  multifaceted disease  marked  by  the  uncontrolled  division  and  growth  of abnormal cells within the body. Globally, it is the second leading cause  of  death,  accounting  for  more  than  19  million  new diagnoses  and  10  million  deaths  yearly. Cervical  cancer  is  a significant public health issue and ranks among the top cancers

Manjula Gururaj Rao NITTE (Deemed to be University), Dept. of Information Science and Engineering, NMAM Institute of Technology, Nitte, Udupi 574110, India

dr.manjulagururajh@nitte.edu.in Venugopala P S NITTE (Deemed to be University), Dept. of Artificial Intelligence and Data Science, NMAM Institute of Technology, Nitte, Udupi 574110, India venugopalaps@nitte.edu.in Ankitha A Nayak  * NITTE (Deemed to be University), Department of Computer Science and Engineering, NMAM Institute of Technology, Nitte, Udupi 574110, India ankitha@nitte.edu.in affecting  women,  particularly  in  low  and  middle  income countries. Cervical cancer originates in the cells of the cervix, the lower portion of the uterus, predominantly caused by longterm infection with high-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV). Alarmingly, each year, approximately 250,000 women globally succumb to this disease due to the human papillomavirus (HPV), an infection that around 80% of sexually active women contract. Some strains of HPV, like Type 16 and Type 18, are known to induce cancer and are thus labelled as high-risk. Cervical cancer and HPV infections are curable if it is detected in the early stage [1]. Although HPV infections often clear up within two years, in some instances, they can trigger precancerous conditions [4]. According to global data from the World Health Organization, approximately 605,000 new cervical cancer  cases and 342,000 related deaths  are reported yearly,  which  can  be  reduced  and  moderated  by  the  early detection  of  the  cancer  [5]. Early-stage  cervical  cancer  often does not exhibit any symptoms, as the gradual transformation in cervical  cells  progresses  to  precancerous  lesions,  which  may eventually develop into full-blown cervical cancer. As a result, regular  screening  is  considered  essential. Pap  smears,  HPV DNA Tests, and Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid are among the well-established screening techniques used these days. The Pap  smear  test,  officially  known  as  the  Papanicolaou  Exam, plays  a  significant  role  in  early  detection. The  test  analyses changes in cells  shed  from  the cervix, including  irregularities like  nuclear  size  [2]. Though  there  is  room  for  improving  its effectiveness, regular Pap smear screenings can help to lessen the  prevalence  of  cervical  cancer. Manual  inspection  of  each patient's smear images is tedious and susceptible to errors, given the  number  of  sub-images  a  cytopathologist  must  scrutinize under  a  microscope  [3]. With  the  advancements  in  machine learning, Artificial Intelligence, and image processing technology, the detection and analysis of cervical cancer have become  much  more  effective  and  easier. Recognizing  the importance  of  automated  solutions  in  this  context,  this  paper proposes  a  novel  automated  AI  approach  to  detect  cervical cancer  at  its  initial  stages,  aiming  to  save  more  lives. Cancer diagnosis primarily relies on data retrieved from irregularities in cell  structure  and  distribution. As  diseases  progress,  notable changes  are  observed  in  the  cell's  morphology,  topology, texture, and color, providing the basic idea for disease classification. Relevant features are extracted to convert images into  a  more  understandable  form  and  detect  any  signs  of malignancy. In this work, Pap smear test datasets are utilized to detect  the  presence  of  precancerous  cells. Positive  results indicating  abnormal cells necessitate further treatment or additional tests. However, in the absence of such cells, no further tests are required. The sample of normal and abnormal cells is shown in Fig 1. <!-- image -->

## II. ROOT MAP OF THE LITERATURE REVIEW

Several existing works have exhibited numerous solutions for early crucial cancer detection and analysis. Over the past few years,  research  work  on  cervical  cancer  detection  based  on Artificial  Intelligence  and  the  CNN  network  has  taken  a  leap ahead in the invention of new solutions. In [7], a detailed review of opportunities and research challenges in cervical cancer using deep  learning  is  presented.  A  more  detailed  study  on  the advancement  in  cervical  cancer  detection  using  whole  side images is shown in [8]. Few researchers [9] have presented work in  which  convolution  neural  networks  were  applied  to  detect multiple cancers such as oral, breast, kidney, lung, colon, and cervical cancer with a validation accuracy of 99.94%. In [10], the  hybrid  model,  combined  with  deep  learning  and  machine learning, is explained to detect cervical cancer with an accuracy of 98.08%. In this work, the integration of the machine learning algorithm with Resnet-152 has shown impressive performance. To understand and analyse more about the role of the dataset in cancer detection, in [11] a review is conducted with 24 practical papers  for  cervical  cancer  detection  based  on  pathology  and colposcopy  images.  In  [12],  a  3D  convolution  model  with  a vision transform module is designed for cervical cancer classification. The paper mainly focused on extracting spatiotemporal features from cervical images. The study achieved an accuracy of 98.6% giving effective performance.

A  method  for  analysing  pap  smear  images  to  find  CC  was introduced  in  the  study  by  W.  William  et  al.[3].  For  scene segmentation, the team used a customizable weak segmentation classifier,  and  to  remove  extraneous  information,  they  used  a sequential  removal  procedure.  Gebeyehu  et  al.  [13]suggested employing a deep learning model to identify and categorise CC. To  help  doctors  more  successfully  remove  ovarian  cysts, Ravishankar, T. N. et al.[14] suggested an automated detection system.  This  method  detects  and  categorizes  cysts  using  the features that were retrieved from the image. An effective CAD called "CerCanNet" is proposed by Attallah et al. [15] for the rapid  detection  of  CC.  In  order  to  simplify  categorization, CerCanNet uses three lightweight CNNs, such as Mobile Net, DarkNet-19, and ResNet-18, with fewer parameters and shallower layers. For automated detection of cervical intraepithelial  neoplasia  (CIN)  in  epithelial  patches  produced from digital histology pictures, Brosnan et al.'s[16] integrated technique was developed. In this study, the authors introduce a tool designed for detection and classification of CC.

## A. Summary of the Literature Review

The  review  section  studies  various  research  papers  related  to cervical cancer detection. The reviewed articles are focused on the types of datasets used for cervical cancer detection and the advancements  in  CC  detection  methods  using  AI.  Various algorithms and models supported for cervical cancer detection are analysed with benefits and limitations. The primary points analysed throughout the review phase are given in Table I.

SIPaKMeD  and  Herlev  have  frequently  used  datasets  in many  research  articles  for  CC  detection  using  CNN and ML.

The hybrid  model  with  CNN  and  ML  algorithms for CC detection gives better performance and accuracy

RCNN and FCNN can be applied for CC detection  with architecture to enhance performance

## III. METHODOLOGY

The proposed hybrid CNN model aims at the classification and detection of cervical cancer and its five cervical cell types. The model is mainly trained on major two datasets, namely the SIPaKMeD  and  Herlev  datasets. The designed approach delivers a simple and efficient user-friendly interface to upload pap smear cell images with a UI to choose segmentation and ROI  operation.  The  proposed  tool  facilitates  UI  to  analyze features such as the area, perimeter, and so on for cytoplasm and nucleus of given pap smear images. This section further explains the  architecture  of  the  proposed  model  and  its  functional modules,  as  shown  in  Fig  2.  The  high-level  design  of  the proposed hybrid CNN architecture is mainly categorized into six modules  namely,  Dataset  collection, Splitting the dataset, Annotation of training images and producing masks, Segmentation,  Feature  extraction  and  selection  and  Cancer detection and classification. The explanation of each module is further discussed as a separate subsection of this study.

Fig 2. Architecture of Proposed Methodology with GUI

<!-- image -->

## A. Dataset Collection

This  study  uses  the  SIPaKMeD  and  Herlev  datasets  for  the training  purposes.  The  SIPaKMeD  dataset  consists  of    4049 secluded  cell  pictures  extracted  from  966  Pap  smear  group images. The extracted cell pictures include ordinary. strange, and harmless cells. The cell pictures are further classified into five types of cells such as shallow transitional cells, parabasal cells,  koilocytotic  cells,  dyskeratotic  cells,  and  metaplastic cells.  The  intermediate  cells  used  in  the  research  were  taken from the Herlev dataset.

## B. Splitting of Dataset

For training and testing purposes, the dataset was partitioned at a ratio of 80:20. The training and testing subsets had 468 and 117 pictures, respectively. Out of the 468 images, the 100 pictures were dyskeratotic, superficial, and metaplastic, with 98 being koilocytotic and 70 being intermediate. The split up  of  the  dataset  is  handled  carefully  to  avoid  corruption between the integrity of the items in the train and the test sets. The  presented  work  has  an  optional  shuffle  operation  in  the validation  set  that  shuffles  images  in  the  dataset  and  allows users  to  collect  random  samples  for  both  the  training  and validation sets. The training and validation values will subsequently be called separately and stored in their respective variables. The detailed illustration given in Fig 3.

Fig. 3. Detailed Dataset Split-up

text:
## C. Segmentation

The segmentation  of  cytoplasm  and  nucleus  is  necessary  for valuable  information  extraction  in  this  approach.  In  the  CC cancer  detection  and  classification  process,  identifying  the region of interest(RoI) is the fundamental step. In the proposed work,  the  UNET  model  is  applied  for  RoI  detection  using  a segmentation technique. The implemented model is designed with  characteristics  to  handle  and  adjust  images  of  various dimensions.  UNET  model  is  a  network  designed  with  an encoder  and  decoders  in  a  U  shape.   The  decoder  assists localization  and  symmetric  expansion  path  using  converted convolution.  The  UNET  model  consists  of  four  encoder  and decoder  blocks  with  a  connecting  bridge.  Cytoplasm  and nucleus  of  the  cell  in  the  given  labelled  image  were  trained proficiently  using  UNET.  Generally,  the  nuclei  play  a  major role in cervical cancer detection, and cytopathologists mainly concentrate on cell-based diagnostic screening to evaluate the characteristics of the nucleus and cytoplasm.  In this work, the labelled images are used for training purposes, which designs the model instrumental in the testing and RoI detection of new input  images.   In  the  implemented  segmentation  method,  the cytoplasm  and  nucleus  are  identified  separately  as  shown  in Fig.  4.  Testing  was  performed  on  117  test  images,  and  the results were accurate, which will be further discussed.

Fig.4. Segmentation of Nucleus and Cytoplasm

<!-- image -->

## D. Feature Extraction and Selection

Feature extraction technique converts images into a highly suitable  format  that  supports  classification  by  distinguishing morphological and textural parameters, focusing on nuclear and cytoplasmic  features  associated  with  the  Bethesda  System. Using  a  scikit-image  package,  contours  give  morphological details such as area, perimeter, and eccentricity. GLCM acquires texture based on pixel relationships. The extracted characteristics  are  necessary  for  distinguishing  abnormal  and normal  cells  that  are  refined  through  feature  selection  to eliminate  noise  and  enhance  classification  performance.  The extracted features were gathered into a single data frame, saved as a CSV file, and prepared for the classification approach. The characteristics used in proposed model is shown in Table II.

## E. Evaluation of the Classification Models

The  evaluation  of  a  model's  performance  is  an  extremely important step in every research study. In this paper, performance metrics such as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score are used for the evaluation model which is discussed in the result  section.  To  enhance  the  robustness  and  accuracy  of cervical  cancer  classification  Random  Forest and XGBoost  is applied after U-Net segmentation. The approach helps to analyse non-linear  relationship  and  complexity  between  the  extracted features.

## IV. RESULTS

The proposed work identifies 5 variants of cervical cancer cells. The approach was built using two different data repositories. The  superficial,  dyskeratotic,  koilocytotic,  and  metaplastic classes are trained using the SIPaKMeD dataset and the Herlev dataset to train intermediate cells. Data annotation is handled manually using the APEER website. 100 images are collected for  three  classes.  To  train  the  UNET  model,  98  koilocytotic class images and 70 intermediate class images are taken.  The tagged dataset is later cascaded into the UNET model for the segmentation.  After  the  region  of  interest  is  extracted,  the attributes  are  collected  from  each  ROI  of  the  image.  The extracted  attributes  are  further  used  for  classification  and identification of cells. In this methodology, the GUI is designed to  make  the  work  more  flexible  and  easier  for  the  user  and clinical  use.  The  designed  GUI  is  illustrated  in  Fig.  5.   The performance analysis of the proposed study is outlined in Table III. To gain a better insight into performance metrics, such as Accuracy,  precision,  recall,  and  F1  score,  is  calculated. ## V. CONCLUSION

The suggested model outlines a method for classifying and detecting cervical cancer from Pap smears utilizing the UNET model  for  segmentation  and  the  Random  Forest  classifier algorithm  for  classification.  Cervical  cancer  and  HPV  have serious worldwide consequences. The burden of these diseases must  be  reduced  globally  through  research  and  advances  in identification and treatment. The proposed methodology gives an accuracy of 89%, which is better than the existing research work.  For  future  enhancement,  the  proposed  model  can  be worked on multimodal data and ensembled with RCNN.

text:
## Impact of Real-Time Posture Yoga on Brain Regions and EEG-based Classification Using Machine Learning

## Rashmi C R

Associate Professor, Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Channabasaveshwara Institute of Technology Gubbi, Tumkur, Karnataka, India rashmi.cr@cittumkur.org

Abstract -  Yoga  is  an  ancient  Indian  practice  that  encompasses various  techniques  for  physical  and  mental  healing.  One  such practice  is  posture  yoga,  or  asana,  which  consists  of  different poses aimed at regulating physical and mental functions. Previous  studies  have  reported  an  increase  in  alpha  activity immediately after yoga practice; however, the real-time effects of posture  yoga  on  brain  activity  remain  unexplored.  This  paper aims  to  investigate  these  effects  using  electroencephalography (EEG).  EEG  analysis  was  conducted  for  41  yoga  poses  and  a control group in a resting state using Enobio-8 device. Features including absolute power, relative band power, total power, and entropy  were  extracted  from  the  EEG  signals.  The  results indicated an  increase  in  alpha  relative  band  power  in  the temporal,  central,  and  occipital  regions,  whereas  beta  relative band power was higher in the frontal region. Wilcoxon rank-sum test revealed significant differences between yoga and rest states for  (a)  alpha  absolute  power  (P  <  0.001),  (b)  total  power  (P  < 0.001), (c) beta absolute power (P < 0.001), and (d) theta absolute power (P < 0.001).  Additionally,  machine  learning  models  were implemented to automatically classify yoga and rest states, with XGBoost achieving the highest accuracy of 94%. These findings suggest that during real-time yoga, alpha brain activity is higher across most brain regions, indicating a greater state of relaxation.

## Keywords - BCI, EEG, Yoga, Machine learning

## I. INTRODUCTION

Since  stress  is  the  leading  cause  of  the  majority  of  mental disorders, many people suffer from it and take medications to treat it. But  the problem  is  that few  people  take  those medications forever. Hence, there are certain practices that can help them  overcome  those  disorders. Yoga  is one  such practice  that  originated  in  ancient  India  to  help  people  heal from physical and mental disorders.

In yoga, there are different practices involving physical and breathing  exercises  (meditation).  These  practices  have  been proven to be efficient in many cases. A lot of researchers have worked  on  the  analysis  of  EEG  to  quantify  the  cognitive improvement  after  following  these  practices.  EEG  can  be  a biomarker to identify the difference in cognitive improvement before and after the yogic practices.

In this paper, rather than analyzing the EEG before and after yoga  practice,  the  EEG  is  analyzed  during  real-time  yoga practice.  This  paper  has  made  a  novel  attempt  to  check  the pattern of EEG during the posture yoga practice and make a comparison with the resting state EEG. Also, different machine  learning  methods  are  implemented  to  classify  the signal during yoga and the resting state.

Shantala C P

Prof & Head,

Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Channabasaveshwara Institute of Technology Gubbi, Tumkur, Karnataka, India shantala.cp@cittumkur.org

text:
## II. BACKGROUND

A  wide  range  of  studies  has  utilized  machine  learning methods  for  automatic  classification  of  EEG  signals  before and  after  yoga.  The  classification  of  mediator's  and  nonmediator's  EEG  is  shown  in  [1]  for  yoga  combined  with sudarshana  kriya.  They  took  EEGs  before  and  after  three months of yoga practice. These signals were classified using Support Vector Machine (SVM), decision tree, logistic regression,  discriminant  analysis,  ensemble  and  weighted  KNearest  Neighbor  (KNN)  classifiers.  SVM  has  shown  the highest  classification  accuracy.  Another  study  showed  that breathing practices can be used to decrease stress in adolescents with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) [2]. In this work,  they  have  shown  SVM  and  deep  learning  models  to classify  mental  stress  with  and  without  guided  breathing practice.  Different  variants  of  LSTM  were implemented, and they  achieved  93%  classification  accuracy.  This  shows  the potential  use  of  deep  learning  approaches  for  the  automatic classification of EEGs with disorders. Meditation and yoga are shown as complementary therapies for stress-related psychiatric  disorders  [3].  They  have  shown  an  increase  in alpha  and  theta  activity  after  the  practice  of  meditation  in neuropsychiatric  disorder  patients.  Takaaki  Komiyama  et  al., [4]  have  demonstrated the effect of acute aerobic exercise in combination with eyes closure on alpha activity. It is observed that exercise significantly increases alpha activity. They have considered eyes closed and open conditions  for collection of EEG data. The effect on alpha and beta activity was observed during  eye  closure.  A.  Tiwari  et  al.,  [5]  have  designed  a Smartphone  application  for  stress  removal  using  yoga  and music  therapy.  The  main  goal  of  this  application  was  to provide relaxation to individuals. Padmavathi Kora et al., [6] have  provided  a  systematic  review  on  effect  of  yoga  and meditation  on  human  brain  activity  using  machine  learning. Mental  states  classification  using  different  machine  learning models like SVM, Fuzzy logic, KNN, Random forest, neural networks are described. Most of the existing work concentrated  on  pre  and  posr-yoga  analysis  but  not  during yoga practice.

## III. METHODS AND MATERIALS

This section gives the details of methodology followed for analyzing  EEG  signals  and  describes  the  machine  learning approaches used for the classification of brain activity during yoga and resting states. The workflow of proposed methodology is shown in figure 1.

Fig. 1.  Workflow of Proposed Methodology

<!-- image -->

## A. Data Description

EEG signal is recorded during the exercise of 41 different posture  yoga(asanas)  and  a  control  group  in  the  resting  state without any prior experience of yoga practice using Enobio-8 device. Enobio-8 is a wireless 8-channel EEG signal acquisition device from Neuroelectrics, Spain shown in figure 2. The electrode positions are O1, O2, C3, C4, FP1, FP2, T7, T8 with sample frequency of 500Hz. The left (A1) and right (A2)  earlobes  are  used  for  reference  ground  and  electrodes respectively.  All  the  subjects  selected  were  normal  without any mental disorders with age between 21 to 35. Yoga data is recorded from experienced yoga practitioners. Also, EEG data is  recorded  from  normal  subjects  in  resting  state.  Figure  3 shows few yoga postures during signal recording. All participants were right-handed, physically healthy, and provided  informed  consent  prior  to  participation.  Individuals taking medications affecting brain activity, consuming alcohol or caffeine within 24 hours of recording, or exhibiting excessive movement or artifacts during EEG acquisition were excluded from the study.

text:
## B. Data Preprocessing

The raw EEG signals contain artifacts induced either from non-physiological or physiological sources. Physiological artifacts  are  eye  blink,  muscle  movements,  deep  breathe  etc which  originates  internally.  Non-physiological  artifacts  are due to cable movements, incorrect reference placement, electrode  pop  etc  which  originates  externally.  In  the  present study,  EEG  signal  is  highly  contaminated  since  signals  are recorded  during  posture  yoga.  Posture  yoga  includes  many body  movements  along  with  breathing  control  so  raw  EEG signal had muscle, eye blink and deep breathe artifacts. These artifacts are removed using Parks-McClellan optimal FIR filter with band pass filter of 2 to 40Hz [7]. The filter range 2-40Hz is considered as per the EEG bands selected. Figure 4 shows almost  a  clean  EEG  after  removal  of  all  the  artifacts  for posture yoga EEG.

## C. Feature Extraction

The filtered EEG signal is used to extract the EEG bands such  as  alpha,  delta,  theta,  gamma  and  beta  using  multiwavelet transform. In multi-wavelet transform, wavelet is used for decomposing the filtered signal into 6 levels with Daubedhies  14  wavelet.  Multi-wavelet  is  considered  since  it gives EEG bands in different levels. Figure 5 shows the bands extracted for one of the posture yoga.

The statistical  features  are  extracted  by  analyzing  each  EEG band individually. Statistical features are used as a feature set to  train  the  different  machine  learning  models  for  automatic classification of mental states. The different statistical features considered  for  our  study  are  mean,  band  power,  minimum, maximum, relative band power, total power, variance, entropy, kurtosis and standard deviation computed in MATLAB [8]. Table 1 shows all the EEG features.

## 1) Power Spectral Density (PSD) analysis with band power

Welch PSD is used to check the power spectral estimate for all  the  EEG  bands.  Welch  PSD  estimate  is  calculated  for alpha, beta, delta, gamma and theta bands for yoga and resting state. This PSD is further used to calculate the absolute band power of EEG signal using matlab bandpower function. This gives the energy of each EEG bands. In practice, the power of a  frequency  band  is  expressed  as  a  percentage  of  the  total signal power, rather than as absolute band power; this measure is  termed  relative  band  power.  The  calculated  relative  band power for each of the bands is compared using the statistical approach  with  error  bars  shown  as  mean±  standard  error. Figure 6 shows the percentage change of relative band power (mean ± standard  error)  for  all  the  EEG  bands.  Rise  in  alpha and  beta  relative  power  is  detected  during  yoga  practice compared to resting state. There is a decrease in delta, gamma and theta relative band power. With this observation, it can be concluded  that  there  is  a  significant  rise  in  alpha  and  beta bands  during  yoga  practice.  Also,  the  percentage  of  alpha relative  band  power  (nearly  0.495  as  shown  in  figure  6a)  is higher  compared to beta relative  band  power  (nearly  0.17  as shown in figure 6b) which indicate increased relaxation.

Posture  yoga  EEG  experiment  comprises  artifacts  due  to head movements, body movements, and deep breathing. If rise in  alpha  and  beta  relative  band  power  during  yoga  is  due  to artifacts  such  as  noise  originated  by  body  movements,  the increments should be witnessed at all the recordings. However, the increase in theta, delta and gamma relative band powers  is  not  observed  rather  there  is  a  decrease  in  band powers of these bands, inferring that the yoga effects on alpha and beta activity are not artifacts. Hence, the increase was not due  to  artifacts,  it  is  due  to  increased  brain  activity  during yoga practice.

## 2) Neurological Assessment

The filtered EEG data is used to extract the features such as absolute  power,  relative  power,  and  entropy  for  each  EEG band, as discussed in Section III. This  section  provides  a discussion of these features for all channels and lobes.

## a: Alpha Absolute power

The  frequency  range  of  alpha  band  is  between  8-13Hz. Absolute alpha band power is determined for each subject in both resting and  yoga  state.  Absolute power is calculated by taking  the  mean  of  all  the  subjects.  The  data  points  are normalized by dividing all the subjects' data with the resting state  data  [9].  The  resultant  absolute  power  for  each  channel and  lobe  is  depicted  in  figure  7. text:
## 3) Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis is performed to check the effect of yoga with the resting group. Wilcoxon rank-sum test is applied for the  selected  features:  absolute  power,  entropy  and  relative power for alpha, beta and theta bands. The test conditions are for yoga vs rest for each channel (C3, C4, FP1, FP2, O1, O2, T7,  T8,)  or  lobes  (frontal,  temporal,  central  and  occipital). Statistical analysis was performed using DataTab online tool. It was a two-tailed test with alpha (significance level) equal to 0.05[18]. Two-tailed Wilcoxon rank-sum test is a nonparametric hypothesis test where the alternative hypothesis is that both yoga and resting group is from different distribution. This  test  is  performed  to  check  the  statistical  significance  of two groups that is  yoga  and  resting  states.  The  result  of  this test is shown in section IV.

## 4) Classification using Machine learning with Feature Scaling

The  automatic  classification  of  mental  states  during  yoga and  resting  state  is  performed  using  eight  machine  learning algorithms. They  are Logistic regression, support vector machine, random forest, Decision tree, XGBoost, Light gradient  boosting  machine,  Gaussian  naïve  bayes  and  KNearest  Neighbour.  These  machine  learning  models  were chosen  because  they  represent  diverse  learning  approaches suitable for EEG  data,  which  is often non-linear, highdimensional, and noisy [10-17]. Feature scaling is applied for all  the  extracted  features  before  using  it  for  training  the machine  learning  method.  It  is  one  of  the  techniques  to normalize the given features by distributing it over a specified range. There are many categories of feature scaling and they are StandardScaler, MinMaxScaler, MaxAbsScaler, RobustScaler  etc.  MinMaxScaler  is  the  most  popular  feature scaling method since the shape of original distribution in the data is preserved. It is also an alternative to z-score normalization or standardization. The scaling range in minmaxscaler is between 0 and 1. It results in smaller standard deviations  which  help  to  suppress  the  effect  of  outliers.  The min-max scaling is applied using equation 1.

Abstract - The increasing demand for organic farming has led  to  the  need  for  efficient  monitoring  and  automation  of traditional  organic  fertilizers  like  Jeevamrutha.  This  paper presents  a  novel  system  titled  'IoT-Based  Image  Processing System  for  Jeevamrutha  Monitoring  and  Automation'.  The system integrates Raspberry Pi, multiple sensors, and decision tree classification to analyse the different stages of Jeevamrutha preparation. Experimental deployment of the system achieved 90%  accuracy  in  stage  classification  and  resulted  in  a  30% reduction  in  manual  labour  during  preparation.  Real-time alerts  and  consistent  microbial  growth  ensured  improved  soil fertility and enhanced crop yield, making the system viable for sustainable and precision agriculture.

Keywords-  IoT,  Organic  Farming,  Jeevamrutha,  Image Processing,  Smart  Agriculture,  Decision  Tree  Algorithm,  Soil Monitoring, Precision Farming.

With the growing concerns about chemical fertilizers and their  adverse  effects  on  soil  health,  organic  farming  has gained  importance.  Jeevamrutha,  a  natural  liquid  fertilizer made from cow dung, cow urine, jaggery, and other organic components,  plays  a  vital  role  in  enriching  soil  microbes. However,  traditional methods  of  preparation  are laborintensive and lack standardization.

Recent  advancements  in  Internet  of  Things  (IoT)  and image processing have enabled smart agricultural solutions. ## IV. PROPOSED METHOD/ ALGORITHM

The proposed IoT and image processing-based system for Jeevamrutha  preparation  was  implemented  in  two  main stages:  (1)  system  hardware  integration  and  (2)  algorithmic processing.  The  implementation  is  described  in  detail  as follows:

## Step 1: Hardware Integration

- A  Raspberry  Pi  The central control unit is a microcontroller.
- To  allow  for  real-time  monitoring,  the  following sensors are connected:
- o Temperature sensor to monitor fermentation heat levels.
- o Moisture sensor to assess water content.
- o Gas sensor to detect gas emissions during microbial activity.
- o pH sensor to measure acidity and alkalinity levels.
- A  camera  module  is  installed  to  capture  periodic images of the Jeevamrutha solution.
- A stirring motor is linked and triggered automatically based on sensor thresholds.
- Sensor readings (temperature, moisture, pH, gas) are collected and logged continuously.
- The  camera  captures  images  of  the  Jeevamrutha mixture at defined intervals.
- The  images  are  processed  using  MATLAB-based functions:
- o Grayscale  conversion  to  simplify  image intensity levels.
- o Noise  filtering  using  Gaussian  or  median filters.
- o Segmentation to isolate the region containing the Jeevamrutha solution.

Step 2: Data Collection

## Step 3: Image Preprocessing

Step 4: Feature Extraction Rationale

The  image  features  selected  are  critical  indicators  of microbial activity and organic decomposition:

- Color variation reflects chemical changes in Jeevamrutha due to microbial growth.
- Texture  helps distinguish  between  turbid (early stage) and uniform mixtures (final stage).
- Edge density indicates surface changes as bubbling and sediment formation stabilize.

Step 5: Stage Classification and System Automation

A  decision  tree  algorithm  classifies  the  extracted  image features into different preparation stages (Initial, Mid, Ready).  Once  the  final stage is identified, the  system automatically  halts  the  stirring  mechanism  and  sends  realtime alerts to the user through a connected interface. If the solution is still in earlier stages,  the  system  continues automated  stirring  based  on  a  feedback  loop  with  sensor input. Table I depicts the feature conditions.

TABLE I Classification Logic (Decision Tree Branches)

| Feature Condition                                     | Decision Tree Rule Applied                | Classification Output   |
|-------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------|
| Color intensity < Threshold1                          | Early fermentation phase                  | Initial Stage           |
| Color intensity > Threshold1 AND Texture < Threshold2 | Moderate decomposition & bacterial growth | Mid Stage               |
| Texture ≥ Threshold2 AND Edge Density low             | Uniform, fully fermented solution         | Ready Stage             |

The  tree  classifies  input  images  by  traversing  these  rules based on extracted feature values.

Step 6: System Testing and Performance Evaluation

The complete system was tested in real farming environments. Evaluation showed a 90%  classification accuracy for Jeevamrutha stages, a 30% reduction in manual labor, and enhanced soil fertility. These results validate the system's  reliability,  usability,  and  effectiveness  in  organic agriculture.

The  decision tree algorithm was  chosen  due to its interpretability,  efficiency  on  small  datasets,  and  ability  to handle mixed feature types. While models like SVM or CNN offer higher complexity, they demand extensive training data and  computational  resources,  which  are  limited  in  field conditions.

The dataset includes over 300 real-time images of Jeevamrutha collected over 10 days at 2-hour intervals using a Pi Camera. Sensor data was logged concurrently. The data is proprietary but available on request.

Images  were  pre-processed  using  grayscale conversion, Gaussian  filtering,  and  threshold  segmentation.  Features extracted include:

- Color histogram bins
- Texture features via GLCM
- Edge density. These were statistically validated for correlation with fermentation stages.

## A. Experimental Setup and Dataset Overview:

To  assess  the  effectiveness  of  the  proposed  system,  a practical experiment was conducted in a monitored organic farming setting over a span of ten days. During this period, approximately 300 images were captured at regular intervals of two hours using a Pi Camera, allowing for consistent visual tracking of the Jeevamrutha fermentation process. Simultaneously, real-time sensor data-comprising pH (with ±0.1 accuracy), temperature, gas concentration, and moisture levels-was  recorded  continuously. Each  image  and  its corresponding  sensor  data  were  carefully  time-stamped, enabling accurate correlation with manually verified fermentation stages  labeled  as  Initial,  Mid,  or  Ready. This integrated  approach  ensured  a  comprehensive  dataset  for validating the system's performance in real-world agricultural conditions. 5- Fold Cross validation is performed to verify the performance of the model. The  term  "Jeevamrutha"  combines  the  Sanskrit  terms jeevan (life) and amrit (nectar or medicine) to signify "life nectar for plants."   In natural farming, this microbial culture and fermented liquid biofertilizer is used to boost soil fertility and  promote  plant  growth. What  Jeevamrutha  do  to  the plants. Instead of feeding plants directly, Jeevamrutha feeds and enriches the soil's beneficial microorganisms. After that, the plants receive nutrients from these microbes. The  recipe  for  Jeevamrutha  uses  readily  available  local ingredients and a simple fermentation process includes:

- Two hundred liters of water. - Ten kilos of manure from cows. - Five to ten liters of urine from cows. - Two  kilograms  of  fermentable  sugar,  such  as jiggery. - Two  kilograms  of  pulsed  flour,  such  as  besan (gram) flour. - A tiny quantity of dirt from a farm or woodland

For 48 hours to a week, the materials are combined in a barrel, covered with a towel, and stirred twice daily. The mixture is kept in the shade during the fermenting process. It is typically diluted with water before being sprayed on leaves or applied to the soil. The  system  was  tested  under  controlled  conditions,  and various stages of Jeevamrutha preparation were monitored. ## Memory Dropout GRU Architecture for Efficient and Generalizable Sequence Learning

Shravan Kumar Department of Mechanical and Robotics Engineering, Sahyadri College of Engineering & management, Mangaluru, India skodiyoor3@gmail.com Jeevith B T Department of Mechanical and Robotics Engineering, Sahyadri College of Engineering & management, Mangaluru, India jeevithbidarakatte@gmail.com

Rathishchandra Ramachandra Gatti Department of Mechanical and Robotics Engineering, Sahyadri College of Engineering & management, Mangaluru, India gattirathish@gmail.com

Abstract -This study proposes an innovative recurrent neural network model employing the Memory-Dropout Gated Recurrent Unit (MD-GRU), which is aimed at enhancing the sequential data ML classification performance. The MD-GRU introduces two key modifications to the standard GRU: (1) dropout applied directly within the memory update pathway to mitigate overfitting, and (2) a learnable activation function to increase model adaptability. The MD-GRU model was evaluated on the UCI Human Activity Recognition (UCI-HAR) dataset and it is observed that this model achieves a remarkable classification accuracy of 95.08% for 50 epochs compared to the conventional GRU, with minimal additional computational cost. These results demonstrate that the proposed modifications improve generalization while maintaining efficiency, positioning MD-GRU as a promising approach for time-series analysis tasks.

KeywordsRecurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Memory Dropout, Dynamic Activation Function, Human Activity Recognition (HAR)

## I. INTRODUCTION ( HEADING 1 )

Recurrent Neural Networks  (RNNs)  are  extensively utilized for modelling sequential information in domains such as  Natural  Language  Processing  (NLP),  Human  Activity Recognition (HAR), and various signal processing tasks[1][3].  Among  the  different  RNN  variants,  the  Gated Recurrent  Unit  (GRU)[10]  is  recognized  for  its  strong computational efficiency and performance, often matching or surpassing the capabilities of the more complex Long ShortTerm Memory (LSTM) models. The GRU[5] was introduced to address the vanishing gradient issue present in traditional RNNs, enabling the effective learning of long-range dependencies in sequence data. It employs two primary gating mechanisms: (i) the update gate (zₜ), which determines how much of the previous hidden state is retained, and (ii) the reset gate  (rₜ),  which  regulates  how  much  past  information  is discarded. Since GRU has fewer parameters than LSTM (no separate  cell  state),  it  is  faster  to  train  and  less  prone  to overfitting on small datasets. This makes them ideal candidates for sequential tasks like HAR, Speech recognition, time-series forecasting and NLP[2][4]. Despite their strengths, GRUs have drawbacks such as overfitting on small or noisy datasets, limited regularization[8], limited model flexibility, Asthik K L

Department of Mechanical and Robotics Engineering,

Sahyadri College of Engineering & management,

Mangaluru, India

asthikkoingaje@gmail.com

Sri Haripriya Rai N Department of Electronics and Communication Engineering, Sahyadri College of Engineering management, Mangaluru, India

&

raishp1@gmail.com

fixed  activation  functions  (typically  tanh  and  sigmoid)  and gradient Issues in long sequences[10].  To  address  this limitation, recent research has explored regularization techniques such as dropout, which randomly omits neurons during training to prevent co-adaptation. While feed- forward dropout is commonly used, recurrent dropout especially when applied  to  internal  memory  updates  has  shown  promise  in enhancing generalization without sacrificing temporal coherence.

Another line of research has demonstrated the benefits of dynamic activation functions that adapt their non- linearities during  training[6].  These  adaptive  functions,  when  made learnable can improve convergence and robustness by learning taskspecific transformations beyond fixed activation shapes like ReLU or tanh.

This paper proposes a unified architecture, the MemoryDropout GRU (MD-GRU), which integrates candidate- state dropout  with  learnable  dynamic  activation  functions.  The MD-GRU introduces dropout at the candidate memory update level to discourage memorization, while embedding a slopeadaptive activation function within the GRU cell to increase flexibility  during  training.  We  evaluate  the  proposed  MDGRU on  the UCI Human Activity Recognition(UCI-HAR) benchmark  dataset.  Experimental  results  demonstrate  that MD-GRU  consistently achieves better results than the standard GRU[10] with respect to accuracy, F1-score, and the Area Under the Curve (AUC), while maintaining acceptable computational overhead. These findings support the efficacy of combining internal dropout and dynamic activations as a practical strategy for robust sequence modelling.

## II. RELATED WORK

RNNs, especially variants like LSTM and GRU architectures[10], have emerged as the standard approach for sequence modelling because they excel at capturing relationships across long time spans. However, these models are prone to overfitting, especially in low-resource settings. To address this, regularization techniques such as dropout and recurrent dropout have been widely explored.

Gal  and  Ghahramani's  work  on  recurrent  dropout  without memory loss demonstrated that selectively applying dropout within  the  recurrent  connections  improves  generalization while preserving temporal coherence[9]. Building upon this, candidate-state dropout was introduced to target the memory update  path  of  RNNs,  offering  a  finer-  grained  form  of regularization. Despite progress in both dropout regularization and adaptive activations-few studies have combined them within a single architecture. The MD-GRU addresses this gap by integrating memorylevel dropout with Dynamic Activation Allocation (DAA) inside the GRU cell[6]. Early experiments on sentiment analysis and HAR indicate that this dual enhancement leads to better generalization and robustness with negligible runtime penalty. Furthermore, prior works on the UCI-HAR dataset typically focus on standard GRU or LSTM-based models. Our approach extends this by applying memory dropout at the candidate state and evaluating  improvements  in  F1-score,  AUC,  and  training efficiency.

## III. STANDARD GRU AND MD-GRU

A standard GRU as shown in Fig. 1 processes data along a single dimension, typically time-updating its hidden state sequentially using reset and update gates to manage temporal dependencies efficiently[10]. In contrast, the MD-GRU is a modified Gated Recurrent Unit that introduces dropout in the memory update path to improve generalization  and  reduce overfitting. Unlike a standard GRU, it introduces dropout to the  previous  hidden  state  before  calculating  the  candidate hidden state. This forces the network  to rely less on memorized patterns and more on relevant input features. This simple  change  retains  GRU's  efficiency  while  enhancing performance, especially on small or noisy datasets.

## IV. DATASET AND PREPROCESSING

## A. Dataset Description

The experiments in this study were conducted using the UCI  HAR  benchmark  dataset,  which  is  a  benchmark dataset  for  sequential  human  activity  classification.  The dataset  comprises  10,299  samples  collected  from  30 subjects, each performing six different physical activities: walking, walking upstairs, walking step is represented by 561 feature values. These features are derived from time and frequency domain signal processing, capturing body motion and orientation patterns relevant to activity recognition tasks. The dataset is well-balanced and publicly available through the UCI Machine Learning Repository.

## B. Data Preprocessing

Before  inputting  the  data  into  the  models,  multiple preprocessing steps were applied to maintain consistency and ensure compatibility with the model requirements. First, the dataset  was  examined  for  missing  or  null  values;  no  such anomalies were found, as the dataset is already pre- processed and clean. Feature standardization  was performed using zscore  normalization,  implemented  with  the  standard  scaler utility from the scikit-learn library. This normalization scales each feature to have zero mean and unit variance, helping to improve training stability and convergence speed[6].

The pre-processed feature vectors were reshaped into a 3D structure  compatible  with  GRU-based  architectures,  with dimensions corresponding to samples, timesteps, and features. In this experiment, the sequences were treated with a timestep of 1 and a feature vector of length 561. Activity labels were converted into integer-encoded categorical classes  (0  to  5),  which  were  later  used  for  multi-  class classification  via  softmax  output.  The  dataset  was  divided into 70% for training and 30% for testing. Additionally, 20% of  the  training  portion  was  set  aside  as  a  validation  set  to facilitate model evaluation during training. Importantly, the temporal sequence of each activity window  was preserved throughout,  and  no  internal  shuffling  of  time  steps  was performed,  ensuring  that  the  recurrent  models  could  fully leverage temporal dependencies[8][9].

## V. MODEL ARCHITECTURES

This section outlines the baseline GRU and the proposed MD-GRU models used for sequential classification.

## A. Standard GRU

The standard  GRU  model,  shown  in  Fig.  2,  comprises  the following components: (i) Input layer, where the input shape is (timesteps=1, features=561), (ii) GRU layer which consists of  64  hidden  units  with  tanh  activation,  (iii)  Dropout  layer where a 0.2 dropout rate is applied after the GRU output, (iv) Dense Layer which consists of 32 units with ReLU activation, and the (v) Output  Layer which is composed  of  six  neurons with Softmax activation and designed for multiclass classification. The training configuration is optimized using Adam (learning rate = 0.001) with categorical cross-entropy loss .

Fig. 2. Block diagram of Standard GRU architecture

<!-- image -->

## B. Memory-Dropout GRU (MD-GRU)

The MD-GRU architecture as shown in Fig. 3, modifies the  standard  GRU  by  integrating  dropout  into  the  memory update path and embedding a learnable dynamic activation function.  It  incorporates  the  following  changes  from  the standard GRU: (i) Candidate Dropout: Dropout is applied to the  candidate  hidden  state  before  it  blends  into  the  final memory  state;  (ii)  Learnable  Activation:  The  activation function  in  the  candidate  state  is  slope-adaptive,  learned during training;(iii) Dropout Mask: A fixed Bernoulli mask is reused across time steps to maintain temporal consistency.

## VI. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed MemoryDropout  GRU  (MD-GRU)  model  against  the  standard GRU, both  architectures  were  trained  on  the  same  UCI Human  Activity  Recognition  dataset  using  a  consistent experimental protocol[10]. Since  the  benchmark dataset was already pre-processed as validated by our exploratory data analysis, it was directly used. Each model was trained for 50 epochs with a batch size of 64 using the Adam optimizer, configured  with  a  learning  rate  of  0.001.  For  multiclass classification,  categorical  cross-entropy  served  as  the  loss function. Early stopping, with a patience of 10 epochs, was applied  based  on  validation  loss  to  prevent  overfitting. Additionally,  20%  of  the  training  data  was  reserved  for validation,  and  model  weights  were  initialized  using  the Xavier initialization scheme.

As shown in Table II, from the ablation study on dropout values (0.0 to 0.5), we observe consistent improvements up to a dropout rate of 0.3. Interestingly, after a dropout of 0.4, the model's performance metrics begin to stabilize, indicating a saturation point in regularization. This suggests an optimal dropout  range  between  0.3  and  0.4  for  this  architecture. Performance metrics begin to stabilize between dropout rates of 0.4 and 0.5. This indicates that the model benefits from strong  regularization  in  this  range,  effectively  mitigating overfitting while maintaining high predictive performance. The MD-GRU model introduces two key innovations: (i) candidate-state memory dropout to combat overfitting within recurrent connections[8], and (ii) dynamic activation allocation through a learnable slope parameter in the GRU cell. Ablation  studies  show  that  removing  either  of  these components results in degraded performance, underscoring their complementary effect. Furthermore, confusion matrix heat maps indicate enhanced class separation, especially for activities like Sitting and Standing , which are often misclassified in standard models. The ROC curves show that MD-GRU maintains  a  higher  true  positive  rate  across  all thresholds, reinforcing its superiority in model ranking and threshold-free classification evaluation. Despite the architectural enhancements, MD-GRU only incurred a 4.5% increase in per-epoch training time, which is acceptable for most real-time applications. Additionally, the model maintained similar parameter counts to the standard GRU, ensuring fairness in comparison and viability for deployment on resource-constrained devices. Overall, the combination of memory-level dropout and learnable non-linearity enables  MD-GRU  to  achieve stronger generalization and discriminative power without compromising efficiency.

text:
## IX. CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK

This  study  presented  the  MD-  GRU,  an  enhanced recurrent architecture that integrates candidate-state memory  dropout  and  dynamic  activation  allocation  to address  overfitting  and  limited  model  adaptability  in sequential  classification  tasks.  By  introducing  memorylevel  dropout  directly  into  the  hidden  state  update  and coupling it with a learnable activation function, MD-GRU promotes  more  effective  regularization  and  expressive capacity within the recurrent unit. Unlike traditional GRUs which may overfit on temporally correlated data, MD-GRU is  designed  to  retain  sequence  memory  while  reducing memorization, leading to improved generalization.

Experimental  evaluation  on  the  UCI  HAR  dataset demonstrated that MD-GRU consistently outperformed the standard GRU in terms of classification accuracy, F1-score, and ROC-AUC, while requiring only a marginal increase in training  time.  Notably,  MD-GRU  showed  robustness  in distinguishing  between  closely  related  human  activity classes,  such  as  sitting  and  standing,  which  are  often confused  in  sensor-based  classification.  The  proposed modifications are lightweight, architecture-compatible, and can be easily integrated into existing RNN workflows.

Despite these promising results, there remain several avenues for further exploration. In future work, we aim to evaluate  the  MD-GRU  on  additional  datasets  exhibiting diverse temporal structures, including long-range dependencies  and  irregular  time  steps.  Datasets  from domains such as speech emotion recognition (e.g., RAVDESS, CREMA-D), physiological signals (e.g., ECG or EEG), and financial forecasting could help validate the generality of our approach. Moreover, dynamic activation functions  could  be  extended  beyond  slope  adaptation  to include  learnable  non-linearity  families  (e.g.,  adaptive ReLU, erf-based activations), potentially boosting performance further. Based on the current results, MD-GRU offers an effective balance between performance, generalization, and computational efficiency, making it a strong candidate for real-world sequential learning applications across various domains.

## MindSync: An Intelligent Journaling Tool for Mental Well-being and Productivity Analysis

Srinivas P M, Prashantha ., Aditya Bhagwat, Dhanush Naik, Kumar Marathe

Department of Computer Science and Engineering Sahyadri College of Engineering and Management Mangaluru, India

Email: { srinivas.cs@sahyadri.edu.in, prashanthprashanth25541@gmail.com,

adityaadi11122@gmail.com, naikdhanush81@gmail.com, kumarsmarathe8317399047@gmail.com }

Abstract -MindSync stands out as a smart journaling platform. It uses Natural Language Processing to help boost mental well-being in everyday ways. Our approach relies on advanced machine learning models that dig into daily journal entries. These models handle emotion detection for things like stress or anxiety. They also cover sentiment analysis and productivity checks all in one go. The system provides feedback that feels personal. It includes easy visualizations drawn from behavioral trends we spot. The results demonstrate solid model performance from the models along with good usability overall. This makes MindSync a useful tool in digital mental health. It connects emotional insights directly to productivity patterns.

Index Terms -Emotion Detection, Machine Learning, Mental Health, Natural Language Processing (NLP), Productivity Analysis, Sentiment Analysis.

## I. INTRODUCTION

## A. Background

These days, in our digital world, everyday stresses have led to a big rise in mental health issues. People of all ages and backgrounds often feel completely overwhelmed by things like school, work, or family demands. That sort of overload tends to cause emotional exhaustion, constant worry, and sometimes total burnout. The World Health Organization reports that hundreds of millions worldwide struggle with depression or anxiety disorders. Our always connected culture just makes the situation even tougher in some ways. This mental pressure affects the way we think as well. It reduces focus, motivation, and the ability to get tasks completed.

## B. Problem Statement

There is a major shortage of tools that allow the individuals to keep track of the delicate interaction between their emotional state and the performance of the day. The majority of the psychological health apps that are available today are onesize-fits-all, providing nothing more than basic mood tracking and task management along with no personalized, data-driven insights. They are usually not capable of giving feedback in real-time that is specifically based on an individual's particular emotional patterns and life context. As a result, the users are not aware of the direct correlation between their emotions like stress, sadness, or happiness with their work efficiency and their overall well-being. This unawareness of one's self may result in a slow but steady decline of both mental health and productivity, since the issues that are at the root of it are neither detected nor addressed.

## C. Contribution and Scope

This research introduces MindSync , an advanced journaling system designed to connect emotional well-being with productivity analysis. In contrast to conventional tools that address mood tracking and task management as separate functions, MindSync offers a unified solution. It integrates both aspects within a single, adaptive framework that prioritizes user privacy.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

- 1) Unified Emotion-Productivity Framework: Simultaneous detection of emotions and productivity patterns from personal journal entries, revealing how affective states influence daily performance.
- 2) Hybrid NLP-ML Architecture: A balanced combination of interpretable models (TF-IDF with Random Forest) and contextual deep learning (fine-tuned BERT) for transparent yet context-aware analysis.
- 3) Personalized Insights and Visualization: Adaptive feedback and intuitive visual dashboards that translate emotional and behavioral data into actionable selfreflection.

In summary, MindSync distinguishes itself through its integration of emotion-productivity correlation, hybrid NLP design, and emphasis on user-centric, interpretable mentalhealth analytics.

text:
## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

Recent studies have demonstrated significant progress in applying natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning techniques to mental health analytics. Notably, Rasool et al. introduced nBERT, a specialized model fine-tuned for emotion recognition within psychotherapy settings [1]. This work highlights the effectiveness of adapting BERT models to specific domains.

In a related development, Scherbakov et al. utilized NLP methods to examine behavioral factors that influence wellbeing [2]. Their approach aligns with MindSync's focus on emotion tracking through journaling. Hameed et al. contributed by developing explainable artificial intelligence models for depression detection, emphasizing the importance of transparency, which is also a central objective for MindSync [3].

Transformer-based models have become widely used for predicting emotions and stress. For example, Pandey and Kumar applied BERT to stress detection tasks [4], while Wu et al. and Gupta et al. advanced the field of contextual sentiment analysis [5], [6]. Sahoo and Wankhade proposed hybrid deep learning methods, supporting MindSync's integration of BERT with Random Forest algorithms [7]. Additionally, Zhang et al. underscored the significance of domain-specific datasets, a principle reflected in MindSync's approach to data curation [8].

Recent research has also expanded sentiment analysis through aspect-based and multimodal techniques. Jayakody et al. focused on aspect-based sentiment detection [10], while Lai et al. incorporated text, audio, and visual data, which informs MindSync's plans for future multimodal analysis [11].

Further, Miah et al. and Pandey and Vishwakarma investigated cross-lingual and ensemble frameworks, enhancing both scalability and multilingual capabilities [14], [15]. Islam et al. achieved balanced results by combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), and Transformers [13]. Huang et al. and Jain et al. improved TF-IDF-based classification through stacking strategies [19], [20].

Together, these advancements support MindSync's hybrid NLP architecture, which integrates contextual embeddings with TF-IDF features to extract emotional insights and analyze productivity patterns.

To contextualize MindSync, Table I presents a comparative overview of related approaches in digital mental health analytics.

TABLE I COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS OF DIGITAL MENTAL HEALTH APPROACHES

| Feature            | Generic Mood Trackers   | Task Managers   | MindSync           |
|--------------------|-------------------------|-----------------|--------------------|
| Emotion Analysis   | Basic (Manual)          | None            | Advanced (NLP)     |
| Productivity Link  | None                    | Indirect        | Direct Correlation |
| Personalization    | Low                     | Low             | High (AI-driven)   |
| Actionable Insight | Limited                 | Limited         | Core Feature       |
| Data Source        | User Input              | User Input      | User Journal Text  |

A variety of tools are available for mood tracking and task management; however, MindSync offers a distinctive solution by combining both functionalities through comprehensive analysis of unstructured text. This approach addresses a significant gap highlighted in the literature [16], [20]. What sets MindSync apart is its ability to move beyond basic data collection. The system provides a holistic perspective on users' daily experiences by linking emotional states with concrete achievements. This integration enables a more complete under- standing of how mood and productivity interact over time.To contextualize MindSync's novelty and scope, a comparative summary of related works is presented in Table I.

## III. MINDSYNC SYSTEM DESIGN

## A. Architecture Overview

The MindSync system is architected as a multi-tier web application designed for scalability and modularity.The highlevel architecture, shown in Fig. 1, illustrates the core system components of MindSync.

- 1) Presentation Layer (Frontend): A responsive web interface where users interact with the system.
- 2) Application Layer (Backend): A Flask-based server that handles API requests, manages user sessions, and orchestrates the data processing workflow.
- 3) Analysis Layer (NLP/ML Engine): The core engine responsible for all text processing, sentiment analysis, and productivity classification.
- 4) Data Layer (Database): A MongoDB database for persistent storage of user data, journal entries, and analysis results.

Fig. 1. System architecture diagram illustrating data flow and processing in the MindSync system.

<!-- image -->

The workflow begins when a user submits a journal entry. The backend API receives the entry, stores it in the database, and triggers the analysis engine. The engine processes the text and returns structured insights (emotions, tasks, scores), which are then stored and made available to the frontend for visualization. This decoupled architecture ensures that components can be updated independently, for instance, allowing the NLP model to be improved without affecting the user interface.
