## A. Hardware Requirements

The proposed IoT and machine learning-based pest detection framework utilizes a range of essential hardware components to ensure effective monitoring and pest detection.

The  DHT11  Sensor  is  used  to  measure  temperature  and humidity  levels  in  the  food  storage  environment,  helping  to maintain conditions that are unfavorable for pest growth.

The ESP32 Microcontroller serves as the core processing unit, handling data collection, communication, and control. Equipped  with  built-in  Wi-  Fi  and  Bluetooth  capabilities,  it facilitates  seamless  integration  of  sensors  and  efficient  data transmission to the central processing system.

The MQ135 Air Quality Sensor monitors the air for gases such as  ammonia and volatile organic compounds (VOCs), which could  indicate  the  presence  of  pests.  This  sensor  adds  an additional layer of proactive environmental monitoring to the system,  enhancing  its  ability  to  detect  changes  that  might promote pest activity.

The Buzzer is incorporated to provide an audible alert when pests are detected or when environmental parameters exceed set thresholds.  This  serves  as  an  immediate  warning  for  facility operators, enabling quick responses to emerging issues.

## B. Software Requirements

A variety of software tools are crucial for the development and implementation of the pest detection system.

OpenCV  is  used  for  image  preprocessing,  including  noise reduction,  contrast  enhancement,  and  edge  detection.  This ensures  high-quality  images  are  available  for  the  YOLOv8 model, which plays a central role in accurate pest detection.

YOLOv8 is the core object detection framework, enabling realtime pest identification. Its high precision and speed make it highly  efficient,  even  in  low-light  environments,  ensuring accurate pest detection across diverse conditions.

MySQL  is  employed  as  the  database  system  to  store  pest detection  logs,  air  quality  readings,  and  historical  data.  It facilitates efficient data retrieval and analysis, allowing operators  to  track  pest  activity  trends  and  environmental changes over time.

Arduino IDE is used to program the  ESP32 microcontroller, enabling  the  integration  of  sensors  and  control  of  system operations.  The  platform  provides  an  intuitive  interface  for configuring sensor operations and communication protocols.

XAMPP is  utilized  to  set  up  a  local  server  for  hosting  and managing  the  web-based  pest  monitoring  dashboard.  This allows real-time visualization of pest activity and environmental data, providing facility operators with actionable insights.

## C. Additional Components for Enhanced Functionality

Several additional components are incorporated to enhance the system's functionality.

HDMI Cables are used to connect the ESP32 to a monitor or display,  enabling  real-time  visualization  of  data  and  system results. This is particularly important during development and testing, allowing easy troubleshooting and performance monitoring. The IP Web Camera is used to capture high- quality images, even in low-light conditions. The camera is essential for detecting pests in dark storage areas, and it works in tandem with the image processing and detection frameworks to provide clear visuals of pests.

The Motion Sensor monitors movement within storage areas, enabling  automated  adjustments  to  the  camera's  focus  and angle  based  on  real-time  sensor  data.  This  enhances  the system's  respon siveness  to  potential  pest  threats  and  helps optimize  operational  costs  by  reducing  the  need  for  manual adjustments.

## A. Experimental Setup

Over  a  continuous  period  of  four  weeks,  an  extensive  and meticulously  curated dataset was  collected, consisting of thousands of high-quality photographs paired with environmental sensor data. These data were gathered as part of multiple  structured  test  cases  designed  to  simulate  various agricultural storage and field conditions. The images captured diverse scenes, including different lighting environments, angles, and pest populations, ensuring the dataset was representative of real-world scenarios. To prepare the images for  analysis,  a  comprehensive  preprocessing  workflow  was applied using OpenCV,  an  open-source  computer  vision library. This preprocessing included sophisticated noise reduction methods aimed at removing unwanted visual artifacts such  as  graininess,  blurring,  and  interference,  which  could adversely affect the accuracy of object detection. The ability to detect  anomalies  in  sensor  data  also  helped  in  identifying unusual pest outbreaks or environmental conditions that might indicate storage issues.

## B. Data Collection and Preprocessing

Over a period of four weeks, a comprehensive data acquisition process was carried out involving the collection of thousands of high-resolution  images  and  a  diverse  array  of  environmental sensor  readings.  These  test  cases  were  designed  to  simulate realistic storage conditions where pest infestations might occur, ensuring the relevance and reliability of the data for subsequent analysis. The captured images were subjected to a meticulous preprocessing pipeline using OpenCV, which involved a series of enhancement techniques such as noise filtering, histogram equalization, and contrast sharpening.

These steps were crucial to improve the visibility of fine details and features in the images, thereby increasing the effectiveness of subsequent image recognition.

Once  preprocessed,  the  enhanced  images  were  fed  into  the YOLOv8  deep  learning-based  recognition  model  for  pest identification and classification. YOLOv8's architecture enabled real-time detection with high precision, making it wellsuited for automated pest surveillance applications. In parallel with the image data, continuous environmental monitoring was conducted using sensors like the DHT11 (for temperature and humidity) and the MQ135 (for detecting air quality and harmful gases). These sensors transmitted readings at regular intervals, which were timestamped and systematically stored in a MySQL relational database.

The accumulated sensor data was then analyzed for patterns and anomalies using statistical and machine learning-based techniques.  This  enabled  the  identification  of  correlations between environmental factors such as increased humidity or the presence of volatile organic compounds and the occurrence of  pest  activity.  Such  insights  were  pivotal  in  developing predictive models that can alert operators about potential pest outbreaks  before  they  escalate.  Ultimately,  this  integrated approach of combining image-based recognition with sensordriven environmental analytics significantly enhances the capability to implement proactive pest management strategies and facilitates  the  optimization  of  storage  conditions  in  realtime.

## C. Performance Metrics

The  system  was  assessed  using  the  following  performance parameters:

- Detection Accuracy: Quantified as the percentage of accurately detected pests against the ground truth.
- False Positives and False Negatives: To deter- mine the consistency of pest detection across various environmental conditions.
- Latency:  The  time  taken  from  image  capture  to generation of alerts.
- Energy Consumption: Tested to maximize IoT device efficiency for long-term usage.

## Evaluation Metrics

- Precision:

Precision = TP / TP + FP

- Recall:

Recall = TP + FN

- F1 -Score: F1 = 2*Precision*Recall / Precision + Recall

Where, TP = TruePositives TN = TrueNegtives FP =  FalsePositives FN = FalseNegatives

- mAP: Average of the area under the precision -recall curve for all classes.

## VII. CONCLUSION

Abstract -Visually impaired individuals encounter significant  challenges  in  navigating  unfamiliar  environments, identifying obstacles, and accessing written information, which impact  their  safety  and  independence.  This  work  presents  a smart wearable device that integrates real-time object detection, text  recognition,  distance  measurement,  and  an  SOS  alert system  into  a  compact,  affordable  solution.  The  system  is powered by a Raspberry Pi 4, equipped with a camera module, and provides audio feedback to the user. Yolov5n is employed for object detection, achieving ~88% accuracy under standard lighting  and  ~92%  in  optimal  conditions,  while  PaddleOCR delivers  ~97%  text  recognition  accuracy.  Distance  to  nearby obstacles  is  estimated  using  a  calibrated  focal  length  method with  an  error  margin  of  ±5  cm,  and  the  SOS  system  ensures emergency  communication  within  3  seconds.  Field  testing demonstrated  improved  mobility,  situational  awareness,  and safety among visually impaired users. This work contributes a multifunctional, accessible assistive device to promote independence and confidence.

## I. INTRODUCTION

In a world filled with vibrant sights, diverse sounds, and intricate details, visually impaired individuals face significant barriers  in  performing  even  the  most  basic  daily  activities. Simple tasks such as crossing a busy intersection, reading a restaurant menu, or navigating through unfamiliar areas can become overwhelming challenges. According to the World Health  Organization  (WHO),  an  estimated  285  million people worldwide live with some form of visual impairment, of which approximately 39 million are completely blind and 246  million  have  low  vision  [1].  As  urban  environments continue  to  become  more  complex  and  fast-paced,  the demand for effective and reliable assistive technologies that can support visually impaired individuals grows increasingly critical [2].

Over the decades, assistive tools designed to help visually impaired individuals have evolved considerably. Conventional aids such as white canes and guide dogs have provided invaluable assistance to countless users [3].

In  addition  to  object  detection,  text  recognition  and speech synthesis are essential functionalities of these devices. Such  capabilities  allow  users  to  independently  read  street signs,  menus,  labels,  and  documents  by  converting  printed text into audible speech [5]. This not only enables users to access vital information but also enhances their confidence and  autonomy.  Hazard  detection  and  timely  alerts  further enhance  the  utility  of  these  systems  by  warning  users  of terrain changes, oncoming vehicles, and unexpected obstacles, significantly reducing accident risk in unpredictable urban settings [6].

Despite these advancements, current assistive technologies face several challenges. Many of the available solutions  are  prohibitively  expensive,  limiting  accessibility for a significant portion of the visually impaired population. Furthermore,  some  devices  require  extensive  training  or technical  skills,  which  can  be  daunting  for  certain  user groups.  There  is  also  a  pressing  need  for  comprehensive solutions  that  seamlessly  integrate  multiple  functionalities into a single, intuitive device [7].

To address these challenges, ongoing research focuses on developing affordable, ergonomic, and multifunctional assistive  devices  tailored  to  the  specific  needs  of  visually impaired  users. Incorporating feedback  from  real users through surveys and usability studies ensures that the resulting  devices  align  closely  with  their  expectations  and daily  requirements.  By  combining  AI  and  ML  with  usercentered  design  principles,  developers  can  create  inclusive and  scalable  technologies  that  empower  visually  impaired individuals  to  navigate  the  world  with  confidence  and independence.

text:
## II. LITERATURE SURVEY

Ashiq et al. proposed  convolutional neural network (CNN)  based application for aiding visually impaired individuals. They analyzed various methodologies and techniques  employed  in  recent  studies,  highlighting  the potential of CNN models in improving object recognition and tracking for visually impaired assistance. The authors examined  the  performance  of  different  CNN  models  on benchmark datasets [8].

Xia  et  al.  designed  a  wearable  smart  system  to  assist visually  challenged  individuals  [9].  They  analyzed  various methodologies and techniques by highlighting the potential of  wearable  smart  systems  in  improving  navigation  and object detection for visually challenged assistance.

Bai et al. proposed a wearable navigation device for blind people.  This  plan  is  the  main  part  of  a  comprehensive navigation system that is installed on wearable optical seethrough glasses to make blind individual's daily walks easier. Tests  on  a  group  of  people  have  shown  that  the  suggested navigation  device  works  well  for  indoor  navigation  tasks [10].

Li  et  al.  introduced  a  new  holistic  vision-based  mobile assistive navigation system to aid blind and visually impaired individuals with independent interior travel [11]. To increase navigation  safety,  the  system  recognizes  dynamic  barriers and modifies path planning in real time.

Katzschmann  et  al.  introducesd  ALVU,  a  wearable technology that is contactless, hands-free, unobtrusive, and intuitive [12]. It enables visually impaired people to identify physical boundaries in their immediate surroundings as well as  barriers  that  hang  low  or  high.  By  allowing  the  user  to differentiate between barriers and clear space, the approach enables safe local navigation in both tight and wide environments.

Zraqou  et  al.  suggested  a  real-time  object  recognition method  to  help  blind  individuals  [13].  Two  cameras  have been installed on blind people's spectacles, and an ultrasonic sensor and GPS-free service are used to offer the information they need about their surroundings. The goal of the suggested approach for the blind is to give those who have vision loss more opportunities to realize their full potential.

A mobile emergency alert system framework was proposed  by  Alsaad  and  Hussien  [14].  Transmitted  and Central Emergency are the two components of the system. The  first  section's  goal  is  to  use  a  global  position  system (GPS)  receiver  device  to  identify  the  event,  determine  its nature, and track its location. Monitoring and evaluating the alarm message and locating the closest assistance center are the objectives of the second section. The suggested system uses  a  unified  modeling  language  and  an  object-oriented software engineering methodology.

## III. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The Smart Wearable Device for Enhanced Mobility and Safety of the Visually Impaired Person leverages cutting-edge AI and machine learning technologies to transform accessibility.  By  integrating  real-time  object  detection,  text recognition, and  distance  measurement  into  a  lightweight wearable, the system ensures accurate, timely, and intuitive assistance. Its decentralized approach, powered by Raspberry Pi, enhances reliability while providing audio-based feedback for real-world navigation.  This  innovative  solution  fosters independence,  addressing  mobility  challenges  and  ensuring the safety of visually impaired users.

System  Architecture: The  system  architecture  is  designed to  handle  real-time  data  processing  and  provide  actionable feedback  to  the  user.  The  wearable  device  consists  of  a Raspberry Pi 4, a camera module, push buttons, and an audio output system (earphones or speaker).

An empty list detected\_objects is initialized to store the labels of objects that meet the confidence threshold. For each detection result, the algorithm extracts the bounding box coordinates (x1, y1, x2, y2), retrieves the object label and its confidence score, and checks whether the confidence exceeds a predefined threshold (e.g.,  0.5). If  so,  the  label  is  appended  to  the detected\_objects list, and the bounding box and label text are drawn on the frame for visualization. The system  captures  images  of  textual  information,  such  as signage or printed documents, processes them, and converts the extracted text into speech. This functionality is particularly useful in public spaces, where reading instructions or signs is essential for navigation.

## V. CONCLUSION

In this study, we present a smart wearable device aimed at improving  mobility,  situational  awareness,  and  safety  for visually impaired individuals in day-to-day life. The device is built around a compact, cost-effective design using a Raspberry Pi 4 platform. It brings together four core functions: real-time object detection, text recognition, distance measurement, and an emergency SOS alert system.

Our evaluation shows that the device achieves about 88% accuracy in object detection under standard lighting, supported  by  the  Yolov5n  model.  The  PaddleOCR  module attains  up  to  97%  accuracy  when  reading  printed  text.  For distance measurement, the device maintains an average error margin of ±5 cm, offering reliable spatial data to the user. The SOS feature enables emergency communication within roughly 3 seconds of activation.

The outlined future work provides a thoughtful roadmap to enhance  the  proposed  smart  wearable  device's  capabilities and broaden its applicability for visually impaired users. Key improvement areas include incorporating GPS-based navigation  to  enable  outdoor  guidance  and  context-aware alerts,  which  would  significantly  extend  usability  beyond indoor  environments.  Adding  multi-language  OCR  support would make text recognition accessible to users from different linguistic backgrounds, adding inclusivity to the device.

## Structured Representation of Free Text and Audio in Medical Records Using Deep Learning

Amrutha 1,2 ,  Raghavendra S 1 ,  Pankaj Kumar 1 ,  Dinesha L 2

1 Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, Karnataka, India, 576104.

2 Department of Computer Science & Engineering, Mangalore Institute of Technology & Engineering, Mijar, Moodabidri, Karnataka, India, 574225.

amrutha2.mitmpl2023@learner.manipal.edu

Abstract -Medical records and decision-making face substantial challenges due to the rapid increase of unstructured medical data,  mainly  in  the  form  of  audio  conversations  and  free-text clinical  notes.  To  deal  with  this  challenge,  we  formulate  a deep learning-based outline that systemizes the extraction and structuring of clinically connected information from both verbal and written medical sources. The system syndicates automatic speech recognition  capabilities  with  dual  NLP  frameworks  for  entity extraction, enhanced with domain-specific post processing methods to guarantee data consistency and accuracy. The framework harnesses  Open  AI's  Whisper  for  ASR,  SpaCy  and  Stanza  for NER, supported by custom rule-based techniques to handle deduplication and data management. The framework is assessed on two freely available datasets:  MedSpeech  (audio)  and  MT Samples  (text-based  medical  transcriptions).  Experimental  and results  demonstrate robust performance, achieving an F1-Score of  90.69.  The  result  shows  strong  potential  for  improving  the accuracy, usability and efficiency of EHR digitization workflows.

Keywords -AI  in  Healthcare,  Clinical  Data,  Deep  Learning, Electronic Health Records, Multilingual Medical NLP

## I. INTRODUCTION

Electronic  Health  Records  plays  a  pivotal  role  in  modern  medicine  by  supporting  better  diagnostics,  customized treatment,  and  clinical  decision-making.  However,  over  80 percent of medical information remains unstructured, as it is found  in  the  form  of  handwritten  prescriptions  and  audiobased  calculations [1].  Extracting  an  organized  data  from these  sources  is  difficult  due  to  handwriting  variations,  poor audio  quality  issues  and  different  languages,  and  domainspecific vocabulary. Optical Character Recognition tools such as Tesseract [2] and ASR systems such as Google Speech to Text and Whisper [3], [4] have shown its ability in digitizing such  data.  Subsequently,  NLP  tools  like  SpaCy,  Stanza,  and BERT based  models  [5],  [6]  are  used  to  extract  the  entities like  Name  of  the  patient,  Age,  Diagnosis,  Symptoms,  and Treatments. However, real-time deployment is delayed due to noisy  inputs,  overlapping  speech,  and  inconsistent  formats. This  paper  proposes  a  combined  deep  learning  framework that integrates both OCR (Tesseract), ASR(Whisper), and NLP tools (SpaCy and Stanza) to organize handwritten and spoken medicinal data. The system is verified on real world datasets involving the prescriptions and audio consultations, and evaluated using precision and recall mainly for the entities such as Name, Age, Symptom, Diagnosis, and Treatment [7] [8] [9]. We develop a complete multimodal framework that flawlessly

processes both handwritten medical documents through optical character  recognition  and  spoken  clinical  consultations  via automatic speech recognition, using parallel natural language processing  models  to  ensure  reliable  entity  extraction  across varied  medical  data  formats.  Designed  and  implemented  a system which is capable of identifying and extracting critical clinical  entities  such  as  Name,  Age,  Symptoms,  Diagnosis and  Treatment  from  an  unstructured  data  source.  This  paper presents the following contributions:

- We  design  a  multimodal  pipeline  which  develops  both audio and text clinical inputs for Named entity recognition.
- We develop a custom annotated dataset combining both real and simulated doctor patient interactions.
- We evaluate the performance of SpaCy and Stanza models  for  clinical  NER  and  implement  a  post-processing plan for entity de-duplication.

Conducted  an  extensive  evaluation  on  publicly  available datasets using precision and recall metrics, demonstrating the efficiency of this method for clinical documentation tasks.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work, Section III describes the methodology, implementation  and  results  are  presented  in  Section  IV,  and Section V concludes the study with future directions.

text:
## II. RELATED  WORK

The  exponential  upsurge  in  unstructured  clinical  data,  including  handwritten  prescriptions,  doctor  patient  dialogues, and  clinical  notes,  has  demanded  intelligent  automation  for extracting structured intuitions. Manual data entry, particularly in rural and resource constrained environments, is inefficient and  prone  to  error.  This  has  led  to  the  combination  of Optical Character Recognition, Automatic Speech Recognition and  Natural  Language  Processing  techniques  to  develop  an multimodal healthcare data pipelines [1] [2] [3].

## A. OCR based Extraction Techniques

OCR systems such as Tesseract [1] and CRNN [2] have been widely  used  for  digitizing  paper  based  medical  documents. Yet, handwritten prescriptions add complexities such as poorly legible  handwriting,  uneven  layouts,  and  use  of  abbreviations  [3].  To  address  these  problems,  deep  learning  methods  leveraging  CNN-LSTM  [4],  attention  mechanisms  [5], and  transformer  models  [7]  have  been  proposed.  However, issues  like  handwriting,  variability,  multilingual  scripts  and low-resolution  images  continue  persistent  hurdles, [6].  A specialized  systems  like  Deep  prescribe [8]  show  domainspecific promise but are still inadequate in scale and language adaptability.

## B. ASR for Medical Conversations

Transcribing  the  doctor  and  patient  communications  requires ASR systems. Traditional tools such as Google Cloud Speech [9], Kaldi [10], and Mozilla DeepSpeech [11] struggle with  medicinal  jargons,  overlapping  speech,  and  background noise. Whisper [12] facilitates prominent improvements due to its  multilingual  and  noise  robust  competences.  Additionally, domain-specific  ASR  model  like  Vosk [13]  has  shown  its ability  in  increasing  medical  transcription  accuracy,  particularly  through  customizable  language  modeling;  however,  the difficulties with scalability and cross linguistic support are still present. Recent developments include commercial answers like Dragon Medical One achieving 95-98% accuracy in controlled atmospheres.  [14], but they do not have they lack multimodal integration  capabilities  that  are  required  for  comprehensive clinical documentation workflows.

## C. NLP and Named Entity Recognition (NER)

After the conversion of OCR or ASR, extracting structured medicinal  information  relies  on  NLP.  The  early  attempts  in rule-based  systems  like  cTAKES  [15]  and  MetaMap  [16] exposed utility but showed restricted flexibility. Statistical and neural  models  such  as  CRFs  [17]  and  BiLSTM  CRF  [18] have exposed improved accuracy in entity recognition. Recent transformer-based models such as BERT [19], BioBERT [20], ClinicalBERT  [21],  and  BlueBERT  [22]  have  significantly progressive  medical  NER  by  leveraging  large  scale  datasets like  MIMIC-III  [23].  The  hybrid  models  that  incorporate domain  ontologies  like  UMLS  further  improve  performance and semantic accuracy [24]. Present limitations include inadequate handling of clinical situation, inconsistent performance across  medical  specialties  [25],  and  limited  integration  with multimodal data sources.

## D. Multimodal Fusion Approaches

Integrating  a  text,  audio,  and  visual  data  has  expanded  its traction  in  clinical  Artificial  Intelligence [26].  The  research has  proposed  disease  classification  models  using  audio  and textual inputs [27]. Studies have employed fusion techniques by combining structured EHR data with radiology narratives to  predict  the  results [28].  Work  has  travelled  cross-modal fusion  to  detect  medical  events.  However,  most  pre-existing systems are limited to specific  modalities  or  rely  on  the  late fusion,  missing  an  end-to-end  pipeline  from  a  raw  clinical input to a structured output. Existing multimodal approaches in healthcare mainly focus on diagnostic prediction rather than a complete clinical documentation structuring [29], leaving a substantial gap in practical EHR digitization workflows.

text:
## E. Clinical Application and Deployment

Despite of a technical improvement, real-world deployment will face more challenges. Many models will either lack offline functionality,  show  high  latency,  or  pose  challenges  when  it integrates into existing hospital systems. Recent work shows the  necessity  requirement  for  scalable,  low-cost,  privacypreserving  clinical  decision  tools  for  rural  and  outpatient care [30] [31]. The challenges regarding data security, ethical AI,  and  the  necessity  for  depth  medicinal  validation  further delay widespread adoption.

## III. MATERIALS  AND  METHODOLOGY

This  section  summaries  about  the  design  and  implementation  of  a  deep  learning  framework  for  transforming  an unstructured  clinical  data  into  a  structured  Electronic  Health Records. The Key stages involve data acquisition, annotation, preprocessing, entity extraction, and evaluation methods.

## A. Datasets

This research is based on 3 datasets. The primary resource is a MedSpeech Corpus, comprising of audio segments which is  about  2  seconds,  and  each  contains  clinical  expressions. The second dataset is a custom-made audio records featuring simulated dialogues done between doctors and patients, which lasts  about  30  seconds  and  labeled  with  essential  clinical expressions including Name, Age, Symptoms, Diagnosis, and Treatment. The third dataset is MTSamples, a compilation of medical  transcripts  that  have  been  curated  to  emphasize  the connections among symptoms, diagnoses, and treatments.

## B. Entity Annotation

To support  structured  extraction  from  both  audio  and  text inputs,  we  annotated  the  datasets  using  five  core  clinical entities:  Name,  Age,  Symptoms,  Diagnosis,  and  Treatment. Table I defines these entity types.

Table I. Entity types used for annotation

| Entity                                | Description                                                                                                  |
|---------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Name Age Symptoms Diagnosis Treatment | Patient's name or alias Age in years Complaints (e.g., fever) Conditions (e.g., diabetes) Medications/advice |

Table  II  presents  example  annotated  records  used  during training and validation.

Table II. Sample annotated patient records

| Name       |   Age | Symptoms     | Diagnosis              | Treatment                 |
|------------|-------|--------------|------------------------|---------------------------|
| John Doe   |    45 | Fever, Cough | Viral Infection Angina | Paracetamol Nitroglycerin |
| Jane Smith |    60 | Chest Pain   |                        |                           |

## C. Audio Preprocessing and Transcription

Audio files were standardized to 16 kHz mono WAV. format Noise  was  reduced  using  bandpass  filtering  (300 -3400  Hz) and log-energy thresholding. Whisper (large-v2) was used for transcription, generating speaker tagged outputs. Handwritten Prescription Processing: Although the current system focuses on  audio  and  typed  inputs,  it  is  designated  for  future  OCR integration  to  process  handwritten  prescriptions.  A  pilot  test on 50 handwritten samples evaluated OCR feasi bility using preprocessing  pipeline  with  image  enhancement,  binarization,  noise  reduction,  and  optimized  Tesseract config uration (PSM 6 with a medical dictionary). The best setup achieved 72variability and limited annotated data, full OCR integration was  deferred.  The  present  work  prioritizes  ASR  and  NLP validation,  with  OCR  reserved  as  a  modular  extension  for future development.

text:
## D. Text Preprocessing

This  phase  prepares  clinical  text  for  NLP  tasks  through normalization and structuring. Text is tokenized using spaCy to handle punctuation and sentence boundaries, and all tokens are lower cased while retaining clinically relevant stop words. Lemmatization  standardizes  terms  to  their  base  forms,  and domain-specific mappings expand medical abbreviations(e.g., 'HTN' → 'Hyperextensions').  Regular  expressions  further unify common medical terminologies. Negation detection uses a  hybrid  rule-based  and  contextual  approach  via  a  modified NegEx algorithm that identifies triggers (e.g., no, not, denies, without) and their scope within a 5-word window. For instance, in 'patient denies fever or cough,' both symptoms are correctly marked  as  negated.  The  negation  module  operates  in  three sequential phases.

- 1) Trigger  Detection: Recognizes  negation  cues  using  a predefined  lexicon  of  35  common  medical  negation keywords.
- 2) Scope  Determination: Applies  syntactic  guidelines  to establish the range of negated concepts.
- 3) Entity Tagging: Marks affected entities with a negation flag in the organized output.

This method achieved 91.3% accurateness in finding negated symptoms in our test set, significantly reducing false positive symptom extraction.

## E. Named Entity Recognition and Structuring

The clinical  transcript  was  cleaned  and  was  preprocessed, and  run  through  two  NLP  frameworks  such  as  spaCy  and Stanza to identify medical entities like name, age, symptoms, diagnosis and treatment. Both models were implemented independently, and their extracted entities were combined to form a unified set. The de-duplicated, and regular expression pattern matching  and fuzzy  string  matching  were  used  to  normalize format  variations  such  as  'fever'  and  'high  fever',  and  em -ployed  fuzzy  string  matching  method  to  merge  semantically similar entities like 'MI' and 'Myocardial Infarction',

## G. Model Training and Evaluation

The  annotated  dataset  was  split  into  80%train  and  20% test,  and  supervised  learning  employed  a  cross-entropy  loss function. We used evaluation metrics comprised of accuracy, precision,  recall,  and  F1-score  to  ensure  stable  performance across  all  clinical  entity  types.  Training  was  conducted  for many  epochs  with  early  stopping  based  on  validation  loss, demonstrating stable convergence across both audio and text modalities. The underlying architecture and training procedure were refined through model optimization, and stratified sampling  ensured  stable  class  distribution  during  training.  Each module  is  intended  to  work  with  clearly-defined  APIs,  to enable independent execution and scalability. The modularity easily allows replacement or upgrading of individual components such as ASR or NER.

## IV. RESULTS  AND  DISCUSSION

The  experiments  demonstrates how  well  the proposed framework  proficiently  converts  unstructured  audio  and  text clinical inputs into a structured EHR entries. The assessment covers  key  aspects  such  as  model  training  dynamics,  ASR performance, entity recognition and clinical interpretability, all of which are essential for successful integration into real world healthcare systems.

To  backing  these  evaluations,  experiments  were  carried  out on an Intel Core i7-12700 with 32GB RAM and an NVIDIA RTX 3080 GPU. The framework was executed in Python3.10 using  Whisperv1.2,  spaCyv3.6,  Stanzav1.5,  Pandasv2.0,  and Scikit-learn for modeling and evaluation.

## A. Training Performance Trends

As  envisioned  in  Figure  3,  across  the  training  epochs  the precision,  recall,  and  F1-score  had  reliable  improvements. Firstly,  during  1  to  5  epochs,  the  model  quickly  learned  the patterns  connected  with  common clinical  entities.  The precision  increased  from  0.60  to  0.88,  recall  peaked  at  0.91,  and F1-score  stabilized  around  0.90  by  epoch  12.  This  indicates effective convergence without overfitting. Notably, the training  process  benefited  from  entity-specific  learning  rates  that weighted  underperforming  categories  such  as  diagnosis  and treatment more heavily during gradient updates. This method not only corrects the medical diagnosis; it also improved overall  decision-making  performance.  Model  Performance across the  Training  Epochs  shows  convergence  of  precision,  recall, and F1-score metrics on the combined MedSpeech and MTSamples dataset (n=2,500 records).

## B. ASR Performance Comparison

The performance comparison of Whisper and Vosk model is  portrayed  in  Figure  4.  Whisper  model  attained  a  word error rate (WER) of 7.2%, significantly outperforming Vosk's 14.5%. This is due to transformer-based encoder decoder architecture and large multilingual training. These features allow Whisper to separate speech from background noise and handle Model Performance across Training Epochs varied  accents.  Its  robustness  was  evident  in  clinical  audio with  overlapping  dialogues  and  machine  noise.  As  a  result, Whisper  produced  higher  quality  transcriptions,  improving NER outcomes.

## C. Entity-Level Extraction Accuracy

The  table  III  compares  the  NER  performance  between SpaCy and Stanza. Stanza performed superior  extraction  capabilities,  achieving  100%  accuracy  on  three  out  of  five entities. In contrast, SpaCy occasionally misclassified or incorrectly classified compound terms and drug names due to limitations in  its  base  model  vocabulary.  In  clinical  situations,  precise entity detection is vital. Missing a treatment or misidentifying a symptom may lead to incorrect diagnosis support or decision making.  Stanza's  higher  accuracy  in  these  important  fields justifies its inclusion in the final deployment pipeline.

## D. Modality-Wise Performance Analysis

Mainly text-based and audio-based inputs were used to compare model performance in order to evaluate the framework's resilience. The analysis exposes that performance decline due to  transcription  errors  or  acoustic  variability  in  audio  data. The  table  IV  presents  a  comparative  evaluation  of  entity extraction  performance  between  two  input  modalities:  text based  (OCR/manual)  and  audio  based  (Whisper  ASR).  The results show that both the inputs were relatively accurate, with slight differences in symptom related entities due to occasional nonrecognition of words related to spoken audio inputs.

The  text-based  pipeline  attained  higher  performance,  with a  precision  of  96.5%,  recall  of  95.2%,  and  an  F1-score  of 95.8%. In contrast, the audio-based system attained a precision of  91.0%,  recall  of  90.2%,  and  an  F1-score  of  90.6%  using Whisper ASR. Therefore while both modalities shows higher accuracy,  the  slight  drop  in  the  audio-based  metrics  can  be attributed  to  speech  transcription  errors  and  variability  in conversation.

## E. Clinical Use-Case Impact

The  structured  outputs  were  evaluated  in  contradiction  of manually labeled ground truth for accuracy and consistency. The compact tabular format improves usability, by providing a quick access to related patient information. Use-case evaluations exhibited that the system can automatically align symptoms  with  matching  diagnoses,  supporting  effective  clinical decision-making.  The  tables V  and VI  provide  structured EHR  records  generated  from  text  and  audio  based  clinical inputs,  signifying  effective  entity  extraction  and  alignment across both modalities.

text:
## Temporal Evolution of Phishing URL Patterns Using Heuristic Features and ML Analysis

S Shyam Kumar, Nitte (Deemed to be University), NMAM Institute of Technology (NMAMIT), Department of Cyber Security, Nitte, India

s.shyam@nitte.edu.in

Abstract -Phishing attacks remain a major threat to users and organizations because of their use through the presence of deceptive URLs that resemble a valid web site.  Although  machine  learning  has  extensively  been used in the detection of phishing, little research on the evolution  of  phishing  URL  has  been  conducted.  The proposed study fills in that gap by conducting an itemby-item comparison of phishing URLs in 2020-2025 and extracting  handcrafted  features  and  comparing  them with  the  benign  dataset  of  legitimate  URLs  found  in Majestic Million. A dataset of 500 URLs (250 phishing, 250 benign) was used with 20 heuristic features extracted per URL, including length, entropy, presence of  suspicious  terms,  and  brand  names.  A  Random Forest classifier achieved 91% accuracy and a macroF1 score of 0.91. Temporal analysis from 2020 to 2025 shows  that  phishing  URL  patterns  remain  largely stable,  with  only  minor  feature  drift  over  time.  The analysis showed that there are some essential structural trends  and  minor  changes  in  phishing  URL  patterns over the years whereas main deceptive strategies have not changed significantly. The results provided a timely component to the area  of  phishing  detection  research and a definite reference point to which future models built on time-based phishing can be anchored.

Keywords-  Phishing  detection,  Random  Forest,  URL features, Machine learning, Cybersecurity, Feature extraction, URL classification, Temporal analysis, URL-based detection, Network security .

## I. INTRODUCTION

Phishing is one of the most common and destructive forms  of cyberattack in today's digital environment, responsible for significant theft of credentials and sensitive information across banking, social media, and government sectors  [18].  Phishing  campaigns  typically  lure  users  to phony websites via deceptive URLs that mimic legitimate sites, and their frequency and sophistication have increased over time, which motivates automated detection approaches.  Conventional  defenses  such  as  blacklists  or rule-based filters are simple to deploy but are often evaded through URL obfuscation and fast registration of domains, limiting their long-term effectiveness [12].

As a result, URL-based machine learning approaches have  become  popular  because  they  extract  lexical  and structural  features  directly  from  the  URL  string  and  can generalize beyond fixed blacklists [1], [2]. Many studies report  high  detection  accuracy  using  handcrafted  lexical features  and  both  classical  and  deep  learning  classifiers; however, much of the prior work analyzes static datasets without explicitly assessing temporal variability in phishing patterns [1] [2]. Understanding whether phishing URL characteristics drift over time is critical for designing robust  detection  models  that  maintain  accuracy  across years.

To  address  this  gap,  we  construct  a  balanced,  timestratified dataset of phishing and legitimate URLs spanning 2020-2025,  extract  20  heuristic  lexical  and  structural features  per  URL,  and  perform  temporal  analysis  to quantify feature stability and predictive importance. Using a  Random  Forest  classifier,  we  evaluate  classification performance  and  highlight  the  features  that  consistently distinguish phishing from legitimate URLs across years.

Besides, the available literature addresses the issue of the evolution of phishing URL structures only infrequently. The  insight into whether  the nature of phishing remains the same or changes over time is vital to the development of detection systems that survive in the long  run.  Even  though  there  are  longitudinal  studies  in adjacent  areas,  such  as  malware  analysis,  a  comparable time-based study of phishing links is rather understudied.

To provide a solution to this research gap, this research involves  year-wise  comparing  phishing  URLs  that  were gathered between the year 2020 and 2025. A sample set was prepared using the phish attack URLs of PhishTank by gathered 250 samples where all the URLs were distributed equally across six years. To make a baseline comparison, 250 valid URLs were taken form the Majestic Million data. All the URLs were converted into vectorized hand-crafted lexical and structural features. The essence of the proposed study is finding an answer to the question of how phishing URL  features  change  over  the  course  of  time  and  to compare those features with the valid ones with the help of the supervised learning methods. Through Random Forest classification, this study is able to detect the classification performance, as well as by pointing out the most important variables that can differentiate phishing URLs apart from regular URLs.

The study is restricted to lexical and heuristic features extraction and content-based and behavioral cues are not included.  Nevertheless,  it  covers  a  wide  range  of  URL shapes  and  offers  knowledge  on  a  year-by-year  basis, which will be handy to create a time-based detection model or an adaptive phishing filter in future. The results show a high level of phishing tendency consistency, but the slight changes in the patterns of features tend upward to reflect adaptive behaviors relative to security countermeasures.

Overall, the paper proposes a new exploration of the trends of detecting phishing on a temporal basis, which is to compare the feature development over several years. It will provide a balanced dataset in addition to a model of analysis that can be expanded or incorporated into phishing defense systems in the future.

text:
## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

In  recent  years,  the  field  of  literature  dedicated  to phishing URL detection has developed dynamically, and it  should  be  noted  that  it  is  especially  focused  on  the inclusion of the most advanced machine learning / deep learning algorithms and the introduction of the process of feature engineering itself, as well as the utilization of large, high-quality labeled datasets. As an example, Ghalechyan et al. used LSTM and CNN models to perform labeling of the dataset of 500 000 URLs classified with 97% accuracy focusing  on  URL  features  only,  including  their  length, entropy, and whether or not they contain suspicious terms or  brand  names  [1].  Shirazi  et  al.  similarly  showed  that gradient boosting may reach high accuracy model with a small  set  of  only  seven  features  indicating  the  high discriminating nature of well-selected URL-based features [2].

Machine  learning  algorithms  and  their  comparative performance has also been in focus. In one of his papers, Kumar et al not only thoroughly considered the comparison of classifiers- Logistic Regression, Decision Trees,  K-Nearest  Neighbors,  and  ensemble  approaches, such as Extra Trees and XGBoost, but also tested them across  several  datasets  and  concluded  that  ensemble classifiers had outperformed simple models because of a higher accuracy rate, which increases to over 99 percent when  k-fold  cross-validation  is  used  [2].  The  same  has been  reinforced  by  the  studies  of  traditional  machine learning combined with deep learning structures. To make a few examples, a stacked generalization ensemble with LSTM as a meta-learner attained 98.76 detection accuracy,  which  validated  the  worth  of  incorporating hierarchical and sequential learning in phishing detection [4].

New detection accuracies have been established with the use of hybrid deep learning architectures with attention-based  LSTM  coupled  with  CNNs  and  LSTM combined  with  advanced  feature  engineering  examples include  TF-IDF  vectorizing  and  principal  component analysis.  According  to  Birthriya  et  al.,  an  accuracy  of above 99.92  %  was  attained  by  their  integrated  LSTMCNN  model,  which  uses  a  hybrid  feature  set  and  thus shows the possibility of using such an architecture in realtime detection of phishing [5]. Between them, additional techniques based on  natural  language  processing  (NLP) have been investigated to further contribute to the feature extraction process of URLs, and increase the resilience of machine  learning  models  to  the  current  phishing  trends [6].

Availability  and  design  of  the  datasets  can  make  an important contribution to the phishing detection research. Additional hybrid approaches combining multiple machine learning techniques have also been explored to enhance detection accuracy [7]. Opara et al. emphasized the  significance  of  integrating  raw  URL  and  HTML attributes which demonstrated that deep neural networks may  automatically  identify  the  salient  characteristics  to detect phishing via automatic extraction and, additionally regular  LSTM  models  performed  better  than  random forests on big corpora [9].

Research always indicates that the length of the URL, entropy of URL, presence of suspicious words, whether HTTPS is used, similarity of brand names, are some of the strongest predictors in regard to phishing detection [10].

Despite  the  variety  of  machine  learning  and  deep learning  approaches  proposed  in  prior  work,  several limitations remain. Most studies focus on static datasets without considering temporal variations in phishing URL characteristics.  Additionally,  many  works  rely  on  largescale  datasets  but  do  not  provide  replication-friendly, balanced  samples,  limiting  reproducibility.  Few  studies explicitly analyze feature evolution over time or quantify feature importance stability across years.  Our  work addresses  these  gaps  by  constructing  a  balanced,  timestratified  dataset  of  phishing  and  legitimate  URLs  from 2020 to 2025, extracting 20 heuristic lexical and structural features,  and  performing  temporal  analysis  to  assess feature stability and predictive importance.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## I. Overview of Experiment

This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of a Random Forest  classifier  in  detecting  phishing  URLs  based  on extracted  URL  features  collected  over  multiple  years.  The objective is to assess how URL characteristics differ between phishing  and  legitimate  URLs  and  to  verify  whether  the selected  features  can  accurately  classify  URLs  into  these categories.  The  dataset  comprises  a  balanced  collection  of phishing and benign URLs, and each entry is analyzed using multiple  heuristic  and  statistical  attributes  such  as  URL length,  entropy,  the  number  of  subdomains,  the  use  of HTTPS,  and  the  presence  of  suspicious  keywords.  These features  were  chosen  based  on  their  potential  to  reveal structural and lexical discrepancies between malicious and legitimate web addresses.

This  approach  enables  a  deeper  understanding  of  which characteristics contribute most to phishing detection accuracy.

Fig. 1. Workflow of the Phishing URL Detection System, illustrating data collection, preprocessing, model training, evaluation, and prediction modules.

Fig. 1 outlines the complete workflow of the phishing URL detection system. It includes key stages such as data collection from open sources, preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, evaluation.

## II. Description of Materials

The source of phishing URLs was the phish tank online-valid CSV dataset of phishing URLs, which had URLs with the time of their submissions. The Majestic Million CSV dataset has been used to retrieve legitimate URLs as the most popular ones on the worldwide basis. The two datasets are obtained in  the  CSV  format  and  pre-processed.  Data  and  feature extraction  as  well  as  model  training  were  conducted  with Python  3.8  and  its  libraries  such  as  Pandas,  Scikit-learn, Matplotlib, and Seaborn. The experiments have been performed  in  the  Google  Collab  environment  on  8GB  of RAM and GPU.

First steps towards cleaning up the data were undertaken on the two datasets, wherein duplicate URLs were removed and unproductive data fields in the URLs were filtered. PhishTank data was sampled specifically in order to extract the same amount of URL occurrences in each year in 20202025 years, so that time analysis can be done.

## III. Description of Procedure

Datasets  were  sampled  and  filtered  with  a  goal  to  match phishing  and  genuine  URLs.  All  URLs  were  converted  to lowercase and standard URL decoding was applied. Duplicate  URLs  and  malformed  entries  were  removed. Missing values were discarded. URL-length, the existence of HTTPS, subdomains, entropy, and the existence of suspicious words were features and were obtained using selfwritten Python functions. The concatenated data was renamed and divided into training and testing data sets with suggested  ratio  80:20  using  the  training  data  to  train  a Random Forest classifier. The Random Forest was configured with n\_estimators=100, max\_depth=None, class\_weight='balanced',  and  random\_state=42  to  ensure reproducibility.

Fig.  2  illustrates  the  breakdown  of  a  URL  and  how  each segment is analyzed to extract lexical and heuristic properties, which are then used for classification

The  feature  engineering  was  also  rather  important  in  the process. The text version of each URL was extracted and it was decomposed into several parts: host name, path, query parameters, and several quantitative and binary features were created. To take an example, the entropy was computed to reflect the randomness rate of URL strings, which tends to vary between phished and legitimate URLs. Moreover, the existing  binary  features  like  suspicious  word  (e.g.  login, verify) or familiar brand names were also added, according to the expertise of phishing techniques regarding the domain.

## IV. Description of Data Analysis

Available scripts extracted text features that extracted URLs and calculated corresponding numeric and categorical features. qualified lines of difference were made between the distribution  of  features  between  phishing  and  legitimate URLs.  Random  Forest  approach  was  applied  with  Scikitlearn, and a measure of accuracy, precision, recall, and F1score were applied. Based on the trained model, the scores needed  to  determine  the  most  predictive  features  were identified using scores of the features importance. Barplots of feature importance and heatmaps on confusion matrices were plotted with Matplotlib and Seaborn.

Also, temporal analysis was performed to answer whether the characteristic of phishing URLs change with time. Performance of the model was also tested on subsets of the phishing  URLs,  that  were  yearly,  over  a  five-year  period between  2020  and  2025.  By  adopting  this  method,  the stability of relevance features and the robustness of detection against phishing strategies that evolved  were possible. The analysis revealed that although there are slight differences, the  main distinguishing characteristics are the same,  which enables the overall generalizability of the model.

In support of the quantitative assessment, error analysis was also done on misclassified URLs to get an insight on possible weaknesses of the model. Other patterns that were checked include those that included URLs that used unpopular toplevel domains or other new obfuscation techniques and where improvements could still be done. The general approach had been aimed at performing a detailed analysis of the  model performance, both statistically and contextually.

## IV. INFERENCES AND FINDINGS

The primary question addressed in this work is whether URL-based features alone can effectively differentiate phishing  websites  from  legitimate  ones.  The  number  of analyzed  URLs  was  500  which  consisted  of  250  phishing URLs, taken with the help of PhishTank and 250 legitimate URLs retrieved as part of the Majestic Million database. The Random  Forest  classifier  was  used  to  assess  the  level  of performance of the classification basing on these handcrafted features.

After fitting  and  testing  the  model,  Random  Forest classifier  gave  a  total  accuracy  of  91  percent  to  the  pooled data. The confusion matrix showed 45 true positives and 47 true negatives, along with a few misclassifications.

These results are consistent across the previously published researches [1][2], thus indicating that the phishing URLs tend to have greater length,  complexity,  and  include misleading words to confuse the users. Also, the classifier was applied on the phishing URLs of the years 2020 to 2025 to measure temporal growth.

The model maintained high classification accuracy across yearly  subsets,  reaching  up  to  100%  in  some  years,  which demonstrates  that  the  basic  deceptive  characteristics  of  the URLs in phishing remain more or less the same over time. This  confirms  the  importance  of  the  chosen  URL-based feature to detect phishing from a long-term perspective.

The importance of suspicious terms and well-known brand names is very high, so the hypothesis that phishing attackers tend to exploit trust through the use of recognizable keywords might  be  accepted.  This  is  congruent  with  the  results  of Ghalechyan et al. [3] and Shirazi et al. [4], who identified such features as highly discriminative in deep learning arrangements. In this study, deeply inherent models were not incorporated, but the strong performance of Random Forest in the  same  characteristics  proves  its  applicability  in  practical scenarios.

The  above  findings  can  be  interpreted  to  mean  that  the URL-based detection can be lightweight and effective, since it  is  particularly  essential  in  systems  with  concerns  of  real- time response and where retrieving external web content is not feasible. Yet, there are certain drawbacks such as the reliance on static features and the absence of behavioral cues, which may limit detection in specific contexts. Larger experiments can be done on the use of this approach to supplement DNS data or user interaction logs to increase the efficiency.

The integration of such complementary signals could help address edge cases where lexical features alone are insufficient for accurate classification. Additionally, incorporating periodic model retraining and drift monitoring would  ensure  that  the  system  remains  robust  as  phishing techniques evolve over time.

text:
## V. CONCLUSION

This study evaluated the effectiveness of a Random Forest classifier in detecting phishing URLs using 20 hand-crafted lexical  and  structural  features  over  a  time-stratified  dataset from 2020 to 2025. The classifier achieved 91% accuracy and a  macro-F1  score  of  0.91,  demonstrating  that  URL-based features  alone  are  sufficient  for  robust  phishing  detection. Features such as URL length, entropy, presence of suspicious terms,  and  HTTPS  usage  were  identified  as  the  most discriminative,  and  their  importance  remained  stable  over time, confirming the temporal consistency of phishing strategies.

The  results  highlight  that  URL-based  detection  is  a lightweight  and  practical  approach  for  real-time  systems, especially  where  external  content  retrieval  is  not  feasible. Limitations  include  the  relatively  small  dataset  and  the evaluation  of  only  a  single  classifier.  Future  work  will explore larger datasets, compare multiple machine learning models (e.g., XGBoost, Logistic Regression, deep learning approaches), and incorporate DNS and user behavior features to enhance detection performance.

Beyond classifier performance, this study also underscores the importance of feature stability in the context of  adversarial  evolution.  The  observation  that  key  lexical features  maintain  consistent  discriminative  power  across multiple years suggests that attackers tend to reuse structurally similar URL patterns, even as campaigns change over time. This stability enables security systems to rely on lightweight URL inspection without requiring page downloads or script execution, making the approach suitable for integration into email gateways, browser extensions, and enterprise  security  appliances.  However,  the  findings  also point toward the need for periodic retraining, since even small temporal deviations in feature behavior may gradually impact accuracy if models are not updated in a timely manner.

In future work, we also plan to conduct longitudinal drift analysis to quantify when and how phishing patterns begin to diverge from learned models. Integrating explainability tools such as SHAP or feature-attribution maps can provide better insights for analysts, support transparent model updates, and assist  in  identifying  emerging  phishing  trends  before  they become widespread. Ultimately, a hybrid detection pipeline combining  fast  URL-based  models  with  selective  deeper content or network-level inspection can offer the best balance between speed and accuracy.

## Temporal Fusion Transformer-Based Framework for Predicting Network Traffic in Femto Cell Infrastructure

Sheela G V

Department of Computer Applications, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India S.P. Shiva Prakash Department of ISE & CSBS, JSS Science and Technology University, Mysuru, India

Email: sheelagv@jssstuniv.in

Email: shivasp@jssstuniv.in

Abstract -Femto cells are responsible for enhancing network capacity and coverage indoors with minimal additional load on the functioning of macro networks. Precise forecasting of network traffic in femto cell environments is vital to the proactive optimization of network performance and optimized use of resources. The present work puts forward a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)-based approach for predicting network element traffic from raw performance management (PM) data. The model can detect both short- and long-term multivariate timeseries relationships, thus enabling early anomaly, traffic surge detection as well as early performance degradation detection. An experimental investigation was performed using real PM counter data to verify the effectiveness of the proposed scheme. The TFT model is compared with some baseline models used in this research, i.e., ARIMA, LSTM, GRU, and Prophet. From the results as shown, the TFT model performed better in terms of prediction performance in all the most important measures. In particular, it achieved the best MAE of 7.2, RMSE of 9.1, and MAPE of 6.3%, while having the highest coefficient of determination (R 2 ) value of 0.94. In comparison, the secondbest model, GRU, had an MAE of 9.5, RMSE of 11.8, MAPE of 8.1, and R2 of 0.90. Conventional statistical models like ARIMA fared poorly with an MAE of 12.5 and R2 of 0.84, and it indicated their failure to capture complex temporal behavior. These results emphasize the strength and accuracy of the new TFT-based approach in predicting femto cell network traffic. With the assistance of the TFT model, network operators are able to make data-driven, informed decisions to dynamically control network load, foresee congestion, and provide good quality of service in dense indoor and urban settings.

Femto cells cover a limited area, typically a home, office, or public building, and divert traffic off the macro network, with the effects of improved spectrum efficiency and congestion alleviation. As there is more number of and greater complexity in femto cell deployments, it becomes increasingly important that their uniform performance. Network providers have to deal with lots of performance indicators that must be tracked to detect anomalies, guarantee service continuity, and optimize resource use. Conventional methods encompass reactive ones like manual drive testing, threshold-driven warning, and fault analysis in hindsight. These are not scalable and instead result in late discovery of network problems. By considering the limitations, ML and DL based data-driven approaches have been proposed for proactive Network Performance Optimization (NPO). The solutions proposed rely on past performance records to forecast future directions, allowing for early improvement in network reliability and customer satisfaction. Traditional models like AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA) and neural networks like Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been the most used timeseries forecasting techniques. text:
## I. INTRODUCTION

With more and more mobile communications in the changing environment, offering reliability as well as high-speed wide coverage, they are likely to suffer indoor penetration difficulties efficiently, leading to coverage holes and bad user experience. In an effort to eliminate these drawbacks, femto cells-small and low-power cellular base stations-have been widely applied to enhance indoor coverage and network

979-8-3315-7364-5/25/$31.00 ©2025 IEEE

This paper proposes a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)based framework for forecasting network traffic in femto cell infrastructure using raw Performance Management (PM) counter data. The TFT model is a recent advancement in deep learning for time-series forecasting that combines recurrent networks, gating mechanisms, and attention modules. It supports multi-horizon forecasting, interprets feature importance, and effectively handles static and dynamic covariates. These capabilities make TFT highly suitable for complex and multivariate prediction tasks such as those found in femto-cell environments.

The organization of the paper is as follows: Section II includes the related work, Section III highlights the system model, and Section IV describes the architecture of the pro- posed framework. Section V presents the proposed algorithm, and Section VI details the experimental setup and evaluation metrics with the performance comparison of the proposed model with a discussion of the results. Finally, Section VII concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research.

## II. RELATED WORK

Recently, Dinh et al. [1] have introduced a new cell identitybased mobility prediction metric for small cell and femtocell networks in 5G. Rather than geographic coordinates, user mobility is represented by the sequence of cell IDs visited. For better prediction accuracy and resilience, the model employs recurrent neural networks (RNNs). The cell-based model was consistently 92% accurate. Lee et al. [2] used the ARIMA model to forecast LTE network throughput. ARIMA successfully modeled the 64-second traffic cycle and produced a low prediction error of 2.84%. In response to the limitations of conventional models, Zhang et al. [3] suggested employing Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT) for shortterm, multistep traffic speed prediction. TFT combines attention mechanisms, gating layers, and sequence-to-sequence structures to improve both accuracy and explainability. The model effectively learned intricate patterns and temporal relationships over various forecast horizons. Lim et al. [4] also implemented TFT for explainable multi-horizon forecasting. Bellahsene and Kloul [5] proposed the Local-Global Profile Model (LGPM), which utilizes local (personal) and global (population) mobility patterns to improve the prediction of locations in femtocell networks. The model resulted in an 80% success rate in highdensity LTE environments, with an indication of its applicability to dynamic user behavior. Nabi et al. [6] proposed a deep learning-based LTE traffic prediction scheme that fuses radio and temporal information. Mahanand et al. [7] developed a hybrid ensemble model that combines LSTM and GRU to predict big traffic data. Tested on the WTTSF dataset, the model performed better (MSE = 0.0007, R 2 = 0 . 921 ) with tanh activation compared to individual networks in both short- and long-range forecasting tasks. The method supported preallocation of femtocell resources, enhancing QoS, and guaranteeing a utility satisfaction level of up to 0.95 in the presence of high mobility. Zhou [8] applied TFT for multistep traffic flow prediction at 31 San Jose locations. The model, which was developed using a self-attention mechanism on top of LSTM, demonstrated strong predictive performance with R 2 = 0 . 9565 , MAE = 97.61, and RMSE = 157.55, proving itself suitable for spatiotemporal prediction tasks. Ben Jemaa and Douligeris [9] developed Femto-Catching, a proactive resource allocation mechanism based on firstorder Markov models. The model predicted user mobility and preallocated femtocell resources, which reduced handover latency dramatically and enhanced performance in highly mobile environments. Khoshkholgh and Leung [10] studied caching and energy optimization techniques in femtocell networks. According to their research, content-aware user associations had the potential to significantly minimize energy consumption and improve load balancing, particularly when used in conjunction with predictive traffic modeling through LSTM-GRU hybrids. Balandat et al. [11] benchmarked Bayesian Optimization (BO) against Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) for blackbox wireless optimization. BO achieved near Pareto-optimal performance on only 1,100 evaluations-many fewer than DDPG's 600,000-proving its sample efficiency and realworld deployability. Dreifuerst et al. [12] also compared BO and DDPG for optimizing LTE physical- layer parameters such as downtilt and transmit power. Both algorithms converged successfully to the Pareto frontier, providing enhancements in interference-coverage balancing. Folorunsho et al. [13] surveyed AI-based solutions in SelfOrganizing Networks (SONs) such as fault detection, traffic classification, and latency optimization. Yao et al. [14] proposed slice allocation and MIMO edge computing for optimizing 5G performance in smart grids. Arulappan et al. [15] focused on NFV-based management of 5G/6G infrastructure.

Existing models for network traffic prediction in femto cell environments often struggle with capturing complex temporal patterns and multivariate dependencies. Traditional approaches like ARIMA, LSTM, and Prophet lack adaptability and precision. There is a need for a more robust, interpretable, and accurate model to improve resource allocation and network optimization.

## A. Data Acquisition and Ingestion

The input information is extracted from raw Performance Management (PM) counter logs gathered from femto cell network equipment.

In particular, two main counters are taken into account, i.e., Counter 70001: Number of incoming Ethernet packets via the 10G port and Counter 70007: Number of outgoing Ethernet packets via the 1G port. Each sample of data corresponds to a 15-minute observation window. Data is stored and retained sequenced in time for each Femto Access Point (FAP) for its FGW ID.

## B. Preprocessing and Input Structuring

The raw counter data collected goes through preprocessing for numerical stability and model preparation. This involves the following steps:

- 1) Missing Value Imputation : Linear interpolation is used to replace small gaps in the time series.
- 2) Normalization : Feature scaling is performed using zscore normalization:

<!-- formula-not-decoded -->

- where µ and σ are the mean and standard deviation of each feature, respectively.
- 3) Sequence Formation : Fixed length ℓ input sequences are formed by a sliding window approach. Sequences are projected onto a target window of size H .

## C. Feature Representation

Input features are divided into two categories:

- Dynamic Features : Time-series counter values x t ∈ R n at every time step t .
- Static Features : Time-invariant attributes such as FAP ID, chassis configuration, or port type are represented as a static covariate vector s ∈ R d .

Each of these features is embedded via learnable transformations and fed through Gated Residual Networks (GRNs) for variable selection and context augmentation.

## D. Model Architecture: TFT

The Temporal Fusion Transformer is the central prediction engine. Its architecture consists of the following components:

- 1) Gated Residual Networks (GRNs) : Select and transform relevant input features dynamically.
- 2) LSTM Encoder-Decoder : Captures temporal dependencies over historical and forecast windows.
- 3) Static Covariate Encoder : Embeds and broadcasts static context across the network.
- 4) Multi-Head Attention Layer : Focuses on important historical time steps to improve interpretability and forecasting accuracy.
- 5) Position-Wise Feed-Forward Decoder : Concatenates temporal and static contexts to produce the prediction ˆ y t + τ for every future step τ .

The network is trained end-to-end by minimizing the Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between ground truth and predicted counter values. During inference, the trained TFT model is presented with the latest sequence of counter values together with static context and produces H future values of the target counter (e.g., Counter 70007). The prediction ˆ y t +1 , . . . , ˆ y t + H is employed to anticipate congestion patterns, predict failures, and maximize femto cell performance.

Static covariates like femto access point (FAP) IDs and hardware features are encoded within a distinct GRN, producing a static context vector indicating static impacts on traffic behavior. The LSTM encoded temporal features are utilized to calculate query, key, and value matrices for a multi-head self-attention block. This attention calculates attention weights to highlight the most important time steps and feature contributions across the sequence. The attention context vectors obtained are concatenated with the static context vector and fed into a decoder GRN. For every prediction step τ in the prediction horizon H , the model makes an output ˆ y t + τ from the decoder's output. The predictions are the expected Ethernet traffic volume for future time steps. The accuracy of the forecasting is measured by the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the predicted values and the true observed counter values. The obtained loss function is used to adjust the model parameters through backpropagation and gradient-based optimization. This is done iteratively over the training data until convergence. The algorithm combines temporal dynamics, static metadata, attentional context learning, and gating mechanisms within an interpretable forecasting framework and allows accurate and proactive traffic prediction in femto cell networks.

## VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS

The model is evaluated based on performance metrics such as MAE, RMSE and MAPE. Models are contrasted with ARIMA, LSTM, GRU, and Prophet models. Preprocessing of data is done for handling missing values, normalizing the counter readings, and splitting into training and validation sets. The TFT model is trained to predict future values of both counters based on past trends and context. The data source adopted for this research is gathered from raw PM files of femto access points (FAPs), i.e., FAP FGW 140014. It consists of time-stamped counter values sampled at 15-minute time intervals. Two Ethernet traffic counters are deemed, and these counters indicate ingress and egress traffic in the femto cell network element and are suggestive of its running state. To assess the proposed model's robustness under different data availability, tested its performance for diverse train-test splits: 60:40, 70:30, 80:20, and 90:10. As evident from Figure 2 , the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) kept on reducing from 7.5 to 7.0 with increased training data, reflecting enhanced predictive accuracy. Likewise, the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) also reflected a decreasing trend, falling from 9.4 to 8.8, as evident from Figure 3 , revealing that the larger deviations of the model from real values reduced with increasing training data. The Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) , shown in Figure 4 , also followed a similar trend, decreasing from 6.7% to 6.0%, showing the model's improving relative accuracy. Moreover, the R 2 Score , an indicator of model fit, also improved from 0.93 to 0.95 over the splits ( Figure 5 ), validating the model's improved capability to account for the variance in the data. These findings confirm that the TFT model not only predicts robustly across all the evaluation measures but also gains a lot of benefit from bigger training sets.

## VII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

This work proposed a Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)based approach for network traffic prediction in femto cell scenarios from raw performance management (PM) data. The model is well-established both short- and long-term multivariate temporal dependencies, thus allowing early detection of anomalies, traffic spikes, and performance degradation. Comparative comparison with conventional models like ARIMA and deep learning models like LSTM, GRU, and Prophet showed that the TFT model was consistently superior to them in all the comparison criteria. The TFT method's higher accuracy and insensitivity to novelty explain its application in making data-driven decisions for network optimization, congestion forecasting, and quality of service in indoor and high-density cities. Future research can include adding spatialtemporal modeling by drawing on neighboring femto cell data to enhance prediction quality. Incorporating this predictive model within an edge computing framework may also support low-latency, real-time network control in future communications systems.
