## Transforming Upper Limb Rehabilitation: RealTime, Holistic Feedback Using Python and Sensor Fusion

Vasantha Kini T Department of Instrumentation and Control Engineering Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India vasantha.mitmpl2024@learner.man ipal.edu Haimanti Basu Department of Instrumentation and Control Engineering Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India haimanti.basu@learner.manipal.edu S Meenatchisundaram Department of Instrumentation and Control Engineering Manipal Institute of Technology, Manipal Academy of Higher Education, Manipal, India

meena.sundar@manipal.edu

Abstract -Over the past decade, Python-based rehabilitation tools have dramatically transformed access to  interactive,  low-cost  therapy  by  combining  powerful technologies such as computer vision, sensor fusion, and intuitive user interfaces. This paper presents the development and evaluation of a novel, holistic real-time hand orientation feedback system which can be used in upper  limb  rehabilitation.  Our  implementation  uses MediaPipe  Holistic,  OpenCV,  and  NumPy  to  estimate elbow, wrist, index finger, and neck angles from synchronized video feeds, comparing live movements to reference  motions.  Corrective  prompts  are  generated immediately, enabling responsive guidance and enhanced patient  autonomy.  Preliminary  results  show  smooth, sinusoidal  angle  tracking,  reliable  phase  segmentation, and accurate real-time feedback, suggesting high potential  for  deployment  in  remote  and  home-based therapy contexts. Future enhancements include adaptive AI  calibration,  engaging  gamification  strategies,  and multimodal sensor integration to personalize and optimize rehabilitation further.

Keywords-computer vision, rehabilitation, sensor fusion, health, Python, home-based therapy

## I. INTRODUCTION

Rehabilitation for individuals with hand motor impairments-whether due to stroke, peripheral nerve injuries, or neuromuscular disorders-is essential for regaining functional independence. However, traditional therapy  approaches  depend  heavily  on  repeated  in-person sessions, which are limited by cost, therapist availability, and geographic constraints. These challenges hinder timely

979-8-3315-7364-5/25/$31.00 ©2025 IEEE

intervention and can compromise long-term recovery outcomes.

With the rapid advancement of digital health technologies, a  paradigm  shift  has  emerged:  therapy  tools  powered  by computer vision, wearable sensors, and artificial intelligence can  now  be  deployed  directly  in  patients'  homes.  These systems provide real time feedback, personalized training, and progress  tracking  without  the  need  for  specialized  clinics. Central to these developments is Python, a widely used and easy to learn programming language that supports an extensive  ecosystem  of  libraries.  Tools  like  MediaPipe  and OpenCV enable real-time body landmark detection and image processing  [1].  Wearable  inertial  sensors,  when  combined with vision systems, further support accurate at-home motor rehabilitation  programs  [2].  Machine  learning  frameworks such  as  SciKit  Learn  and  TensorFlow  support  intelligent prediction and classification, and web-based or desktop GUI libraries-Streamlit, PyQt5, and Kivy-enable the design of adaptive, user-friendly interfaces [3].

These  tools are  enabling the creation of accessible, scalable,  and  effective  rehabilitation  systems.  Patients  can follow guided exercises using a  simple  webcam  while receiving  continuous,  automated  feedback.  Simultaneously, therapists can review exercise logs and provide insights based on precise joint angle data and motion patterns. In this paper, we review existing research on Python-powered rehabilitation tools and introduce our novel system, which leverages videobased tracking to compute joint angles and generate posture feedback in real time. This approach reduces dependency on expensive hardware while enhancing engagement and therapeutic outcomes. This shift has significantly widened the scope of remote physiotherapy, allowing rehabilitation protocols to be standardized, monitored, and adapted in real time. As a result, home-based systems now offer a level of

## II. RELATED  WORK

Python's accessibility and library ecosystem have empowered numerous rehabilitation innovations over the past decade. G. Amprimo et al. [4] showcased how webcam-based MediaPipe  systems  could  track finger joints with high precision, rivalling therapist accuracy. Park, Mina & Kim [5] extended  this  approach  by  estimating  hand  grip  strength through 3D kinematic modelling and ML regression.

In  remote  feedback  systems,  N.  E.  Saleh,  B.  Debs,  E. Moussallem, A. R. Sarraj and S. Saleh [6] developed a live Python  dashboard  to  stream  movement  data  for  therapist oversight. Similarly, V. S. Chaithra, M. S. Vikas, B. Pankaja, and N. S. Sowmya [7] created a PyQt5 desktop application for posture visualization and feedback customization. Meanwhile,  Ahmad  Anwar  Zainuddin,  Nurul  Hanis  Mohd Dhuzuki [8] addressed variability in home environments by introducing calibration protocols for personalized hand gesture  detection,  improving  system  performance  across lighting and positioning differences.

Sensor  fusion  systems,  such  as  that  by  Rossi  et  al.  [9], integrated  surface  EMG  readings  with  functional  electrical stimulation.  By  deploying  Python  on  a  Raspberry  Pi,  they enabled  localized,  autonomous  muscle  response  triggering. Wearable technologies also benefited from Python's modularity. For example, Colli Colli Alfaro, J.G.; Trejos, [12] combined EMG and IMU signals, achieving gesture recognition  accuracy  above  93%,  while  Ekambaram  & Ponnusamy [11] embedded LSTM-based classifiers in Streamlit dashboards for form validation.

Several systems emphasized gamification and immersive interaction. Gherman, B.; Zima,. [10] applied MediaPipe and OpenCV to mirror  healthy  hand  movements  onto  impaired limbs  via  pneumatic  gloves,  while  Park,  Wonjun  &  Heo, Hayoung  [13]  used  Kivy  to  design  game-like  robotic  arm control systems, enhancing user motivation and engagement.

Furthermore, S. Zhou, G. Zhang, R. Chung. [14] Shen, Y.; Huang,  [18]  provided  comprehensive  reviews  of  AI-driven rehabilitation  systems,  emphasizing  the  value of  combining vision-based  and  sensor-based  inputs  for  holistic  motion tracking.  Dalal,  Urav  &  Thadhani,  Aasmi  [15]  devised  an efficient method to perform sign language detection using a similar  algorithm.  These  projects  illustrate  the  breadth  of applications  and  potential  of  Python  as  the  backbone  of modern rehabilitative technology.

In order to calculate important joint angles, such as those of  the  elbow,  wrist,  index  finger,  and  neck,  in  real  time,  a sensor-fusion  method  was  created  that  combines  computer vision  techniques-using  MediaPipe  and  OpenCV-with hand-landmark data. In order to extract landmark positions, compute joint angles using the cosine law, compare them to reference postures, and provide instantaneous corrective feedback, video input from a standard webcam is processed frame by frame. All data are also logged for future examination. Initial findings demonstrate how well the system can differentiate between appropriate and inappropriate postures during common stages of rehabilitation exercises.

By modifying a single-track side variable, users can switch between left- and right-side monitoring thanks to the system's modular design and configurable side-tracking. This improves the system's usability and flexibility by removing the need to change  the  core  code.  Additionally,  Electron  is  used  to package  the  core  Python  script  into  a  standalone  desktop application  that  runs  on  multiple  platforms  and  has  an interactive, user-friendly interface. This eliminates the need to install external dependencies and enables users of Windows and macOS to launch the therapy tool with ease.

text:
## III. METHODOLOGY

The proposed feedback system integrates three modulessensing, processing, and feedback-forming a unified pipeline. A webcam  captures both a reference video demonstrating proper movement and a live stream of the user. MediaPipe  Holistic  is  employed  to  extract  body  and  hand landmarks. Using vector geometry, the system computes joint angles for the elbow, wrist, index finger proximal interphalangeal (PIP), and neck in real time. The  calculated  angles  are  compared  against  predefined reference  thresholds.  When  deviations  exceed  the  allowed range,  the  system  provides  visual  prompts  indicating  the specific  discrepancy,  e.g.,  'Adjust:  elbow  off  by  12°,' ensuring that even subtle deviations are corrected promptly. Previous studies have explored similar rehabilitation dashboards; for instance, Prabha and Akilashri [16] developed an interactive dashboard for healthcare rehabilitation, while  Gopura  et  al.  [17]  implemented  a dashboard using EEG-based monitoring. For landmark detection, MediaPipe Holistic was selected due to  its  lightweight  architecture,  real-time  performance,  and reliable  tracking  of  full-body,  face,  and  hand  landmarks. Compared  with  other  pose  estimation  models,  such  as OpenPose or BlazePose, it offers faster inference on standard hardware and minimal setup requirements, making it suitable for  home-based  rehabilitation  applications.  OpenCV  was employed  for  image  processing  tasks  due  to  its  extensive functionality and robust community support. TensorFlow and SciKit-Learn were utilized for machine learning due to their versatility, ease of integration, and comprehensive documentation.

## A. Component Selection

Hardware  requirements  are  minimal:  a  standard  720p webcam and a mid-range computer suffice. Python, OpenCV, MediaPipe, and NumPy constitute the primary software stack due to their accessibility, speed, and extensive documentation.

## B. System Description

Figure  1  illustrates  the  steps  involved  in  developing  a computer  vision-based  real-time  posture  feedback  system. First,  a  reference  video  and  webcam  feed  are  opened,  and variables  are  set  up.  In  order  to  extract  body  joint  angles (elbow, wrist, index finger, and neck) based on a designated tracking  side,  a  loop  continuously  reads  frames  from  both sources,  pre-processes  them,  and  then  processes  them  with MediaPipe. To produce performance feedback (such as "Good form"  or  suggestions  for  adjustments),  these  angles  are compared between the reference and live video. The system shows the annotated feed as in figure 4 and figure 5, records data to a CSV file, and superimposes landmarks and feedback text on the live video. When you hit "q," the system releases resources and uses the logged data to create summaries and visualisations before stopping.

where A, B, and C are the landmark points. The calculated angles are passed through a 1D Kalman filter to suppress noise and maintain responsiveness. The elbow and neck angles in figure  2  and  figure  3  display  smooth,  sinusoidal  patterns, measuring about 179° for the elbow and 180° for the neck.

This indicates they are in sync with the exercise cycles. On the other hand, wrist and finger angles have more noticeable shifts and higher noise levels. The system provides posture feedback in real-time. When both the elbow and neck angles are  within  a  10°  range  of  their  reference  values,  it  gives  a positive cue: "Good form!" If not, it gives specific corrective messages pointing out which joint, either the elbow or neck, needs adjustment.

Beyond these immediate corrective cues, the angle trajectories also reveal important characteristics about the user's movement  quality  across  each  repetition.  When  examined over longer windows, the filtered signals expose gradual drifts in joint orientation, compensation patterns, or subtle hesitations  that  may  not  be  visible  in  a  single  frame.  Such behaviours,  often  caused  by  fatigue  or  incorrect  muscle activation,  appear  as  slight  asymmetries  between  the  rising and falling edges of the angle curves or as small but repeated deviations at the same phase of the exercise cycle. Monitoring these  trends  enables  the  system  to  differentiate  between random  noise  and  systematic  form  errors  that  require  user attention. Additionally, the temporal consistency of the elbow-neck  relationship  provides  insight  into  upper-limb coordination, allowing the platform to flag cases where one joint  stabilizes  earlier  than  the  other  or  where  movement sequencing becomes erratic. By capturing these fine-grained variations in real time, the system not only ensures immediate posture accuracy but also builds a richer data profile that can support long-term assessment and personalized rehabilitation planning.

Building  on  this,  the  system's  continuous  monitoring  also uncovers  how  users  adapt  their  movement  strategies  over time.  Even  when  the  overall  angle  patterns  appear  correct, subtle  shifts  in  joint  contribution  or  posture  alignment  may develop  as  repetitions  progress.  For  instance,  a  user  might gradually rely more on shoulder elevation to compensate for limited elbow extension, or begin tilting the neck slightly to maintain  visual  focus  during  complex  movements.  These compensatory  behaviours,  although  small,  can  accumulate and  affect  the  long-term  effectiveness  of  the  exercise.  By identifying such patterns early, the system provides clinicians with  valuable  information  to  refine  exercise  prescriptions, ensure  proper  muscle  engagement,  and  prevent  undesirable habits from forming during unsupervised rehabilitation sessions. Together, these capabilities make the angle-analysis module not only a tool for instantaneous correction but also a reliable indicator of overall movement quality. This comprehensive understanding strengthens the system's role as a continuous, data-driven support mechanism throughout the rehabilitation process.

## D. Thresholds and Feedback

A real-time posture feedback system captures and compares joint angles (elbow, wrist, index finger, neck) from a  reference  video  and  live  webcam  feed  using  MediaPipe. User-configurable thresholds-±10° for elbow/neck and ±15° for  wrist  (determined  by  trial  and  error)-trigger  overlaid corrective  feedback  as  shown  in  figure  4  and  figure  5  and logging  of  timestamps,  angles,  and  comments;  pressing  'q' ends the session and produces summary plots and tables.

## E. Visualization and Logging

Joint angles and posture feedback are recorded in a CSV file.  After  the  session,  Matplotlib is used to plot angle-time graphs. Peaks and troughs indicate flexion/extension cycles, while annotated deviations highlight incorrect form occurrences.

## IV. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

The  developed  system  was  able  to  track  hand  and  arm postures across test scenarios in preliminary experiments. The measured wrist angles quantitatively agreed with the ground truth (motion-capture baseline) within a few degrees. Sample angle traces are shown in Fig. 2, where posture corrections are indicated by distinct step changes. Within one video frame of detection, the system immediately provided feedback in the form of a beep and an on-screen visual cue.

These findings show dependable real-time performance: angle  calculations  introduced  very  little  latency,  and  the combined  vision  pipeline  preserved  15  frames  per  second. Crucially,  the  webcam  capture  was  sufficient  to  infer  joint positions without the need for wearable calibration.

## B. Testing and Validation

Even though the system consistently monitors joint movements and offers pertinent  feedback,  some  anomalies were noted. For example, infrequent calibration errors resulting  from temporary occlusions or changes in lighting caused  short-term  errors  in  measured  angles,  which  were evident as outliers or spikes in the recorded data (e.g., Table 1, Rows 2 and 5). The feedback loop was not considerably disturbed by these differences, which hardly ever went above 20°. Due to real-time processing limitations, a slight latency was also observed between live posture changes and feedback generation;  nevertheless,  this  latency  was  within  tolerable limits for exercise scenarios. In order to ensure traceability and clarity for both user guidance and post-session analysis, each data entry records important metrics such as timestamp, joint angles, and feedback.

The system's primary goals of providing individualized corrective  feedback  and  real-time  posture  monitoring  are effectively met. As can be seen from Table 1's structured data log,  posture  evaluations  are  regularly  in  line  with  angle thresholds,  allowing  for  prompt  and  useful  advice.  The system's overall reliability is high, even with small variations brought on by hardware or environmental constraints. With future improvements concentrating on lowering latency and enhancing  robustness  under  various  lighting  and  camera conditions,  these  results  validate  its  applicability  in  sports training, physiotherapy, and rehabilitation. ## C. System performance metrics and limitations

While the setup can be well utilised in-home environments, there are limitations that might need to be worked upon in the future  for  improvements. Occlusion,  a  condition  where  a user's hand or arm is blocked from the camera's view, maybe by  another  body  part  or  any  other  external  object,  still remains a challenge. When the camera cannot see the hand or the arm, it fails to decide whether the positioning is right or wrong. Also, the background greatly impacts the accuracy. The more complex the background, the lower the accuracy will  be. Although  the  system  can  still  be  robust,  with background  patterns  similar  to  human  forms,  the  system might wrongly consider those as the user's hand or arm and give  wrong  interpretations. The  lighting  conditions  under which  the user is  performing have  a vital impact on reliability. Poor  lighting  conditions  can  reduce  landmark visibility  and  result  in  erroneous  outputs. Despite  these constraints, the system has 89% detection accuracy, and with further  improvements  and  by  addressing  these  issues,  the accuracy  and  reliability  can  be  further  improved. ## V. CONCLUSION

A  Python-based  hand  posture  feedback  system  was developed  that  fuses  computer-vision  outputs  to  support rehabilitation. Leveraging MediaPipe for high-speed hand and body landmark detection [18], the system tracks joint angles and issues corrective cues whenever deviations are detected. Initial evaluation confirms that the system meets its objectives, accurately monitoring posture and providing realtime  feedback  using  only  a  standard  webcam.  This  noninvasive, low-cost approach has the potential to complement traditional therapy by enabling personalized, continuous monitoring  outside  the  clinic.  Future  work  will  focus  on clinical validation with patients and refinement of algorithms to handle more complex movements. Furthermore, integration with telehealth platforms could expand accessibility, allowing therapists to remotely monitor progress and guide interventions.  Overall,  this  project  underscores  the  growing role of open-source computer vision in healthcare, combining sensor  fusion  and  machine  learning  techniques  to  make rehabilitation exercises more effective and widely accessible [19].

## Unveiling Sentiments in Movie Reviews: A Comparative Study of Computational Approaches for Sentiment Analysis

Rupesh Sai Ram Kotha Dept. of Computer Science Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham Amaravati, India roopeshkotha@gmail.com Raghu Ram Sai Lingutla Dept. of Computer Science Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham Amaravati, India lingutlaraghuramsai@gmail.com

Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham Amaravati, India nmohangopal05@gmail.com Mohana Gopala Krishna Reddy Nalamalapu Dept. of Computer Science Sarin Kumar Sathunuri Dept. of Computer Science Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham Amaravati, India sarinsathunuri@gmail.com M. Srinivas Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham Amaravati, India Dept. of Computer Science m srinivas@av.amrita.edu

Abstract -In today's digital age, where opinions are readily shared and accessible, understanding public sentiment through movie reviews has become increasingly important. Three computational methods-Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs)-have been the primary basis for this research, which focuses on sentiment classification. For this research, we consider both traditional ML algorithms and a hybrid deep learning approach with Bayesian Networks (BNs) due to their explanatory power. With the IMDb dataset, the DL model achieved the best performance of 88%, closely followed by the traditional ML methods at 87%. The PGM model, however, considerably lagged at 52% accuracy. These findings illustrate an existing performance-interpretability tradeoff which contributes to model selection for real-world applications in SA .

Index Terms -Sentiment Analysis, Natural Language Processing, Machine Learning, Deep Learning, Probabilistic Graphical Models, ConvLSTM, Bayesian Networks.

## I. INTRODUCTION

People's sharing and consumption of opinions has changed dramatically in the digital age. In the past, individuals relied on personal interactions to gather opinions about movies or products. With millions of people now voicing their opinions online, Sentiment Analysis (SA) has become vital to learn about public opinion. Being a major area of Natural Language Processing (NLP), SA identifies and classifies emotion, opinion, and other subjective information from text. It generally classifies input as positive, negative, or neutral to inform about the sentiment of the user [1]. Moreover, SA uncovers complex elements within textual data including sarcasm and irony alongside other features. Varying levels of emotional intensity in text offer deeper insights during analysis [2].

The use of a lot of high-quality labeled data is one of SA's main challenges, which are employed to train supervised machine learning (ML) models.for instance, NaiveBayes (NB) and SupportVectorMachines (SVM), have been adapted from general machine learning to text categorization, and are effective for flat text classification,they could not capture some linguistics nuances and subtle changes of sentiment they often miss linguistic nuances and subtle variations in sentiment [3]. This constraint resulted in the design of more sophisticated methods in DeepLearning (DL) that employ several layers of processing to learn hierarchical representations of data.Hybrid models, like Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM), integrate Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) to extract spatial and temporal data, effectively addressing related challenges. [4]. Outside of DL and ML, Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGMs) provide an interesting insight by using probabilistic word-word, word-phrase, and word-sentiment correspondences. Bayesian networks, an emerging subclass of PGMs, enable interpretable models capable of modeling dependencies between variables, which are particularly useful for studying the text structure [5]. However, their use in sequential data has been relatively less studied than DL models This contribution to the field of sentiment analysis research comes from a thorough comparative evaluation of three computational paradigms: conventional ML algorithms (e.g. NB, SVM), cutting-edge DL architectures (e.g.ConvLSTM), and PGMs (e.g., Bayesian Networks). This research provides a unified evaluation of these distinct methodologies, directly comparing their respective strengths, weaknesses, and suitability for real-world sentiment analysis applications.

text:
## A. Contributions

This research work suggests a comparative study of three computational frameworks, Machine Learning (ML), Deep Learning (DL), and Probabilistic Graphical Models (PGM) for sentiment analysis of cinema reviews.

The primary contributions of this research are:

- In-depth performance study of ML, DL, and PGM methods with discussion on accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency trade-offs.
- Development of a preprocessing pipeline with an unambiguous order of operations, including lemmatization and feature extraction using TF-IDF and GloVe, for effective text representation.
- Application of Bayesian Networks as an explainable replacement for deep networks with a demonstration of its performance and limitations in sentiment classification

## II. LITERATURE REVIEW

In ML and DL, sentiment analysis has been an area of extensive academic research. Conventional methods were heavily based on Conventional machine learning classifiers, include Na¨ ıve Bayes, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Decision Trees. Although these techniques worked well in text data classification, they faced the issue of identifying contextual relationships and linguistic dependencies in text data sets [4] [5].

In recent years, deep learning techniques have brought substantial improvements to sentiment analysis. Models based on LSTMs and CNNs have been especially influential. According to Fei Long et al. [5], incorporating multi-head attention into a bidirectional LSTM leads to strong performance in classifying sentiments, especially for comments taken from a Chinese social networking application. Their work also shows that using regularization strategies such as Dropout, L2 penalties, and early stopping further enhances the model's robustness.

Similarly, Yadav and Vishwakarma [6] presented a review, emphasizing the outstanding performance of hybrid CNNLSTM models in the area of sentiment classification. They discovered that convolutional layers are specifically made to extract geographical and local contextual information from text input, identifying minute patterns that are important for sentiment analysis. On the other hand, LSTMs are optimally designed to model sequential relationships and long-range dependencies, allowing the system to extract context from long sequences of text. The synergy of CNN for feature learning and LSTM for sequence handling achieved significantly higher classification accuracy than traditional machine learning methods or standalone deep learning architectures.. Their work also reflects a general trend toward the use of deep learning architectures in sentiment analysis, claiming that hybrid models are significantly robust in dealing with intricate linguistic structures, domain variability, and the subtleties of sentiment. Our work draws inspiration from their insights.

Probabilistic graphical models (PGM) are a promising direction for sentiment analysis because of its ability to quantify uncertainty. Ukachi et al. [7] were among the first to apply sentiment analysis in the form of Bayesian Networks and demonstrated that PGMs offer better interpretability compared to black-box deep learning models. Their research also demonstrated that PGMs improve semantic representation of sentiment by capturing word dependencies. However, one of the biggest challenges is in the form of computational complexity, particularly for large data collections.

Recent work continues to highlight the importance of text vectorization in sentiment analysis tasks. TF-IDF [8] still remains a good baseline for sentiment analysis tasks, especially when it comes to interpretability, relevance of terms, and low computational costs. However, some of the new advanced techniques include Glove embeddings [9], which are effective at capturing word meaning by combining global statistics with local context. While transformer-based models like Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) are adept at handling homonyms, or words with various meanings, Glove struggles with them. BERT dynamically captures the contextual meaning.

According to Bharal et al. [10], Sentiment categorization is significantly enhanced by hybrid deep learning models that integrate Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) and Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) networks, especially in highly context-sensitive datasets with intricate sentence structures. Their Twitter sentiment analysis experiment leveraged CNN's ability to extract local textual features effectively while BiLSTM enabled the exploitation of long-range dependencies through its bidirectional information processing ability. The model utilized Word2Vec embeddings, where words were represented as dense vector representations that captured semantic relationships and enhanced contextual understanding. This CNN-BiLSTM setup achieved an accuracy of 78.86%, surpassing conventional approaches. While it has its merits, the study outlined some of its weaknesses, including susceptibility to overfitting and limited generalizability by virtue of biases in the data. Several optimizations like fine-tuning of hyperparameters, incorporation of attention mechanisms may enhance its robustness and effectiveness in real-world sentiment analysis applications.

Deep learning models are accurate but less interpretable, while probabilistic models are more interpretable but less accurate. This work fills this gap by comparing traditional ML approaches, DL models, and PGMs, and showing a general comparison in performance in sentiment analysis.

## III. METHODOLOGY

This study follows a systematic methodology comprising four key steps: data collection, preprocessing, feature extraction, and model implementation. Each stage is outlined below, with detailed explanations of the techniques and tools employed (see Fig. 1).

## A. Preprocessing

Preprocessing plays an essential role in preparing textual data for analysis. The Raw text usually includes various forms of noise, such as duplicate entries, missing values, HTML tags, special characters, and links, which can adversely affect the model's performance [11]. To address these challenges, the following steps were carried out:

- Data Cleaning: Unwanted components including HTML tags, hyperlinks, and special characters were eliminated from the raw text data. This ensured that irrelevant information did not influence the model.
- Tokenization: After cleaning, the text was divided into individual words using a tokenizer. This step simplifies the analysis by breaking down sentences into their basic components.

A frequency analysis of common words was conducted during the initial phases, with the top 30 most common words in the dataset illustrated in (Fig. 2), providing insight into the distribution of terms before further preprocessing.

Fig. 2. Top 30 most common words in movie reviews.

<!-- image -->

The remaining steps involved further refinement of the data:

- Lemmatization: All tokens were subsequently lemmatized into their base form, which eliminated morphological differences while maintaining the original meanings of the words. This process improved the consistency of the data set.
- Vectorization: Lastly, the text processed was converted to a numeric form by vectorization. Every word was given a special numeric code so that the models could effectively understand the text.

## B. Feature Extraction

It captures relevant patterns and representations that are used as input for models, feature extraction is a crucial step in text analysis [11]. Two methods for feature extraction were used in this study: GloVe embeddings and Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF).

1) TF-IDF: Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) is a statistical metric that is frequently used in natural language processing to compare the frequency of words in a particular document to their relevance in a broader body of material [8]. TF-IDF downplays the significance of common terms that are not very relevant while emphasizing words that are only used by specific publications. TF-IDF can be computed as follows:

The TF-IDF score is calculated by multiplying the TF and IDF numbers, thereby balancing word relevance within a document against its general occurrence across the corpus.

- 2) GloVe Embeddings: An algorithmic method for learning word embeddings is called GloVe (Global Vectors for Word Representation). suggested to produce dense word embeddings by Pennington et al. [9]. By examining word co-occurrence patterns over a large corpus, it encodes both syntactic and semantic word-word relations.

Each cell in GloVe's word co-occurrence matrix, X ij , counts the instances in which words i and j co-occur inside a specific context window. GloVe looks for word vectors where the log of the co-occurrence probability of the missing word equals the dot product.

In this study, pretrained GloVe embeddings (300dimensional) were used to initialize the embedding layer in the neural network. Out-of-vocabulary words were given zero vectors, and every word in the dataset was mapped to its matching GloVe vector. The hybrid ConvLSTM architecture was built on these embeddings, which allowed the model to capture the semantic linkages in text.

text:
## C. Techniques

This study compares the performance of three computational paradigms: machine learning models, deep learning architectures, and probabilistic graphical models. Each approach is designed to handle sentiment analysis uniquely, leveraging its inherent strengths.

- 1) Multinomial Na¨ ıve Bayes (MNB): The Multinomial variant of the Na ıve Bayes classifier is suitable for multiclass classification problem distribution. MNB estimates the probabilities from word frequency in the text and processes every word independently. This light but efficient algorithm is best used for text classification tasks.
- 2) Linear Support Vector Classifier (SVC): Linear SVC is a supervised learning algorithm designed to classify data points into individual classes by finding the best hyperplane. This hyperplane is computed so as to maximize the margin between the closest points from each class, guaranteeing strong classification. Linear SVC is optimized for performing with large datasets and is suitable for linearly separable data.
- 3) Hybrid CNN and LSTM Architecture: Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN), Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) layers, and a self-attention mechanism are all part of the proposed deep neural network design. CNN is used as a feature extractor to detect salient local patterns and n-grams of text, which is useful in detecting short-term dependencies. CNN is, however, not able to detect long-range dependencies in text sequences. To combat this, BiLSTM layers are used to preserve sequential information and word dependencies. The combination of CNN and LSTM takes advantage of the strengths of both architectures CNN captures spatial features, while LSTM captures long-term dependencies giving an enhanced sentiment classification performance. A self-attention mechanism is also used to pay attention to the most significant words and phrases that induce sentiment, leading to an interpretable and accurate model. Architectural Flow:
- 1) Input Layer: Text reviews begin with pre-trained GloVe embeddings of 300 dimensions. This choice ensures the initial data representation includes established semantic relationships.
- 2) Feature Extraction (CNN): A 1D Convolutional layer processes the embedding output. This layer identifies local, key phrases (n-grams) with 128 filters and a kernel size of 5. Feature maps progress to a Global Max-Pooling layer, which consolidates the most relevant patterns. This reduces data dimensions.
- 3) Context Modeling (BiLSTM): A pooled feature set is fed into a Bidirectional LSTM layer of 64 units. The BiLSTM runs text forward and backward, a critical function for accurate sentiment classification over lengthy reviews. This step bridges the sequential dependencies that the CNN cannot perform alone.
- 4) Attention Mechanism: A Self-Attention layer is dedicated to the BiLSTM output. It differentially weights the sequence tokens, enabling the network to hone in on key sentiment-bearing phrases (like strong adjectives or qualifiers). This mechanism enhances accuracy and supports model interpretability.
- 5) Classification: The final representation is classified using a fully connected layer with a sigmoid activation function and a single neuron. The model is optimized using Adam and the BCE loss function.

The integration of these three sequential mechanisms CNN, BiLSTM, and Attention is designed to capture a broader range of textual features than any standalone approach, yielding enhanced overall performance.

4) Bayesian Networks (BNs): BNs are a graph-based representation of the joint probability distribution where dependencies between variables are represented in a directed acyclic graph. With the integration of expert knowledge and conditional probability distributions, BNs offer an interpretable framework for managing uncertainty in the process of classification tasks.

Applying Bayes' theorem, posterior probability of a hypoth- esis with observed evidence is computed as:

This property makes BNs particularly useful for modeling relationships in text-based data and addressing uncertainty in sentiment classification.

## IV. EXPERIMENTATION

The experiment was conducted on the Google Colaboratory cloud platform, leveraging its GPU support for efficient deep learning model training. The implementation utilized standard libraries, including Scikit-learn (sklearn) for traditional machine learning models, TensorFlow for deep learning models, pgmpy for probabilistic graphical models, pandas for data manipulation, and NLTK for text preprocessing.

text:
## A. Dataset Information

This work made use of the IMDb database, a well-known standard for sentiment analysis. More than 50,000 movie reviews, equally divided into positive and negative sentiment categories, make up this dataset. The dataset is highly helpful for those conducting binary classification tests because each review is tagged as either positive (1) or negative (0). Table I displays a subset of the dataset items.

The dataset originally contained raw text data, which included HTML tags, special characters, punctuation, and stopwords that can influence model performance. These elements were eliminated systematically during preprocessing to get clean and structured input for feature extraction and model training.

To get some idea about the dataset before preprocessing, a frequency analysis of common words was conducted, which revealed common words that do not have a major influence on sentiment classification. The dataset was then converted using TF-IDF and GloVe embeddings to get it ready for subsequent model evaluations.

## V. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

In this section, we look at how well various models do when given the task of categorizing textual sentiment. Multinomial Na¨ ıve Bayes, Support Vector Classifier, a hybrid CNN-LSTM model with bidirectional layers, and a Bayesian Network are among the models examined. To determine how well each of these is able to comprehend and accurately classify sentiment, typical assessment metrics like as accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score are used. The complete performance evaluation is summarized in Table II. while accuracy provides a general overview, a deeper analysis has been made, especially given the close performance of top contenders.

TABLE II PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF SENTIMENT CLASSIFICATION MODELS

| Models                          |   Accuracy |   Recall |   Precision |   F1-Score |
|---------------------------------|------------|----------|-------------|------------|
| Multinomial Na¨ ıve Bayes       |       0.86 |     0.87 |        0.87 |       0.85 |
| Support Vector Classifier (SVC) |       0.87 |     0.89 |        0.89 |       0.88 |
| Hybrid CNN-LSTM                 |       0.88 |     0.87 |        0.85 |       0.87 |
| Bayesian Graphical Model (PGM)  |       0.52 |     0.40 |        0.56 |       0.47 |

## A. Performance Assessment

The MNB classifier achieves around 86% accuracy and an F1-score of 0.85, which is a pretty solid result overall as shown in II. Its speed and efficiency make it popular for text-based tasks. That said, since it 'views' each word as standalone, it doesn't know about the bigger picture, which limits its use in more complex reviews.

The SVC model got about 87% accuracy, which puts it slightly behind the CNN-LSTM model. However, a more detailed look at the metrics reveals a more complex picture. The SVC model achieved the highest F1-Score of all models as shown in Table II. This F1-Score was supported by the highest and most balanced precision (0.89) and recall (0.89) scores. This indicates that SVC model was the most reliable model, exceptionally minimizing both false positives and false negatives.

The CNN-LSTM hybrid model reached the highest accuracy at 88%, slightly higher than the SVC model. However, its F1score (0.87) was slightly lower than the SVC's. Looking at Table II, this is due to a less balanced precision-recall profile, its precision of 0.85 and recall of 0.87 were lower than other ML models. This suggests that while it was good at finding positive cases (high recall), it was more prone to false positives than the SVC model. The specific classification performance is detailed in the Confusion Matrix (Fig. 3), and the model's training was stable (Fig. 4). While the model's architecture is theoretically powerful, these results show its performance is highly comparable, and not definitively superior, to the simpler SVC model.

Conversely, the Bayesian Network Model performed much lower than the others. Although Bayesian models are excellent in uncertainty and interpretability, their inability to model good sequential dependency in text data is a drawback to their capacity to classify. In contrast to deep learning models, which can learn hierarchical features from text, Bayesian Networks are better for structured probabilistic reasoning rather than high-dimensional text classification.

text:
## B. Discussion and Observations

Our work has found that the performance difference between the traditional SVC and the hybrid CNN-LSTM is marginal, making the results inconclusive for declaring a definitive 'best' model. While the CNN-LSTM yielded the highest accuracy (88%), the SVC achieved the highest F1score (0.88), which is often considered a more robust metric for classification tasks as it balances precision and recall. This suggests that for this dataset, the powerful feature representation from TF-IDF combined with an optimized linear classifier (SVC) is just as effective as a more complex deep learning architecture.

Fig. 3. Confusion Matrix of CNN-LSTM Model

<!-- image -->

A visual comparison of the accuracy, precision, and recall across all models is provided in (Fig. 5). This graph clearly illustrates the close race between SVC and CNN-LSTM. To give these results more analytical weight (addressing Review 2), future work should include a comparative graph focusing specifically on the F1-scores. Furthermore, the small difference in accuracy is likely not statistically significant. Future experiments should incorporate k-fold cross-validation and other statistical tests to determine 'best' model.

In contrast, the performance of Bayesian Networks was significantly weaker than the other approaches. There are fundamental reasons for this shortfall, the most important being their inability to effectively model sequential data. while deep learning models process text as a sequence, Bayesian Networks do not inherently depend on sequence instead model probabilistic relationships between features. It is difficult to construct these dependency relationships from sequential data. when building a BN using Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAG), we must define the dependencies between features. However, when using TF-IDF vectors, the dependencies between individual word features are not explicit, which presents major challenge in building an effective network for this type of data.

The model's reliance on the feature independence assumption is also a significant constraint. To simplify the probabilistic calculations, Bayesian models often assume that features are conditionally independent, thereby ignoring the complex inter-dependencies inherent in Natural Language. While models like SVC can manage this through engineered feature encoding and deep learning architectures are less constrained by this, Bayesian Networks are not well-equipped to handle these dependencies, which limits their classification accuracy.

Fig. 4. Loss Curve of CNN-LSTM Model showing training and validation loss across epochs.

<!-- image -->

Bayesian Networks are not well suited when it comes to working with very large data sets. Unlike deep learning which relies on GPUs to train fast, using BN's can be difficult because they require a lot of expensive computations. This computational overhead is why Bayesian Networks are less effective for analyzing opinions on large scale.

Despite these limitations, Bayesian Networks are valuable in applications where probabilistic reasoning and interpretability are critical. Unlike 'black box' deep learning models, BNs can offer clear explanations of the relationships between different factors, making them useful in applications where explainability is a primary concern

The CNN-LSTM approach outperforms other models by providing a slight increase in accuracy and is able to catch the order in which text is presented. It is possible for future research to try combining Bayesian probabilistic techniques with deep learning-driven feature extraction or attention methods to get improved explanations and higher classification performance.

text:
## VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK

The entertainment industry relies on public opinion to determine the popularity and success of films. Sentiment analysis is essential for gauging public sentiment, especially when it comes to large-scale internet reviews. This research evaluated performance of ML, DL, probabilistic models for sentiment classification. These models were pre-trained with GloVe and TF-IDF embeddings to extract richer text information.

Fig. 5. Performance comparison of sentiment classification models in terms of accuracy, precision, and recall.

<!-- image -->

Experimental outcomes revealed a highly competetive performance between the deep learning and the traditional machine learning approaches.Although the CNN-LSTM hybrid model has the best accuracy (88%), the SVC demonstrated superior reliability, attaining the highest F1-Score (0.88). This suggests that for this dataset, a well-tuned model like SVC is exceptionally effective, and its performance is highly comparable and statistically inconclusive when weighed against the more complex CNN-LSTM architecture. MNB also performed competently, while BN models were clearly unsucessful due to their limitations in modelling sequential data.

Despite such findings, there are limitations. The work focused primarily on English-language IMDb comments, which may limit generalizability to multilingual datasets. In addition, Bayesian Networks were restricted by the inability to capture long-term dependencies and computational restrictions, thus resulted in poor performance for complex sentiment classification tasks.

Future work can address these limitations by:

- Expanding the dataset to multilingual movie reviews for broader analysis.
- Exploring transformer-based architectures (e.g., BERT, RoBERTa) to improve sentiment classification using contextual embeddings.
- Using ensemble learning techniques to leverage the strengths of ML, deep learning, and probabilistic models for improved sentiment prediction.

With the aid of robust deep learning and ensemble-based techniques, sentiment analysis can further enhance predictive power and provide greater insight into viewer sentiment in the film industry.

Abstract -  Visually impaired and blind students face significant barriers in programming and IT education due to the reliance on visual elements in traditional tools, which limits their ability  to  engage  with  coding  environments.  While  Braille remains a vital accessibility tool, the lack of adaptive programming resources further complicates the learning process. To address these challenges, we developed a platform that integrates Natural Language Processing (NLP) technology using the BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) algorithm to enable automated code verification and real-time error detection. The system is designed to offer audio-based  feedback  along  with  theoretical  programming concepts,  ensuring  that  visually  impaired  learners  can  access and  interact  with  coding  environments  independently.  The platform's performance was evaluated using Python and HTML error  detection.  It  achieved  92%  accuracy  and  90% precision for Python code detection and 82% accuracy and 80% precision for HTML code detection. These results demonstrate the platform's reliability and its potential to enhance programming  accessibility.  By  combining  NLP-based  code analysis  with  audio-assisted  learning,  the  platform  empowers visually impaired students to navigate programming concepts confidently and participate fully in IT education. Furthermore, the platform's adaptability allows it to support various programming  languages,  offering  flexibility  for  students  to explore diverse coding environments. The integration of realtime  error  detection  and  corrective  feedback  ensures  that learners can efficiently progress through their coding exercises with minimal external assistance.

Digital literacy is, therefore, an important component of their education, ensuring that they can utilize these technologies effectively. It's also important to foster an inclusive environment, where visually impaired individuals are encouraged to participate in mainstream educational and vocational  settings  [3].  This  requires  not  only  specialized training  for  the  individuals  themselves  but  also  awareness and  sensitivity  training  for  educators,  employers,  and  the general public. ## II. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY

The proposed system integrates Braille recognition, syntax validation, and  audio  feedback  to  create an accessible programming interface. The Fig. 1 illustrates the architecture of a programming learning platform specifically designed for blind students, emphasizing its components and their interactions.  The  platform  begins  with  the  user  interface, which serves  as  the  primary  interaction  point  for  students. Through  this  interface,  students  can  input  their  code  and receive feedback, with auditory outputs ensuring accessibility.

Fig. 1. Architecture Diagram for Proposed Model

<!-- image -->

The system integrates advanced Natural Language Processing (NLP) capabilities, including an NLP engine and a  BERT  model,  to  analyze  and  evaluate  user  input.  This processing unit identifies errors or issues within the code and generates relevant feedback for the students. A robust content management module provides structured educational materials,  including  lesson  content  and  code  examples, which  are  essential  for  comprehension  and  practice.  Once errors  are  detected,  the  error  handling  module  takes  over, employing  an  error  detector  and  a  feedback  generator  to create  constructive  feedback.  This  feedback  explains  the identified  mistakes  and  suggests  improvements,  ensuring students receive actionable  guidance. The platform's audio management component utilizes text-to-speech technology to convert text-based feedback and lesson materials into auditory  formats.  This  feature  ensures that all content, including feedback and code explanations, is delivered in an accessible  manner.  Collectively,  this  architecture  offers  an interactive,  inclusive,  and  audio-driven  learning  experience tailored to the unique needs of visually impaired students.

## A. Data Collection

The data collection process for this study is meticulously designed to ensure the development of a robust and inclusive programming learning platform  tailored  for  blind  students. Three primary datasets are utilized:

## · Programming Data:

A curated collection of programming examples and common errors is obtained. This dataset includes code snippets ranging from beginner to advanced levels, focusing on syntactic and logical errors to train the error detection system effectively. Publicly  available  programming  repositories  and  datasets from educational platforms serve as the primary sources.

## · Braille Input Data:

Data on Braille inputs, including tactile-to-digital translations,  is  gathered  from  Braille  standards  and  user studies involving visually impaired individuals. This dataset includes  common  patterns,  frequently  used  shortcuts,  and real-world input scenarios to ensure compatibility with user needs.

## · Educational Content:

Lesson modules, tutorials, and structured educational material  are  collected  to  support  the  content  management module.  These  materials  are  sourced  from  open-access programming resources and adapted for accessibility, ensuring relevance for visually impaired learners.

## B. Data Preprocessing

The data processing workflow utilizes  a  BERT-based algorithm to classify  programming  errors  and  generate structured feedback for users. This integration enhances the system's ability to process code inputs effectively, ensuring accurate and accessible feedback  for visually  impaired learners.

## · Sorting:

The  input  data  is  loaded  from  a  JSON  file  containing timestamped entries. The entries are sorted by timestamp to prioritize the most recent user input for analysis.

text:
## · Error Detection and Classification:

When the programming language is identified as Python, the algorithm  thoroughly  examines  the  code  to  detect  errors related to syntax, semantics, and logic.  The process  begins with  parsing  the  code  to  uncover  syntax  errors  such  as missing colons, improper indentation, unmatched parentheses,  or  invalid  variable  names.  Following  syntax analysis, the algorithm proceeds to perform a semantic check by  analyzing  the  code's  logic  and  data  flow. This step is essential for identifying issues like type mismatches, undefined variables,  incorrect  function  calls,  and  improper use of standard  libraries.  The  detected  errors  are  then classified into categories, including syntax errors,  semantic errors, and logical errors, with clear  and  informative messages  generated  to  assist  users  in  comprehending  the nature  and  location  of  the  errors.  For  HTML  code,  the analysis  focuses  on  detecting  structural  and  accessibilityrelated  issues.  The  algorithm  begins  by  validating  HTML tags, checking for problems such as missing or mismatched tags and incorrectly nested elements. Additionally, it inspects attributes to identify invalid or deprecated ones while ensuring that essential attributes are correctly specified.

## · Feedback Storage:

The classified  errors  and  feedback  messages  are  saved to a secondary JSON file (json file1). This structured feedback serves  as  input  for  the  subsequent  stages  of  the  platform's architecture, including text-to-speech conversion.

## · Exception Handling:

The algorithm  incorporates  error  handling  mechanisms to address potential issues, such as missing files, JSON decoding failures, or missing keys in the JSON data. These measures ensure that the processing pipeline re- mains robust and reliable.

## · Output Preparation:

Feedback saved in json file1 is integrated into the  user interface  for  seamless  delivery  through  accessible  formats, including audio feedback.

## C. Feature Extraction

Feature  extraction  plays  a  pivotal  role  in  the  effective functioning of the programming learning platform designed for blind students. This step focuses on deriving meaningful patterns and insights from the input data, enabling accurate code  analysis,  error  detection,  and  personalized  feedback gen- eration. Textual Feature Extraction (NLP Engine): The NLP engine processes the code input by tokenizing it into smaller  com-  ponents,  such  as  keywords,  variables,  and operators. Using models like BERT, contextual features are extracted from  the code to understand its syntax and semantics. These  features help identify patterns, detect logical or syntactical errors, and understand the intent behind the code. Error Identification Features: Error detection involves ex- tracting error-related features, such as missing syntax, unde- fined variables, or logical inconsistencies in the code.  The  system  analyzes  sequences  of  tokens  to  detect code-specific anomalies, leveraging the advanced contextual understanding of BERT. These features allow the system to pinpoint error locations and their probable causes.

Feedback-Oriented  Feature  Extraction: Once  errors  are identified, additional features are extracted to tailor feedback to the user. These features include the type of error, the code context in which it occurs, and the frequency of similar errors in  past  submissions. Such detailed features ensure that feedback  is constructive, actionable, and customized for the learner's level of expertise.

Audio  Adaptation  Features: For  auditory  feedback,  textbased features, such as error descriptions and explanations, are converted into audio-ready formats. Features like sentence  complexity  and  tone  modulation  are  extracted  to ensure the generated speech is clear, engaging, and accessible.

User  Interaction  Features: The  platform  captures  user interac- tion patterns, such as frequent code submissions or common errors, to identify learning gaps. These interaction features  are  used  to  adapt  the  lesson  content  and  feedback dynamically, creating a more personalized learning experience.

## ZKPass: Making Authentication Invisible: A ZeroKnowledge Proof Approach

Sahyadri college of Engineering & management Mangalore. srinivas.22phdecs213@student.nitte.edu.in S rinivas P M Research Scholar Nitte (Deemed to be University), NMAM Institute of technology (NMAMIT), Nitte and Assistant professor , department of CSE

Ravi Babu Nitte University, NMAM Institute of Technology, Department of Information Science and Engineering, Nitte ravib671@nitte.edu.in

Abstract-This work proposes ZKPass, an emerging authentication platform making use of Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) and blockchain to provide passwordless, decentralized digital  ID  proofing.  ZKPass  does  away  with  conventional passwords and crypto key storage by tying authentication to a human-intelligible user identifier (UID) and locally generating zk-SNARK proof on the user device. The platform comprises an off-chain  deterministic  mnemonic  recovery  phrase  from  the UID and device-specific secrets allowing for self-sovereign offline account recovery independent of centralized entities. ZKPass stores only hashed UIDs and device  metadata on the blockchain, minimizing costs, maintaining privacy, and allowing multi-device management. On-device proof generation coupled with on-chain smart-contract-based verification provides  rigorous  security,  preserves  privacy,  and  makes  the solution practically usable. Performance comparisons indicate better  proof  sizes,  verification  times,  gas  usage,  and  recovery success over prevailing ZKP-based  ID solutions.  ZKPass overcomes key drawbacks  of prevailing decentralized ID solutions by fusing powerful crypto security with user-friendly design to bring reality closer to adoption potential in healthcare, financial services and government sectors.

Keywords-zero-knowledge proof (ZKP), passwordless authentication, blockchain, decentralized identity, cryptography,  device  management,  zk-SNARK,  self-sovereign identity, recovery phrase

## I. INTRODUCTION

## A. Background

As  the  rapid  digital  evolution  of  healthcare,  finance, education,  even  government  services  raises  the  need  for reliable and secure proof of identity, traditional-based systems are  identified  by  multiple  architecture  paradigms.  Centrally managed identities where one vetted authority is responsible for  user  credentials  awarded.  Federated-identity  supports cross-site  log-in  through  the  intermediary  of  some  central provider (Google, Facebook, etc). Most recently, SelfSovereign Identity (SSI), trying to provide didactic authority over  the  data  of  an  identity.  While  privacy  as  well  as autonomity are merits of SSI, viable implementation remains out of reach due to the absence of common criteria or technical

ZKPs by means of which users are able to attest that they have particular information but they have -- without simultaneously which the information possession is revealed, so we have very good privacy as well as  security  features  [6].  And  also  blockchain  by  means  of whose  immutable  as  well  as  distributed  nature  provides foundation  for  trustless  as  well  as  transparent  functioning decentralized  identity  systems  [3].  The  implementation  by means of blockchain tech as well as ZKPs is an issue by means of identity proofing since implementing them within practical world-based  systems  adds  unnecessary  complication,  puts additional stresses on computational power, as well as incurs usability issues [7]. Even with all those obvious security holes, the likes of phishing assaults, credential re-use, centralization remains the standard among most digital domains [8].

## B. Problem Statement

A number of identity systems have been built using Zero Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs) over the last several years. This design  aim  is  to  ensure  that  the  privacy  is  augmented  and decentralization of the checks on identities is achieved [5][7].  They  are  also  promising  but  do  not  always  work  with common users [20]. They are too complicated, too resourceintensive or demanding to the non-technical masses [7], [19]. This  renders  them  difficult  to  operate  in  addition  to  being unpopula  [20].  The  most  serious  thing  is  the  absence  of passwordless login [19]. Most of the systems also continue to use stored credentials, cryptographic key stores or third-party verifiers  [19].  Such  a  need  of  sensitive  information  is  a security risk, and is against decentralization as well [5]. The other problem is obscurity of the cryptography. The users are usually compelled to create, save or operate with cryptographic key pairs and go through the technologically cumbersome,  multi-stage  sign-up  procedures  [19].  This  is difficult to the laymen and a greater threat of an error or loss of  qualifications  [20].  Moreover,  there  is  a  problem  of  the inadequate or incomplete self-recovery technologies with the ZKP-based systems [19]. The majority of them rely on the centralized forces or the social recovery strategies where the former  involves  the  need  to  trust,  which  goes  against  the principle of self-sovereign identity [5], [20]. The interface of the existing system is not an excellent one. The majority of the most are unfriendly as users and consume much effort [7]. This  discourages  people  against  the  adoption  and  reduces their  adoption  within  the  various  groups  or  industries  [20]. They are problems that demonstrate that there is a necessity of  an  easy,  passwordless  solution  of  the  self-sovereign identity [19].

## C. Contribution and Scope

The new authentication model utilizing ZKPass blockchain  to  provide  an  improved  authentication  system technically passwordless yet secure is presented in this paper [9]. It also eliminates the need for password and conventional cryptographic storage as it crypto-verifies on a UID that is printable by the human and utilized more easily and securely [12].  To  make  recovery  more  resilient,  ZKPass  makes utilization  of  the  deterministic  mnemonic  recovery  phrase, generated locally based on device secrets as well as UID so that  recovery  will  be  self-sovereign  and  not  dependent  on trust [19].  The  architecture takes up  less area on  the blockchain by hashinging the UID and the metadata of the devices to make the solution much less costly and maintain the privacy of users [4]. The system is effective in supporting multiple  devices  per  user,  straightforward  device's  simple registration  as  well  as  device's  easy  revocation,  and  secure device's  recovery  process  yielding  flexible  user-centric  ID management [19]. It  consequently  means  that  utilizing  zkSNARK  circuits  generated  with  Circom,  ZKPass  realizes scalable as well as functional security through device-level proof as well as chain-level smart contract-based verification [18]. ZKPass is an important step toward reasonable adoption of the decentralized as well as privacy-conscious authentication mechanism suitable for the most vital infrastructures including the region's healthcare sector, financial institutions, as well as government ecosystem [19].

## II. RELATED WORK

text:
## A. Traditional Identity Models

In  the  last  20  years,  the  change  in  the  digital  identity systems  is  immense,  which  involved  the  transition  of  the central models into the federated models to the Self Sovereign Identity (SSI) models. In the centralized model one body  has  the mandate  of issuing out, controlling  and authenticating user credentials. This is a basic model, yet it raises issues of large-scale nature, in that we know of single points of failure, which are then used to generate large scale data  breaches  and  unauthorized  access  when  there  is  a security breach [1]. To rectify these issues out there has been development of federated identity models wherein users can access other platforms with credentialing issues issued by a trusted third party (ex: Google and Facebook via OAuth/SAML) [1]. These technologies do not fully remove centralization and use of such technologies provides little or no  control  to  the  user  over  his  or  her  information  sharing among different services [1].  Self-Sovereign  Identity  (SSI) enables  users  to  create  and  manage  their  own  identifiers

(DID) and credential verifiable without a centralized system, which is a paradigm shift in the other approach.

## B. Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Identity Systems

It  has  been  made  possible  with  the  assistance  of  ZeroKnowledge Proofs (ZKPs) which have provided privacy and protection [6]. ZKPs enable users to prove learning that they have  knowledge  about  secrets  such  as  age,  citizenship  or credentials  without  disclosing  them  [5].  Some  identified evidences are zkSNARKs, zk-STARKs that are different in their performance, security circumstances and cost of computation  [12],  [18].  Despite  offering  rapid  verifications and tiny proofs, zk-SNARKs also have the drawback that they entail a trusted setup, whereas this aspect is highly valuable to toolssets such as Circom [18]. This poses issues to the mobile and edge devices that demand high computation powers [12]. Although there is no trusted setup in zk-STARKs, the proof size  is  bigger  and  therefore  verification  and  blockchain storage are more unfortunate [12]. In anonymous authentication  systems,  ZKPs  have  been  applied  to  ZAMA [11] and BAuth-ZKP [8] and zkLogin [19].

## C. Blockchain in Identity Systems

The blockchain technology enhances ZKPs by offering a distributed and resilient environment in which identity data is recorded  and  does  not  require  centralized  authorities  to validate them, and it is audit-able [1]. Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs) have been stored using blockchains, as well as to operate credential revocation registries and apply access control mechanisms [2]. Nevertheless, in reality, there are still a  number  of  acute  problems.  The  storage  of  large-scale cryptographic demonstrations and metadata on-chain is still practiced by many blockchainbased identity solutions making it  a  significant  storage  overhead and an expensive gas cost, especially  on  public  chains  such  as  Ethereum  [3].  Key management is another unresolved issue: users have to safely store private keys or seed phrases, and a loss of credentials usually implies that there is no backup, which invalidates the philosophy of self-sovereign identity [4]. Models like LedgerMaze [3] and HyperMaze [4] do include secure and private  transaction  mechanisms,  but  are  too  complex  in architecture  and  too  heavy  in  infrastructure  to  be  useful  in consumer-grade applications [11].

Concretely, ZKPass  supports  client-side  proof  generation  [4],  adopts  a recovery phrase that  is  human-readable,  and  minimizes blockchain  footprint  to  the  UID  hash  only.  This  set  of properties  makes  ZKPass a  strong  contender  for  consumercentric digital identity systems' real-world adoption.

## III. METHODOLOGY

## A. Architecture Overview

The ZKPass solution provides passwordless, decentralized authentication  with  the  help  of  Zero-Knowledge  Proofs (ZKPs) and blockchain smart contracts [19]. The architecture provides secure, privacy-respecting identity verification with minimal  on-chain  storage  and  maintainability  for  user  selfsovereignty [4].

The architecture is comprised of four big components.

- Client Interface: Receives the UID input from the user and triggers generation of proof locally by Circom and SnarkJS [18].
- ZKP Circuit Engine: Circom compiled circuits produce zk-SNARKs that attest to the knowledge of the devicespecific key without disclosing the secrets [18].
- Smart  Contract  Layer:  A  Smart  Contract  written  in Solidity on an Ethereum-compatible blockchain checks zk-SNARK proofs and hashes UID comparisons to onchain data [4], [18].
- Minimum On-Chain Storage: Only the hashed UIDs and device public key hashes are stored on-blockchain, minimizing the cost of gas while still achieving privacy [4].

Fig.1. System Architecture

<!-- image -->

Fig 1 illustrates the overall ZKPass architecture, including registration, authentication, device management, and recovery flows.

## B. Passwordless Authentication

ZKPass  supports  passwordless  authentication  by  utilizing device-specific derived key per device [19]:

- Hash-Derivation with Salt: The UID from the user is coupled with the device/session-specific salt generated randomly. The pair is hashed by SHA-256, yielding the device-specific private  key. This  key is never reused but is instead discarded the persistent attack risk [12].
- Proof Generation: Locally, the Circom circuit generates  an  zk-SNARK  proof  by  showing  that  the proof  is  of  the  derived  key's  knowledge  without disclosing the key [18].
- On-Chain  Verification:  The  proof  is  provided  to  the smart  contract,  where  the  smart  contract  checks  the correctness  and  bindingness  to  the  hashed  UID  [4], [18].
- Security Benefits: Without stored secrets or passwords, ZKPass is resistant to phishing, credential stuffing, and server-side breaches [19].

## C. Self-Sovereign Recovery

ZKPass  supports  self-sovereing  recovery  without  the need for third-party custodians, SMS, or even emails [19]

- Recovery  Phrase  Generation:  The  UID  and  devicespecific random salt are hashed during the process of registration and then transformed into  a  humanreadable mnemonic [19].
- User Privacy: The recovery phrase is only shown once and is never stored or transmitted [19].
- Client-Side  Restoration:  If  the  device  gets  lost  or  is revoked, typing the recovery  phrase  supports  secure, client-side restoration of the UID and the generation of a new device key pair [19].

Fig. 3 presents the performance of ZKPass compared to Traditional and Basic ZKP-based authentication mechanisms. The column chart compares verification time, transaction  cost,  and  recovery  rate.  Verification  time  is reduced to 1 second by ZKPass, compared to 4 seconds for Traditional and 3 seconds for Basic ZKP. Transaction cost is around 1¢ for ZKPass, versus 8-12¢ for the others. Recovery success is also higher for ZKPass at 95%, compared to 60% for  Traditional  and  70%  for  Basic  ZKP,  based  on  100 authentication instances per mechanism.

text:
## V. DISCUSSION

ZKPass  accelerates  decentralized  verification  through zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) and blockchain, delivering a deployable,  user-friendly,  and  privacy-preserved  solution. Unlike conventional systems trusting in passwords or authoritative hubs, ZKPass achieves passwordless verification relying on device-specific derived keys and zkSNARK proofs, preventing phishing, credential stuffing, and server compromise. Deterministically generated locally mnemonic recovery phrases facilitate self-sovereign recovery, and users own it (no third-party dependencies).

For efficiency, ZKPass reduces evidence size, accelerates client-side calculation, reduces verification latency and decreases on-chain storage and gas fees compared to zkLogin, BAuth-ZKP, and ZAMA. Accommodating  numerous  devices  per  user,  user-friendly device  registration,  and  secure  device  revocation,  ZKPass provides  flexibility  and  user-ease  of  deployment  in  realworld scenarios. ZKPass achieves a good trade-off between security,  privacy,  and  efficiency.  It  also  supports  seamless multi-device synchronization and rapid recovery in case of device loss, enhancing usability and reliability.

## CONCLUSION

In this study we developed ZKPass, a passwordless and decentralized verification system that uses Zero-Knowledge Proves and blockchain minus key storage or use of typical passwords.  Authentication  comes  attached  to  a  humanreadable UID, and self-soverereign recovery comes through a deterministic mnemonic phrase, keeping control strictly in the  user's  hands  and  not  a  authority.  Device  metadata  are hashed and stored once-on-chain and only the UID, thereby reducing gas costs yet allowing for secure handling of multidevices. Performance analysis shows that ZKPass outperforms existing ZKP-secured ID systems tremendously when it comes to verification rate, proof size, gas usage, and recovery  rate.  With  a  blend  of  cryptographic  high-level security and user friendliness, ZKPass provides a practicable foundation for decentralized ID implementations in sectors ranging  from  healthcare  and  finance  to  government,  and future improvement avenues include enhancing postquantum security and supporting emerging self-soverereign ID requirements.
